# TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS
## AND MOST NOBLE HOLY ROMAN
### EMPIRE COUNT AND LORD,

# LORD ERNST,

->of Gehmen, etc.<-

->Dedicates, Presents, and Devotes.<- <note>original Latin: "D. D. D." (Dedicat, Dat, Dicat). This is a traditional formal formula used in book dedications.</note>

### MICHAEL MAIER, COUNT PALATINE
->*Imperial Exempt Noble, Doctor of Philosophy and Medicine, Poet Laureate.*<- <note>Michael Maier (1568–1622) was an influential German physician, counselor to Emperor Rudolf II, and a famous writer on alchemy and Rosicrucianism.</note>

<insert>LIBRARY OF THE ROYAL COLLEGE OF PHYSICIANS OF LONDON.</insert> <note>original Latin: "BIBLIOTHECA REG. COLL. MED. LONDIN." This is a stamp indicating the book was once part of the historic medical library in London.</note>

**S**OCRATES the Philosopher, most illustrious Count, who by the judgment of the Delphic oracle and all of Greece was held to be the wisest of all, used to profess that he knew only this one thing: That he knew nothing. And Heraclitus <note>A Greek philosopher (c. 535 – c. 475 BCE) famous for his idea that "everything flows" and his focus on the hidden nature of reality.</note> used to say that truth is held confined, buried in subterranean enclosures, from which it is extremely difficult for it to emerge, unless it is at last revealed and dug out by its father—that is, by Time. These two most excellent men, as— <note>The text ends mid-sentence at the bottom of the page.</note>

<summary>This page contains the formal dedication of Michael Maier’s alchemical work to Count Ernst von Holstein-Schaumburg, opening with a philosophical reflection on the difficulty of uncovering truth.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Epistle Dedicatory" to Count Ernst von Holstein-Schaumburg. On the previous page, Maier introduced the philosophical humility of Socrates and Heraclitus. This page develops that theme, arguing that human perception is inherently flawed and prone to error when seeking the truth.</meta>

# EPISTLE

<meta>catchword: science</meta>

*...although they may not have agreed at all on other theorems of their doctrine, yet in this part, though they used different words, they are very much in agreement on the same meanings. Namely, that the **weakness of the human mind** is so great that it is only very rarely able to penetrate to true **Beings** <term>Entia; a philosophical term for things as they exist in their true reality, rather than how they appear to our senses.</term>, as they are, but for the most part, it captures and carries about shadows instead of a solid body, like the **dog in Aesop's fables** <note>Maier refers to the fable of the dog who drops a real piece of meat to snap at its larger-looking reflection in the water, losing both.</note>. From this come those diversities of minds and opinions regarding one and the same thing; from this come so many sects in all disciplines, which are again split into infinite opinions and separated from one another and from the **unity of Truth**. From this come so many dreams of those who are awake and the **phantasms of those possessed by the itch to write**. Whatever one person establishes as certain, another mocks, and vice versa. What is believed by one to be the naked and plain truth itself, to another seems to reflect scarcely a footprint of truth, let alone its face. Just as one of the aforementioned philosophers <note>Referring to Heraclitus, mentioned on the previous page.</note> best expressed the cause of all these things, so the first of them <note>Socrates.</note> frankly acknowledged the effect in himself. In addition to the obscurity of things themselves and the dark garment with which truth is covered, there is the **cataract of the mind's eyes** <note>original: "glaucoma oculorum mentis". In this period, "glaucoma" was often used to describe any clouding of the eye or cataract that obstructs vision.</note> and the variety of languages. Since these two factors differ greatly across the whole world according to the depression or elevation of the sun and the pole <note>Maier is suggesting that different geographic locations and climates affect the physical and mental disposition of peoples.</note>, it follows that those with eyes that are either too dull or imbued with another color do not see the truth lurking in the shadows, but they think they see it—much like certain old men suffering from this defect who mistake one thing for another. Or, through ignorance of a foreign language, one person understands another differently than he intended. Thus it happens that, like archers [pursuing] a wild beast hiding in thick thickets...*

<summary>Maier explores the fallibility of human reason, comparing our search for truth to a dog chasing shadows or a blind man misidentifying objects. He blames this confusion on both the inherent "darkness" of reality and the biases caused by geography and language.</summary>
<keywords>human error, epistemology, Aesop, philosophy of science, perception, variety of languages, Michael Maier</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Michael Maier's "Epistle Dedicatory" to Count Ernst von Holstein-Schaumburg. The previous page discussed the limitations of human perception and the tendency for people to follow "shadows" of truth rather than truth itself. This page introduces the central subject of the book: the hidden truth of Chemistry, which Maier presents as a unifying secret known to the wise of all ages and nations.</meta>

# DEDICATION

(:) 3

### DEDICATION

*...of those who know, yet they do not know at what point in space to aim; they attack the mark with arrows from all sides, but very few graze or wound it.* <note>Maier is using an archery metaphor to describe how many scholars attempt to find the truth but miss the target.</note> *Yet one thing truly offers itself among these <term>sublunary</term> <note>original: "sublunaribus"; in the worldview of the time, this referred to the Earth and everything below the moon, which was subject to change and decay.</note> matters, which, although it seems most abstruse and almost like a non-entity to all those philosophizing in every age and place, and is deemed unworthy of investigation; nevertheless, if it is well considered by the countless many who do not stick to the surface but penetrate into the depths of the matter, it is like a certain immobile point, noted by the eyes, perceived by the mind, and expressed more than a thousand times in the most diverse idioms of language, albeit under <term>tropes and figures</term> <note>Literary devices and metaphors used to hide secrets from the uninitiated.</note>; and that is held to be the* **SUBJECT OF CHEMISTRY**. *For in this, with all other ignorant people excluded, the philosophers of all ages—even the most ancient—and the first poets in their chief allegories and fictions, are in agreement. The peoples of all nations, differing in character, languages, customs, religion, laws, and other institutions of life; indeed, the wise men of all places, not only of so many kingdoms of Europe, but also of Africa and Asia: When I had weighed this, and observed that from this point—concerning Chemical truth—the desires of all men (as many as exist who are eager for knowledge, capable, or unlearned) are divided into two opinions. On one side, I have set those devoted to and favoring Chemistry from twelve principal nations who were at hand, as if a certain* **APOLLO** <note>Apollo, the Greek god of music, truth, and light, here represents the harmony and enlightenment of the alchemical art.</note>; *on the other side, those contradicting the same, who are a mixed and larger multitude, I have set as* **PAN** <note>Pan, the god of the wild and shepherds, often depicted as earthy and unrefined, represents the "coarse" masses who do not understand the higher arts.</note>: *By whom [Pan], since Apollo has been so often challenged to a singing contest—that is, Chemistry and those devoted to it by the ignorant and the foolish...*

<meta>catchword: ni</meta>

<summary>Maier identifies "the Subject of Chemistry" as a universal truth hidden beneath metaphors and recognized by the wise across all cultures, framing the conflict between alchemists and their critics as a contest between the refined Apollo and the rustic Pan.</summary>

<keywords>Chemistry, Alchemical Subject, Apollo vs. Pan, Universal Truth, Allegory, Ancient Philosophy, Twelve Nations</keywords>

--- Page 8 ---
<meta>This page continues Michael Maier's "Epistle Dedicatory" to Count Ernst von Holstein-Schaumburg. In the preceding text, Maier discussed how the "Subject of Chemistry" is a singular truth shared by wise men of all nations, hidden under allegories. This page explains his rhetorical strategy: he has staged a symbolic debate at a "Golden Table" where the wise men of various nations defend alchemy against a mocking opponent, and he now asks the Count to serve as the judge of this contest.</meta>

->EPISTLE<-

...doms, [men] harassed by insults and mockery not unlike those of hairy and brutish feet and horned head <note>Maier is likely comparing the critics of alchemy to satyrs or Pan-like figures, known for their unruly and mocking nature.</note>, I could not pass over the opportunity to finally set them against one another from both sides, so that they might fight for victory—not so much for the sake of a sweet song, but for the sake of expressing the Truth. Since this plan of mine cannot but be praiseworthy to any honorable man—for it is often said: 
**Socrates is a friend, Plato is a friend, but truth is a dearer friend** <note>original: "Amicus Socrates, Amicus Plato, veritas magis amica"; a famous philosophical proverb meaning that while one respects great thinkers, the pursuit of truth is the highest priority.</note>, 
I have reduced it into a form which would best suit so many nations and the presentation of their decrees in order. Specifically, I have arranged for them to be seated at a Table—called **"The Golden Table"** on account of the dignity and art of the philosophers—where each, surrounded by his own countrymen, might wait for and receive the fighting Adversary (namely, <term>Pyrgopolynices</term> <note>A character archetype from ancient Roman comedy meaning "Tower-Town-Conqueror." Maier uses this "braggart soldier" to personify the arrogant and ignorant critics of alchemy.</note>, delegated by all the aforementioned) and convince him with firm reasons.

Therefore, most Illustrious Count, since it is especially necessary in such a distinguished and hitherto unheard-of assembly and skirmish of philosophers of all ages and nations that some renowned <term>Arbiter</term> <note>A judge or referee chosen to settle a dispute.</note> be appointed—one distinguished by the splendor of his lineage, by justice, by judgment, and by a talent not averse to the <term>Muses</term> <note>The Greek goddesses of inspiration in the arts and sciences.</note>, whom both sides would not fear but would willingly acknowledge and submit to—I could find no one more worthy than Your Highness, more illustrious, or more distinguished by all the virtues and gifts of mind, body, and fortune. For your house holds a most ample place among the more ancient and illustrious houses within the **Holy Roman Empire**, as well as possessing its own dominion. Furthermore, since a few years ago I was in Your Highness's region...

<meta>Catchword: [I] was,</meta>

<summary>Maier explains his decision to frame the book as a debate at a "Golden Table" between the wise men of various nations and a personified critic named Pyrgopolynices. He formally invites Count Ernst von Holstein-Schaumburg to act as the noble judge (Arbiter) for this intellectual contest.</summary>
<keywords>Michael Maier, Golden Table, Pyrgopolynices, Holy Roman Empire, Count Ernst von Holstein-Schaumburg, alchemy as truth, philosophical debate</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes Michael Maier's dedication to Count Ernst von Holstein-Schaumburg. The previous page ended mid-sentence as Maier described his plan to stage a debate between the champions of alchemy and a boastful critic (Pyrgopolynices) at a "Golden Table." Here, he formally offers the book to the Count, praising his patronage and requesting protection for the art of chemistry.</meta>

->DEDICATION<-

# DEDICATION.

*...ons; and so that I might offer my services, such as they are, whenever the opportunity arose—as if in passing—in the presence of the most watchful Chancellors and the Physician at Bückeburg* <note>original: "Bokelburgi"; the residence of Count Ernst. Maier served as a physician and counselor here.</note>, *which I understood were not unwelcome to him. Hence, I could not pass by without dedicating, transmitting, and presenting to Your Highness* <note>original: "Celsitudo"; a formal title of address for a high-ranking noble.</note> *these* **Symbols of the Golden Table of the 12 Nations**. *Although this work was born from a weary hand, I believe it will be very useful and well-received by many. I wish it might seem sufficiently elegant and polished to Your Highness, who delights above all in the most refined and precious things. Furthermore, Your Highness’s inclination toward the learned order and toward literature is so great that the philosophers who champion* <term>Chemistry</term> <note>original: "Chemiæ"; in Maier's time, this term referred to both practical lab work and the philosophical pursuit of the "Philosopher's Stone."</note> *may rightly congratulate themselves on having such a great Guardian to defend them against any force or injustice. Nor, in truth, do I value this labor of mine so highly as to think it worthy of being offered to such a great Count. Yet, because Your Highness possesses such innate kindness and favorable support for studies that you do not neglect even the smaller sketches of the learned, but receive them with a benevolent look and hand, surveying and unrolling them with a curious eye and mind; hence, I have somewhat boldly inscribed Your Highness’s name upon my pages. I strive with the greatest prayers I can offer that you might receive this with a kind spirit. Your Highness will always find me most ready in your service. I commend you to God, the Best and Greatest. Given at Frankfurt on the Main, in the month of December, in the year 1616.*

<summary>Michael Maier concludes his dedication to Count Ernst by presenting his book as a defense of alchemy, praising the Count as a protector of scholars. He officially dates the letter December 1616 in Frankfurt.</summary>
<keywords>dedication, Bückeburg, patronage, alchemy, Michael Maier, Count Ernst von Holstein-Schaumburg, Frankfurt, chemistry</keywords>

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page serves as a formal honorary title page and commendatory poem following the author’s portrait and personal motto. It transitions from Michael Maier's self-description to an external validation of his status and intellect provided by a contemporary colleague, Petrus Finxius. The poem specifically references Maier’s alchemical and medical interests through classical metaphors.</meta>

# ON THE
# ARMS AND TITLES
## OF THE MAGNIFICENT AND MOST NOBLE MAN, LORD
# MICHAEL MAIER
## <term>COUNT PALATINE</term> <note>original: "Comitis Palatini"; a high-ranking title of nobility granted by the Holy Roman Emperor.</note>, KNIGHT,
### <term>EXEMPT</term> <note>original: "Exempti"; referring to his "Noble Exempt" status, meaning he was answerable only to the Emperor’s court.</note>, DOCTOR OF PHILOSOPHY AND MEDICINE,
### <term>POET LAUREATE</term> <note>original: "P. L." (Poeta Laureatus); a prestigious title for excellence in Latin poetry.</note> & FORMER PHYSICIAN
### TO HIS IMPERIAL MAJESTY.

> *Just as Nature opens her secret places to you, Maier,*
> *And reveals whatever she holds submerged in the depths;*
> *Since the <term>Muses</term> <note>original: "Pegasides"; literally the daughters of the fountain created by Pegasus, referring to the Muses who inspire the arts.</note> favor you, and <term>Apollo</term> <note>original: "Delius"; an epithet for Apollo, god of medicine and music.</note> himself has granted*
> *The art of healing and his other skills to you;*
> *What wonder is it that you were the charge of the Divine <term>Rudolph</term> <note>Emperor Rudolf II (1552–1612), a famed patron of the occult and sciences.</note>,*
> *That you are loved by Princes, a sacred Leader of the <term>Muses</term> <note>original: "Aonidum"; another name for the Muses from their home in Aonia.</note>?*
> *Continue, like the <term>winged armor-bearer</term> <note>the eagle, the symbol of Jupiter and also an alchemical symbol for volatility.</note> of great Jupiter, to lift*
> *The sluggish <term>toad</term> <note>a common alchemical symbol for the "fixed" or earthy matter of the Great Work.</note> from the cold earth in victory.*
> *Thus the brow that adorns and supports the open helmet*
> *Upon the shield shall survive in eternal bloom.*

->Petrus Finxius, Doctor of Medicine<-

--- Page 12 ---
<meta>This page continues the introductory front matter of Michael Maier’s work. Having established his titles and portrait on the preceding pages, the text now transitions to heraldic poems (ekphrases) by his peers, which interpret the symbolic meaning of his coat of arms—specifically the eagle, the toad, and the turtle-dove.</meta>

### On the same man's Coat of Arms.
*What is the bird of Jupiter <note>The eagle, which in heraldry represents high status and in alchemy often symbolizes "volatility" or the spirit rising from matter.</note>, Maier, gliding through the heavens?*
*Is it thus you are famous in mind, thus famous in intellect?*
*The high-flying Eagle is King of birds in the wide world:*
*Is it thus you are famous in mind, thus famous in intellect?*
*What does the Toad represent, creeping on the ground with a collar?*
*You shape the body and the intellect according to the mind:*
*You flourish by art, and are decorated by a triple degree from art:*
*Hence the **TRIPLE LAUREL**, hence the double Diadem.*
*It lacks black bile <note>original: "Atro felle"; in ancient medicine, black bile was associated with melancholy and malice. The turtle-dove was believed to have no gall bladder, making it a symbol of purity.</note>, nor does it wound with a hooked beak,*
*The Turtle-dove, which stands as your bird by omen.*
*These are the praised insignia of Maier; lively*
*virtue and good reputation ennoble the man.*

->Master Petrus Ailberus of Oelsnitz, Imperial Poet Laureate:<-

### Another on the same coat of arms.
*What do the Eagle and the Toad mean? She flying above the stars,*
*But he creeping on the ground? She represents Virtue going to the Gods,*
*Spurning the weights of the human torch <note>A metaphor for the heavy, mortal body or earthly burdens.</note>.*
*The Toad is like a brutish man, clinging to the earth,*
*Who, lacking reason, places the lower things above heaven,*
*Unless, carried by the bird of Jupiter, he reaches toward the golden ether,*
*As, Maier, virtue carries you across all celestial*
*things, and the Gods gift you with a turtle-dove's heart.*
*And your name flourishes on earth like the splendid laurel,*
*Until the laurel seeks the high ceilings of heaven.*
*Hence you are bright with twin helmets and the arms of Gods and men,*
*You even deserve the hearts of both Gods and men.*

->Master Samuel Rulingius, Imperial Poet Laureate.<-

### On the same coat of arms.
*O Maier, you have achieved a name among Counts,*
*The <term>Lateran Court</term> <note>original: "Aula Palatina"; the court associated with the Holy Roman Emperor's power to grant titles, specifically referencing the rank of Count Palatine.</note> calls you a Palatine.*

<summary>This page contains several commendatory poems by fellow poets laureate interpreting Michael Maier’s heraldic symbols—the eagle, toad, and turtle-dove—as metaphors for his intellectual and alchemical achievements. It reinforces his social status as a Count Palatine and a man of balanced earthly and spiritual wisdom.</summary>
<keywords>heraldry, Michael Maier, eagle, toad, turtle-dove, laurel, alchemy, Count Palatine, Petrus Ailberus, Samuel Rulingius</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the sequence of laudatory poems celebrating Michael Maier’s coat of arms. The previous page introduced the symbolism of the eagle and the toad; this page concludes that heraldic interpretation and begins the author’s own epigram regarding the confusion of languages at the Tower of Babel, a common theme in Maier’s work concerning the lost "language of nature."</meta>

(:) (:) 2
<meta>catchword: Intel-</meta>

*Indeed, because you shine with remarkable virtue (a marvel!),*
*And can scarcely have an equal to yourself:*
*Behold, Caesar <note>Referring to the Holy Roman Emperor, Rudolf II, who granted Maier his titles and nobility.</note> has granted you these splendid insignia,*
*Which fittingly contain something of a secret.*
*For just as the swift bird of Jupiter <note>The eagle, which in alchemical symbolism represents the volatile spirit or the "sublimation" of matter.</note> flies toward the sun*
*And gazes into the rays of light with a sharp eye:*
*In no other way do you, swift with the sharpness of your mind, search out*
*The mysteries of nature, which have long lain hidden.*
*Just as you also see in the toad, a lover of the earth,*
*Who, unless he is lifted up, crawls on the ground as before:*
*So unless virtue lifts a man up, he cares only for mortal things*
*And is accustomed to seek earthly things, just like a toad <note>The pairing of the eagle (volatile) and the toad (fixed) is a famous alchemical emblem representing the union of the spirit and the body.</note>.*
*What of the double helmet? Arising from bright virtues,*
*For you indeed shine with a twofold nobility.*
*As for what remains: use these insignia happily,*
*O Laurel-bearer <note>original: "Lauriger"; a reference to Maier's status as a Poet Laureate.</note>, and hold this title of nobility.*

->Johannes Knorr of Mittenwalde, Imperial Poet Laureate.<-

## THE AUTHOR'S EPIGRAM.

*A single work is said to have divided the unanimous peoples*
*Of the primeval time into various sounds:*
*That is to say, it was the Babylonian tower, when its peak*
*Was meant to be made equal to the ethereal poles.*
*So that the tongue might pay the penalty for the crime of the insane mind,*
*Alas for me, how many different modes of speech it brought forth!*
*Here the people poured out idioms never heard before,*
*And here brother gave to brother barbarous words.*
*Here "stone" is not "stone" <note>original: "Non lapis hic lapis est"; a play on words suggesting that when language failed, the very names of the building materials became confusing or "barbarous."</note>—though it might seem to be one thing,*
*It began to have ambiguous meanings.*
*There was no harmony of mind and mouth for the peoples;*
*No one could speak the true feelings of their soul.*

For one understood what the other did not wish, and one,

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**Alchemy** <note>original: "Chemia"</note> constructed by various sages.
So that the tongue might keenly grasp the dictates of the mind,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Even though it be varied by alternating sounds.
Here the peoples begin to have understood themselves in speaking,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Although they do not give forth their words in one single way.
Here a stone is a stone to this man—though nothing of the sort is said—
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;They are unanimous in things and equals in love.
All harmony has returned to the whole world in this,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;So that anyone may grasp the mind of another.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;By a thousand names, and must be cooked in various hearths. <note>A reference to the "Philosopher's Stone," which alchemists famously claimed had hundreds of different names to hide its true nature from the uninitiated.</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Just as Pallas <note>Athena, the goddess of wisdom.</note> is believed to have been brought forth from Jove: <note>original: "Ioni"; likely a variant of "Iovi" (Jove/Jupiter). In myth, Athena sprang fully formed from the head of Zeus.</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Who does not undergo wars for the sake of the female flock. <note>This "female flock" likely refers to the Muses or the personified Alchemical arts.</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Love fights for you, and the chaste virgin is yours.

# Preface to the Reader.

<margin>The table of Lucius Verus the Roman.</margin>
<margin>Ulrich von Jungingen. Year of Christ 1410.</margin>
Whenever, honest reader, I consider the opinion of that Majorcan Philosopher <note>Referring to Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315), a polymath and mystic. Though he likely did not practice alchemy, many influential alchemical texts were attributed to him in the centuries following his death.</note>, that most sharp investigator of nature, which he reports as a conclusion in his *Theory of the Testament* <note>original: *Theorica Testamenti*; one of the most famous alchemical works attributed to Pseudo-Llull.</note> in this manner: **HE WHO HAS COME TO SUCH A TEMPERAMENT** <note>In alchemy, "temperament" refers to the perfect balance of qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) achieved in the Philosopher's Stone.</note> **shall be worthy to be seated at the TABLE OF THE TWELVE PEERS**, I am reminded of the ancient custom by which men distinguished by martial virtue and military glory, and as it were equals [peers], were accustomed to recline at the Golden Table—that is, one most magnificently furnished with golden utensils, cups, and platters. Just so, in ancient times among the Romans, Lucius Verus, having returned to Rome from Syria, celebrated a banquet to which only twelve guests were admitted, at a cost of one hundred and fifty thousand crowns. For he gave to the guests all the servants waiting on the banquet, the gold and silver vessels, the couches, the tapestries, and the rest of the feast's apparatus. 

Moreover, a little before our own age, we have noticed something similar practiced most honorably very frequently in the Tournaments of the Germans (to say nothing of other nations) and, within the memory of our ancestors, in Prussia <note>original: *Borussia*</note> by a certain Master of the Teutonic Order <note>Ulrich von Jungingen (1360–1410) was the 26th Grand Master of the Teutonic Knights. He is famously associated with the Battle of Grunwald.</note>. For just as this was, like a prize <note>original Greek: *brabeion*, meaning the award given to the winner of a contest.</note> of virtue and a cloak <note>original: *paludamentum*, a ceremonial cloak worn by Roman commanders.</note> of martial honor, always praiseworthy in every age, so it was an especially useful invention for this nation, since it so animated the nobility devoted to arms toward virtuous deeds and noble exploits that very many thought life bitter to them if [they did] not

<meta>The text breaks off here at the catchword "not," continuing onto the next page.</meta>

<summary>Michael Maier begins his preface by linking the alchemical concept of a "Table of Twelve Peers" (derived from Ramon Llull) to historical traditions of elite banquets and chivalric honors, such as those of the Roman Emperor Lucius Verus and the Teutonic Knights.</summary>

## TO THE READER.

For they would not devote themselves to magnificently performed deeds, despising all danger, unless they aspired to reach at last such a table of virtue, as if to the highest peak of dignity. It appears that the same goal was proposed in the various games of the Greeks—the Olympic, Pythian, Isthmian, and Nemean—to which the youth of Greece once flocked with such zeal that Xerxes <note>The Persian King (c. 518–465 BCE) who invaded Greece. This anecdote is often used to contrast Persian greed for gold with Greek passion for honor.</note>, not without cause, wondered that so much effort and labor was spent for a crown of oak or poplar leaves, as much as might perhaps be spent for a golden crown. Nor were the gates wide enough to receive an Olympic victor, for he would enter his fatherland through torn-down walls <note>It was a Greek custom to dismantle a part of the city wall for an Olympic victor, symbolizing that a city defended by such men had no need for stone fortifications.</note>, received most honorably by all.

<margin>The crowns of the Romans.</margin>
To say nothing here of the Roman crowns—Triumphal, Mural, Naval, Civic, and others—by which they were raised to such a height of Empire, as long as they established rewards for virtue and punishment for vice. For whatever is praised by a praiseworthy man tends to increase, while that which is despised tends to suffer decline. Thus, so that virtue may grow daily, it demands its own praise; but that crimes might be rooted out, they have earned infamy. But if the contrary should happen, then it is inevitable that almost all virtue is extinguished and vice flourishes. It is most lamentable that something not unlike this is happening in our own age, not only in military service and the camps of Mars, but also in the arts of Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, goddess of wisdom; here referring to scholarly and academic pursuits.</note> and the more humane disciplines.

<margin>The dignity of the Chemical Arts.</margin>
Among these, nothing is more secret, sublime, and praiseworthy than Chemistry <note>original: *Chemiâ*; in this context, Maier refers to the high art of Alchemy.</note>; for, to speak of profane matters, it is the <term>Art of Arts</term> and <term>Science of Sciences</term>. This is established not by the common crowd of deceived alchemists, who do not understand even a letter of it, but from a long series of the most learned men of every age, who were otherwise famous in the other sciences. These men investigated it over a long time, finally obtained it after their investigation, and having obtained it, left proof of it to posterity, partly in their writings and partly by the labor of their hands. Nevertheless, many have been found who proclaim the art itself to be no art, and its practitioners to be most frivolous, vain, and deceitful men, for no other reason than that

<margin>Detractors of Chemistry.</margin>
they themselves, as judges, do not see or understand how that art can be true—that is, because they do not perceive how a natural work can be advanced through art, or an artificial one through nature. But I would wish the censorious rod of too-hasty judgment to be snatched away from these immature evaluators of the <term>Gifts of God</term> <note>original: *Donorum Dei*; a common alchemical term implying that the Stone cannot be found by effort alone, but must be granted by Divine grace.</note>. For the occult arts are not learned through insults or injuries...

PREFACE

# PREFACE

*...and by slanders heaped upon the practitioners, rather than by their labors, expenses, and studies continued day and night; nevertheless, unless the free-giving kindness of the Highest Bestower <note>Maier refers here to God as the "summi largitonis," emphasizing that alchemical success is a divine gift rather than a purely human achievement.</note> flows forth, nothing worth the effort is acquired by force, nor by boldness, nor by the cleverness of one's wit:*

<margin>Alchemical practitioners are worthy of praise and honors—and here is why.</margin>
*Truly, if a person ought to receive a reward according to how they have served the Republic or literature, then those men should be followed with accolades and honorable titles—not with so many slanders and the insults of great men—who, though they discovered and worked out things for themselves alone, nevertheless wished them not to remain unknown to posterity. Granted, they intended this not so much for the unworthy, the unlearned, and the stiff-necked, as for the intelligent and teachable <term>Sons of Adam</term> <note>A common philosophical term for humanity, implying those who seek to regain the knowledge lost after the Fall.</note>. But if very many are deceived by the writings of these men—having twisted the literal meaning or the sense into something foreign to nature—they have been the cause of their own error.*

<margin>Chemists are not the cause of other people's errors.</margin>
*For they often hear it emphasized by the practitioners that only the most learned, those of sharp wit and the best understanding, of constant will, and patient in labors, sleepless nights, and studies—the true philosophers—are invited to the feast of the <term>Philosophical Table</term> <note>The "Aurea Mensa" or Golden Table, a metaphor for the highest level of alchemical achievement and communion with ancient masters.</note>. They are not the unlettered or those only commonly educated, nor the sufficiently wealthy nor the extremely poor; if anyone else should turn up and taste nothing of what is set before them, that must be attributed to their own rashness. In the meantime, I cannot excuse my own readiness to believe; like countless others, both learned and unlearned, suitable and unsuitable, I entered the path of common errors, trusting in nothing of my own. Thus, I do not wish to testify to experience in these such rare matters. Only so much experience has come to me, among the other things I have handled, that I presume to judge more freely about those things which are outside the <term>Court of Chemistry</term> <note>original: "Aula Chemiae"; the symbolic space where the secrets of the art are guarded.</note>, such as those things contained in this treatise.*

*As for what goes on within those walls, let the dead counselors <note>Maier is referring to books and the writings of ancient authorities as "dead counselors" who provide honest advice without the biases or greeds of the living.</note> be heard, as they are witnesses greater than any exception—the most faithful and eyewitnesses. One of them is worth more, as the <term>Comic poet</term> <note>original: "Comicus"; Maier refers to the Roman playwright Plautus, specifically his line: "One eyewitness is worth more than ten who have only heard."</note> says, than ten who have only heard. These men, though they relied on their own innocence and purity of life, have now shed that human desire for a bit of glory and small profit which usually torments the living. Having passed on to the place common to all mortals, they can neither be suppressed by the insults of others nor elevated by their praise. Thus, they make light of the threats and slanders of their detractors, while they might accept our recommendation and, as it were, our restoration to wholeness...*

<meta>The text cuts off mid-word "restoration" (restitutionem), which is continued on the following page as indicated by the catchword "tionem".</meta>

<summary>Maier defends alchemists against slander, arguing that their work requires divine grace and is intended only for the learned. He positions ancient authors as "dead counselors" whose written testimony is more reliable than the opinions of the living.</summary>

# TO THE READER.

<margin>The reason motivating this writing.</margin>
<margin>Four things to be achieved by this type of writing.</margin>
*...hardly need praise; yet, lest like ungrateful mules we kick the mother who nourished us with the milk of wisdom, or allow her to be attacked by others, we return this favor in place of a teacher's fee: that, as far as we are able, we may free and defend their spirits from the barking of dogs, the tongues of vipers, and the hands of the most wicked men. We hope to achieve this by this style of writing, by which, unless I am mistaken, we shall paint four walls with one brush:* <note>original: "una fidelia parietes tingemus" — a variation of a Latin proverb meaning to accomplish multiple tasks with a single effort, similar to "killing two birds with one stone."</note>

<margin>1.</margin>
*First, we will introduce here the antiquity of true <term>Chemistry</term> <note>Maier uses "Chemia" to refer to the high art of alchemy, which he views as a sacred and ancient science of nature.</note>, as well as its authority and its continuous lineage and propagation through so many centuries, nations, peoples, and languages. By this, the adversaries—if they are not entirely devoid of judgment—can easily be weakened and convinced, or at least softened, so that they might perhaps speak more mildly (and not so lethally) about the Chemical art and its authors.*

<margin>2.</margin>
*Second, we shall rescue the legitimate and true authors of Chemistry, both ancient and modern, along with their supporters, from the slanders of the malicious and the insults of the envious, restoring them to the glory and honor of their excellent reputations—which is a duty of the highest order.*

<margin>3.</margin>
*Third, we shall hurl back the leaden and overly blunt arrows of the adversaries against their own necks; that is, we shall show that their fallacies and illegitimate cleverness in reasoning should be brought back to their own doorsteps.*

<margin>4.</margin>
*Fourth, we shall take upon ourselves the defense of the affirmative side of Chemical truth, as much as is permitted and sufficient, so that we do not seem to be provoked by them in vain, by bringing forward a steel-like edge—or certainly one threatening a blow. From this, it will be apparent to those "retired veterans"—or rather, old tricksters and horse-doctors <note>original: "veteratoribus & veterinarijs" — Maier is using a biting pun here, mocking his opponents by shifting from "veterans" to "sly old foxes" and "beast-doctors."</note>—who sang of victory before the battle,* 

<margin>Chemistry is not yet defeated or ruined.</margin>
*and who sounded the triumph before even seeing the enemy, that Chemistry—that pure and innocent maiden hiding in her most fortified Citadel—is not yet prostrate, ruined, or utterly removed from our midst so that she could never (as they boast) recover her strength. Instead, the madness of these old men will be a laughingstock; having fled from the Chemical war, even while in flight they boast that they have laid the enemy low—truly worthy of everyone's laughter. On the contrary, Chemistry, which...*

<margin>That she is the Queen of the Arts.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the Preface from Michael Maier's "Symbola Aureae Mensae" (Symbols of the Golden Table). It picks up from the previous page's discussion on the reputation of the alchemical art, specifically addressing the contrast between its true nature and its public perception.</meta>

# PREFACE

<margin>Pyrgopolynices, the common enemy of Chemistry and a deputy for others.</margin> <note>Pyrgopolynices is a character from the Roman playwright Plautus; his name literally means "Tower-town-taker." Maier uses him to represent the arrogant, loud-mouthed critic of alchemy.</note>
*...fame held by them, which is most true, though it is considered cheap; most noble, though it is treated as a prostitute by the common crowd; most chaste, though it is cast down; and that she truly exists as the Queen of all arts. Before the entrance of her court, we have prepared this <term>Golden Table</term> <note>The "Mensa Aurea" of the title, a symbolic gathering place for the greatest alchemical authorities.</note> for the twelve Peers. We presuppose that a skirmish was initiated by them against the enemy Pyrgopolynices (who, at one and the same time—as is clear from Plautine Comedy—has, if the gods please, beheaded with a single stroke all the chemical craftsmen living until now across three thousand years in Europe, Asia, and Africa, scattered across a hundred different provinces and separated by such vast distances of time and space). This skirmish was begun for the reason that an enemy is no more permitted to enter the approaches of <term>Chemistry</term> than is a stranger.*

*Since that excellent man, <term>Bonus of Ferrara</term> <note>Petrus Bonus (14th century), an influential alchemist and author of the "Precious New Pearl."</note>, proves that the Chemical art can neither be sufficiently proven by logic, nor undermined by arguments; and that almost all arguments brought against it proceed from nothing other than ignorance of those things which are done in the art:*

<margin>The insults of the adversary.</margin>
*The Adversary denies she is a virgin; these men demonstrate she is. He asserts she is stained by every vice of nature and character; they assert she is pure and chaste. He declares her poor; they declare her rich. He says she is defenseless, powerless, and deceptive; they contradict him. In short? The lawsuit is conducted on both sides, uncertain and varied, not with swords but with tongues, not with a dagger but with reason; nor does an Arbiter intervene to settle it. The Adversary calls for an eyewitness demonstration, so that Chemistry might show herself publicly—what and how great she is—and offer herself naked to be handled by everyone, making known her power, riches, and other gifts. He demands she not hide the manner in which she obtained and possesses these things, but reveal each of her goods and gifts. And indeed, this would be the most convenient way to shut the mouth <note>original: "rostrum" — literally "beak" or "snout," used here derisively for the critic's mouth.</note> of Pyrgopolynices (as once happened to <term>Lully</term> <note>Ramon Llull, a legendary figure in alchemy.</note> by <term>Arnold</term> <note>Arnald of Villanova, a famous physician and alchemist.</note>),*

*by manual experience often repeated and by adding the clearest reasons for such a great operation,*

<margin>The reason why the maiden Chemistry is not to be met in public or prostituted.</margin>
*were it not for the most serious reasons which forbid the maiden Chemistry from making herself public and prostituting herself to the common crowd. For first, consideration must be given to the weakness of her sex and her virginal chastity; second, it is not safe enough for a Queen to descend from her otherwise inaccessible citadel...*

<summary>Maier defends alchemy as a noble "Queen of Arts" against arrogant critics, personified by the comedic character Pyrgopolynices. He argues that alchemy's truths cannot be found through mere logic but through experience, while explaining why the "secrets" of the art must remain hidden from the unworthy public.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the preface of Michael Maier's "Symbola Aureae Mensae" (Symbols of the Golden Table). It elaborates on why the "Queen of Arts" (Alchemy) remains veiled in allegory and why Maier uses a "battle" metaphor to defend her against critics like the character Pyrgopolynices.</meta>

# TO THE READER.

...to go forth and offer herself naked and ready to be captured by the adversary; which has often been observed to happen in practice, unless the most cautious provision is made for these matters by fair hostages. But what hostages could be equal to so great a Queen? Thirdly, such a great gathering of spectators and idle people would occur that, even if danger to the life of the virgin did not loom, nevertheless many damages would seem to be imminent, which any rational person will easily perceive for himself.
<margin>Let the adversary be incredulous.</margin>
Hence it was judged safer that one **Pyrgopolynices** <note>A "braggart soldier" character from the plays of Plautus, used here by Maier to represent the arrogant, loud-mouthed critic of alchemy.</note>, an adversary and an unbeliever, should remain so out of either ignorance or envy, rather than such a great Queen be stripped or despoiled of her goods along with his belief.
<margin>The truth of Chemistry can be demonstrated by a single argument.</margin>
For just as it is easy to demonstrate a geometric problem (for example, that every acute angle above a straight line, together with its neighboring obtuse angle, is equal to two right angles), so it would be just as easy to demonstrate the Truth of **Chemistry** <term>Chemia</term> <note>While Maier uses the word "Chemia," in the 17th century this referred to the "Hermetic Art" or alchemy.</note> against its enemies and haters by revealing all its secrets. But because it is a crime and a sacrilege to open these things to everyone, except through riddles, twists, and various turnings—just as sailors sometimes shift their sails against the wind by pushing obliquely toward where they want to go—hence the virgin **Chemistry** has remained unblemished until now.
<margin>Why weapons are handled during feasts.</margin>
Nor will anyone truly wonder why we mix weapons among feasts, like music in mourning, if they consider that in the banquets of the ancients, gladiators were often matched against each other among the **Romans**, as in the **Saturnalia** <note>A Roman festival in honor of Saturn, characterized by role-reversal and feasting.</note>, which are the same as the **Mercurialia** <note>Festivals of Mercury; Maier links these to the "mercurial" nature of alchemical work.</note> in their first institution and origin; or among the **Athenians** in the festivals of **Minerva**, where they fought with various games of arms and spears. Furthermore, these spears of ours are not bloody, such as might create a loathing of the feast at the banquets, but are rather **Platonic** dishes of reason and speech, which heal the person they wound, like the spear of **Achilles** <note>According to Greek myth, the spear of Achilles could heal the very wounds it inflicted.</note>; what they refresh today, they may also affect tomorrow. To these—whether they be dishes or spears, according as anyone is minded toward this Virgin (while she, as one pure, carries friendship and enmity ready on her brow)—we invite and refer all who are judges of this dinner or battle: namely, the well-meaning suitors of this girl to the former, and the malevolent haters of the same to the latter; so that both, to the praise of Almighty God and the utility of the **Republic**... <note>original: "Reipublicae utilita-" (The text cuts off mid-word "utilitatem").</note>

<summary>Maier defends the use of allegory and "intellectual combat" in alchemical writing, arguing that exposing the art's secrets directly would be a sacrilege. He compares his argumentative "spears" to the spear of Achilles, which heals the wounds it makes.</summary>

<margin>Symbols to be brought together at the golden table.</margin>
**He** <note>The critic/enemy of alchemy mentioned on the previous page, Pyrgopolynices.</note> must be stripped of those arms with which he carries himself so swell-headedly. With these words, they sat down, each according to his own order and place, and all directed their faces and minds most politely toward **HERMES**, as if toward a King.

<margin>A philosophical table, which is also unique.</margin>
This table was round like the World, composed of two semicircles, one of which appeared to be of a very bright red color, the other snowy white; for no other reason than that the seated guests might be reminded by this quasi-hieroglyphic <note>A symbolic or mystical visual sign.</note> that these colors especially are the true and legitimate ones belonging to the **Moon** and the **Sun** <note>In alchemy, Luna (Moon/White) and Sol (Sun/Red) represent the two main stages of the "Great Work": the Albedo (whitening) and Rubedo (reddening).</note>, which the shape-shifting chameleon could in no way imitate or express. For while simple truth is denoted by these colors, counterfeiters assume all others, but not these.

<margin>What order is to be observed in each entry.</margin>

<margin>1.</margin>
First, we shall relate the nation, homeland, life, deeds, works, and other relevant matters of each **CHIEF** <term>Primas: A leader or foremost authority in a specific field.</term>, insofar as they have come to our knowledge.

<margin>2.</margin>
Next, we shall add for each his fellow countrymen who were likewise devoted to **Chemistry**.

<margin>3.</margin>
From here, the arguments and weapons of the adversary attacking **Chemistry**...

It remains for him to seek another father, since he himself, as has been said, acknowledges Hermes—not Philo—as his father. <margin>Books of Hermes.</margin> *Iamblichus* <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote on Egyptian mysteries</note> *in his book on the Mysteries* recounts that Hermes wrote a great many books, where he made mention of the COLUMNS OF MERCURY <note>Legendary pillars upon which ancient wisdom was said to be inscribed to survive natural disasters</note> in this manner: *The whole universal principles,* he says, *as Seleucus narrates, were handed down by Mercury himself in twenty thousand volumes; or, as Meneteus recounts, he handed them down in thirty-six thousand, five hundred and twenty-five volumes, and in them he perfectly demonstrated all things.* The same author says that *Mercury wrote about the Ethereal, Empyreal, and Celestial Gods, and that he composed one hundred books on the Empyreal, as many on the Ethereal, and a thousand on the Celestial:* very many of which he records were translated into the Greek language in these words: *For those books which are circulated under the title of Mercury contain Mercurial opinions, even if they often speak in the style of the Greek philosophers; for they were translated from the Egyptian language into Greek by men not unskilled in philosophy.* Indeed, it might seem incredible and beyond all belief that so many writings were published by one man—writings which alone might suffice for the entire world in philosophical matters. But it must be considered that this man, most perfect in every respect, consecrated these as the sacrifices of his mouth to God the Creator, filled with innumerable divine hymns and praises; and that he, without doubt, wrote individual books about individual created things, as if they were <margin>From the books of Hermes that still exist.</margin> the pages of the Universe. Of his books, very few still survive and have reached our age, namely the *Pimander* <note>Also known as the *Poimandres*, a foundational text of Hermeticism</note>, the *Asclepius*, the *Treatise of Seven Chapters*, and the so-called *Emerald Tablet*: <note>The *Tabula Smaragdina*, a brief, cryptic text highly revered by alchemists as the foundation of their art</note> Apuleius <note>A Roman philosopher and prose writer</note> rendered the *Asclepius* into Latin more than fifteen hundred years ago, and Marsilio Ficino <note>A key figure of the Italian Renaissance who translated many Hermetic and Platonic texts</note> translated the *Pimander*. <margin>Why Hermes is called Trismegistus.</margin> He is called HERMES by the Greeks because he acted as the interpreter of God among men; and TRISMEGISTUS <note>Meaning "Thrice-Great"</note> because he was a most great Philosopher, Priest, and King, and the first inventor and institutor of the Egyptian laws, for which reason he was left as an advisor to Isis...

<margin>Why Socrates drank hemlock.</margin>
Hence we see that Socrates willingly underwent death by drinking hemlock <note>A poisonous plant used in ancient Athens for executions; Socrates was sentenced to death in 399 BCE, partly for "impiety."</note> because he taught that one God, the creator of all things, ought to be worshiped; and that Plato, Theophrastus, and many others, having followed this opinion according to the doctrine of Hermes and the most learned Egyptians, risked their lives. Since, in the course of time, *Egypt* was targeted by foreigners, and expeditions were frequently attempted against it by *Chaldean*, *Persian*, and *Greek* kings, the priests who recognized the truth of that science gradually passed away. <margin>Isis and Osiris are not from the celestial gods.</margin>
By these points, he demonstrates sufficiently that he does not mean "celestial gods" here, and that Isis or Osiris were not such gods as later pagan writers believed—and the poets who followed them—but were rather earthly things made by human hands. This interpretation of ours is not forced, but agrees with the very circumstances prescribed by Hermes.

<margin>Gold is held as an earthly God by the worldly.</margin>
Even if most people in this world do not call **G O L D** an "earthly God" with their voices, in reality they possess and worship it, carrying it in their minds and eyes; at its command they speak, fall silent, run, stand, and leave nothing undone. Indeed, for most, the God of heaven is on their lips, while the god of the earth is in their heart, their prayers, and their sighs. It is notorious to anyone how many labors, sleepless nights, dangers to life—through right and wrong, waters and lands, even infamy, exile, capital punishment, and the cross—most people undergo and endure to obtain this earthly good, gold. Hence the Poet <note>The Roman poet Horace, *Epistles* 1.1.45</note> says: *Fleeing poverty, the merchant runs to the Indies*; and, *O citizens, citizens, money must be sought first; virtue after coins* <note>original: "ô ciues, ciues, quaerenda pecunia primum, Virtus post nummos"</note>.

<margin>The chemical statue made of herbs and stones.</margin>
But if it is said that Hermes speaks of statues, which can in no way be understood as chemical matters since in Chemistry there is neither mention nor use of statues: I admit that statues in themselves have nothing to do with Chemistry; but if they are made of "herbs, stones, and spices," as Hermes says, they look precisely toward that art and are specific to Chemistry <note>Maier argues that "herbs and stones" are alchemical code for the organic and mineral components of the Philosopher's Stone</note>. Since some more recent writers have understood this, they have mentioned these statues more than once in various places. Senior <note>Senior Zadith, a famous 10th-century Arabic alchemist often cited by Maier as an authority</note> says in the allegory or archetype of the *Hunting of the Lion*: *Then I collect the head, hands, and feet, and I warm for them the water extracted from the hearts of statues made of white and lemon-yellow* <note>original: "citri-"</note>

<meta>The text breaks here at the syllable "citri-", which the catchword "nis" at the bottom of the page indicates will complete the word "citrinis" (lemon-yellow or citrine) on the following page.</meta>

<summary>Maier argues that the Egyptian gods Isis and Osiris were not literal deities but alchemical metaphors for "earthly gods" like gold. He uses the writings of the alchemist Senior Zadith to prove that ancient descriptions of "statues" made of stones and herbs actually refer to chemical substances.</summary>

...[of the dew] which falls from heaven at the time of rain, and we collect it and store it for the **decoction** <note>A process of heating or boiling a substance to extract its essence</note> of the head, hands, and feet of this **Lion**: <note>original: "nis, quae cadit de caelo tempore pluuiæ & colligimus eam & referuamus ad decoctionem capitis, manuum ac pedum Leonis huius." The "Lion" in alchemy often symbolizes a strong mineral acid or a specific state of matter like antimony or mercury.</note> The same author mentions a statue in the form of a wise man, when he says: *I will reveal to you openly the things which that wise man concealed, who made that statue in that house, in which he described all that science as if in his own form, and taught his wisdom in his stone, and revealed it to those who understand:* I knew that this statue is in the form of a wise man, etc. For that is the same statue from whose heart water is extracted, which **Ramon Lull** <note>A 13th-century philosopher and polymath whose name was frequently attached to alchemical texts</note> also mentions in his *Codicil*, chapter 47. *And therefore,* he says, *through the washing with water and the drying by fire, you always extract God from the hearts of statues.*

<margin>Hermes was worshiped after death by the Egyptians.</margin>
Because of the aforementioned reasons and countless other merits, they say that Hermes was not only worshiped with the highest reverence by the Egyptians while alive—and called **Thoth** <note>Theut</note> as if by the divine name of Mercury—but also that after his death, the city of **Hermopolis** was founded in his honor, and the first month of the year (which among the Egyptians corresponds to September) was named after him. To these things we may add that he was honored with divine rites after his death, not only in Egypt but throughout the entire world, with temples, altars, and sacrifices dedicated to him.

<margin>A statue of Hermes dedicated after death.</margin>
Among his other statues, there was one made of stone in **Pharai, Achaia** <note>A region in Greece</note>, which used to deliver oracles. At that statue, toward evening, incense was burned on the altar, lamps were filled with oil, and a bronze coin was placed at the right hand of the image. Prayers were whispered into the ears of the God; when these rites were finished, the seekers would leave the temple for home with their ears plugged. Once they had gone out into the marketplace, the very first voice they heard upon opening their ears was interpreted as the answer, as if sent by **Mercury**.

<margin>Superstition arising in honor of Hermes.</margin>
But these things must be attributed to the superstition of men, who thus abused the posthumous memory of this most excellent man. In the same way, we consider as fables those things which [are attributed] to Hermes...

Magical trifles are falsely ascribed to such a great man, which are most unworthy of so grave and pious a person.

<margin>Falsely ascribed to Abel.</margin>
Just as *St. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), a major medieval theologian, though the specific magical works mentioned here were often falsely attributed to him in the Renaissance.</note> in the book he published On Being and Essence*, relates that **Abel**, the son of **Adam**, wrote certain things about the virtues and properties of the planets; and since he knew the world would perish in a general flood, he designated this with certain characters and enclosed the signed secret within a stone, so that the writings would receive no damage from the inundation of the **Cataclysm** <note>The Great Flood of Noah</note>. Many centuries after the flood, these writings came into the hands of **MERCURY TRISMEGISTUS**, from which he was taught many things, all of which he claimed as his own—namely, the method of consecrations and many secrets pertaining to **natural Magic** <note>The study of hidden powers within nature, such as magnetism or herbal properties, considered distinct from demonic magic.</note>. These same writings, handed down from that ancient time, finally came to *St. Thomas*, from which he learned the making of certain small images which, when consecrated to certain planetary influences and the position of the sky, ward off the encounter of harmful animals; and when placed in springs, they cause jars to be broken upon contact with the water.

<margin>With what the Patriarch Abel was occupied.</margin>
Be these things as they may, the fact that they are ascribed to the Patriarch **Abel** is completely contrary to reason. For why would they have attributed such things to him? He was one who merited being pleasing to **GOD**, though hated and killed by **Cain**. He did not occupy himself with these magical trifles, but with true piety and divine worship—namely, through constant prayers poured out to God, frequent acts of thanksgiving for gifts received, and trust in the Son of God who was to come in the flesh according to the Gospel promise given to **Adam** after the fall: *The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent* <note>original: "Semen mulieris conteret caput ferpentis." A reference to Genesis 3:15, viewed by Christians as the first prophecy of Christ.</note>. Through these and similar religious practices, he became the first to offer his blood for the earth to drink and his soul to heaven, from whence it had arisen.

<margin>Whether Abel was able to write is unknown.</margin>
Who could affirm for certain that any kind of letters or writing was known to **Abel**, by which he could have committed anything to memory? Indeed, what others report concerning **Seth** <note>The third son of Adam, often credited in mystical traditions with inventing writing or astrology.</note>, these people report concerning **Abel**.

<margin>The origin of chemistry is falsely attributed to Adam and his sons.</margin>
In a similar way, those who trace the origin and use of the *chemical* <note>original: "Chymicę"; in this period, "chemistry" and "alchemy" were often used interchangeably to describe the art of transmuting metals and creating powerful medicines.</note> art—and the most excellent medicine derived from it—to *Adam* or other Patriarchs <note>The biblical fathers listed in Genesis, such as Seth, Enoch, and Methuselah.</note> are to be convicted of vanity. They claim that those who lived before the flood used this gift of **GOD** to achieve their longevity, as if it would have been impossible for God to extend their lives to eight or nine hundred years without such a means, or for them to have fathered sons and daughters even after several hundred years. For that cause [chemistry] in human medicine is neither sufficient nor proper for extending life for such a vast time, since without God’s will, one cannot prolong a person's age even by a year, a day, or an hour, as this remains in God's hand alone.

<margin>The natural cause of the longevity of the fathers before the flood.</margin>
However, the natural cause of the Patriarchs' longevity before the flood is recorded as follows: they always maintained a simple diet, were not devoted to luxury or gluttony, and did not indulge in excessive idleness, nor in immoderate labor, sleeplessness, or anxiety over immense riches, precious clothing, the pursuit of honor or kingdoms, or delicate banquets—for these and similar things were not valued then. Much less were they concerned with leaving estates and goods to their children as an inheritance, because they possessed more land than could even be cultivated. But the chief natural cause was the power infused into the human seed in its highest vigor and efficacy, which resulted in robust and long-lived parents begetting similar children. Beyond all these, however, was the divine blessing, which out of its singular providence granted the first fathers such great longevity and reproductive power to multiply the human race, and to adorn and populate a world still empty of inhabitants. Opposite causes produced opposite effects, namely the gradual shortening of life after the flood until this present time. For as *luxury*, *gluttony*, empty worries, and other vices began to prevail, sickly parents produced sickly offspring, who were neither so power-

Thus, if those Fathers had no need for the practice of the chemical art to prepare medicine, they had much less need for it to acquire riches. I consider this certain: if the Patriarchs before him knew Chemistry theoretically <note>original: "speculatiuè"; meaning they understood the principles through divine revelation rather than laboratory work.</note> as a gift from **GOD**, they nevertheless did not practice it.

Where Plato derived his divine ideas.

The false opinions of certain Christians regarding Alchemists.

What shall we say now of those who, in this our own time, sacrilegiously and most impiously attempt to transfer the Creation of the world, the birth, passion, death, resurrection, and ascension of Christ—indeed, almost all the articles of faith—to the <term>Alchemical art</term> <note>original: "Chymicam artem." These men, however, though calling themselves Christians, leap over all bounds of piety, break through the limits of modesty, and attempt to procure a mixture of Truth and falsehood; of whom we shall speak elsewhere.

Alexander the Great finds the tomb of Hermes.

Now we shall turn ourselves to the alchemical books of Hermes, among which a certain very brief one exists under the name of the *Emerald Tablet* and has reached our age. Regarding this, *Albertus Magnus* <note>A 13th-century Dominican friar and philosopher known for his work in the natural sciences.</note> *relates in his book on Alchemical secrets* that Alexander the Great, *during his travels*, found the tomb of Hermes—the father of all philosophers—filled with every treasure; not metallic treasures, but golden letters written upon the *Zarad Tablet*, which others call the *Emerald Tablet*. Yet there is no doubt that this Tablet, or its inscription, was among the Egyptians long before the time of Alexander...

<margin>What Alexander the Great learned from the Egyptian priest Leo.</margin> 
Alexander the Great, from his conversation with the *Priest Leo*, received as a secret to be revealed to no one that the Gods—*Jupiter, Mars, Juno, Osiris, Isis,* and all the rest, then undoubtedly accepted as gods and worshipped throughout the greater part of the known world—are not, and were not gods, but men; a fact which *Alexander* wrote to his mother *Olympias*, though he ordered the letter to be thrown into the fire once read. But what if they were not even men, as in truth they were not? What then? They were surely not nothing at all, but rather "chemical gods," 
<margin>The Egyptian gods were chemical symbols used by them like letters of an alphabet.</margin> 
hieroglyphic figures, which the ancients invented and introduced to be used like literary elements or axiomatic sentences to declare the feelings of their minds to one another. They did this so that others seeing those figures could not read them, and those reading them could not understand them in the least; just as we have demonstrated more copiously in our own work on hieroglyphics <note>A reference to Maier's *Arcana Arcanissima*, where he argues that Egyptian myths were actually alchemical instructions.</note>. Once the *Emerald Tablet* <note>original: "Tabula Smaragdina"; the foundational text of Hermeticism, traditionally attributed to Hermes Trismegistus.</note>, as has been 
<margin>Many recognized the chemical artifice from the Emerald Tablet.</margin> 
said, was found or in whatever manner made public, there were innumerable people who, looking upon its brevity joined with its obscurity, imagined—not without cause—that some great mystery was hidden within it. Indeed, there was no doubt that it ought to be explained as concerning the <term>philosophical mastery</term> <note>original: "magisterio philosopho"; the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note> or the <term>chemical artifice</term>, of which *Hermes* was the author. *Morienus* <note>An 8th-century legendary alchemist said to have taught the Ummayad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> (who says the divine mind of *Hermes* fully touched upon all parts of philosophy) records that after the death of *Hermes*, his disciples studied the precepts of this book for a long time until they achieved the desired effect. Afterward, these disciples gave forth innumerable precepts out of envy, so that others following them might not reach the art because of its obscurity and difficulty. 
<margin>Summary of the Emerald Tablet.</margin> 
*Count Bernard* <note>original: "Bernhardus Comes"; likely Bernard of Trevisan, a famous 15th-century alchemist.</note> says that the entire work is contained in that little book, of which he provides this summary: **IT IS TRUE, CERTAIN, & most true. That which is above has the nature of that which is below, and that which ascends has the nature of that which descends: You shall join them by a single way and arrangement...**

*The SUN is the father of this union and the white moon the mother; a third succeeds them as the governor: fire. Of this Tablet also—to pass over others—Johannes Pontanus <note>A 15th-century alchemist famous for his "Epistle" claiming to have found the "secret fire" after much study.</note>, a more recent author, makes mention, and testifies that he studied for three continuous years in the books of the philosophers (namely, after many years of prior errors) specifically in Hermes alone, *whose words,* he says, *though brief, encompass the whole stone, even if he speaks obscurely of the upper and lower, and of heaven and earth.* <note>The "Stone" refers to the Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the alchemical Great Work.</note>

<margin>
The Emerald Tablet is admirable to all ages.
</margin>
Thus, in all ages, that Emerald Tablet has been deservedly held in admiration by the most learned men, both because of the supreme excellence and celebrity of the author, and because of the dignity of the contents within it, since it has opened the way of truth to many. Furthermore, there is a *certain Treatise of Seven Chapters, truly Hermetic and Chemical*, which the alchemists of all ages have acknowledged and received as authentic up to this point. In this work, those things which were delivered more obscurely and briefly in the aforementioned Tablet are unfolded more clearly and extensively.

<margin>
The Treatise of Seven Chapters is Hermetic.
</margin>
Some think this treatise is by a certain anonymous Arab, since it was translated from Arabic into Latin, which is clearly apparent from the translation itself. But here it must be considered that the books of the Egyptians were translated into their own languages partly by the neighboring Greeks and partly by the Arabs, who are very close to the Egyptians and were at one time subject to them; from these widely used idioms, they were finally translated into Latin...

...into Latin. Hence the *Asclepius* and *Poimandres* <note>original: "Asclepius & Pimander." These are core texts of the *Corpus Hermeticum*, a collection of Greco-Egyptian wisdom attributed to Hermes Trismegistus.</note> seem to be by Greek authors, but this *Treatise of Seven Chapters* <note>The "Septem Tractatus" is an alchemical work traditionally attributed to Hermes, but likely of medieval Arabic origin.</note> appears to be by an Arabian or Mohammedan author, since these nations became famous for chemical works long before others near us, as will appear later. But if anyone, through ignorance of mind or slowness of wit, cannot yet perceive the light of truth from the philosophical sayings and writings mentioned so far—so as to realize that Hermes is the Restorer and standard-bearer of the chemical art among the Egyptians, and in general, and that this art has been practiced in Egypt for many centuries as if it were native to the land—let him believe what he wants and persuade himself of what pleases him. Meanwhile, he will do no violence to the truth of the matter, nor will he subvert the true essences with his contrary opinion. It is necessary for human minds to be free, but only in such a way that the intellect, which is of divine origin, is not subjugated or led captive by imagination or fantasy, which is common to the beasts.

<margin>History of the most true gold-making of Egypt.</margin>
For others, who are lovers of true chemistry, we shall produce a most certain and irrefragable history of the gold-making of Egypt, beyond what has already been said, with infallible testimony—and indeed in the very words of the authors. Paul the Deacon, in his *Life of Diocletian Caesar*, says: *After Diocletian had defeated Achilleus <note>A Roman usurper who declared himself Emperor in Egypt.</note>, the leader of the Egyptians, having besieged him for eight months in Alexandria of Egypt, he burned all the books of the chemical art, sought out with diligent care, so that they [the Egyptians] might not resist the Romans again by restoring their wealth.*

<margin>Around the year of Christ 296.</margin>
Orosius <note>Paulus Orosius, a 5th-century historian and student of St. Augustine.</note> testifies to the same in Book 17, Chapter 16. And Suidas <note>The *Suda*, a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the Mediterranean world.</note> under the word *CHEMIA* <term>Chemia: Maier identifies this ancient term specifically with the "confection" or creation of gold and silver</term>. *Chemia*, it says, *is the making of gold and silver; Diocletian burned the books of this art after they were sought out, because the Egyptians had plotted new revolts against Diocletian, and he treated them harshly and as enemies. At which time he also sought out and burned the books on the chemistry of gold and silver written by the ancients, so that wealth should not thereafter fall to the Egyptians from that art, nor, relying on an abundance of money, should they rebel against the Romans in the future.* So says that author. This occurred around the year of Christ two hundred...

</margin>
This was the reason why so many most clear-sighted men from the Greeks and other peoples traveled through Egypt and other most remote places, so that they might clearly see the sun without shadows—that is, the thing itself.

## 2. EGYPTIAN COLONIES
### Chemical.

**C**olonies have very often been led from various nations into different parts of the world for certain well-known and political causes. But we suspect that, besides these, certain Egyptians—acting as private men, as it were—left their homeland and migrated into other far-off regions, and there established either a city or a kingdom at their own expense. Most of these were descended from the priests, on account of the Hieroglyphic works placed by them in honor of the Gods or themselves; they were not unskilled in 그that Chemical art <note>Maier uses "Chymica" to refer to the Hermetic art of alchemy, particularly the transmutation of metals.</note> which was honored and practiced in the Temple of *Vulcan* at *Memphis*. <margin>*The Phoenicians.*</margin> Among these, we have already demonstrated elsewhere that the *Phoenicians*, or some of their primary Princes, were foremost. They say that *Cadmus’s* brother was *Phoenix*, his sister *Europa*, his father *Agenor*, and his grandfather *Belus*. *Cadmus*, however, was sent by his father to seek his sister (whom *Jupiter*, in the form of <margin>*Cadmus, founder of Thebes in Boeotia.*</margin> a bull, had carried off to that part of the earth now called *Europe*); he founded *Thebes* in *Boeotia* near a spring, where his companions were killed, one after another, by a horrible *Dragon*. <margin>*The Dragon, son of Typhon and Echidna, killed by Cadmus; a subject of chemistry.*</margin> But this dragon, the son of *Typhon* and *Echidna*, was slaughtered by *Cadmus*, and its teeth were scattered as seed for the earth; these soon brought forth armed "Earth-born" men rushing at *Cadmus*. When he had struck one of them with a stone, the others then stirred up a civil war and laid hands upon each other, and were all slain and destroyed to a man. No one fails to see that this is an allegory and not history. <margin>*Cadmus skilled in the art of metals.*</margin> They openly report that *Cadmus* was a man skilled in the art of melting gold and metals; this is nothing other than a description of *Chemistry*, in which *Cadmus* greatly excelled, and, from the tradition <note>original: "institutione"</note> of his homeland, he acquired immense riches. *Thebes* in *Boeotia* [was founded] as if by the indication of a cow...

### 3. THOSE BORDERING THE EGYPTIANS.

<margin>An objection of some.</margin>
There are many who, upon hearing our most true assertion regarding the continuity of the chemical art, ask: *How is it that if this art was once in human use and practice, it did not become hereditary for some nation, King, or city, so that it might endure forever, rather than always needing to be sought anew with the intervention of so much expense, time, and labor?* 

<margin>Chemistry is a gift granted by the will of God.</margin>
But let them know this: Just as no one in this life is overlooked or neglected by God—for one meets their death either sooner or later by God’s gift—so too this most noble Gift <note>original: "Munus." Referring here to the "Donum Dei" or the secret of the Philosopher's Stone.</note> does not come into anyone's hands without God's knowledge; indeed, it is by His will, His sight, and His permission. If this is true, then no one has ever received this from the divine hand unless they appeared worthy to God. And if an unworthy person should obtain some of the <term>Medicine</term><note>In alchemical literature, the "Medicine" refers to the Elixir or Philosopher's Stone, capable of "curing" base metals into gold or healing the human body.</note> itself by hook or by crook <note>original: "per fas et nefas," literally "through divine or human law," meaning by any means possible.</note>, they nevertheless would by no means possess the science of it. 

<margin>Why the experts of the art concealed it.</margin>
This is the reason why those who have enjoyed this Gift of God—whether they were kings and public figures or private individuals—have always concealed the art itself and veiled it under the shadows of obscure speech. They did this to such an extent that the common people did not know what subject was being introduced through such allegories, fictions, fables, or animal characters and signs. Hence, the craftsmen were bound and tied to one another by the strictest oaths, so that no one might reveal anything of their secrets to another by voice, writing, a nod, or any other way whatsoever. 

<margin>Why the statue of Silence was used in Egyptian rites.</margin>
For that same reason, whenever the priests celebrated the <term>Isiac rites</term><note>The sacred mysteries of the Egyptian goddess Isis, which Maier interprets here as alchemical in nature.</note> (which were performed by priests wearing mitres, with shaved heads and all parts of their bodies clothed in white, ankle-length linen garments), they did not allow their mysteries to be expressed in words, as they were covered and unknown to the common folk, but instead protected them with a sacred silence. Therefore, a statue of SILENCE (which was called <term>Sigalion</term><note>A name for the god of silence, often identified with the Egyptian Harpocrates, who is depicted with a finger to his lips.</note>) was erected at the beginning of the altar, and the people were commanded to "favor with their tongues" <note>original: "fauere linguis." A ritual formula used in ancient religious ceremonies to command the audience to keep a holy silence so as not to interrupt the rite with ill-omened words.</note>.

<summary>Maier explains that alchemy is a divine gift (Donum Dei) granted only to the worthy, which explains why it is not a publicly inherited science. He links this tradition of absolute secrecy to the Egyptian priests of Isis and the ritual use of the statue of Sigalion to enforce silence.</summary>

## 2. THE COLLEGE OF THE MAGI
### Among the Persians.

<margin>The College of the Magi among the Persians.</margin>
<margin>What Magic signifies now and in the past.</margin>
<margin>A king was chosen from the Magi among the Persians and Medes.</margin>
The name of **MA**gic has come into such contempt that in our time it is understood as nothing but an illicit art, *Necromancy* <note>The practice of communicating with the dead or using demonic influence.</note>, which uses the invocation of evil demons to accomplish certain things; whereas anciently among the *Persians*, it was accepted as wisdom and the most perfect knowledge of natural things.
