<margin>Osthanes the Persian magus.</margin>
*Osthanes drove the Greek peoples to a madness, not just a greed, for this science.*
<margin>Greek philosophers who traveled abroad for the sake of magic—namely, natural magic.</margin>
Certainly *Pythagoras, Empedocles, Democritus,* and *Plato* sailed abroad to learn this, undertaking what were more like exiles than mere travels.

<margin>Tantalus the Alchemist.</margin>
I maintain that he was a man who was not only eloquent, but also most highly skilled in **Alchemy**; this appears not only from the institution of these **Brahmans** <note>The Brahmans were the priestly caste of India, whom Maier views here as keepers of ancient alchemical wisdom.</note>, who saw fit to honor him with a statue, but from many other signs as well. <margin>The allegory of Tantalus.</margin> They assert that he was the King of Phrygia, who, when he had received the Gods at a banquet, served them his son **Pelops**, cut into pieces and cooked, to be eaten. ## The Response of Hermes.

**T**he major premise <note>In a formal logical argument (a syllogism), the "major premise" is the first general statement used to reach a conclusion. Hermes is attacking the very foundation of his opponent's logic.</note> is false, however it may be understood: For certain entire species pass over into other different species; or individuals of certain species migrate into individuals of other species. For instance, eggs, legumes, and seeds are species within their own respective kinds: an acorn is not an oak, nor is a walnut the walnut tree. Nevertheless, the latter are produced from the former. Similarly, the "seeds" <note>Hermes refers to silkworm eggs as "seeds," a common term in early biology.</note> of silkworms remain in winter when the species of the little animal has perished, and from there a caterpillar is soon born; this caterpillar differs from the seed, and from the caterpillar comes a <term>bombyx</term> <note>original: *bombyx*; a silkworm or the silk moth</note> or winged butterfly, which differs in species from the caterpillar. Indeed, this whole nature of things shows nothing else through its daily change—whether natural or artificial—than the falsehood of this major premise, so there is no need for other specific examples. *Nevertheless, I shall overthrow that premise, as if it were the base of this syllogism, with this **BATTERING RAM**.* <note>Hermes uses the "battering ram" (*aries*) as a metaphor for a forceful logical argument intended to demolish the opponent's "wall" of reasoning.</note>

If species were not changed into species, nor an individual of one species into an individual of another, then silver would not be naturally generated from lead, nor gold from silver.

But we must learn from the miners and from daily experience that this does happen (though not as quickly as hen's eggs are hatched and changed into chicks). Therefore, etc. <note>The "etc." indicates the conclusion of the formal logical proof: that transmutation is therefore possible.</note>

To the minor premise <note>The second, more specific statement in his opponent's argument.</note> I respond: that lead, copper, and metals similar to these are indeed species—just as gold is—in their own right. However, one is produced after the other, just as a hen comes after the egg, or each exists by itself in its own perfection. For an egg, beans, wheat, and other things of that sort are further perfected when they are propagated into a new species; or they are not further perfected when they are instead converted to the use of men. <note>Hermes argues that just as a seed's "perfection" is to become a tree, a base metal's "perfection" is to become gold, unless humans interrupt the process to use the lead or copper as they are.</note>

<summary>Hermes refutes the skeptic's logic by citing natural metamorphoses, such as seeds becoming trees and caterpillars becoming moths, to prove that one "species" can indeed transform into another. He argues that metals follow this same natural law, maturing from lead toward gold over time.</summary>

## 2. *The Argument of those attacking Chemistry.*

From a privation of form, there can be no return to a state of possession. <note>original: *A privatione formae non potest regressus fieri in habitum.* This is a principle from Aristotelian logic. "Privation" refers to the absence of a quality that a thing should naturally have (like blindness is the privation of sight), while "habit" or "possession" refers to having that quality.</note>
But if gold were to be made from lead, copper, etc., they would first have to be deprived of their prior form, and then a return would have to be made to the form of gold.
Therefore, gold cannot be made from lead, copper, and the like.
The major premise <note>The first general statement of the argument.</note> is evident from the accepted axiom: *From privation to possession, no return is granted*, or, that which has been destroyed by death can be brought back to life neither by art nor by nature.

### *The Response of Hermes.*

**T**he major premise is true regarding the form of the same species, but not of another: For if a privation of the form of some thing has occurred, the same form is not introduced again by nature, but another, either more noble or less noble, as appears in all mutations. For if the exact same form were immediately introduced, it would not be a change, but a permanence of the form; just as we see in a fire, where always new and newer fire succeeds in the same form. <note>Hermes argues that if you burn wood, the "form" of the wood is lost, but it is replaced by the "form" of fire/ash, which is a change, not a restoration of the wood.</note> Nor indeed is there anyone among the Chemists who would say that a metal to be transmuted into gold must be so destroyed that it possesses no form at all before it receives the form of gold. For this does not happen in other changeable things, as is clearly seen in man, who first utilizes the life of a vegetable plant—namely as an <term>Embryo</term> <note>original: *Embryo*; Hermes is following the Aristotelian view that a human fetus passes through stages of "souls": first vegetative, then sensitive, then rational.</note> in the womb; then...

...from this, it is gifted with an animal soul, and finally with a rational soul, which succeeds the other forms just as a pentagon succeeds a quadrangle, and a quadrangle a triangle, of which the more perfect contains the less perfect, and the later contains the earlier. <note>Maier uses a classic philosophical metaphor: just as a square "contains" the triangles used to build it, a "higher" soul or form (like a human's) includes the functions of "lower" ones (like a plant's or animal's).</note> 

Truly, a distinction must be made between the privations <note>The loss or absence of a quality.</note> of forms. Some forms perish entirely through corruption and resolution into their original elements; thus an egg that is cast into the dung-heap is corrupted there into the elements from which it was composed, because its corrupted form cannot be put back into that same thing again by either art or nature. 

Other forms are removed, but not entirely through corruption and resolution into their elements; rather, they are removed through a successive ennobling, or change. This is seen when the form of an egg takes into itself the more perfect form of a chick, just as the triangle becomes the quadrangle. The "major premise" <note>The opponent's starting argument on the previous page.</note> speaks of that first kind of corruption, but not the second, which is how the "minor premise" should be understood.

*Regarding the minor premise, I say it is false that a "return" to gold is made from the privation of the form of lead or copper. Instead, it is a single progress from the less perfect to the more perfect, just as was said regarding the egg. In the succession of forms, there is a great difference:* 

*In corruption into the elements or "prime matter," <note>The fundamental, formless "stuff" that makes up the universe in ancient physics.</note> another simple elemental form succeeds it. But in maturation or ennobling, a new form does not succeed prime matter that has been stripped of every form; rather, it succeeds a cruder form, and perfects it in an instant. To strike down the minor premise of this argument, I shall oppose it with this Ballista:* <note>original: *Ballistam*. A ballista was a heavy ancient siege engine used for throwing stones or bolts; Maier is using it as a metaphor for a powerful, "heavy-hitting" logical counter-argument.</note>

> *A form that perfects a thing does not entirely remove the*
> *form of the thing to be perfected, but rather perfects it,*
> *and does so in an instant.*

But the form of gold, which comes upon the metals—lead, copper, and the like—is that which perfects them,

Therefore, the form of gold does not entirely abolish the forms of the metals to be perfected, but rather it perfects them in an instant.

The *major premise* of this syllogism cannot be refuted by any contrary example, whether in the works of nature or of art. Even our adversaries admit that when an ant becomes winged, or a fly emerges from a worm, an ennobling <note>Latin: *nobilitatio*; the process of a thing moving to a higher, "nobler" state of being.</note> takes place there; the prior form does not depart entirely, but is changed for the better. Nevertheless, there is a migration from one species into another species—that is, a crawling creature becoming a flying one—which is exactly what they deny happens in metals. If an Aedile becomes a Praetor, or a Praetor a Consul; or if a Nobleman becomes a Baron, a Baron an Earl <note>original: *Comes*</note>, and an Earl a Prince, is that the destruction of the prior form, or is it truly an ennobling? Just as a greater light does not take away but merely obscures a lesser one, so does a nobler form act upon a less noble one. The *minor premise* is proven true by experience or by a sound hypothesis.

<meta>This page continues the refutation of the third argument against alchemy, specifically addressing the concept of "circular generation"—the idea that nature or art might move in a loop from one substance to another and back again.</meta>

# THE GOLDEN TABLE. BOOK I.

...from a corrupted metal, another is made: If the corruption of the form of lead, copper, and similar metals had to occur all the way back to the "prime matter" <term>First Matter: the original, formless substance from which all things are made</term>, or into the four elements, then the first part of their argument would proceed. *But even so, the logical connection would not follow; because for that reason there would not be a Circular Generation <note>Circular Generation: a process where a substance changes through various stages only to eventually return to its original form.</note>; as a worm comes from a dog, a fly from that same worm, and if this fly settles on meat, it sows little worms, and from here again, if they mature, they become flies; and thus it is the mutation of one small animal into another: but for that reason, however, it is not to be called exactly "Circular." For from one into another, or from the more imperfect into the more perfect, a circle is not made, since the more perfect does not here regress into the more imperfect.*

To the minor premise I say: that "circular generation" is not granted, at least as far as it is known to us exactly; but nevertheless, similar transmutations are granted in nature, as we have already said regarding the fly from the worm and the worm from the dog. What if mercury <term>quicksilver: literally "living silver" or *argentum vivum*</term> passes into lead, this into silver, silver into gold, and gold back into silver, and silver into copper or lead? Would this not be a Circular Generation in nature? Which is, however, admitted to be so, from the increase and decrease of metals, just as <margin>Andreas Solea, who wrote the *Septentrias* on the knowledge of metals.</margin> *Andreas Solea demonstrates, being a most skilled practitioner in these matters.*

But this is not the work of the chemical art, whose purpose is to perfect nature or to assist it in acquiring perfection, not to lead it back from perfection to imperfection. Although it is indeed certain that all metals, even gold itself, can be reduced into running mercury <note>original: *argentum vivum currens*</note>, from which they took their origin; yet this does not happen by the regression of the "cooked" into the "raw" <note>Alchemy often compared the maturation of metals to "cooking" or digestion; gold was considered "fully cooked."</note>, but rather by the separation of the more cooked and "tinctured" <term>tinctured: "tincting" or "dyeing" refers to the alchemical process of infusing a substance with a specific color or quality, such as the power of gold</term> from the raw and untinctured, by a certain separation of their natures. Other circular generations can also be found, if they are sought: Does not air come from water, water from air, and again—

<summary>Michael Maier argues that alchemy is not a "circular" process of decay, but a linear path toward perfection, though he admits metals can be reduced to their original mercury through separation rather than regression.</summary>

<margin>Affirmative Reason 1.</margin>
### I. Hermes’ Affirmative Reason for **CHEMISTRY**. <note>The author uses "Chemia," which in this period (early 17th century) referred to both chemistry and alchemy without distinction.</note>

> If silver is naturally generated from lead, and gold from silver, there is nothing that prevents the same from being done by art—though perhaps not by the same path or method, but by the possibility and potential of nature.
> And the first premise is true.

<margin>In his *Sarepta*, in which he most truly relates the natures of all metals.</margin>
*The minor premise <note>original: "assumptio"</note> of this syllogism <term>Syllogism: a form of logical reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two assumed premises</term> is most true and has been sufficiently demonstrated elsewhere to the eye by us and by others. Above all others, however, this affirmative proposition is most clearly proven by the famous Johann Mathesius.* <note>Johann Mathesius (1504–1565) was a German cleric and mineralogist whose book *Sarepta* combined mining knowledge with theology.</note>

The connection of the major premise cannot be severed by any logical distinction, even if it does not demonstrate the exact necessity of the method. It is enough that it is evident that there is a certain natural potential among these metals, by which one passes into another—as an egg becomes a hen, or the more imperfect becomes the more perfect.

...which we call imperfect, they are in a movement toward the perfection of form.

Therefore, these same things can be perfected as much by art as by nature.

The *Major premise* <note>The first part of a logical argument</note> is established in the vegetable and animal kingdoms—namely, by the grafting of different trees, one into another; the production of flowers and leaves from shoots in winter time in heated rooms <note>original: "hypocaustis," referring to rooms warmed by underfloor heating</note>; the hatching of chicks from eggs by artificial means, and so on. In the mineral kingdom also, steel <term>chalybs: a hardened form of iron</term> is made from iron, etc.

The *Minor premise* <note>The second part of a logical argument</note> seems doubtful to the opponent, but not to those who have experienced that in every imperfect thing something of the perfect lies hidden—and even more so where the location is more exposed to the midday sun, even within the same mountain fertile with ores. And if the time were not so long—amounting to as much movement toward the perfection of form in one day as now occurs in a hundred years—imperfect metals would be changed into gold as quickly as an egg into a chick. Then everyone would have the perfection of metals before their eyes, just as they now see the hatching of eggs. Because this does not happen, no perceptible change of metals is noticed in the entire lifetime of a human. To this point belongs what *Albertus Magnus* <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a famous philosopher and theologian who wrote extensively on nature and minerals</note>
<margin>*Dionysius Zacharius.* <note>A 16th-century French alchemist</note> Imperfect metals are always ennobled in their perfection.</margin>
relates, and others after him, of what happened in his time in *Slavonia* <note>A region in modern-day Croatia</note>: when the miners had come upon a less perfect metal, they closed the mines for thirty or more years so that a greater maturation might occur. From these examples it is clear that imperfect metals move by a continuous motion to occupy a nobler form, which is first silver, and then gold; once this is attained, they rest, unless some evil should befall them.
<margin>Perfect metals can be consumed.</margin>
For the same previously cited *Mathesius* <note>Johann Mathesius, mentioned on the previous page</note> proves that if metals reach their peak <term>acme: the highest point of development</term> or perfection, they can, by some accident occurring, be consumed again and as if "burnt up." From this, the miners then say that they have come too late. *Andreas Solenander* <note>A 16th-century physician and writer on mineral baths</note> attests to the same in his treatise on the increase and decrease of metals.

### 3. Hermes’ Argument for Chemistry.

<margin>3. An affirmative argument.</margin>
**I**F from grass, orache <note>original: "artiplice," likely *Atriplex* or saltbush</note>, chrysanthemum, and other decayed vegetables; likewise from mice in Egypt, eels, fleas, and other animals that have rotted and been reduced to their smallest parts <note>original: "atomos," referring here to the fundamental particles resulting from decay</note>, these same things are generated; if also copper is made from iron decayed in vitriol-enriched water <note>A common observation where iron placed in a copper sulfate solution appears to "turn into" copper as the copper precipitates out</note>, and quicksilver <term>quicksilver: mercury</term> is made from other metals, why should metal not be generated from decayed metal, and thus a circular cycle of generation be established?
But all the former premises are true.
**Therefore, the latter is also true.**

The connection to the preceding statement is evident from this: if it happens in every one of the three kingdoms <note>The animal, vegetable, and mineral kingdoms</note>, then it is possible for it to happen in one of them in that same way. Furthermore, it is more marvelous that a small animal with various organic parts, or some plant, should be regenerated from its own putrefaction and decay, than that a uniform <note>original: "homogeneum"</note> metal should be.

*The truth of this assumption is evident from experience.* For if decayed grass turned to manure, or burned to ash, is spread over a field or earth stripped of all turf, it will soon be regenerated. The same is true for the chrysanthemum <note>Likely referring to the Corn Marigold, known as a persistent weed</note>, as farmers testify; even if it is eaten by oxen and turned into dung, it still brings forth a new generation from itself into the fields where that dung is spread—a generation most harmful (since it chokes the crops and always multiplies). Regarding the *mice of Egypt* produced immediately from the mud, see the historians, especially *Diodorus Siculus* <note>A 1st-century BC Greek historian who described mice spontaneously forming from Nile mud</note>. Regarding *iron converted into copper*, consult the mines of *Spiš* <note>original: "Zepusienses," a region in modern Slovakia famous for mining</note>, *Goslar* <note>A historic mining town in Germany</note>, and *Kutná Hora* <note>original: "Cuticenses," a famous silver and copper mining city in the Czech Republic</note>, as well as *Ercker* <note>Lazarus Ercker (c. 1530–1594), a renowned metallurgical author</note> and others, along with daily experience. <term>Chemists</term> <note>At this time, the term encompassed both laboratory science and alchemy</note> truly testify that they can reduce all metals into running <term>quicksilver</term> in many ways, and they should be believed in this regard. Truly, as said before, we do not intend to cor-

Although these women might perhaps belong to another nation, they are assigned by authors to her company <note>original: "gynæceo"; literally the women's quarters of a house, here used to describe a female circle or peer group.</note> so that **Mary the Jewess** might not be left alone. <margin>Question concerning Solomon: whether he possessed knowledge of Chemistry or not.</margin>
let us first settle the question that arises here as best we can: Very many assert that **Solomon**, King of Israel and son of David, had a perfect knowledge of **Chemistry**; many more deny it. 

<margin>Reasoning of those affirming it: 1. Because Solomon was the wisest.</margin>
Those in the affirmative seem to use these signs: *First*, because he sought and obtained wisdom from God. Therefore, he emerged as the wisest of all men. His wisdom would not have been so perfect without the knowledge of **Chemistry**, the Queen of Arts, as it was with it added. Since, therefore, perfect wisdom was given to Solomon, which other chemical practitioners could not surpass in their operations, it follows that he was as skilled in **Chemistry** as any other. 

<margin>2. Because from being the wisest, he became the richest.</margin>
*Second*, because he is celebrated not only as the wisest but also as the wealthiest of all kings. For since he chose wisdom over riches, it is clear that having been made wise, he was also made rich, as if riches were born out of Wisdom—which is a most true axiom. If he had chosen riches as his wish, he might have seemed rich to others, like **Midas**, who through the weakness of judgment [preferred] **Pan**, sounding on his rustic and unrefined pipe... <note>Referring to the mythological contest where King Midas foolishly judged the music of Pan to be superior to that of Apollo, leading to his ears being turned into those of a donkey.</note>

<margin>The source of **Solomon’s** riches.</margin>
Therefore, **Solomon** acquired immense riches from wisdom, as all histories testify. But how? Was it by exactions from his subjects, by taxes, or by burdens imposed on individuals or property? Or was it truly from the yields of the fields? Certainly, all these things would not have filled his Kingdom with gold and silver, but would rather have emptied it; for as much as the prince’s treasury <term>fiscus<gloss>The public treasury or the emperor's privy purse.</gloss></term> increases by this means and becomes richer, so much do the subjects decrease and become poorer. 

Wherefore, some have not inaptly compared the treasury to the **spleen** of the human body: when it swells, the whole body wastes away. Indeed, this way of growing rich is extraordinary, nor does it seem to have proceeded from the true wisdom of God, which **Solomon** had obtained. To act as a tyrant is not the part of a wise King or one endowed with reason—what shall I say, even the wisest? For such a man is not, as **Homer** calls a King, a **Shepherd of the people** <note>original: *Pastor populi*; a common Homeric epithet for a leader.</note>, 

<margin>A saying of the Emperor **Tiberius**.</margin>
but a wolf, whose part it is to flay the flock; whereas the shepherd’s part is to shear them: <note>Maier alludes to a famous quote attributed by Suetonius to the Emperor Tiberius, who told his governors that a good shepherd shears his sheep but does not skin them.</note>

<margin>The reasons given for Solomon's riches.</margin>
*Others answer* that he received a great sum of gold from his father David as an inheritance, and then perhaps doubled the revenues of such a large kingdom. *In addition*, he received great gifts from foreign Kings. Finally, he dispatched his ships to India <note>The text refers to the biblical voyages to Ophir, often associated with India or East Africa in the 17th century.</note> every three years, which brought back a wealth of gold and silver from there. However, these points are easily answered: the sum of gold and silver he received from his father was easily spent on the construction of the Temple of the Lord and his own most precious royal palace; likewise, the annual revenues of the kingdom were consumed by his lifestyle, through which he presented himself as a more magnificent King than even his father had been. As for the gifts received from foreigners, these are usually balanced out by reciprocal gifts of equal value. *There remain the Indian ships*, which did indeed bring much gold and silver, but the journey was long, involved many expenses, and was fraught with the occasional loss of ships, men, and cargo; therefore, this maritime trade should not be considered as profitable as is generally thought. Furthermore—

<margin>Hiram, King of Tyre, a partner to Solomon in the Indian trade.</margin>

Even after ending the commercial partnership they held for a time with Solomon, they continued to sail there alone, just as before. If, therefore, immense riches came from this Indian navigation, they were shared with the King of Tyre—and were perhaps even greater for him, because the King of Tyre had an abundance of ships and all the materials necessary to equip them. King—

<margin>5. Solomon’s riddles concerning the secrets of nature which must not be revealed.</margin>
It is applied to Alchemy <note>original: *Chemiæ*</note>, and thus it can be applied to nothing else by any of the truly learned—unless they stubbornly resist the truth. <margin>Illicit magic is extremely far removed from alchemy.</margin>

To the extent that Solomon practiced illicit magic, we do not admire his supreme wisdom; but to the degree that he practiced licit magic, and with it Alchemy, we rightly look up to and venerate him. Truly, one should not think that Solomon’s wisdom was celebrated in writing for certain deceptive trifles, but surely for the most profound...

## Neighbors to the Hebrews.

<margin>The Syrians.</margin>

For from ancient times they mourned Adonis, who was killed by a boar, and performed funeral rites for him with wailing and lamentation as if he were dead; yet on the following day they said he lived and sent him into heaven: 
<margin>The cult of Apis among the Egyptians.</margin>

## 4. Argument against Chemistry.

If metals are carried by a natural appetite toward the best of their kind, and having acquired that state, they rest and delight in being preserved in it, then no transmutation of lower metals into gold can occur.
But the first part is true.
Therefore, the second follows as well.

### *Maria the Jewess's Response to the 4th Argument.*

**T**he sense of this *Argument* is as follows: If imperfect metals are not transmuted into perfect ones by nature, but remain in their own state, then neither can they be transmuted by art.
But the first is true; therefore, etc.

<margin>
Many things are done by art which are not done by nature.
</margin>

*But there is no logical connection in the premise:* namely, that what does not happen by nature cannot happen by art. For we see many things done by art which do not happen by nature alone: For instance, nature does not set dislocated limbs, only art does; nature does not distill spirit of wine <note>original: spiritum vini; referring here to concentrated alcohol or aqua vitae</note>, but art does; nature does not make cheese, bread, or glass, but art does. Likewise, nature does not create active <term>Tinctures</term> <note>In alchemy, a "Tincture" is a potent medicinal or transmutative substance capable of "staining" or transforming the inner nature of a base metal into a noble one</note> abstracted from the passive matter, although she creates them combined with matter and prepares the materials from which Tinctures are made—to say nothing now of the grafting of trees and other such aids to nature provided by art.

But as for the assumption, I deny it entirely: For in the realm of Nature, imperfect metals do not remain in their own state, but always...

## Maria’s Response to the 5th Argument of the Adversary.

**I** respond to the proposition; <note>Maria is addressing the Adversary's first premise: "To that which is perfect, nothing can be added."</note> That which is in its highest state of natural being, nothing can be added to it: If here you mean <term>Art|The human application of skill and technique to natural materials, often synonymous with Alchemy in this context</term>, you are mistaken. For Art frequently adds something to Nature so that she may be perfected toward her ultimate end, just as we see in bread-making. Nature produced the wheat so that men might eat it; but Art, not Nature, perfects it for this purpose. In the same way, <term>medlars|A fruit that is hard and acidic until it undergoes "bletting," a process of softening and ripening</term> are ripened by Art. By the grafting of trees, wild fruits grow mild and become more noble; all of these things are added to Nature by things generated by Art. 

In ancient times, as well, one kind of gold was considered far more noble than another: such as Arabic, <term>Obrize|Pure, refined gold, a term often used in biblical and classical texts</term>, or Indian gold compared to Hungarian, or Hungarian compared to Rhenish <note>Refers to gold from the Rhine region</note>. This was because Art did not yet know the method of separating silver from gold. Once this method was discovered, Art now makes all gold equal; by separating the silver, it reduces it to a single state of perfection. Therefore, if gold does not emerge with the same value, color, or grade in every place, but must be reduced to that state by the <term>separatory art|The metallurgical process of "parting" gold and silver, usually using acids or fire</term>, it is clear from this that something is added to its natural perfection. That is, by subtracting the immature parts—just as in hard pears and medlars, where the unripened parts are dispersed through the air—they are ripened by Art. Thus, all <term>cooking|original: "coctio"; in alchemy, this refers to the application of heat to mature or "ripen" a substance</term> is the dispersal of rawness and the gathering of heat. In whatever way gold is considered, perfection is always added to it by Nature or Art through cooking, the separation of the crude, and the increase of heat.

### *I refer back to the Assumption and its proofs.*

<margin>Regarding the 1st proof: that species are perfect.</margin>
**T**hat those metals are perfect not in regard to their ultimate end, but an intermediate one, which can vary. Just as from unripened grapes...

She refutes the idea that "perfect" natural species cannot be further improved through human skill and heat.</summary>

...from mature [grapes] we make vinegar; from immature walnuts we make preserves to strengthen the stomach; from immature olives we produce <term>omphacine oil|Oil pressed from unripe olives, often used in ancient medicine and perfumes</term> and preserve them for our own use. All these things and others like them have a double use: one is an intermediate use, such as we have just described, and the other is the final use, which occurs when these individual things have fully ripened.

In the same way, the younger fruits of orange trees, as well as any animals, vegetables, or minerals, are utilized before they reach their full maturity. For is it perhaps not permitted to eat the meat of calves, lambs, goats, chicks, pigeons, and the like before they have reached their perfect end <note>That is, adulthood or full growth</note>? Is it not permitted to extract that grain of silver—which lies hidden in all imperfect things like an <term>embryo|In alchemical theory, the "seed" of a perfect metal was believed to exist within base metals, waiting to "grow" into gold</term> in its mother’s womb—before those imperfect things have fully matured? The same must be said of the gold lurking within silver. Is it not permitted to eat eggs, simply because mature hens are not always present? It is clear, therefore, that each of these things are distinct species, even if they have not yet reached their highest perfection, and yet they still possess their own peculiar uses.

<margin>Regarding the second point: That which is imperfect is not the best-made thing.</margin>

Therefore, the Best [God] has ordained all things toward their best or ultimate end, but not all at once or in a single moment. These are of innumerable use to us, even if certain individual pieces of them never reach the state of silver or gold. There is, however, no reason why you should fear that if imperfect things pass into gold, there would remain only one metallic species, and that all things will eventually turn into gold. We see that there are diverse forms of metals and we recognize this from their diverse uses. Those things which have once been taken from the earth for human use will not return to the earth and the <term>mines|Latin: "mineras", referring to the ore veins where metals were thought to "grow"</term> to return to the state of silver and gold. The third cause is because immature metals—such as lead, tin, <term>quicksilver|Mercury</term>, and even silver itself—cannot hasten toward perfection in these colder regions <note>The author is likely referring to Northern Europe, particularly Germany</note> as they do in India, Arabia, and other very hot regions, because the cold accidentally hinders the process. Hence, among us, these immature metals are found more often than gold and silver (which are more "mature"), and these are mixed with many parts of cruder metals. Among the peoples of those hot regions, however, gold and silver exist in greater abundance, and immature metals are rarer. For this reason, silver and lead are greatly desired by the Indians, because there these metals are rarer; and we carry these metals to them, exporting their gold in return, as has been done since the time of Solomon <note>Refers to the biblical accounts of King Solomon’s fleet bringing gold from Ophir, often associated by early modern writers with the East or West Indies</note>. 

Because of these three causes, different forms of metals remain, just as they have always been from the beginning even to the end of the world. They were thus ordered by the Creator, even though one thing can be changed into another through nature and art. In the same way, there is no fear that all men should die at once and at the same time, leaving the world empty with no generation of men...

### Maria’s Response to the 6th Argument.

**I** deny the connection of this proposition: because even if nature performed no transmutations, no one could for 그 reason deny it to Art. For Art often transcends and surpasses nature—it does not only correct and perfect it. We omit other examples here: Does the body of a dog, crawling worms, and flying flies possess a single essence? Why then do I not say to a flying fly of this kind, **BEWARE** <note>original: "CAVE"</note> the dog, or to the dog, *Look, a fly*? Does an egg differ from a rooster only in its accidents? Does the seed of a man, or an animal, or any plant differ only in accidents from the man, animal, or plant of its own species, when the former are transmuted into the latter? 

Thus, we do not say that lead, copper, and the other base metals differ from gold and silver only in their accidents, but that each has its own <term>essential forms|the inner blueprint or "soul" of a substance that makes it a specific element</term> in the same way that an egg has its own subordinate form, upon which the form of the chick follows; and the worm has its own form, to which the form of the fly is added for its perfection. The reason for this was that in his writings—although they were obscure according to the literal letter—there breathed and manifested something divine and hidden, which is to be desired by all. 

He had a father so <margin>Democritus was wealthy by inheritance.</margin> wealthy that he was able to provide a feast for the army of **Xerxes**, that is, for seven hundred and eighty thousand men. (This is also said to have been done by that **Pythius the Bithynian**, who also gave that famous golden plane tree and noble vine to King **Darius** and moreover promised five months' pay and grain to Xerxes, on the condition that at least one of his five children might be granted to him in his old age from the military draft; but the barbarous and inhuman King ordered his chosen son to be killed, as recorded by **Pliny**, Book 33, Chapter 10). Being liberally aided by these gifts of fortune, Democritus was able to more conveniently advance the cultivation of his mind. 

When he had come into **Egypt**, it is said he stayed there for five years and fell into the most intimate familiarity with certain priests, from whom he received all the most hidden secrets. Some add that <margin>Democritus received a book from the tomb of Dardanus.</margin> in that same place he opened the tomb of a certain Priest named **DARDANUS**, and from it he unearthed a book containing a philosophical secret, which contributed much to his attaining a perfect knowledge of the art. ->OF THE GOLDEN TABLE. BOOK III.<-

Among the interpreters of Aristotle, Michael Psellus <note>An 11th-century Byzantine monk and scholar known for his work on philosophy and the occult.</note> not only mentions him, but writes that his secrets were revealed by himself. <margin>The Democritean sect.</margin> From **DEMOCRITUS**, the Democritean sect—which is also called the Abderite sect <note>named after his home city, Abdera</note>—took its origin. Indeed, as many of the later Greeks as there were after him who treated chemical matters <note>technical vocabulary for alchemy</note> drew their teachings from the books of Democritus. But because of the rarity and nobility of the material, Democritus was forced to always assign new names to things and use figurative expressions; to those who understood them only according to the literal sound of the words, they mostly seemed impossible and clearly false. For this reason, he was accused of lying and vanity by Cicero and certain others who stuck only to the surface of the words and did not look into his mind or the actual subject matter. Pico della Mirandola <note>Giovanni Francesco Pico della Mirandola, the author of *On Gold* mentioned on the previous page.</note> writes of him thus:

<margin>Democritus was obscure.</margin>
> *He lived for more than a hundred years and discovered many things that were hidden from the common crowd of scholars. He wrote his instructions somewhat obscurely, not indeed for the reason that he did not want to appear knowledgeable in chemistry, but so that those instructions would be known only to his followers and friends, and unknown to the common people. For that reason, he changed the names of things, so that he might be understood only by those who already held the matter in hand. And hence I cannot help but wonder that Hermolaus Barbarus <note>A famous Venetian scholar and translator of Aristotle (1454–1493).</note>—a man otherwise well-deserving of literature—condemned this style of writing only in the Democritean school and attributed it to either malice or arrogance. He could have remembered that from antiquity, all the way from Homer, different names were given to the same things, and that some used the language of the gods <note>original: "superis"</note> and others the language of mortals <note>original: "imis"</note>, and that the leaders of nations were not accustomed to use the same words as the common people. Nor would it have been difficult for him to recall—for I certainly do not doubt that he read this—that it was a most praised and primary rule in every sect held to be more excellent among philosophers to hide their teachings, especially among the Pythagoreans and the Heracliteans. For the former used silence and symbols, while the latter—as Plato writes—used riddles; and to those who sought an explanation of the riddles, they replied with yet other riddles. Thus he speaks on behalf of Democritus.* Two

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Democritus’s reputation, moving from his historical biography to the specific nature of his writing style. It addresses the common criticism that his work was nonsensical by explaining the tradition of alchemical metaphor.</meta>

# SYMBOLS

<margin>Two kinds of chemical writers.</margin>
It is well established that there have always been two kinds of writers in chemistry: the poetic, which is the most ancient, and the philosophical, which is a little more recent. The poetic style, woven from fables and allegories, did not change the words themselves, but rather the underlying intent or the entire meaning of the speech; this was the method used by the ancient poets, and among the Greeks, by the first seers and theologians. The philosophical style uses metaphorical sayings and terms transferred from their common meaning to a foreign one <note>This refers to the use of "deck names" or *senivivus*, where common words like "sun" or "lion" represent specific chemicals.</note>, which are often renewed or exchanged for others. This was the style used by the philosophers, especially **DEMOCRITUS**; for this reason, he is accused of excessive obscurity by those who are ignorant of the underlying cause. On this point, **CICERO** affirms somewhere concerning him that *he had never heard a man of greater authority speak greater nonsense* <note>original: "sese non audiuisse virum maiori authoritate maiores nugas dixisse"</note>. It was perhaps from these sources that it seemed so to Cicero, because **DEMOCRITUS** is reported to have taught that there are certain birds from whose mixed blood a certain kind of serpent is born; and if this serpent is eaten, the voices of birds would not be unknown to the eater <note>i.e., they would gain the magical ability to understand birdsong</note>. From this figurative way of speaking, others have deduced that **DEMOCRITUS** diluted his own drink with the blood of certain birds, adding other herbal juices, through which he perceived and understood the chirping of birds by a secret sense and communicated with them.

<margin>Those who are said to have understood the voices of birds.</margin>
However, although this same faculty is ascribed to many others—such as **THYADAMAS**, **MELAMPODUS**, and **APOLLONIUS OF TYANA**—I would scarcely believe that **DEMOCRITUS** ought to be understood literally in that passage. Rather, he denoted something else entirely by the "serpent" and the "birds," namely that which the Chemists proclaim a thousand times <note>original: "sexcenties" — literally "six hundred times," a Latin idiom for an innumerable amount</note> under the name of the serpent. Indeed, one can hardly find a chemical allegory in which mention is not made of the serpent as a primary requirement. <margin>See *Hieroglyphics*, Book 3, p. 126.</margin> Hence the twin serpent is depicted on the caduceus <note>The winged staff entwined with two serpents</note> of **MERCURY**, and associated with **AESCULAPIUS**, the labors of **JASON**, as well as those of **HERCULES**, **CADMUS**, and countless others. The birds, or "flying things," are the same as what the Chemists call <term>volatiles</term> <note>substances that easily vaporize or pass into a spirituous state</note>; that is, things that are not fixed, whether they be bodies or spirits, which through...

...by the capture and ripening of that serpent <note>In alchemical allegory, the "serpent" often represents volatile Mercury; "ripening" refers to the process of fixation where the substance is made stable under heat.</note> are understood things manageable for human capture, or things that do not flee. What collections or scattered excerpts from his writings survive may be seen in the works of Flamel <note>Nicolas Flamel (c. 1330–1418), the famous French legal scribe and legendary alchemist.</note>, and these are purely chemical. Psellus <note>Michael Psellus (11th century), a prominent Byzantine scholar and philosopher.</note> read most of his writings and declares them to be entirely about the making of gold. He is said to have learned theology and astrology from the Magi and the Chaldeans.

<margin>Democritus learned various arts.</margin>
He also met with the Gymnosophists <note>Literally "naked philosophers," a group of ancient Indian ascetics known for their wisdom and simple lifestyle.</note> in Ethiopia, from whom he obtained many secrets. Hence, he progressed so much in every kind of philosophy that he seemed to have completed the entire circle of education <note>original: "Encyclopædiam"</note> and was not undeservedly seen as a ***Five-fold Athlete*** <note>original: "Pentathlos seu Quinquertio." In ancient Greece, a Pentathlete was an expert in five different physical disciplines; here Maier uses it to describe Democritus’s mastery of five branches of knowledge.</note>. For he was skilled in ***natural, moral, and mathematical sciences, the liberal disciplines,*** and the expertise of all arts. Therefore, Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, the Roman naturalist.</note> reports that he was a shrewd man and most useful to life, but that he fell into an excessive desire to help mortals.

<margin>Democritus gives a large part of his inheritance to his fellow citizens.</margin>
Having returned home to his fatherland from his long travels, he distributed a large part of the remainder of his inheritance to his fellow citizens of Abdera. He himself retired to a suburban garden, where he diligently devoted his efforts to the contemplation of nature. 

<margin>He devoted himself to the contemplation of things.</margin>
For his concern was not only to know minerals and vegetables and to investigate their properties, but also to practice the anatomy of animals. For this reason, he arranged for animals of all kinds to be brought to him, which he dissected, examining their entrails, veins, and fibers. 

<margin>Democritus was judged insane, though he was the wisest of all.</margin>
Because of this, when the citizens of Abdera (to whom he was very dear) gathered around him and thought his behavior—being unheard of and unusual—was that of a madman, they sent for Hippocrates <note>The most famous physician of antiquity, often called the "Father of Medicine."</note>, the most celebrated doctor of that time. They begged him to come immediately to cure the "insane" Democritus with his divine remedies. Hippocrates, arriving and being met by the wailing and lamenting citizens, [found] the matter...

# SYMBOLS

...informed of how the matter stood with Democritus, he was led to him.

But when this divine philosopher understood the reason for Hippocrates’ arrival, he used such a type of speech and reason toward him that Hippocrates, struck with amazement, most severely rebuked the "sane" people of Abdera <note>The citizens of Abdera, Democritus's home, were ironically called "sane" while they believed their wisest citizen was mad.</note> because they had sent him to cure this man of delirium or madness <note>original: "mania"</note>. For he was the wisest of all wise men, and Hippocrates felt he himself ought rightly to be instructed in true wisdom by him. To Hippocrates, who inquired into the cause of why he was thus dissecting animals, Democritus replied that he was seeking the cause of human folly <note>original: "stultitiæ"</note>, and of their diverse and contrary appetites—why they were so prone to vanities and the most trifling things, yet turned away from virtue and true goods. Since these things arise from the humors <note>In ancient medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to regulate health and temperament.</note> contained in the veins or organs, or from elsewhere, he was investigating them through the anatomy of beasts, since it is a divine crime <note>original: "nefas," referring to a violation of divine law or a religious taboo.</note> to perform it on humans.

<margin>The cause of Democritus’s laughter.</margin>
Regarding this human vanity and the things that change with any stroke of fortune, whenever he heard of or thought about them, he would dissolve into laughter (just as Heraclitus <note>Heraclitus of Ephesus (c. 535 – c. 475 BCE), known as the "Weeping Philosopher," contrasted with Democritus, the "Laughing Philosopher."</note>, for the same reason, would dissolve into tears); hence he was named the Laugher <note>original: "Gelasinus," from the Greek word for laughter.</note>. Hippocrates himself recorded this whole history quite extensively in a specific book or letter, which may be examined among his works. As for what some say—that he lived in extreme poverty in a small garden near the walls of his city—this ought to be understood in context. For he did not live as he could have if he had wished, or as delicately as others; otherwise, he would not have given his goods to the people of Abdera only to remain in extreme want himself. Nor indeed is that the mark of a wise man. Without a doubt, he retained enough goods for himself—not from his inheritance, but for his studies—which he needed to complete those contemplations and animal dissections, and for the rest of his life, which he lived until his hundredth...

<margin>The age of Democritus.</margin>
He withdrew himself from the world because of its vanities and its known follies and malice; for this reason, he lived in a solitary place truly as a philosopher. He taught that the world was made of atoms—
<margin>Democritus’s opinion on atoms.</margin>
that is, that the elements of the world consist of indivisible substances <note>original: "atomis." Democritus is famous for "atomism," the theory that everything is made of tiny, indestructible particles.</note>. If this opinion had not been proclaimed as too absurd by Aristotle and the Peripatetics <note>The "Peripatetics" were the followers of Aristotle, known for walking about while debating.</note>, he might perhaps have had his own supporters and followers. Jean Fernel <note>Jean Fernel (1497–1558) was a highly influential French physician who attempted to reconcile ancient medicine with new observations.</note>, in the preface to his book *On the Hidden Causes of Things*, greatly favors him and perhaps judges that his view agrees best with the experience of many things.
<margin>Democritus established many worlds.</margin>
As for his saying that there were many worlds, and that these were corruptible, both past and future, that must be forgiven him in light of his greatness of mind and freedom of thought. We Christians know no other worlds besides this one, except for the "Microcosm" <note>original: "Microcosmum." Literally "little world," a term used to describe man as a reflection of the entire universe.</note> found in man, or the intelligible world <note>The "intelligible world" refers to a spiritual or mental realm, such as the afterlife or the realm of ideas.</note> that remains after this mortal life has passed for all.
<margin>Democritus is said to have blinded himself.</margin>
Cicero, in the fifth book of the *Tusculan Disputations*, relates that Democritus blinded himself so that he might examine the secrets of nature more subtly. Whether this cause is sufficient and worthy of a philosopher, I do not see. Did he not wish to look upon the sun, the sky, and the earth? Did he not receive every good, after God, from these things? Others offer a slightly more probable cause: namely, that he dazzled his own eyesight with a highly polished golden mirror held against the sun’s rays. Perhaps longevity itself and continuous reading first destroyed his sense of sight, as usually happens.
<margin>That longevity itself takes away the sight of some first.</margin>
Indeed, we saw an old woman in Danzig, Prussia <note>original: "Gedani in Borussia." Modern-day Gdańsk, Poland.</note> (who had lived in Livonia, though she was born in Meissen <note>A town in Saxony, Germany.</note>) who was about one hundred and thirty years old. Her eyes gradually fading, she had not seen the light for over thirty years; indeed, the sockets of her eyes could scarcely be noticed, as they were covered over with solid, flat skin. Nor had she used her feet for as many or more years, which also (wondrous to relate!) had suffered such a decrease that they were scarcely like human feet; although the woman herself possessed excellent reason and a voice as ready as if she were forty...

...he reached [one hundred and nine] years of age. But when there was doubt about such great longevity in a woman (who, being carried by two other women, sought alms from door to door), I inquired about certain historical events from a hundred years ago that I knew had been celebrated in Livonia <note>Livonia is a historical region on the eastern shores of the Baltic Sea, comprising parts of modern-day Estonia and Latvia.</note> by the Masters of the Cross <note>original: "Magistris Crueigeris." This refers to the Teutonic Knights, a crusading military order that ruled parts of the Baltic.</note>. She recounted these in order with all the details, as she had lived in those places at that time. Therefore, in such a grand old age, it does not seem necessary to "eliminate the sight" <note>The author is likely refuting the legend that Democritus intentionally blinded himself to think more clearly, arguing that old age does this naturally.</note>, since old age either makes the eyes dim or takes vision away entirely.

<margin>Democritus, sated with life, said farewell to the world through fasting.</margin>
Furthermore, this is also marvelous regarding him: when he had grown weary of this life as if he were sated by it, and had decided to waste himself away through fasting <note>original: "inedia." This refers to a voluntary death by starvation.</note> even unto death, he was moved by the pleas of his sister. She begged him not to turn the wedding joys of her daughter, who was soon to be married, into funeral dirges <note>original: "nænias." These were traditional Roman laments sung for the dead.</note>, which would disturb the whole family of relatives. He, being obliging, restored his vital spirits for a while by having the scent of fresh bread brought to his nose. He took neither food nor drink, yet remained alive until the wedding time had passed. When that time was over, the scent of the bread was removed, and he soon expired.

<margin>To what thing human life is similar.</margin>
In the life and death of this illustrious man, that most true saying is proven: that one must depart from this life as if from a stage <note>original: "scena."</note> or a supper <note>original: "cœna."</note>. For when we have been spectators of the Comedians <note>original: "Comœdorum." In the ancient world, this referred to any stage actors.</note> who present various things and characters—kings, fools, women, devils, kingdoms, wars, joys, jokes, songs, and countless other such things—at length, after a few hours, we become so exhausted and sated by those simulated masks <note>original: "laruis." The actors' masks, but also implying phantoms or illusions.</note> and fictional deeds that it is a pleasure to leave the theater. In the same way, when we have been refreshed with the best foods at a supper and are well-filled with drink, all the pleasure of the food vanishes, the appetite disappears, and finally, the desire to leave comes upon everyone. Therefore, those who reach such a decrepit age undoubtedly have it in their wishes to say farewell to the world and to renounce themselves.

<margin>Which Greeks migrated to Egypt for the sake of learning.</margin>

<margin>The parents of Orpheus.</margin>
There is some dispute regarding his parentage; some establish him as the son of Calliope and Apollo (who never existed in the natural world, except as a philosophical fiction), while others say he was the son of Oeagrus <note>In Greek mythology, Oeagrus was a Thracian king. Maier dismisses the "godly" parents as metaphors for Orpheus's skill.</note>. But because of his knowledge of singing or of diverse subjects, and the sweetness of his songs, subsequent poets bestowed these parents upon him. For this reason, they say he was provided with a lyre by Mercury—though others say it was by his father Apollo—with which he attracted wild beasts, rocks, trees, and birds, held rivers still in their courses, and even entered the underworld to lead back his wife Eurydice from there, and returned.

<margin>Orpheus wrote concerning the Golden Fleece.</margin>
He was the first to describe that most beautiful allegory concerning the **Golden Fleece**, where indeed in the *Argonautica* <note>original: "Argonautica." Maier attributes the "Orphic Argonautica" to Orpheus himself, though modern scholars view it as a much later work.</note> he says: *The rest I have narrated, which I saw when I approached Taenarum:*

> *The shadowy homes of Dis <note>Dis is another name for Pluto, the king of the underworld.</note> and the sorrowful realms,*
> *Trusting in my lyre, and compelled by the love of my wife.*

What he truly wished to be understood by the **Golden Fleece** is now known to anyone from the second book of my *Hieroglyphics* <note>Maier refers to his 1614 work, "Arcana Arcanissima," where he argues that the Golden Fleece represents the Philosopher's Stone.</note> and from what has been said above.

<margin>Orpheus instituted the rites of Bacchus at Thebes.</margin>
He was the first to institute the rites of Bacchus, or the Dionysia, and those which are called "Orphic" after him, at Thebes as a form of religious worship. All writers attest to this concerning him, including Lucian in his *Dialogue on Astrology*: *Orpheus,* he says, *son of Calliope and Oeagrus, was the first of all to introduce the rites of Bacchus into Greece, and first instituted those sacred rites called Orphic on the mountain of Boeotian Thebes.* The story that he was torn apart by women during these rites and his limbs scattered through the fields to be devoured by dogs is a fable <note>original: "fabulosum." Maier often tries to separate historical fact or "chemical" truth from what he considers poetic exaggerations or slanders.</note> invented by a certain poet hostile to him; for others assign a different cause for his death, as we shall say shortly.

<margin>The Dionysian rites are chemical.</margin>
Regarding the Dionysian rites, we have demonstrated abundantly in the fourth book of our *Hieroglyphics* that they are entirely chemical <term>chymici: alchemical</term> institutions. Pausanias, in his *Description of Boeotia*, testifies of Orpheus that he discovered many things useful for human and political life. For he was the first to reveal the initiations of the Gods and universal Theology, and he devised the expiations for wicked deeds, as well as many...

<margin>The Eleusinian Mysteries</margin>

<margin>The Olympic Games.</margin>
**THE OLYMPIC** Games—regarding what types of sports were played, the timing, the judges, the wrestlers, the victors, or for what public purpose they were once celebrated not far from Mount Olympus, near the city of Pisa in the region of Elis—is not a question we shall pursue here, since such things should be sought from other sources.

<margin>The Olympics established in memory of Alchemy.</margin>
However, we are convinced by various circumstances that these games were first conceived and organized by the philosopher-authors and those most skilled in the Chemical Art <note>Original: "Chemiæ." Maier uses "Chemistry" and "Alchemy" interchangeably to describe the sacred art of transmutation.</note> as a slight beginning to honor the Creator and the Art granted by Him. Although we have considered this at length elsewhere—namely in the fourth book of our *Hieroglyphics*—we shall nevertheless present it here succinctly. There are four opinions regarding the authors who instituted these games. We reject two of these as having no foundation: namely, that they began with the Idaean Dactyls <note>Mythical beings said to have discovered iron working and copper smelting on Mount Ida.</note> or with Iphiclus, both of which we have refuted elsewhere.

<margin>Apollo beat Mercury in the race.</margin>
But the claim that Jupiter himself established these contests after defeating the Titans—in which Apollo surpassed Mercury in the race and Mars won at boxing—seems more consistent with the truth, provided it is understood allegorically. Alternatively, it is probable that Hercules, the son of Alcmene, established this contest in honor of Olympian Jupiter after he had defeated Augias, the king of Elis (who was said to be the son of the Sun and Iphiboea), because he had not received the promised reward for cleaning the ox dung from the stables; thus, it is named "Olympic" from the spoils and plunder of the devastation of Elis.

<margin>What Jupiter’s battle with the Titans represents.</margin>
Yet, since Jupiter’s battle with the Titans—wherein Dionysus <note>The god of wine and rebirth; in this myth, he is torn apart by Titans before being restored.</note> was torn to pieces and Pallas brought his still-throbbing heart to Jupiter—is nothing other than the mutual action and commotion of materials joined together, we accept this as referring solely to the Chemical Subject <note>The "Subject" refers to the base matter or "Prima Materia" placed into the alchemical vessel.</note>. Regarding Apollo and Mercury, we and others have demonstrated to the point of nausea what kind of gods they are: namely, those specific to the Chemists. If Apollo surpasses Mercury in the race, the <term>solution of the work (solutio operis): the stage where a solid substance is dissolved or "liquefied" by the philosophical fire</term> has been rightly performed, and the Titans with Jupiter...

<margin>Pythagoras, the author of the migration of the soul.</margin>
Pythagoras was the author of metempsychosis <note>original: "τῆς μετεμψυχώσεως" — the Greek term for the transmigration of souls</note>, that is, the transfusion and migration of souls into other bodies, or at least he published this opinion through his teaching. They believe and teach that there is one supreme God who is eternal, almighty, the creator and preserver of the whole world; but they also believe that the souls of the righteous are carried to heaven after death to assist the Supreme Deity. <margin>The trick of Pythagoras.</margin>
They also say that Pythagoras himself performed a *Pythagum*—that is, a stage-trick—by means of a mirror. This is recorded by Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> under the entry "Thessalian woman" <note>original: "thettalē gynē"</note>, and by Caelius Rhodiginus <note>A Renaissance scholar known for his "Ancient Lessons"</note> in Book 9, Chapter 23.

<margin>Magical herbs named by Pythagoras.</margin>
For instance, Pythagoras names <term>Coracesia</term>, <term>Callicia</term>, <term>Menaidem</term>, <term>Corinthadem</term>, and <term>Aproxin</term>. But if someone treads upon the same juice poured out on the grass, or if they happen to be splashed by it, they die an incurable death.

Democritus lists these herbs as being suited for sorcery: <term>Chirocineta</term>, <term>Aglaophotis</term>, <term>Marmaritis</term>, <term>Achemenis</term>, <term>Hippophauas</term>, and <term>Adamantis</term>. If the roots of <term>Achemenis</term> are reduced into lozenges, and thieves and guilty men drink them with wine during the day, they will confess everything they have committed during their torments at night—things that could not be extorted through physical torture. However, I do not think that for this reason anyone should assert that he was a magician—

->### BOOK III OF THE GOLDEN TABLE<-

...can be asserted, if he used medicinal herbs in part, and partly more common or magical ones, or if he placed their names in his writings. It is established that Democritus did this, who called one thing by innumerable names because of some similarity, and likewise used the terms *Achemenis* <note>A legendary herb mentioned by Pliny, said to cause terrors</note> and *Marmaritis* <note>Another magical herb, likely a type of anemone or bear's breech</note>. 

<margin>Whether the conjurations of Pythagoras were magical.</margin>
As for the conjurations of Pythagoras which he applied to animals, let others judge whether they were magical or diabolical. I now proceed to the other question, which is proper to this treatise: 

<margin>Pythagoras cured diseases.</margin>
They write that Pythagoras was exceptionally practiced in the precepts of medicine and the cure of diseases, and that he wrote a book *On Nature*. Ammianus <note>Ammianus Marcellinus, a 4th-century Roman historian</note> reports that once, when he was at Olympia, he showed his thigh to the bystanders, and it was made of gold. 

<margin>The golden thigh of Pythagoras.</margin>
And although he prohibited the use of gold in external clothing and ornaments, he himself is nevertheless read to have walked about at times with a golden crown placed upon his head. 

<margin>A golden crown.</margin>
His *Golden Verses* <note>A collection of moral exhortations attributed to Pythagoras</note> also exist to this day, which are like Rules of life prescribed for his disciples. In these, he makes mention of the association of the soul and spirit with bodies, an event which clearly takes place in occult philosophy <note>That is, alchemy or the "Hermetic" science</note>. 

<margin>Golden Verses.</margin>
To these things they add that while Pythagoras was teaching at Croton, there was a "golden harvest." 

<margin>A golden harvest.</margin>
Furthermore, the fact that Pythagoras studied in Egypt, and among the <term>Gymnosophists</term> <note>Literally "naked wise men," a group of ancient Indian philosophers known for their asceticism and wisdom</note> and Chaldeans, serves as the strongest testimony to his "Chymic" or alchemical art, which others mentioned before him brought back from those same places. Two other facts support this: first, that he imposed such a strict silence upon his disciples for a five-year period, following the custom of the Egyptians and the <term>Brahmans</term> <note>The priestly caste of India</note>; and second, that he taught the transmigration of the soul into other bodies alongside them. 

<margin>In the projection of the tincture or of gold, there is a transmigration of the soul.</margin>
For when the "soul" of gold—that is, its form and tincture—is cast into imperfect metallic bodies, this is a certain true <term>metempsychosis</term> <note>Greek: "transmigration of souls." Maier is arguing that the alchemical transformation of lead into gold is a physical version of the soul moving between bodies</note>. There are also those among the Alchemists who affirm that Pythagoras was secretly devoted to alchemy. For this reason, the book *The Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum," one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts</note> records the opinions of the sages in the third Pythagorean synod...

<margin>The Pythagorean synod.</margin>

-># S Y M B O L S<-

...[alle]gorical <note>original: "gorica"</note> writings were collected, and that Pythagoras, the philosopher and master, was introduced; his words in that same place are as if from a presiding leader. <margin>Pythagoras declared as the master of the Chymists <note>The term "Chymic" or "Chymist" refers to what we now call alchemists</note>.</margin> *Well have you arranged, O sons of doctrine, the descriptions of these natures from which God created all things; therefore, persevere.* And thus, in that entire book, Pythagoras holds the first place, as the master of that art, and the other philosophers are his disciples. There is no doubt, therefore, that Pythagoras was most expert in this kind of doctrine and truly a master, since the ancient alchemists—who perhaps investigated his writings and life through other evidences—unanimously establish this. Indeed, some of the more recent lovers of alchemy write in this manner concerning the <margin>What the Pythagorean bean is.</margin> Pythagorean bean, among whom is Johannes Chrysippus Fanianus <note>A 16th-century legal scholar and alchemist who wrote on the transformation of metals</note>. *Aristotle himself,* he says, *in the book "On the Secret of Secrets" <note>original: "Secretis Secretorum"—a famous medieval text attributed to Aristotle, covering medicine, alchemy, and statecraft</note> (if indeed that book is by Aristotle), calls the animal, vegetable, and metallic stone an "egg," and this Pythagoras, if we believe Marcellus, calls a **BEAN**. These are his words.* 

If, therefore, Pythagoras understood the philosophical egg <note>The vessel or the substance within which the alchemical transformation occurs</note> by the "bean," he seems to have had a reason why he commanded: *do not eat the bean*. Moreover, he thought one should abstain from the Egyptian bean because he believed this to be the seat of the soul. <margin>What Colocasia is.</margin> This bean is called **Colocasia** <note>The Egyptian water lily or taro root, which had symbolic and medicinal significance in antiquity</note>; it is black in color on the outside and red on the inside, and it is seen to carry something like an **Embryo** in a womb. Mixed with mud, it is cast into the water, and thus it grows into a vegetable most useful for many things. By these points, we seem to have sufficiently demonstrated that Pythagoras stood out as an alchemist rather than a mage.

<margin>Zamolxis, the companion of Pythagoras.</margin> **Zamolxis** <note>A legendary social and religious reformer of the Getae, often described in Greek texts as a student or former slave of Pythagoras</note> was a companion to Pythagoras on his journey, who, having used the same teachers as he did, brought the same doctrines back home with him to Samothrace. From this, he obtained the name of a great and divine philosopher in his homeland. He taught the unskilled common people a new religion and laws, <margin>Laws received from the goddess Vesta—that is, the goddess placed in charge of fires.</margin> which he did not so much pretend as affirm allegorically to have received from **Vesta** (the Goddess presiding over fires), and he [instructed them] in many useful institutions of life...

# THE GOLDEN TABLE. BOOK III.

...[inst]ructs <note>original: "rudit"</note>: There are some who have recorded that his teachings were more precious than gold, and called him the most just, and the Golden one, a Demigod and a Hero.

<margin>Anaxagoras also visited Egypt.</margin>
*Anaxagoras of Clazomenae* <note>A 5th-century BCE philosopher who moved to Athens and was known for his scientific theories</note>, also visiting Egypt, brought back occult <note>hidden or secret</note> sciences from there: he most diligently investigated the more secret Physics, being the first to observe the moon, and attributing <margin>Anaxagoras was the first to teach the causes of eclipses.</margin> eclipses of the sun not to a "disease" or anger of those gods, but to the meeting of two shining bodies. He did not consider the moon and sun as gods, but the sun as a red, burning, and revolving stone—a view for which he came into danger of his life <note>Anaxagoras was prosecuted in Athens for impiety because his scientific explanation of the sun challenged traditional religious views</note>. He also established that the Nemean Lion, slain by Hercules, had fallen from the moon. <margin>What he predicted.</margin> He predicted that a stone of immense size would fall from the upper air <note>the Ether</note>, which did indeed happen <note>This refers to the famous meteorite fall at Aegospotami in 467 BCE, which Anaxagoras supposedly predicted</note>. He is frequently cited as a chymist <note>an alchemist</note>, not only among the general crowd of philosophers, but <margin>Anaxagoras the Chymist is cited.</margin> also by others, such as Petrus Bonus of Ferrara <note>A 14th-century alchemist</note> and Zacharias <note>Dionysius Zachaire, a 16th-century French alchemist</note> in these words: *"Anaxagoras testifies this to be true, saying: Our Sun is red and burning, which is joined to the white soul and the nature of the moon, by means of the spirit, although the whole is truly nothing else but philosophical quicksilver <note>mercury</note>."* Because he derived all bodily substances from similar particles <note>This refers to his theory of "homoeomery," where matter is composed of infinitely divisible parts of the same substance</note>, he was without doubt looking toward occult philosophy, not the common kind, in which he is plucked at and censured by Aristotle, as are all the others.

<margin>Heraclitus was obscure in his writings.</margin>
*Heraclitus* is said to be a philosopher famous for the obscurity which he applied to his writings: he indulged in weeping, just as Democritus <margin>What were the teachings of Heraclitus.</margin> indulged in laughter, for the same reasons: he lamented that Truth lay hidden and neglected in a deep cave. He also established a sect or school in which, among other teachings, he held fire to be the principle of all things. His books are mentioned by Virgil in the poem *Aetna*, when dealing with metals, in these verses:

<margin>Apollonius of Tyana, where he was born.</margin> **APOLLONIUS**, called *of Tyana* because he was born in the city of Tyana in Cappadocia <note>A region in central Turkey</note>. He had a father named Apollonius, a nobleman. It would be far too long to attempt to recount his life, his travels, and all his deeds here. <margin>What testifies that Apollonius was a chymist.</margin> Regarding the first point, that he was a Chymist <note>an alchemist</note>, this is demonstrated by all the travels he undertook even to the most remote places where Chemistry was most in use: namely, to the Magi and Chaldeans, the Brahmans of India, the Egyptians, and the Gymnosophists <note>literally "naked philosophers," a group of ancient Indian or Ethiopian ascetics</note> of Ethiopia.

<margin>Regarding which chemical matters Apollonius debated among the Brahmans.</margin> The matters about which he specifically debated among the Indian Brahmans were recorded above: namely, the Water of Gold, the Phoenix, the Pantaurea stone (which mimics the magnet), and other things of this kind. It is known to everyone that these are Chymical matters and the very kernel of all chemistry.

<margin>Apollonius drinks from the cup of Tantalus.</margin> Hence, he is also said to have drunk from the Cup of Tantalus <note>In this context, a symbolic vessel used by Indian sages; to drink from it signified being sworn to secrecy</note>, so that he would never reveal to anyone the secrets he had learned from those with whom he lived. Indeed, he lived intimately among the wise men of India for four full months, and was instructed by them in all wisdom and doctrine concerning the hidden secrets of Magic and nature. Leaving them as one now perfected in chemistry and the mysteries of all philosophy, he proceeded to other regions, both to learn more and to see their customs and way of life firsthand.

<margin>He averts the plague from Ephesus.</margin>
He showed his friends at Ephesus a certain old beggar, filthy and clothed in tattered rags, with a horrific face. *"Overwhelm this man with stones," he said, "and let it be done immediately,"* and the contagion of the plague was stilled: A little while later, however, when the heap of stones was removed, the body of a dog was found, which Apollonius affirmed to be a Demon, the manager of that pestilence; and having performed sacrifices, he purified the Ephesians and reconciled them to the highest Divinity.

At Tarsus, he healed a youth bitten by a rabid dog by summoning the dog itself.
<margin>Apollonius accused at Rome and cast into prison.</margin>
At Rome, he was cast into prison by Domitian <note>Roman Emperor, reigned 81–96 AD</note>, upon the accusation of Euphrates <note>A Stoic philosopher and rival of Apollonius</note>, because he had given oracles concerning the plague at Ephesus, and because he allowed himself to be regarded as a God.

## ON THE MIRACLES OF APOLLONIUS, the judgments of others:
Anastasius, Bishop of Theopolis <note>Theopolis, or "City of God," was a name given to Antioch in the 6th century.</note>: *In certain places,* he says, *to this very day the works of Apollonius of Tyana still stand and have their efficacy: some for turning away harmful four-footed beasts and birds; others for restraining disordered outbursts of the soul; others for warding off other things that might bring harm to men. <margin>Apollonius restored a girl, who was suffocated from the womb and taken for dead, to life.</margin>
As for his restoring to life a girl who had died on her wedding day, it is perhaps proclaimed by those who trumpet his praise <note>original: "ebuccinatoribus"</note> more loudly than is right, or more than the truth allows. For it is common for girls of that sort, especially those of a more advanced and marriageable age, to collapse as if dead from a "suffocation of the womb" <note>original: "praefocatione uteri." This was a common historical diagnosis for a severe fainting fit or seizure where the pulse became imperceptible, leading onlookers to believe the patient had died.</note> or strangulation, without any sensible movement of the pulse or breathing. Hence it has often been known that such "suffocated" women—their hearts being enclosed by poisonous vapors evaporating from the matrix—have been carried out for burial as if dead, and afterwards revived on their own, or rather, felt a little better. It is likely, therefore, that Apollonius restored such a maiden, who was as if dead (because she appeared entirely like a corpse), to movement and speech by applying certain good remedies which he had at hand, while prayers were nevertheless poured out to God. But if he had raised a man or a youth who was truly dead, then we would judge that he did this not by magical force, but by divine power granted to him by God, and not by his own power.

<margin>It is scarcely believable that Apollonius was devoted to diabolical magic.</margin>
Nor is it truly credible that this man was excessively devoted to **diabolical magic** <term>Diabolic Magic: Magic performed through an explicit or implicit pact with demons.</term>, as is demonstrated first by his good works and the benefits he performed, which were always for the utility of men and never for their harm. Secondly, because in his life he stood out as such an observer and advisor of virtue, abstinence, and chastity, and as an extirpator of all vices and impiety. Thirdly, because the outcome of his life or his death proves him to be nothing other than a good man, since he is not found to have been punished for illicit magic, even though he was accused; he always escaped as if innocent.
