### *Democritus’s Response to the 7th Argument.*

**I** respond that the logical connection of your premise does not align with the truth of the matter. For as to your fear that the species might be mixed, and your subsequent claim in your assumption that the species are *not* mixed, this must be considered: If by "species" you mean that all individuals of a certain species are mixed with individuals of another species, this is clearly false in your premise. If, however, by those same species you mean that one individual of one species does not mix with an individual of another to become a single thing, then your assumption is clearly false. If either interpretation is applied to both sides of the argument, then the reasoning is faulty.

This is because it is not all, but rather certain individuals that are mixed together and become one in actuality. Has nature not produced wine from the **spirit of wine** <note>original: "spiritus vini"; distilled alcohol or the "essence" of the wine</note>, watery moisture, and the **earthy substance of tartar** <note>original: "tartari terrea substantia"; the potassium bitartrate sediment found in wine casks</note>? If these can be separated by art <note>referring to chemical or alchemical distillation and separation</note>, are they not distinct substances in actuality? Nevertheless, they were one single substance composed by nature.

Indeed, consider the wine itself, or the **must** <note>original: "mustum"; freshly pressed grape juice that has not yet fermented</note> and the grapes from which it was pressed; were they not once one? The same must be thought of milk, in which there are three different substances: the **cheesy** <note>original: "caseosa"; the solids or curds</note>, the **whey-like** <note>original: "serosa"; the liquid portion</note>, and the **buttery** <note>original: "butyrosa"; the fats</note>, which are separated from one another and each treated as a distinct species. 

But you will say that these were once one thing. I know this; but after separation, they are not. Therefore, you see that before separation they are joined, and that nature has made one body out of them. The same must be said of the four **humors** <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which ancient medicine held must be in balance for health.</note> in the **mass of the blood** <note>original: "massa sanguinea"</note>, which are blended by nature and yet are distinguished by that same nature through the kidneys, the spleen, and the **gallbladder** <note>original: "vesiculam fellis"</note>. If you wish for yet another example, look to the seeds of two animals, such as those of a donkey and a mare resulting in a **mule** <note>original: "mulum"</note>, or of a leopard and a lioness... <margin>Leopards and Lionesses</margin>

...lionesses crossing into Leopards, or Hens and Pheasants passing into a mixed kind. But you will say these are females; yet even females are **species** <note>Here, "species" refers to the specific "kind" or "nature" of a being in a logical and biological sense.</note> in their own right, and when they coalesce from different kinds into a single substance, a new species is formed that was not originally created by nature. The same is seen in the world of plants, where you see a graft from one tree coalesce with the trunk of another species and become a single thing. And so you have enough examples. 

Nevertheless, all these things have not yet sufficiently explained how lead passes into gold. For lead and gold—those two—ought not to come together into a single species, nor does lead, properly speaking, *become* gold. By this I mean that this lead, which I hold in my left hand, will not be converted into that specific gold which I hold in my right hand—as those **stage-performers** <note>original: "gesticulatores"; Maier is likely referring to "puffers" or fraudulent alchemists who use sleight of hand to trick audiences into believing they have turned a specific coin into gold.</note> promise, claiming that one thing existing in actuality must be transubstantiated into another thing that also previously existed in actuality. 

If you frequently bring up these "species" of yours for this reason, asserting that it is impossible for one species (the lead in the left hand) to be changed into another species (the gold in the right hand), then you should either call the Chemists insane for thinking so, or indeed consider yourself the most inept and foolish of men for interpreting it that way. 

The Chemists never thought such a thing. But so that you may briefly understand their true meaning, take it thus: They say that in this lead there is a dual substance. One part is **quicksilver** <note>original: "argenti vivi"; literally "living silver," the common name for mercury.</note>, which makes up the greater portion; the other is **combustible sulfur** <note>original: "sulfuris combustibilis"; in alchemical theory, sulfur was the principle of flammability and impurity that "corrupted" metals.</note>, which is present in a small amount. Now, if one possesses a certain substance of quicksilver that is red, most pure, stable in every fire, and capable of being mixed—which is called and truly is the **tincture** <margin>What the Tincture is.</margin>—and if this is mixed with the aforementioned lead, then, through the action of fire, it will separate that combustible sulfurous substance from the lead and substitute itself in its place. <margin>How gold is made.</margin> Thus, from these two mercurial substances, one single thing is made...

### *The Response of Democritus to the 8th Argument.*

**T**he proposition is utterly false, since through art and nature one thing is made daily from two beings <note>original: "entibus," or entities.</note>, as from yeast and the dough to be leavened, from rennet and milk, and from the spirit of wine and water...

<meta>catchword: to shut <note>original: "cludere," likely from "intercludere" (to shut off or block), continuing into the next page.</note></meta>

...its substance, is formed from two animal seeds, from the white and the yolk. What shall I say of the parts of a house—the walls, the roof, and the foundation? Does not one single house in number consist of these entities through themselves, even though each part might seem to be something on its own? I need not bring up other artificial works.

Indeed, regarding the assumption, we say that there is no danger in the nature of things if, from two entities existing through themselves, one single thing is made in the transmutation of metals <term>transmutation: the alchemical process of changing one metal into another, specifically base metals into gold</term>. Imagine that there is "cooked" quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuum coctum," referring to mercury that has been processed or stabilized by heat</note>, a tincture, which, if it is projected into the quicksilver of lead—either separated from the lead or into the lead itself to separate the quicksilver from it—then it is the same as if the seed of the male is mixed with the female, or rennet <note>original: "coagulum," the substance used to curdle milk into cheese</note> with milk. Is it not permitted for one thing to be made from these two entities if it is possible, or if it is permitted, is it not possible? There is no difficulty which prohibits this; nor will your incredulity or ignorance stand in the way of it happening.

### 9. The Argument of Pyrgopolynices against Chemistry.

<margin>9. The argument of those who deny:</margin>

*If the change of a caterpillar into a silkworm and of a silkworm into a butterfly is not a change of species into species, as the Chemists <note>In this context, "Chemists" (Chymici) refers specifically to Alchemists.</note> pretend, but only a change of accidents <term>accidents: in Aristotelian philosophy, these are non-essential qualities (like color or shape) that can change without changing the underlying "essence" of the thing</term>, then they can by no reasoning prove the change of one metal into another, and consequently the art is false. But the first premise is true: Therefore, the second is also true.*

### Response of Democritus to the 9th Argument.

**N**ow I understand that the Adversary <note>Pyrgopolynices, a name borrowed from Roman comedy meaning "Tower-town-taker," representing the boastful opponent of alchemy.</note> is without any mercy, who thus shuts off <note>original: "intercludere"</note> all the subterfuges of the Chemists...

<summary>Democritus argues that distinct components (like an egg's yolk and white) can form a single substance, justifying alchemical transmutation. The opponent Pyrgopolynices counters by arguing that insect metamorphosis is merely a change in appearance, not a change in species, and therefore metals cannot change species either.</summary>

The caterpillar is a crawling thing, the butterfly a flying thing; they differ therefore among themselves as creatures living in the air and upon the earth. Lead and the tincture do not differ from gold if the "combustible sulfur" <note>In alchemy, sulfur was thought to be the principle of "combustibility" and impurity in metals; removing it was key to purification.</note> is separated from the lead; then those two are **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum viuum" (living silver), the common name for mercury.</note> and nothing else. Gold is quicksilver and nothing else. Indeed, these two differ from gold by nothing except for the mixing and a little cooking. What then does the chemist have to do with the caterpillar and the butterfly, except that such little animals are suited to the Adversary's pleasure and grasp...

# THE REASONS OF DEMOCRITUS
## IN FAVOR OF CHEMISTRY.

### 7. *The ARGUMENT of Democritus for Chemistry.*

<margin>7. Affirmative argument</margin>
**IF** liquid honey and honey cooked to hardness, pitch, resin, gum, milk, and other such things do not differ in species <note>original: "specie"; meaning their fundamental nature or category.</note> from themselves, and when joined they make something numerically one and indivisible; Then neither does the **philosophical tincture** <note>The transforming agent, often the Philosopher's Stone.</note>, which is **cooked quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum," or mercury. Alchemists believed that mercury "ripened" or "cooked" in the earth eventually became gold.</note>, differ from other raw quicksilver existing in metals, but is one thing in species when joined with it.

->But the first is true, therefore also the second.<-

*The cause of the connection in this proposition is clear: because cooked honey and raw honey do not differ in species: And cooked quicksilver and raw quicksilver do not differ in species: Whence if cooked quicksilver is joined to raw, there results from it a middle substance, which is **gold**.*

<summary>The author mocks critics who use Aristotelian logic to deny alchemy while ignoring other natural wonders like the 'tree-born' geese of the Orkneys. He then presents a logical argument attributed to Democritus, asserting that 'cooked' (processed) mercury and 'raw' mercury are the same species, and their union produces gold.</summary>

*This assumption follows from what has already been stated and is evident by its own nature; it requires no further proof. Although this argument might not be of the kind that forces a necessary conclusion, it is nonetheless among those most closely resembling the truth and nearest to it. From this, the possibility of the philosophical tincture <note>The "tincture" refers to the Elixir or Philosopher's Stone, believed to have the power to "stain" or transform base metals into gold.</note> and the absurdity of the petty arguments directed against it are clearly seen.*

<margin>8. Affirmative reasoning.</margin>
### 8. Reasoning for the truth of Alchemy.

**If from two beings that are by their nature homogeneous <note>original: "homogeneis"; meaning of the same kind or substance.</note> and capable of being mixed, of which one differs from the other only in its maturation <note>Alchemists believed that all metals were essentially the same substance, but "base" metals like lead were "unripe," while gold was "perfectly ripe."</note>, a single thing can be made by itself; then from the tincture and lead, one thing can also be made, which is gold.**

**But the first part is true. Therefore, the second is as well.**

*The connection of this proposition is evident from what follows, as is the premise itself. This is because those two beings which are homogeneous and miscible with each other, and differ from one another only in their maturation, are effectively one in nature, even if they are separated in their capacity to act or be acted upon—as is the case with the tincture and lead. And although lead, before its union with the tincture, differs from it by its "combustible sulfur" <note>In alchemical theory, "combustible sulfur" was an impurity that made metals corruptible and dark; the alchemical process aimed to remove this.</note> and its blackness, nevertheless these heterogeneous parts are separated after the union, and the "agent" [the tincture] is joined to the "patient" [the lead] inseparably into a single, uniform substance.*

<margin>9. Affirmative reasoning.</margin>
### 9. Reasoning of Democritus for Alchemy.

**If there are many things in the nature of things which possess a singular origin and hidden properties, of which—**

### But the first part is true. Therefore, the second follows.

The connection of this proposition depends on this: that any person may presuppose that he could know how the artificial generation of gold would occur, if it were to exist; but since he does not know that it is [not possible], he wishes to impress his denial upon others. But let that man notice for himself that there are innumerable things even before our eyes every day, for which no one has yet been able to give a true explanation; or if he has conceived of it in some way, yet in truth, he cannot express what it is. Examples include how vision occurs, and how the visual species <note>original: "species visiva"; in early modern science, this referred to the "likeness" or image of an object that was thought to travel through the air to the eye.</note> is extended through the illuminated air and carried to the eye; how hearing and understanding happen; or the source of the power of the magnet <note>original: "vis magnetis"</note> turning itself toward the pole and attracting iron, and infinite things similar to these. Indeed, there are so many wonders of nature <term>miracula naturae</term> <note>These are natural phenomena that appear miraculous because their underlying "efficient causes" are hidden from human observation.</note> that they draw even the wisest person into stupor and wonder rather than toward an explanation of each one; they shut out and elude even the most daring. Therefore, it is no wonder if the same thing happens regarding the generation of gold <note>original: "generatio auri"</note>, so that he who begins to probe with his own intellect <note>original: "intellectus"</note> how it might or might not be, may easily find himself mistaken, rather than those who testify that they have understood, performed, seen, and touched it, by their intellect, art, eyes, and hands.

# THE GOLDEN TABLE. BOOK IV.

...he assists and acknowledges, and also understands how that which seems impossible to the whole world is produced by the art. Therefore <term>Morienus</term><note>A legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist, said to have been the teacher of the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> truly said, *that this art leads man back to the knowledge of future blessings, and draws him away from the vanities of the world;* to which the pious and truly God-devoted life of such a great philosopher corresponds in all things.

<margin>The nature of Morienus's doctrine.</margin>
His doctrine in <term>Chymical</term><note>The early modern term "Chymia" encompassed both what we now call chemistry and alchemy, viewed as a single sacred science.</note> matters is steadfast and serious, not filled with poetic fictions or metaphors and unknown terms, but of the kind that suits the Chymical art—neither to be revealed to everyone, nor entirely hidden.

<margin>The virtues and character of Morienus.</margin>
How great the virtues were that shone forth in his conversation with King <term>Calid</term><note>Khalid ibn Yazid (d. c. 704), a historical prince often credited in alchemical lore as the first Muslim to study the art.</note>, the author of that book, <term>Galip</term><note>Often identified as the narrator or scribe who recorded the dialogues between Morienus and Khalid.</note>, testifies when he says: *The King was therefore greatly pleased by this man’s prudence, his humility, his patience, his modesty, and his grace: for he was not wordy of tongue or puffed up in mind: but he was humble, prudent, and benevolent, as it was fitting for such a man to be:*

<margin>Why Morienus was a hermit.</margin>
Indeed, when asked by the King why he lived in the mountains and solitudes rather than in the assemblies of those who pray to God in churches, he replied, *The good which I now have and expect in the future is from God and placed in His hand; let Him do what He wills: nor do I doubt that a greater rest might be found for me among assemblies and gatherings than in solitudes and mountains where there is labor, but no one reaps unless he sows, and what he sows, this he shall also reap:* <note>A reference to Galatians 6:7.</note> *I hope, therefore, that the goodness of the Divinity will not abandon me in the life of this world: for the entrance to rest is too narrow, nor can anyone enter into it except through the affliction of the soul.*

<margin>The constancy and seriousness of Morienus.</margin>
Regarding his constancy and seriousness, these words testify, which follow shortly after: *O King, may almighty God turn you toward better things: for I am not one at whom you ought to marvel much. I am one of the sons of Adam: we all indeed proceeded from one, and shall return again to one, though by a different path: the long change of times truly confounds and changes a man placed within time: nor have I yet been changed so much that many others who were before me [were] not more [changed]*

<margin>Colors of the Stone.</margin>
Concerning the colors of the Stone, by the testimony of the philosopher Datin: "Our *Lato* <term>Lato</term><note>Latin: lato. The Romans singularly applied themselves to this one thing: that they might extend their empire.

The Romans were dedicated to Mars from boyhood.

The Romans did not even think about the art of Chemistry.

The birth of the Phoenix is an allegory, not history.

Indeed, it appears from Tacitus <note>Cornelius Tacitus (c. 56–120 AD), a Roman historian who mentioned the Phoenix in his *Annals*</note> that very few among the Romans, though they were prudent, entertained deeper thoughts about this very thing. <margin>Gods of the greater nations.</margin>

<margin>Vesta and Vulcan, Egyptian gods. The rites and life of the Vestal Virgins.</margin>
Thus ***Vesta***, as well as ***Vulcan***, was among the Egyptian Gods. The Virgins dedicated to her, called the Vestals, who were the guardians of the undying fire, had a most ancient origin. It was necessary for them to apply the most diligent care so that the sacred fire, which was kept in the inner sanctuaries, should not be extinguished. For thirty years they remained pure from marriage: in the first ten years they were instructed in those things which pertained to religion; in the second decade they performed the priesthood; in the third they taught the younger ones. Afterwards, if they wished to marry, it was permitted to them; but this happened to few, and usually with great misfortune for the marriage.

<margin>The size of the Roman army.</margin>
...defending the public interest: These are said to have had 80,000 infantry and 10,000 cavalry. The former led out forces no smaller, by whom Cassius and Brutus were finally defeated <note>Referring to the Battle of Philippi in 42 BC, where the forces of Octavian and Mark Antony defeated the assassins of Julius Caesar</note>. Later, after a dispute arose between Antony and Octavius, Antony had 100,000 cavalry and 500 ships; Octavius, however, had 80,000 infantry, the same number of cavalry, and 1,000 ships. This so admirable multitude of men could not have been gathered without infinite expense, nor could wages <note>original: "stipendia"</note> be paid to the soldiers and other matters pertaining to military service be provided for. In this, besides power, it is apparent how great the wealth of the Roman Empire was at that time, as it collected tribute from the greater part of the entire world.

<margin>Revenue of the Romans from Africa.</margin>
From Africa alone, seventy-five thousand small measures of grain were collected by them every day, which amounts to nearly seven thousand <term>crowns</term> <note>original: "coronatorum"; a gold coin used as a standard of high value in the author's era</note> each day.

<margin>Revenue from Egypt.</margin>
Thus Africa paid 1,400,000 crowns annually. Alexandria in Egypt, which was very fertile in grain, gave half of this sum. At that time, according to the testimony of Strabo <note>A famous Greek geographer and historian who lived during the transition of the Roman Republic into the Empire</note>, Egypt contained seventy-five million people <note>This figure from the original text is a significant historical exaggeration; modern scholars estimate the population of Roman Egypt was closer to 5–8 million</note>. If each of these paid five <term>shillings</term> <note>original: "solidos"; a late Roman gold coin, used here as a general unit of account</note> in tribute annually, the sum prescribed above would be fulfilled. From this, it can be gathered how much money could be collected from the remaining provinces, since Egypt alone paid six million. And Ptolemy Auletes <note>ruler of Egypt and father of the famous Cleopatra VII</note>, the father of Cleopatra, exacted this same sum from his people shortly before. Certain curious and learned men, based on specific calculations of the revenues of the kingdoms and princes of the Christian world, as well as collections from the provinces subject to the Turk <note>Referring to the Ottoman Empire, the contemporary rival to Christian Europe when this was written</note>, conclude in this manner:

<margin>The Romans: how they scraped money together.</margin>
...were. Concerning the ancient Romans, others state most certainly that they scraped together a sum far larger than this from the subject peoples. Whenever an opportunity presented itself—whether through violence, exactions, gifts, or wills—they extorted whatever they could, so that they might be enriched whether by right or by wrong; this happened especially after the Roman princes began to dissolve into luxury and lust.

<margin>Revenue of the Romans at different times.</margin>
In the year 690 of the city <note>64 BC</note>, the revenue of the Roman Empire, according to the testimony of Plutarch in the *Life of Pompey*, did not exceed five million gold pieces. But after the Gauls were subdued under Julius Caesar, and Egypt and Syria were reduced to provinces, it possessed fifteen million in annual revenue under Augustus. Appian writes in Book 2 of the *Civil Wars* that Caesar, after the Pompeians were defeated, carried sixty-five thousand <term>talents</term> <note>A talent was a large unit of weight and value; in the Roman context, Caesar's haul was astronomical</note> in his triumphs, which are valued at thirty-nine million gold pieces. Furthermore, there were two thousand eight hundred gold crowns, which weighed three thousand marks of gold, that is, two million gold pieces. From these forty-one millions, he bestowed four hundred coins or smaller <term>sesterces</term> <note>A basic Roman denomination of currency</note> upon each citizen, which amounts to 10 crowns, so that this distribution <note>original: "congiarium"; a gift of money or food from a leader to the people</note> approached two million gold pieces.

<margin>The vast number of Roman citizens.</margin>
<margin>The wonderful liberality of Julius Caesar.</margin>
For Appian writes that after the civil wars, there were two hundred and thirty thousand citizens in Rome. On the banquets which Caesar celebrated in his triumphs, he spent one million. He moreover gave to the veteran soldiers five hundred crowns each, which amounted to ten million, since at that time more than twenty thousand veterans were counted. Likewise, to the leaders, tribunes, and centurions who had followed his side, he paid out two million, as Suetonius relates in his *Life*, chapter 38. The expenses of the five triumphs, and what was spent on games, tragedies, mimes, athletes, hunts of lions and bears, as well as the gifts he bestowed upon private friends—all of these were estimated at five million gold pieces.

<margin>The liberality of Augustus Caesar.</margin>
Augustus Caesar, who enlarged Rome and adorned it with public and private buildings, was therefore accustomed to say: "I found it a city of brick, and I leave it a city of marble" <note>original: "Lateritiam accepi, Marmoream relinquo"</note>. He offered to the temple of Jupiter Capitolinus...

<margin>
The difference between Mars and Art.
</margin>
The former requires enmity, dissensions, hatreds, lawsuits, and battles; the latter requires friendship, concord, rest, and peace, by which each is nourished.

<margin>
Whether those devoted to Mercury are found among the Martial ones.
</margin>
But let us see whether among these martial men, some were also devoted to <term>Mercury</term> <note>The god of commerce and communication, but in alchemical literature, the patron of the "Hermetic" or chemical art.</note>, though most secretly, in ancient times, or rather recognized after their death; and whether certain Latin poets caught some scent of Egyptian philosophy from obscure rumor:

<margin>
Two Chemical monuments found in Italy.
</margin>
Truly, as far as could be observed, they speak of two famous monuments found in Italy, which can sufficiently attest that among those ancient pagans some were skilled in the <term>chemical art</term> <note>original: "artis Chymicæ"; the term used for alchemy during the Renaissance.</note>, as appears from their cenotaphs and tombs: The first is at *Bologna*, the other was found in the territory of *Padua*:

<margin>
The Epitaph of Bologna.
</margin>

->**AELIA, LAELIA, CRISPIS, NEITHER MAN, NOR WOMAN, NOR ANDROGYNE, NOR GIRL, NOR YOUTH, NOR OLD WOMAN, NOR HARLOT, NOR CHASTE, BUT ALL: TAKEN AWAY NEITHER BY HUNGER, NOR BY SWORD, NOR BY POISON, BUT BY ALL:**<-

<margin>Those who have commented on the Bolognese Epitaph.</margin>
Many of those occupied with Chemistry have perceived the inner meaning of this <term>Cenotaph</term> <note>A monument or empty tomb built in honor of a person whose remains are elsewhere or lost.</note>, and for that reason, they have published their commentaries upon it; such as *Johannes Turrius of Bruges*, *Richard White* <note>original: "Richardus Vitus," a British scholar who wrote a famous 16th-century commentary on this riddle.</note> and *Nicolas Barnaud*. Without detracting anything from the opinions of these learned men, we shall likewise examine the same matter succinctly. No one—unless they have never read, heard, or believed anything regarding the <term>Philosophical Tincture</term> <note>original: "Tinctura philosophica"; another name for the Philosophers' Stone, particularly in its power to "tinge" or transform metals.</note>, or is utterly unrefined and unskilled in chemical matters—could deny at first sight <margin>Why the Bolognese Epitaph was placed.</margin> that this monument was established by an ancient artist for the honor of God and the commendation of the chemical art. And as indeed others also conjecture, it may have something of the <term>perfect work</term> <note>The completed Philosophers' Stone.</note> enclosed and hidden away in the secret places of that marble. This would perhaps be of such a small quantity (namely a <term>drachm</term> or less, for why would he have stored a great weight there?) that for this reason, the Epitaph should not be cast down, nor the place <margin>Why it should not be torn down.</margin> overturned and searched even to its foundation, as some people urge; it would not be worth the effort. ...reduced to a very fine powder: If you were to call these two persons shining forth from one body a "man," you would be mistaken; for while he is a man or a male, he is understood as the active principle with respect to a female. Here, however, that distinction is lacking, although it was present during the preparation of the <term>Tincture</term> <note>The "Philosophical Tincture" is the refined substance capable of transforming base metals into gold or healing the body.</note>. Therefore, it is not 

<margin>Not a woman: Nor androgynous.</margin>
a man, though it once was. Similarly, it is not a *woman*, though it once was; because here there is no longer any power of being acted upon by a man. Nor is it *Androgynous*; it was so indeed in the beginning, with respect to the man and woman joined together, but now it is so no longer.

<margin>Nor a girl.</margin>
Nor is it a *Girl*, for she is untouched; yet in the philosophical work, a virgin gave birth and suckled the infant with her own milk; for which reason she is called a mother and not a girl, even though she remained a virgin. These words, however, are allegorical and have nothing to do with the Virgin Birth by which the Savior of the world was brought forth, except in a figurative sense.

<margin>Nor a youth.</margin>
Nor is it a *Youth* or an adolescent, because living in marriage, it has approached the peak or manly age through its own perfection.

<margin>Nor an old woman.</margin>
Nor is it an *Old Woman*, because it is not decrepit or weak in its powers.

<margin>Nor a harlot.</margin>
Nor is it a *harlot*, because it has not prostituted itself to any other for the sake of money or gain, as the common street-walkers and harlots are accustomed to do.

<margin>Nor chaste.</margin>
Nor is it *Chaste*: for if it had desired eternal chastity, like the <term>Vestal Virgins</term> <note>Priestesses of Vesta in ancient Rome who took a thirty-year vow of chastity.</note>, it would not have been found formerly coupled with a man.

<margin>But all things.</margin>
BUT IT IS ALL THINGS; that is, according to certain respects. It is a *man*, because it performed the action of a man; it is a *woman*, because it performed that of a woman. It is *Androgynous*, because these two were joined together like a single <term>Hermaphrodite</term> <note>In alchemy, the Hermaphrodite (or Rebis) represents the perfect union of opposites, such as sulfur and mercury or male and female principles.</note> made from two. It is a *girl*, because it has not reached any age but that of youth. It is a *Youth*, because it has not yet lost the fruits of youthful age or adolescence—which are the abundance and goodness of the blood, and thus the best temperament of the body. It is an *old woman*, because it now endures through every age and has survived for a very long time. It is a *harlot*, because <term>Beia</term> <note>Beia and Chabritio are allegorical figures representing the feminine/mercurial and masculine/sulfuric principles whose "incestuous" union leads to the birth of the Stone.</note> is lustful, prostituting herself to <term>Chabritio</term> even before the true marriage, which occurs in the <term>whiteness</term> <note>original: "albedo." The second major stage of the alchemical process, representing purification.</note>. Therefore, during the entire time of the <term>blackness</term> <note>original: "nigredo." The first stage of alchemy, characterized by rot and the breakdown of substances.</note> and before it, she can be called a harlot. It is *chaste*, because through the subsequent marriage, she will not be judged as unchaste: for marriage is like a cloak...

171

Whatever this defect is, it covers and hides it. If anyone wished to explain these words by a name halfway between two opposites, provided it agreed with the reality of the matter, he could do so in the manner of that 

<margin>The Platonic Enigma.</margin>
**Platonic Enigma**, which goes: *A man, and not a man, seeing, and not seeing, in a tree, and not in a tree, sitting, and not sitting, a bird, and not a bird, struck it, and did not strike it, with a stone, and not a stone.* <note>Maier refers to a famous ancient riddle often attributed to Plato or Clearchus. The solution is: A eunuch (man/not man) who is one-eyed (seeing/not seeing) sees a bat (bird/not bird) perched on a fennel stalk (tree/not tree) and hits it (struck/not struck) with a pumice stone (stone/not stone).</note> It is as if one said: a eunuch, one-eyed and half-blind, saw a bat leaning on a shrub, and lightly grazed it with a pumice stone. So here one might say: if it is neither man, nor woman, nor <term>Androgynous</term> <note>In alchemy, the 'Androgyne' or 'Rebis' represents the union of male and female principles (Sulfur and Mercury).</note>, it is therefore a **Hermaphrodite** leaning toward the masculine sex. If you say it is neither girl, nor youth, nor old woman, but of middle age, these words are preserved; yet their contradictions—that it is both girl, youth, and old woman—are scarcely satisfied, unless one wishes to take a single middle state as an affirmative for both extremes. Neither a harlot nor a modest woman, yet both a harlot and a modest woman: that is, it is contained within that middle ground which lies between chastity and immodesty.

<margin>An interpretation too harsh.</margin>
This interpretation is too harsh, neither suited to the matter nor clear; therefore, we leave it behind for these others: *Taken away neither by hunger, nor by the sword, nor by poison, but by all of them.* **Hunger** is the appetite for more solid nourishment, which is not truly granted to the matter unless it wishes to prey upon its own entrails. Hence it dies by hunger, and by the **sword**, because it is diminished and its solid parts are softened and thinned. And by **poison**, that is, the poison of the dragon <term>Typhon</term> or <term>Python</term> <note>Maier equates these monsters with the 'chemical poison' or the corrosive stage of putrefaction where the substance 'dies' and turns black.</note>, for they are the same thing. Python was slain by Apollo, and the Olympian monster is called Typhon. By the putrid poison of this dragon, the philosophical matter also succumbed—that is, it was putrefied even unto death. Therefore, it was taken away by three kinds of death at once, and not by one alone. In the same way, the following words must be understood: that it lies neither 

<margin>The philosophical matter is found everywhere, that is, in all the elements.</margin>
in **heaven** (that is, in the visible air extending to the heaven), nor in the **waters** (the element of water), nor in the **lands** (the element of earth), individually by themselves, but in all of them at once—or rather, it lies everywhere. For everything that exists in the sublunary realm <note>The 'sublunary' realm refers to the Earth and its atmosphere, everything below the Moon, composed of the four changing elements.</note> is prohibited from being in any one of these three visible elements; if it is in none of them, it is nowhere; if it is in all of them, it is everywhere. **Fire** is not included because it is not visible—namely, that fire which resides above the region of the air.

<margin>The container turning the contained into itself.</margin>

<margin>Lot's wife was her own tomb:</margin>
Just as the wife of **Lot** <note>In the Book of Genesis, Lot’s wife looked back at Sodom and was turned into a pillar of salt. Alchemists viewed this as a metaphor for "fixation," where a volatile substance becomes a solid, permanent stone.</note> is said to have been her own tomb without a corpse and a corpse without a tomb: a tomb, because she was made of stone; a corpse, because, retaining the form of a human, she was not buried. This is a corpse having no tomb outside it; because the container or tomb passed into the content or corpse, and those two were made one. But the corpse is the same as its own tomb: which words declare the whole matter sufficiently. For the volatile matter, which was the container and tomb, has been made one thing without division with the fixed matter, which was the content and corpse, like water mixed with water, because they were of one genus and origin; let these things suffice for this place.

That the vials are chemical works, not water.

It is easy to conclude that those two vials were chemical works and effects. For in them, the elements, digested with heavy labor, were enclosed—not in water, which easily evaporates into the air and is consumed, even if it had been distilled and redistilled for ten years to induce its fixation <note>The alchemical process of making a volatile substance stable under heat so it does not evaporate.</note> or permanence, unless it be reduced into a golden and thus perennial liquor. Whether this can be done is demonstrated by the nature of water and the suitability of the means by which it must be achieved.

<margin>
Mercury can be reduced into gold; other water, by no means.
</margin>
If it be Mercurial <note>original: "Mercurialis"; referring to the alchemical principle of Mercury, the "First Matter" of all metals.</note>, it can be promoted to that dignity; otherwise, not at all. Therefore, let those who speak of incorruptible water and divine liquor besides fixed Mercury <note>original: "Mercurialem fixam"; mercury that has been chemically "fixed" to remain liquid and stable even when heated.</note> see to it themselves; to me, this does not seem likely. 

<margin>
Spirit of wine is fiery under the form of water.
</margin>
Similarly, we must think of the flame of the fire which is thought to be nourished by this water: Fire can be nourished by no water unless it be spirit of wine <note>original: "spiritus vini"; high-proof distilled alcohol, which looks like water but is highly flammable.</note>, but always by oily, fatty, and sulfurous substances. Hence, all combustible things <note>original: "cremabilia"</note> give as much flame in proportion to the amount of oily substance they possess, and vice versa. 

<margin>
Fire needs air and earth, otherwise it is extinguished.
</margin>
Furthermore, it is the nature of common fire that it needs both earth and air if it is to remain, and that water, as its greatest enemy, should not approach it. Earthy substance is to it like a support and a hearth, in which the most rarefied and fleeting element might be sustained as if in a firmer and solid element. In place of this are kindling, wicks <note>original: "Elychnia"</note>, tinder, linen rags, and other corporeal yet porous oily matter, which, as stated, acts like food. But the surrounding air acts like ventilation and cooling, without which no fire—whether flaming or otherwise—persists, even if it has enough oil and kindling; instead, it is soon extinguished, 

<margin>
Fire is extinguished in deep underground tunnels.
</margin>
as is evident in caves and deep underground tunnels <note>original: "cuniculis"</note> where the free air cannot penetrate unless passages are made for this purpose; and from the experience of other things, it will not be necessary to demonstrate here how this flame, firmly enclosed in vessels, and these within others...

# SYMBOLS

...placed in another urn, and this in turn in another, it will not be extinguished. And why is it extinguished when air enters? Why is it nourished by its opposite element, water? Certainly, all these things regarding a flame of fire and <margin>Doubts concerning the perpetual flame of the Paduan monument.</margin> incorruptible water cause me to doubt their reliability. Furthermore, if two vials of this sort remain underground for several hundred years, applied to one another, even if the place is tightly closed, nevertheless subterranean vapors penetrate through <margin>Water collected by itself in a vial.</margin> all cracks and work their way into the vials. By the coldness of these vials, the condensed vapors are reduced into clear water; thus, it is always possible for some very clear water to be found in vessels of this kind. The same must be said of sulfurous breaths <note>Vapors or exhalations rising from the earth.</note> which are said to <margin>A sulfurous flame appearing where treasures are hidden.</margin> accumulate in those places where treasures of gold and silver are hidden; it is very well known from experience that a sulfurous flame is seen there around the surface of the earth. What if such a sulfurous flame was also seen by those peasants who opened the monument? 

But the verses of *Olibius* must be considered. In the first hexameter <note>A line of verse consisting of six metrical feet.</note>, he openly testifies that he has vowed this gift to *Pluto* <note>The Roman god of the underworld, whom alchemists often associated with the hidden riches of the earth.</note>. In the second, or pentameter, he shows that no human body was hidden in this urn, as is usual in other urns, but that such a work, sacred to *Pluto*, is unknown to the common people. The third verse declares what kind of work it is and who its author is: for the "digestion of the elements" was performed there by Maximus *Olibius*, which is entirely Chemical, and of no other intention than to perfect the Tincture <note>The "Philosopher's Stone" or the agent of transmutation.</note>. Then he says, "let plenty, the guardian, be present with a fruitful horn," which words mean nothing else than that riches and wealth are always present to take care that the value of such a great liquid <note>original: "laticis"</note> does not perish. Philosophers very commonly call the Tincture itself, and the substances required for it, "waters," "waves," "lymphs," or "liquids"—namely, mercurial ones. By "liquid," therefore, he understood the perennial water that was very well known to *Hermes* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical father of alchemy.</note> and *Democritus* <note>An ancient philosopher to whom many early alchemical texts were attributed.</note>, who understood it to refer to the Tincture. For those who [use] the name of water, of the serpent, of vi... <note>original: "serpentis, vi-"; the text cuts off, likely continuing "vini" (of wine) or "vitae" (of life) on the next page.</note>

<margin>The Paduan monument: it uses the style of the age of Plautus.</margin>
This writing and monument seem ancient enough based on the patterns of speech, since the author uses words in the style of Plautus <note>Titus Maccius Plautus (c. 254–184 BC), a Roman playwright known for his archaic Latin.</note>, such as *you wish*, *your*, *greatest*, and *to Pluto* <note>original: "voltis, vostris, vostro, Maxumo, Plotoni." Others follow among the more ancient Romans who lived then, who tasted at least a little of the philosophical secret <note>The "philosopher's stone" or the secret of transmutation.</note>, even if they were perhaps not admitted to the banquet itself.

<margin>Apuleius, the Platonic Philosopher.</margin>
Among these, the most distinguished is **Apuleius of Madaura, the Platonic Philosopher**. Although he was not Roman by birth, but an African, he lived in Rome and wrote in a most delicate Roman style his *Golden Ass*, or the truly golden book of *Metamorphoses*. In this work, he sprinkled various most pleasant allegories, besides the fact that the entire book is written in figures and metaphors.

<margin>Psyche married to the Dragon.</margin>

In the silent night, or at midnight, when her husband was held oppressed by deep sleep (whom she believed to be a horrible dragon with nothing human about him), she approached him with a lamp lit and a razor in her hand. <margin>What the descent to the underworld signifies among the poets.</margin>
The ancient poets, as we have shown elsewhere, understood nothing else by the "descent to the underworld"—the places dedicated to <term>Pluto and Proserpina</term> <note>The Roman King and Queen of the Underworld; Pluto was also associated with the mineral wealth of the earth.</note>—than the exploration of minerals hidden in their mines. This is evident in the stories of Orpheus, Hercules, Theseus, Pirithous, and others. Thus, Virgil, in describing the descent of Aeneas to the underworld, imitates this and adds a metallic allegory to it; namely, that within a shadowy tree—that is, within the minerals spread under the earth like the branches and roots of trees—lies hidden the golden bough. Because of this, some even call the veins of ore "the subterranean tree," projected through the earth in the manner of a tree. This branch of the mineral tree is golden in itself and in its leaves, and because it is a "pliant twig," it is flexible rather than brittle. Virgil says "the whole grove covers it," etc., because shaded woods always surround places fertile in minerals, unless they have been cut down. Or, he means it is hidden in the shadows of the earth so that it cannot be easily found, since it is concealed beneath the ground. But he says "it is not granted to enter," etc., meaning that no one can approach the innermost places of the earth unless they have plucked this golden bough, which must be brought as a gift for Proserpina. "Once the first is torn away," etc.

<margin>Ore under the earth is spread like trees through the ground.</margin>
<margin>The multiplication of the golden branch.</margin>
Here, an infinite multiplication is suggested, which relates most closely to the <term>Chemical art</term> <note>In this era, "Chemical art" (Ars Chemica) was synonymous with Alchemy, specifically the creation of the Philosopher's Stone or the multiplication of metals.</note>. Therefore, Virgil says, "search deeply with your eyes," etc.; he says it is to be sought in a high place of the tree, and this is indeed most true; for it rests upon the peaks of the mountains. And "when found, pluck it rightly with your hand": in the plucking, a certain method must also be observed. "It will follow easily," that is, you will find it with ease,

# Now the arguments of the Adversaries are expected.

### *10. Argument attacking Chemistry, brought forward by Pyrgopolynices against Morienus.*
<note>In this dialogue, the author uses "Pyrgopolynices"—the name of the "Braggart Soldier" from ancient Roman comedy—to represent a loud-mouthed opponent of alchemy. Morienus is a legendary hermit-alchemist said to have taught the secrets of the stone to the King of Egypt.</note>

<margin>10 Negative Argument.</margin>
Whatever things are not living, and are stable, and have reached their intended end, in those things no subordination or mutual transmutation is allowed.

But metals are not living, and they are stable, and have reached their intended end.

Therefore, in metals, the transmutation of one into another is not allowed.

The proposition is thus made clear: Hence it is no wonder if a butterfly emerges from an egg through a caterpillar and a silkworm; because these are living, and have not yet reached their intended end.

## MORIENUS’S RESPONSE.

<margin>Response to the 10th Negative Argument.</margin>

**T**his distinction is indeed cautious, provided it is not yet too broad and wandering. You have craftily, but according to your own whim, invented this exception regarding a species not being changed into another species; we will hardly place any faith in these claims, since we see that you are laying snares for the truth. What if we show you very many exceptions even here? Are there not the same changes, and perhaps more, in the vegetable kingdom? Rye is said to turn into darnel <note>original: "lolium." This refers to tares or "cockle," a weed that closely resembles wheat until it matures, which was often cited in antiquity as a "degeneration" of grain.</note>, and sometimes into wheat, and wheat into rye, according to very serious authors. Are not the kinds of daisies, roses, lilies, and hyacinths mixed, colored, brought forth, and propagated by art in great number? A single grafting of trees would convict...

<margin>Atmospheric phenomena also change into one another.</margin>
...[into] a net of vanity and ignorance. If you say that vegetables are also living—even if they are not sentient—then at least your distinction would be restricted to things dug from the earth or to "meteors" <note>In the 17th century, the term "meteors" (meteora) referred to all atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, and lightning, not just falling stars.</note>. But here you fall into the same difficulties as before, since even these atmospheric phenomena change into one another very often: such as rain into snow or hail, the freezing of clouds into stone <note>Likely referring to hail or "thunderstones," which were once believed to fall from the sky during storms.</note>, and lightning into air.

<margin>Minerals also change into one another.</margin>
If we speak of minerals, there is a great variety of changes from one into another. What of iron into steel? Or iron or steel into copper (as many insist), or into vitriol <term>vitriol: a metallic sulfate, often appearing as glassy green or blue crystals</term> from both iron and copper? Are all these things impossible to you, so that you might demonstrate as impossible that which is actually possible? These are long, winding paths from which you will hardly ever extricate yourself. It would have been better to produce your opinion without reasoning than to want to prop it up with so many ruinous and doubtful ruins. It would have been better to have said once:

> *Thus I wish, thus I command; let my will stand for reason;* <note>original: "Sic volo, sic iubeo, sit pro ratione voluntas" — a famous quote from the Roman satirist Juvenal (Satire VI), used to describe someone who rules by whim rather than logic.</note>

than to have so often twisted reason to your will, and to have heaped up so many trifles and tangles to confirm an opinion that is both the worst and clearly contrary to the truth.

...in countless works peculiar to art and not nature. If, however, it is understood as natural works to be expressed or finished by art in the manner of nature—namely, that one metal is changed into another according to art, provided this happens through nature—then this proposition seems to have some weight. For if transmutation is possible for art, it will depend on the natural power that individual metals have within themselves, by which they pass into one another, the more imperfect into the more perfect; although we have already demonstrated before that in this exchange of a baser metal into another more precious one, it does not happen that one individual member passes into an individual of another species; but if at least mercury <term>mercury: original "argentum vivum" (living silver). In alchemy, this refers not just to the element, but to the essential fluid substance believed to be the "seed" of all metals.</term>, which is in imperfect metals, is joined and mixed with another mercury produced by art; by the mixture of these two, gold is made from two things which before, on their own, were not gold—just as from the seed of an ass and a horse a mule is produced, differing from either seed. <note>This "mule" analogy was a popular way for alchemists to explain how the "Art" could produce a new substance (gold) by combining natural materials in ways nature might not do on its own.</note>

But the assumption must be denied as clearly false: Because even if art does not imitate the same mode of transmutation that nature uses in the generation of metals, nevertheless the transmutation of metals also occurs underground, as has been shown more often.

<margin>12. A negative argument.</margin>

## Response of Morienus.

<margin>Fabulous authors:</margin> **I** respond to the major premise, that there is an equivocation <note>In logic, an equivocation is the use of a term with multiple meanings to mislead.</note> in the word "fabulous."
For authors are understood as "fabulous" in two ways: either as those who truly never existed in the nature of things, but are mere fables; or those who indeed existed, but whose lives have been obscured by fables and enigmas so that they *seem* fabulous to us, and this is due to the weakness of our own reason. If "fabulous" is taken in the first way in the major premise, the premise is true; if in the second way, it is false.

*Regarding the major premise*, I say that the authors are called "fabulous" in the second sense, not the first. For <term>Chemy: alchemy, derived from the Latin "Chemia."</term> has its own authors, but much obscurity has been attached to their names; not because they did not exist at all, or are mere fables.

*As to the proof of the minor premise*, it does not prove that the authors of alchemy are fictional. For even if *Hermes* were *Moses*, or were not, nevertheless nothing is taken away from alchemical truth. This is evident in the case of cities and towns whose founders are unknown, or about whom there is doubt; does one then doubt whether those cities are fables, or whether they exist in the nature of things? Who is accustomed to reason this way, except a madman? That we are ignorant of the authors of Alchemy should not be blamed on Alchemy itself, but rather on its great antiquity; and it results in its honor rather than its disgrace.
<margin>The authors of Alchemy are not unknown.</margin>
In truth, we do not say that the authors of Alchemy are entirely unknown; rather, we proclaim *Hermes Trismegistus* <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure, "Hermes the Thrice-Greatest," credited with the founding of the Hermetic arts, including alchemy.</note> to be its chief restorer, who, although by you...

## Affirmative Reasons of Morienus for Alchemical Truth.
### The 10th Reason of the Affirmers.

<margin>10th affirmative reason for Chemy.</margin>
**Into whatever components a thing is resolved, it is composed of those same things.** <note>This is a fundamental principle of Aristotelian physics: to understand what a thing is made of, you look at what it breaks down into.</note>

Gold is resolved by certain people into <term>quicksilver: also known as liquid mercury; original: "argentum vivum"</term> and Tincture, and other imperfect metals are resolved into <term>Mercury: in alchemy, this often refers to the philosophical "Mercury of the Wise" rather than common quicksilver.</term>

Therefore, gold is composed of quicksilver and tincture, and the others are composed of Mercury.

> *And consequently, if they are composed of these things, they can and ought to be able to be composed from them again. For since art desires to express the works of nature, it is bound to imitate nature as far as it can in its matter, form, and end, even though the <term>efficient cause: the agent or force that brings a thing into being.</term> may vary; as is apparent in the artificial hatching of eggs, in which the efficient cause seems different—namely, the heat produced in a furnace—differing from the heat of a brooding hen.* <note>Alchemists frequently used the example of an incubator (the "Athanor") as proof that human art could replicate natural processes like gestation.</note>

The major premise cannot be in doubt, because it is a most true axiom in every field of learning: Milk is resolved into three substances <note>Likely referring to whey, curds, and cream/butter.</note>, wine likewise into as many, and a man into his members, organs, and humors.

->### The 11th Affirmative Reason of Morienus.<-

<margin>11th Affirmative Reason.</margin>
If all the proper natural causes of any thing, especially the internal ones, can be appropriately gathered together by art, then that same thing which is produced by nature will be produced by art.

But all the proper natural causes for producing natural gold, especially the internal ones, can be appropriately gathered together by art.

Therefore, it is also possible for natural gold to be produced by art.

**This proposition is most true**, because whatever a thing is, it comes from its causes; it is generated, preserved, and known by them.
<margin>Causes that concur in the making of gold.</margin>
There are exactly four causes: two internal, <term>Matter</term> and <term>Form</term>; and two external, the <term>Efficient</term> and the <term>Final</term>. <note>These are the four causes defined by Aristotle: what a thing is made of (matter), its essential nature (form), the agent that brings it about (efficient), and its purpose or goal (final).</note> Those internal causes are proper to the thing and remain with the thing as long as it exists. The remaining external causes are outside the thing: these can vary, but the internal ones cannot. The Final cause is that which disposes the principles through certain means toward the end. The principles and the end must be of the same nature; the means, extending between the principles and the end, can vary. The Efficient cause is the heat, which also varies according to the diversity of the means. Both Matter and Form must be the same in both nature and art.

The minor premise is established: <note>original: "Assumptio constat." Nature works out this *Form* in concrete reality, but art works it out in the abstract. In this, the Chemists imitate the Platonic **Ideas** <note>Refers to Plato’s theory that perfect, abstract templates exist for all things in the physical world.</note> or mathematical figures, which are also considered in the abstract. Nature draws forth the form from the womb of matter in a wonderful way over a long period of time; Art chooses for itself the matter remaining from that ancient Chaos, <note>In alchemy, "Chaos" refers to the "Prima Materia" or the raw, unorganized starting material of the Great Work.</note> which possesses more of form in potential than any other thing—indeed, which is so close in potential that it becomes entirely form. From this tradition, **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), one of the most influential philosopher-physicians of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> and many others were most excellent practitioners in medicine, so much so that in certain matters, departing from the Greeks, they provided countless highly useful medical precepts along with various forms of medicines which are still in use throughout almost the entire world.

<margin>
The nature of Avicenna’s medical writings.

Avicenna the Prince.
</margin>

How great **Avicenna’s** knowledge and practice in medicine was is sufficiently declared by his most complete medical writings, which encompass the whole art in a most convenient method. For this reason, he was not undeservedly called "The Prince" <note>original: "Princeps"; a title reflecting his status as the "Prince of Physicians."</note> in an absolute sense, and he is still called so today. Whether he truly held the title of a prince in a political sense, as many affirm, seems to have no bearing on the matter. It is credible that he was a great and preeminent man in his homeland who had no need to hire out his services for pay to cure the sick—even though he helped them through others with his medical knowledge. Nor is this surprising, since even Kings are found to have practiced medicine and written about it. But Christians, hearing that **Avicenna** and other Muslims had knowledge of so many arts and sciences—and especially of that peculiar gift of God, **Chemistry** <note>In this 17th-century context, "Chemia" refers to alchemy, the "hidden art" of transmuting metals and seeking the Philosopher's Stone.</note>—might think:

<margin>
Whether Muslims should be considered by Christians as unworthy of God’s gifts.
</margin>

<header>SYMBOLS</header>

<margin>Geber is the most obscure of all in his apparent clarity.</margin>
...he obscured [the truth] by his clear method of teaching more than any other of the ancients or <unclear>moderns</unclear>: Since he himself admits that he has hidden the secrets of the art throughout the various parts of his volumes, and <gloss>where they speak plainly and clearly, it amounts to nothing</gloss> <note>original: "vbi plane & clare loquuntur fic quod lib: nihil"</note>, but where he has spoken under an allegory, there he has said something. Hence,

<margin>Geber’s declaration.</margin>
his declaration will excuse him from the slander of readers and practitioners; and all the more so because he asserts that he wrote the art not for others, but for himself, so that he might recall it from his own mind, and not for those who are ignorant. He claims to have given various aids and instructions by which one can reach the goal of the art. Since he seems to have used such sincerity in his forewarning, most people reading

<margin>Many reading Geber’s volumes fall into labyrinths because of their apparent clarity.</margin>
his volumes—presented with such ease and, as it appears, clarity—pore over them with great fervor of spirit. Nor is anyone of so lowly a wit that he does not persuade himself that he can see something hidden in his writings and discern the wheat from the chaff, or even that he has grasped Geber’s entire mind. Animated by this opinion, everyone tries all kinds of distillations, as well as all materials, whether mineral or non-mineral, and subjects them to the practical exercise of the hands with the required furnace fires, now in this way, now in another,

<margin>That Geber’s clearer words are deceptive is evident from the errors they cause.</margin>
until at length, after some years, he understands that Geber’s clearer words were deceptive, and his more obscure ones require a Delian swimmer <note>original: "Delio natatore"; a reference to a comment by Socrates about the deep philosophy of Heraclitus, which required a strong swimmer from Delos to navigate without drowning</note>, or some Oedipus <note>The mythical hero who solved the riddle of the Sphinx</note>, who might lead them from the depths into the sunlight and untangle and explain the riddles of the Geberian Sphinx. <margin>Geber called "harsh" by Bernard.</margin>

<meta>This page transitions from the discussion of Geber’s obscure writing style to a broader historical analysis of Egyptian hieroglyphs. # THE GOLDEN TABLE. BOOK V.

<margin>
The nature of the Hieroglyphic type of letters.
</margin>
The style called **Hieroglyphic** consists especially of animals, and other images taken from plants or things crafted by art. Because this style looked toward the hidden natures of each animal or thing—which the philosophers applied to parts of their <term>Chemical</term> <note>original: "Chymici"; referring here to the alchemical art of transformation</note> work—it could be read or understood by no one except those to whom the doctrine or revelation had been passed down by others. This revelation was strictly guarded, forbidden by oaths and the symbol of <term>Harpocrates</term> <note>The Greek adaptation of the Egyptian god Horus the Child, traditionally represented with a finger to his lips as a symbol of silence.</note> or <term>Sigalion</term> <note>A Roman name for the deity of silence, derived from the Greek word for silence, 'sigé'.</note>. Using this genre, the philosophers wrote down whatever they wished concerning the art, and there was no one besides the craftsmen themselves who could perceive what was written. The "sons of the philosophers" <note>A traditional term for initiated students of alchemy.</note> undoubtedly understood what art these letters concerned, as it was considered a divine crime for anything to be revealed by the fathers to outsiders.

<margin>
The common people in Egypt did not know what those hieroglyphs of animals were about. Hence they worshiped them as sacred.
</margin>
The rest of the common people, however, understood nothing of this; they instead worshiped those images as holy animals and filled every town with them as if they were deities. For this reason, in Egypt itself—where that art had its own temples and priests (who were nevertheless called the priests of <term>Isis</term> and <term>Osiris</term>)—the art remained unknown to the public. Not even <term>Horapollo</term> <note>The legendary author of the 'Hieroglyphica', a work that attempted to explain Egyptian symbols but often provided moral or naturalistic allegories rather than linguistic translations.</note>, the Egyptian interpreter of hieroglyphs, reached their true meaning or scented out the <term>Chemical Art</term> <note>Alchemy</note> within them.

<margin>
The chemical art existed even in Egypt.
</margin>
There was another kind of writing depicted with certain letters and marks, like the letters of any nation, which can be recognized and read by anyone according to the twenty-four-letter sequence. They used that for noting down and committing to memory any other matters. The inconvenience that attended the first kind of writing [hieroglyphs] was this: the common people, seeing those animals painted on all works, pyramids, walls, and books, and seeing them kept as sacred and hidden by the priests, applied themselves to the divine worship of brute beasts.

<margin>
The commoners and Egyptians took the opportunity to approach the worship of beasts.
</margin>
Hence Egypt was filled with brutish idols. This did not bother the priests who were ignorant of the art, since a religious reason was always woven into the fact; however, it suited those who were "in the know" quite well.

Errors arising from the ambiguity and synonymy of Chemistry.

In the philosophers who write, or in those who inquire into the art? Truly, it is not in the former; because it is impossible to pass down these secrets otherwise, unless they were to be made public to everyone and prostituted to the lowest, unlearned commoners. The fault lies, therefore, with those who imagined in their own minds that they could grasp the secrets of the philosophers, yet were found unfit and unworthy by God.

->### SYMBOLS<-

<margin>The writings of Geber</margin>
...we have reached the completion of that mastery we have investigated. *Geber* <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, though the works cited here are from the 13th-century Latin author known as Pseudo-Geber.</note> wrote, besides the *Sum of Perfection* <note>original: "summam perfectionis"</note>, a book on the *Investigation of Truth*, another on the *Discovery of Truth*, and the *Book of Furnaces*, all of which have reached us; but there are still others, including his *Testament*, which we have not yet seen. *Count Bernhard* <note>Bernhard of Trevisan, a famous 15th-century alchemist who spent decades seeking the Stone.</note> and many others devoted several years to studying *Geber*.

<margin>Geber’s writings are adapted to each person's mindset.</margin>
For the writing of *Geber* is like a mirror, in which the form of anyone—or rather, the preconception of their mind—is most perfectly reflected. If someone chooses metals for the work, *Geber* assigns priority to these individually in various places; if they choose minerals and quicksilver <note>Mercury</note>, he offers the primary place to these. Whoever delights in distillation, calcination, solution, coagulation, and fixation will see *Geber* quickly providing assent with every kind of furnace and vessel.

<margin>Geber’s many cooks.</margin>
Hence so many of his "cooks" <note>A derogatory term for pseudo-alchemists or "puffers" who followed literal, practical recipes without understanding the underlying theory.</note> are found who, while they try to put his precepts into action like obedient servants, dedicate a great part of their goods and time to *Vulcan* <note>The Roman god of fire, here representing the alchemical furnace.</note>. Yet, from their long and hard labors, they bring back nothing but glass, or ashes, or the waters of the Styx and Lethe <note>References to the rivers of the underworld, signifying death, failure, and oblivion.</note>.

<margin>What is to be expected from Geber’s works.</margin>
This is the salary with which *Geber* blesses those who are too obedient to him, about which honorable men ought to be forewarned. *Geber* is indeed a good author in his own right and a most true champion of Chemistry,

<margin>* Geber’s strategy in handing down the art. Geber expanded a brief art into something immense to deceive the reader.</margin>
but in his description of the art, he seems to have used this stratagem: just as *Dido* <note>The legendary founder and first Queen of Carthage.</note>, when asking the Libyans for only as much land as could be covered by a bull’s hide, cut the whole hide into continuous and tiny strips, and thus encompassed a vast space of land; so too has *Geber* extended the essence of the Chemical art—which is small in itself—into the widest descriptions. He has dispersed it through all the parts of his books (as he himself testifies) so that even a *Lynceus* <note>In Greek mythology, an Argonaut famed for his keen sight, able to see through walls or into the earth.</note> could hardly recognize or distinguish the truth from the sophistical falsehoods that are a thousand times more abundant in quantity and number. By this cunning, she obtained a kingdom among the Libyans, and he obtained one among the Chemists. Truly, if anyone [wishes] to read *Geber* with profit...

<meta>This page continues the examination of Geber’s writings, transitioning from how his work reflects the reader's own biases to the necessity of using critical reason—a "sieve"—to distinguish his true alchemical secrets from intentional decoys.</meta>

->## OF THE GOLDEN TABLE. BOOK V.<-

<margin>The sieve of reason must be applied to Geber.</margin>
...to manage and handle [this art], he must sieve all of Geber’s precepts and axioms through the sieve of reason <note>The "Sieve of Reason" (cribrum rationis) is a common alchemical metaphor for using logic to separate truth from symbolic "chaff."</note>, according to the rule that Geber himself prescribes: that where he speaks most clearly, one should consider his words as vain, false, and unrelated to the art; but where he speaks in allegory and figure, there he has truly said something. In this way, through a kind of "sieving," rational ideas are distinguished from those of the brutish sort—those endowed with very long horns but possessing very little brain or reason. However, this task is not for just any inexperienced person or novice. For this reason, Geber himself describes at the beginning of his *Sum of Perfection* <note>original: "summae." Referring to the *Summa perfectionis magisterii*, the most famous work attributed to Geber.</note> what kind of craftsman and operator the art requires, so that if someone is not of that sort (or only imagines himself to be), and subsequently falls into error, he should blame his own ignorance and the dullness of his own mind, rather than the truthful authors of the books.

<margin>Geber describes his ideal craftsman.</margin>
In many places throughout his numerous volumes, **Geber** proposes many and various warnings and cautions. By these, anyone could be kept within the truer path of the art and prevented from wandering easily, provided they did not rush in the opposite direction out of sheer desire. *But we always strive for the forbidden, as the Poet says, and we desire what is denied:* <note>original: "At nitimur in vetitū, inquit Poeta, semper, cupimusq; negata." This is a quote from the Roman poet Ovid, *Amores* 3.4.17.</note> We wish to try everything, even things harmful and dangerous, until, like children, we burn our fingers and are finally made more cautious. Or indeed, we possess something of the character of that woman who, being flirtatious and bold, was left at home by her husband as he was about to travel abroad. 

<margin>Human nature, a lover of novelty, leaning toward the forbidden. A ridiculous story of a woman exploring a new way of riding, though it was forbidden.</margin>
Having barely left the house, the husband sent back a servant with a command that she should not invite the priest to dinner. The servant, knowing the woman’s nature—that she leaned toward whatever was forbidden—instead told her that the master's command was that she must not ride upon the **Molossian hound** <note>A Molossian was a large, powerful ancient breed of dog, ancestors of the modern Mastiff.</note>. The woman asked if he took her for a fool and sent the servant away with insults. But the servant had hardly turned his back when the woman, thinking that some sweetness or secret must lie hidden in this forbidden act, climbed onto the back of the Molossian dog; it is said she was immediately thrown off and severely bitten. Such a thing can happen because we all lust after prohibited things, after the manner of our first parents. Thus, when **Geber** proposes things to be avoided, do others not try to experience them to their own ruin? Who is at fault: the servant or the woman? Geber, or the experimenter? Rather the latter than the former.

...without doubt, they signify something of his mind: he introduces his teacher **Bolemus** the philosopher into the dialogue, who was also an **Arab**.

<margin>Alphidius.</margin>
**ALPHIDIUS** is also counted among the lineage of the **Arabs**; he is known to us only through the Latin language, as are the others. Otherwise, he is an author cited by many and held in high regard. Though his writing is filled with many "mists" <note>The "mists" refer to the intentionally obscure and metaphorical language (Decknamen) used by alchemists to hide their secrets from the unworthy.</note>, he is nevertheless quite clear in certain parts. In his recapitulation, he expresses the main summary of the work, having applied many precautions. He says: *Among other things, know, my son, that you cannot possess this science until you purify your mind for God, and God knows that you have a certain and upright spirit; only then will He cause you to rule over the world.* He says the same: *Know that God did not set this stone—which is the subject of this secret—to be bought at a great price, for it is found cast out in the road, so that it can be possessed by the poor as well as the rich, provided that anyone may easily reach it through reason and science.*

<margin>Gilgil.</margin>
<margin>Gilgil's opinion as relayed by Geber.</margin>
**GILGIL** the **Moor** is mentioned by **Geber** <term>Geber: The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), the most influential figure in early Islamic alchemy and chemistry.</term> as an artisan who held a unique opinion on the generation of metals, which he handed down in his book (which, however, we have not seen). First, he asserted that something earthy is generated from quicksilver <term>Quicksilver: mercury; traditionally called "living silver" (argentum vivum) because of its liquid, moving state.</term> in subterranean caves where ores lie hidden, through the strongest heat—just as appears in the furnaces of glassmakers—which is resistant to all flame. He claimed this is washed and penetrated by a continuous flow of mineral water until a union of the two is made; that is, until the watery substance has been coagulated through the earthy, and the earthy dissolved through the watery, by one and the same operation.

<margin>Gilgil's opinion, posited as a hypothesis. Roasting and boiling are done with different intentions and through the will.</margin>
This opinion of his is believed to have been posited as a hypothesis rather than set forth as established doctrine. For Nature does not produce the Tincture <note>The "Tincture" or "Elixir" is the powerful substance capable of perfecting or transforming base metals into gold.</note>, nor gold, in this way, since she is destitute of will and intellect. For one who wishes first to roast something by the fire and afterwards to boil <note>original: "elixare," referring to a wet-heat extraction or cooking process.</note> it, just as he has a different intention, so he requires different instruments, which are discerned and discovered by the intellect.

...are born, but by the will [of the artisan] they are applied to use in various ways at this or that time. Indeed, nature proceeds in its work gradually and step by step, destitute of will, acting upon cold and moist **mercury** <term>argentum vivum: literally "living silver," the common name for mercury</term> with its own added and external **sulfur**—acting like a fire mixed into it—and out of the cold and moist, it creates something not supremely hot and dry, but balanced; that is, retaining much natural moisture within itself and much heat, which is the substance of gold.

<margin>Hamuel.</margin>
**HAMUEL**, the *Author of the Table* which sets the entire rational art before one's eyes, is an **Arab** and a most experienced **Chemist** <note>In the 17th century, "Chymicus" referred to a practitioner of alchemy who focused on laboratory experimentation.</note>, who is cited by everyone and accepted as an authority. A certain author, no less proven, commented on that Table, whom they give the name **Senior** <note>Senior is the Latin translation of the Arabic title "Sheikh." This refers to Zadith ben Hamuel, a 10th-century alchemist.</note>; however, I think this name is derived from the "Senior" (the Old Man) who holds the table itself in his lap, and that the commentator is anonymous.

<margin>A brief explanation of Senior's Table.</margin>
The ***Old Man*** <note>The "Senex" or "Senior" is a recurring figure in alchemical illustration, often depicted as a sage sitting in a stone chamber holding a tablet of secrets.</note> holds a twofold tablet, the first part of which contains **one bird without wings** in the lower position, and **another with wings** in the upper; and one of these grasps the other’s tail with its beak.

<margin>The first part of the work in two birds:</margin>
One is indeed ready for flight, but is held back by the other so that it cannot fly. <note>This famous image represents the "fixation of the volatile": the winged bird (spirit or gas) is tethered by the wingless bird (body or solid) so they can be united into a stable substance.</note> And this is the first part of the philosophical work, which is free of all mixture; once this is well understood and prepared, one must proceed to the other part. This is the base and foundation of the work, without which, even if well placed, nothing firm or stable can be built upon it. The other part of the table encompasses **three suns**: two in the upper position, one of which appears with one ray and the other with two; and a third below, distinguished by three colors. The two suns are the two aforementioned birds, and the lower sun represents the transformations that follow.

<margin>Senior.</margin>
**SENIOR**, or by whatever other name the author is called, who gave a most copious explanation of the pictures of the already mentioned **Hamuel**, is of the same nation and family. This man explained the matter not only in plain words but also through beautiful parables...
