...has illuminated. Among his other remaining works is this: <margin>The parable of Senior.</margin> *If the most beloved parents taste of the vine and are nourished by my milk, and are intoxicated by my white substance, and marry in my little bed, they shall beget the son of the Moon <note>In alchemy, the "Son of the Moon" often refers to the white stage of the work (Albedo) or a specific silver-based compound.</note> who will prevail over all his kin. If my beloved drinks from the stream of the red **STONE** <note>original: PETRAE</note> and tastes the fountain of his mother, and is coupled thereafter and intoxicated with me by my red wine, and lies with me friendly in his bed, and in my love his seed enters into my chamber, I shall conceive and be pregnant, and in my time I shall bring forth a most powerful son, ruling and reigning over all the kings and princes of the earth, crowned with the golden crown of victory.* Other things that could be brought forward from this author, we omit for the sake of brevity.

<margin>Rhazes</margin>
**RHAZES** <note>Abu Bakr al-Razi (c. 865–925 AD), a Persian polymath and physician whose works were foundational to both medieval medicine and alchemy.</note>, who is not the least among the physicians of the Arabs, also possessed a perfect knowledge of Chemistry, as is clear from his book published on this art called *The Light of Lights*, although it is full of sophisticated terms due to envy <note>The "envy of the philosophers" (invidia philosophorum) is a common trope where authors claim to have obscured their secrets to prevent them from falling into the hands of the unworthy.</note>. And especially from the letter which begins: <margin>The First Epistle of Rhazes.</margin> *The pattern of our science is an old man upon a mountain; in him the natures are joined with the completion of earth, water, his fire and air. And all these are in Saturn <note>In alchemical code, Saturn usually represents the metal lead or the beginning stage of the work (the Blackness or Nigredo).</note>; with him the gates of the sciences are opened, as Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the founder of alchemy.</note> and his first predecessors say.* These words, if they are well understood, explain a great part of the work. "With this," he says a little later, "you shall have the science in which the Arabs have been idle. Our gum <term>gumen: likely referring to a resinous or sticky substance formed during the chemical process</term> coagulates our milk, and our milk dissolves our gum, and afterwards the Oriental redness and the redness of blood will appear." That he was a follower of Muhammad is clear from his words, when he says: *I have spoken the truth by the family of Muhammad. And soon: Our earth turns skillful methods into silver first, and finally into gold; it grows old, and you shall have the science in which the Arabs have been idle.* <margin>This epistle is equal to many volumes.</margin> Indeed, this epistle, although brief, far surpasses the great volumes of many others in learning and clarity. For it has within itself all things which seem to look toward the completion of the art. The same author says in his *Great Book of Precepts*: *Whoever is ignorant of weights should not labor in our books; for the philosophers have placed none of their things, nor hidden anything else, except these.*

# SYMBOLS

<margin>Rosinus.</margin>
**ROZINUS** <note>original: "ROZINI". Rosinus is the Latinized name for Zosimos of Panopolis, a 3rd-century Greco-Egyptian alchemist whose works were highly influential in the Arabic and later Latin traditions.</note> *or Rosinus* also seems to be ascribed to the Arabs, even though he wrote certain things to Bishop Sarratanta. For even *Avicenna* <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the famous Persian physician and philosopher.</note> the Arab entered into such familiarity with many bishops that he even learned certain things from them, as he himself admits. 

<margin>The books of Rosinus.</margin>
He published various small books: one to Euthicia, two to Sarratanta (of which the first belongs to another, namely Arnold <note>Likely referring to the medieval alchemist Arnold of Villanova.</note>), others on divine interpretations, on definitions, and the like; all of which are very full of chemical doctrines. At the beginning, he relates that he came to a certain place where many "philosophers" in name only were gathered. When Rosinus sought certain matters regarding the art from them, he was in no way understood. For they held in their hands, he says, books which describe to them *Alkabric Alkakir* <note>A Latinization of an Arabic term, likely referring to "Al-Kibrit" (Sulfur) or a related substance, though the author defines it here as "vain things."</note>, that is, vain species or things which they know and which occupy them. These are the things that would deter those occupied by them; they persist in their own questions and deviate from the truth, blinded by ignorance. He promises in the same place that he wishes to explain the words of the wise, for unless he does so, his books would be like theirs—that is, obscure and most difficult to understand. *Which is unsuitable,* he says, *and a disgrace to him who acts thus.* And a little later: *Unless I do this, we shall not manifest our industry, and my sayings will be without administration and utility.* These promises he truly fulfills in countless ways; let one or two examples suffice for us.

<margin>The Eagle Stone.</margin>
> *This is the stone,* he says, *which the wise men of the art liken to the Eagle Stone <note>term: Eagle Stone <gloss>Lapis Aquilae or Aetites. A geode found in eagles' nests, believed to contain a smaller stone that rattles inside. In alchemy, it symbolizes the "stone within a stone" or the hidden essence within matter.</gloss></note>. For the Eagle Stone is a well-known stone, and there is a stone in its belly which moves.*

He declares in various ways what kind of stone this is, and then relates certain memorable things.

<margin>Different species are not born from different things.</margin>
> *The ignorant man,* he says, *ignorantly sows colocynth <note>A bitter cucumber or "wild gourd" known for its purgative properties; used here to represent a bitter or useless starting material.</note> and hopes to eat honey from it; but when he does not see what he had hoped for, he returns to his own thought and stretches it out, saying: "This is from misfortune." And if it were said to him, "a sheep gave birth to humans," or "grains of wheat bear galbanum <note>A bitter, aromatic gum resin.</note>," or "a palm tree carried pomegranates," or "birds give birth to fish," he would answer: "You speak falsely; things do not generate except their like, nor do they fruit—* <note>The text cuts off here mid-sentence, illustrating the law of nature that like begets like, a fundamental principle in alchemical transmutation.</note>

It introduces the metaphor of the Eagle Stone and the principle that chemical results must follow the natural laws of kind and species.</summary>

<margin>Euthicia, a woman philosopher.</margin>

<margin>Galen.</margin>
**GALEN** <note>The famous Greek physician, whose authority was often co-opted into alchemical literature.</note> says: Prepare the bodies and purge them of the blackness, in which there is corruption, until it becomes white and red; then dissolve both into water—namely, the spirit and the body—and coagulate them, and then cast them upon the washed body.

<margin>Arsicanus.</margin>
**ARSICANUS** <note>Likely a corruption of a Greek name like Anaxagoras, common in the *Turba Philosophorum*.</note> the philosopher says: *Now the four elements—that is, heat, cold, moisture, and dryness—proceed from one source, and some of them are made from others of the same: indeed, of these four, some are like roots and some are like things composed from them, namely earth and air.* Also Arsicanus to Maria <note>Maria Prophetissa, or Mary the Jewess, a foundational figure in Western alchemy.</note>: *Our water,* he says, *has our earth overcoming it, which is great, bright, and pure. For even from the thickness of the water, the earth is created.*

<margin>Datin.</margin>
**DATIN** the Philosopher; *Although our laton* <note>original: *lato*; an alloy resembling brass, often used in alchemy to represent an impure or base metal that must be "whitened."</note> *is red at first, it is nevertheless useless; but if it is turned into white after the redness, it will be worth much:* Therefore, for this reason, the same **Datin** says to **Euthices**; *O Euthices, let these things remain firm here and be entirely well-believed: for the wise have said concerning this: We have already removed the blackness, and with salt of anatron* <note>original: *sale anatron*; a naturally occurring soda/nitre used as a flux.</note>, *that is, salt of nitre and almizadir* <note>original: *almizadir*; the alchemical name for sal ammoniac (ammonium chloride), used for its volatile properties.</note>, *whose temperament is cold and dry, we have fixed the whiteness; wherefore we give it this name Borreza, which in Arabic is called Tincar.* <note>original: *Tincar*; the historical name for borax, used here as a stabilizing agent.</note> *And soon after: Datin the philosopher says: if, however, the Laton is burned with sulfur, and softness is frequently poured over it, its nature will be converted from good to better with the help of God. The same man's saying is: that every thing is nothing except of it and with it, and that every tincture proceeds from its own likeness. And a little later: Whence it is indeed, that it proceeded from it and shall return into it.*

<margin>Euthices.</margin>
**EUTHICES** the philosopher is named by the aforementioned **Datin**; he brought philosophical questions to **Datin**, which we pass over.

<margin>Adarmath.</margin>
**ADARMATH**, a sage and philosopher, says: That all the names and similarities of these things are called or varied by the ancients for no other reason than that you might understand that the beginning of this matter bears witness to its end, and its end bears witness to its beginning.

<margin>Azinabam.</margin>
**AZINABAM**, a philosopher, when asked by **Oziambe** how the philosophical matter is named, responded: naturally this is *vulphi*—that is, it is called an "animal." <note>In alchemical vitalism, the "animal" nature suggests the matter possesses a soul or life-force necessary for growth and transformation.</note>

<margin>Elbo the Killer.</margin>
**ELBO** *the Killer* <note>original: *Interfector*; likely a symbolic title referring to the "mortification" or chemical "killing" of metals to prepare them for rebirth.</note> *says: Whiten the Laton and tear up your books, lest your hearts be corrupted.*

<margin>Ademarus.</margin>
**ADEMARUS**, who is said by the author of the *Rosary* <note>Referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous 16th-century alchemical compendium.</note> to have commented on **Geber**, says: *However much the stone may be cleansed by sublimation, and its combustibility* <note>original: *adustio*; the "burning" or oily impurities of the metal.</note> *be deleted through the extraction of its oil...*

<meta>This page continues the catalog of alchemical authorities from the previous page, specifically focusing on those identified with the Arabic tradition, even if they bear Greek-sounding names. It highlights "Plato the Alchemist" as a distinct figure from the famous philosopher.</meta>

->SYMBOLS<-

<margin>Plato the Alchemist</margin>
**PLATO** the Alchemist is neither Latin nor Greek, but appears to be Arabic, because Greek names of this sort became frequent when their studies spread among the Arabs. Hamech wrote commentaries or explanatory notes on this Plato's *Aphorisms*; Hamech published his own works in Hebrew, but he knew Arabic perfectly, as the Arabic language was very commonly used in the East. There exists a work called *The Path of the Wanderers* <note>original: "Semita errantium"</note> written by this same Plato, to whom the following sayings are attributed by other authors: *Our Stone (citing the Great Rosary) is a thing which fire has not touched; water, our Mercury, rises.* <note>original: "Lapis noster... est res, quam ignis non tetigit, aqua noster Mercurius surgit."</note> And elsewhere: *Note that without corruption, generation cannot occur; therefore, you should focus your study on putrefaction.* <note>original: "sine corruptione generatio fieri non potest; Vnde studeas in putrefactione." <term>putrefaction: the alchemical stage of "death" or decay, usually represented by the color black, necessary for new life to emerge.</term></note> And soon after: *We have an example in the egg, which first rots, and then the chick is born; after it is completely decayed, it becomes a living animal.* Likewise: *The first rule of Saturn <note>In alchemy, "Saturn" usually refers to the metal lead or the beginning stage of the work characterized by darkness and heaviness.</note> is to cause rot and to place it in the sun: the composition is indeed completed over four nights.* The same Plato says in his summary: *You have a need to labor in the dissolving of bodies: therefore it is necessary to maintain a slow fire over the substance until it is dissolved, and through this the work is accomplished.* Calid <note>Prince Khalid ibn Yazid, an early patron of Arabic alchemy.</note> also mentions him in chapter 8 with these words: *Thus says Plato in his discourses, in his book: fire adds benefit or progress to the perfect, and disadvantage or corruption to the corrupt. Therefore, when the amount of fire is good and appropriate, it will be beneficial; but when it is increased beyond measure in things, it will destroy both—namely, the perfect and the corrupt.*

<margin>Other Arabs.</margin>
**IESID** of Constantinople is numbered among the Arabs. His surname alone does not make him Greek; he is cited by Count Bernhard and others whom we will pass over here.

Any art whose experiments are performed through deceptive magic and other frauds is itself deceptive and detestable.

## THE RESPONSE OF AVICENNA.

<margin>Response to the 13th negative argument.</margin>
**W**e grant the major premise <note>The first part of the opponent's logic</note> if such experiments are always the result of the art itself and its instructions; however, if they occur by chance or because of the specific practitioners, we do not grant that it is simply true. To the minor premise <note>The second part of the opponent's syllogism</note>, we respond that it is clearly false. For nothing magical, contrary to the commands of God, or displaying deceptions is contained in <term>Chrysopoeia: the art of making gold</term>. Sometimes the worst of men devote themselves to the best arts; since they cannot master them, the art meanwhile suffers some insult from them. This ought not to happen, and it occurs only because of men who either abuse the art or judge it poorly. Just as in *Africa*, during the greatest heat, dragons and various kinds of poisonous beasts flock to the most healthful and coldest springs for their own benefit, so too do the most greedy and wicked men flee to <term>Chemistry</term>—which is by its nature most healthful and harmless—because of the "sacred thirst for gold" <note>original: "sacra auri sitim"; a reference to Virgil’s "Aeneid" regarding the corrupting power of greed</note>. But here, every honest man of good will ought to imitate the *Unicorn proper to Chemistry*, which, as they say, before it drinks, dips its horn into the waters to draw up healthy liquids, pure and free from all poison. That is to say, by the sharpness of his mind, he discerns which authors are good and to be read, and which are otherwise. The more precious a thing is in its legitimate use, the more ruinous it is in its abuse. The greatest remedies are <term>Alexipharmaca: medical antidotes or preservatives against poison</term> if used well; if used poorly, they are harmful and poisonous. Indeed, even poisons become remedies if they are applied at the right time and place. Such is the power of the use or abuse of any thing.

<margin>Because Chemistry is an allegory and not a deceiver, it should be estimated as more precious for that reason.</margin>
But who would prove the <term>Chemical</term> art to be deceptive? Perhaps because it employs allegories and figures of speech <note>original: "tropis"</note>, rather than plain and simple words? In truth, it is all the more worthy and noble for this: just as a Queen is not seen without her procession, nor *Diana* <note>The goddess of the moon and the hunt, often symbolizing the "pure" matter of alchemy</note> without her garment. For those things prostituted to the common crowd become cheap. *What is rare is dear. Do not throw what is holy to dogs, nor pearls before swine. Sugar for the parrot, hay for the ox. A diamond is nothing to a rooster, nor marjoram ointment to a cricket* <note>A series of classical adages suggesting that high arts are wasted on those who cannot appreciate them</note>.

<margin>Sacred Scripture is also allegorical.</margin>
Is not almost the whole of Sacred Scripture figurative, as much in the prophets as in the teaching of Christ himself and the Apostles? Should it therefore be called full of deceptions, when it [contains] the most certain cau—

<margin>Errors arising from misunderstood allegories.</margin>
It is considered sacred why the art was handed down in such a way, and how impossible it is that it could or should be taught otherwise, just as those reasons were noted previously (under <term>Geber: Jabir ibn Hayyan, a prolific 8th-century polymath often called the "Father of Chemistry"</term>); let them be considered in that same place. From this, errors happen to most people looking at the art, so that out of ten thousand, scarcely one aspires to the true understanding of the <note>original: "occultæ scriptionis"; the intentionally obscure "deck-names" and metaphors used by alchemists to hide their secrets</note> secret writing of the philosophers and the truth of the matter itself. Because of this, so many family fortunes are consumed, so many lifetimes are worn away, and such great labors are performed that it is incredible to state. From this arise so many false craftsmen, who, after they were unable to grow rich by the truth, turn themselves to fraud and vanity, promising much to many, but providing little or nothing except loss. <margin>Certain pseudo-chemists defect to deceptive arts.</margin> Most of them fall away into the <term>juggling arts: referring here to prestidigitation, magic, or sleight-of-hand used to fake alchemical results</term>; but all these things ought not to be blamed on true Chemistry, just as they are not blamed on true Theology simply because so many heretics and apostates are active within it—men who win both soul and body for the devil. Not to mention other good arts badly used by bad men. <margin>True Chemistry deceives no one.</margin> Chemistry truly wears no mask for anyone; it intends no trickery or deception for any person. But if such a thing occurs, it is perpetrated by authors of ill will, who shall never penetrate to the entrances of this art; rather, they are looked down upon by it as guests unworthy of such a feast.

<margin>Response to the 14th negative argument.</margin>
**I** concede the major premise; but I completely deny the minor one. I confess there are arts—or rather, not arts, but frauds—which, under the pretext and name of Alchemy, teach how to adulterate silver, gold, and coinage, and to commit such wicked crimes. This is true even if they claim for themselves the name of "chaste Chemistry," from which they ought to be most clearly distinguished. And if anyone confuses these frauds with the true art, they do so out of a sickness of the mind rather than sound judgment. If there were certain wretched

prostitutes, most deceitful pests, and most debauched temptresses in a city, should a most chaste virgin, conscious of no stain, be publicly shamed and confused with them under the same name? For one who judges thus, one would hope a bridle were placed on his tongue to restrain it, so that he might keep himself within the <note>original: "dentium vallum"; a classical metaphor referring to the lips and teeth acting as a defensive wall for speech</note> wall of his teeth. Thus should one judge regarding the fraudulent arts and true Chemistry: fraud is worthy of punishment, while truth is worthy of reward. 
<margin>The gold of Chemistry is of the same nature as natural gold in all its properties.</margin>
Furthermore, that the gold produced by Chemistry is genuine, true, and legitimate is evident from this: *first*, because according to countless witnesses who have tested it, it withstands all examinations and trials of gold, even if subjected to them a hundred times. *Second*, it possesses all the properties, virtues, efficacy, color, weight, and other <term>accidents: in traditional philosophy, "accidents" are the physical characteristics of a thing (like color or weight) that do not change its underlying essence</term> of natural gold itself. *Third*, it is made by nature (at least through the arrangement of the art) from the very same principles from which natural gold arises. Therefore, it is the truest gold, and should be called natural rather than artificial. Who

<margin>Chicks hatched by art are not artificial.</margin>
Who would doubt whether the chickens hatched by art in **Egypt** from eggs in ovens are real or fake? Surely only a false and deceitful judge would do so. Here, he argues that the purpose of all physical things—whether animals like horses or metals like lead and gold—is ultimately defined by their utility to humanity.</meta>

God, **GOD** exists alone from Himself, in Himself, and for Himself. The Heavens likewise have their own boundaries and ends; so too the lights <note>Referring to the sun, moon, and stars.</note> and the same must be said of the air, water, and earth, and their contents and creatures.

<margin>The various purposes of the horse.</margin>
The horse serves man with its swift and strong body, as well as its courage, for racing, for carrying loads, and for war. Meanwhile, there are those who eat them, namely the *Tartars* <note>A historical term for the various nomadic Turkic and Mongol peoples of Central and Northern Asia.</note>; just as we are nourished by the ox, they are nourished by the horse's milk and blood. Some horses are trained for games, such as mules; others for circling birds <note>Likely referring to falconry or using horses as "stalking horses" to approach wildfowl.</note>; to omit the rest, which of these is the more important purpose of the horse? Surely, it is to serve man, a purpose which encompasses all the others. The same must be said of metals, whether imperfect <note>Base metals like lead, tin, or copper.</note> or perfect <note>Gold and silver.</note>: they have many and diverse purposes, but the ultimate one is that they be applied to human uses. Therefore, whether gold is generated naturally from lead under the earth in *India*, or artificially anywhere above the ground, it still serves man under the form of gold just as it served him under the form of lead. But you will say that those uses are different; I respond that this is irrelevant. Because

<margin>The valuation of sheet lead in India.</margin>
man finds for himself the utility of any given thing. *That sheet lead, which is now carried by ships from Europe to India to the regions of the Great Mogul <note>The Mughal Emperor of India.</note>, is held in admiration there and is traded for an almost equal weight of pepper. Among us, it is of a much lower price. Because to them it is rarer, and thus more precious, it is perhaps employed for different uses than it is by us.*

<margin>The purposes of metals are not fixed, but depend on human judgment.</margin>
How, then, can anything be determined concerning the fixed purposes of gold and other cheaper metals, when they are employed now for these uses, now for others, according to human judgment? One hears of some who were hung from golden chains—indeed, even from gilded gallows; others have drunk from glass and used gold for dishonorable purposes. <meta>This page continues the argument regarding the "final cause" or ultimate purpose of substances. Maier is refuting the Aristotelian objection that if the purpose of base metals is to be themselves (e.g., lead's purpose is to be lead), then turning them into gold would "frustrate" or violate their natural purpose. He continues by discussing how human utility defines these purposes.</meta>

...the curious. On the contrary, iron was held in greater delight by certain nations than gold; for others, it was silver. Thus, human beings find various **ends** <note>The "end" (Latin: *finis*) refers to the philosophical purpose or goal for which a thing exists.</note> for metals under that one single overarching end: that they may enjoy them for their own utility, whether for medicine or other services. From this it is clear that the connection of the preceding proposition is like **loose brooms** <note>original: *scopae dissolutae*. A Latin idiom for a disjointed or weak argument that falls apart because its parts are not bound together by logic.</note>: even if certain metals are converted into gold, the remaining ones that are not converted will not be frustrated of their purpose, nor will those that are converted. For each will have its own forms, and thus its own purposes and uses. Nor is anything taken away from man by this; rather, as I believe, much utility is added.

<margin>The subordinate purpose of metals is to be converted into gold.</margin>

*Regarding the Minor Premise or assumption, I say that gold is not the ultimate purpose of the other metals, because their purpose is—as we said before—to serve humanity just as gold does. But it is a **subordinate purpose**; although all the more imperfect metals do not reach the ultimate state of gold, they will nevertheless achieve other purposes closer to that ultimate one. For instance, various vessels or instruments are fashioned from them which human use requires. Just as chicken eggs, if they are eaten by men before they reach their destined end—namely, the hatching of chicks—cannot be said to have been entirely frustrated of their*

<margin>Eggs eaten without reaching their ultimate end are not frustrated, but fulfill a subordinate one.</margin>

*purpose, since the chicks and the hens themselves are subject to the same end: being destined for human food. From this it appears that those are mistaken who, from the denial that gold is the end of other metals, conclude that **Chrysopoeia** <term>Chrysopoeia: The alchemical art of making gold.</term> is not true. For in their major proposition they speak of a subordinate end, and in their minor assumption they speak of the ultimate end. And thus nothing is concluded, namely*

### 13. Avicenna’s Affirmative Argument.

<margin>
13. Affirmative argument for Alchemy.
</margin>
If <term>Chrysopeia</term> <note>original: "Chrysopeia"; the alchemical art of making gold from base metals.</note> were an imaginary thing and a mere fable, there would not be such agreement regarding its principles, methods, and end among the peoples of all ages and languages; nor would there be any reason why those matters were veiled in mystery and not clearly handed down, nor would any experiments proving the truth of the art exist.

But all these things are exactly the opposite.

Therefore, gold-making is not an imaginary entity, but something real and true.

<margin>
Lies refute themselves.
</margin>
The <term>major proposition</term> <note>In traditional logic, the "major proposition" is the first part of a syllogism—a general statement used to reach a conclusion.</note> is evident from the light of nature; for it is often said: *a liar must have a good memory.* For unless he arranges everything he says so that what follows coheres with what went before and vice versa, and so that effects correspond to causes and attributes to subjects—so that times are matched with times, places with places, and persons with persons, whether examined by arithmetic or geometric proportion—he will easily refute himself and expose himself to the ridicule of all. Indeed,

<margin>

## 14. Avicenna’s Reason for Chemistry.

<margin>
14. An affirmative reason for chemistry.
</margin>
Everything that is pure, homogeneous, and uniform in all respects is more easily constructed than that which is a composite: impure, heterogeneous, and uneven in all respects. <note>Maier is citing Avicenna (Ibn Sina), the famous Persian physician whose views on alchemy were debated throughout the Middle Ages.</note>

Gold is pure, homogeneous, and uniform in all respects, whereas the other imperfect metals are the opposite of these.

Therefore, gold is more easily constructed than they are.

He addresses why it is easier to create "pure" gold than to manipulate "imperfect" metals, using principles of geometry, physics, and music to illustrate that certain, uniform things serve as the standard for all others.</meta>

->SYMBOLS<-

<margin>
The cause of the difficulty in producing imperfect metals, compared to gold.
</margin>
Whether the Adversary <note>The skeptic or opponent of alchemical theory.</note> has conceded that imperfect metals can be constructed or not, we do not labor much. In the meantime, you might ask others whether iron is not turned into copper in **Goslar** in **Saxony**, and in **Smolnik** in **Transylvania**, and elsewhere; or whether iron is not reduced into steel, and lead into mercury. Read **Alexander von Suchten** <note>A 16th-century physician and alchemist famous for his work on the medicinal properties of antimony.</note> regarding his **antimony**, and what he achieved with it. Truly, the cause of the difficulty in these cases, and the relative ease in the generation of gold, lies in this: that pure things are more easily discerned than impure things. Let an example be found in water that is distilled and pure; it cannot have more or less of one quality than another, except as its nature requires. That which is not pure, or is mixed, can be of infinite varieties—namely, as many as there are types of impurity.

<margin>
A homogeneous thing does not admit diverse elements.
</margin>
Thus, that which is **homogeneous** <note>Meaning "of the same kind" throughout; a substance of uniform structure.</note> rejects all diverse things; for instance, **quicksilver** <note>Mercury.</note> takes nothing into itself except what is of its own kind. However, if combustible sulfur is mixed in, that quicksilver can no longer be homogeneous, but becomes **heterogeneous** <note>Consisting of diverse or dissimilar ingredients.</note>. The homogeneous is one in substance; the heterogeneous is diverse. Likewise, if something is equal, it appears uniform in its equally extended qualities.

<margin>
A circle is equal to itself in all its parts.
</margin>
So the **circle** is equal to itself, more so than any other figure. Next is the equilateral quadrangle, or the equilateral **cube**, among solid bodies. Other figures are unequal and of infinite variety. From this it is clear that the pure, the homogeneous, and the equal are more easily produced, because there is a certainty of operation concerning them, whereas the opposite brings uncertainty.

<margin>
The certain is the rule for the uncertain.
</margin>
This is the reason why the **certain** is a perpetual rule for the **uncertain**, just as the circle is the rule among rounded things, the right angle among angles, the axis or straight line among lines, and the perpendicular line among those that stand upright. Hence, in every science and art, that which is equal and certain in all respects stands as the measure for the other, unequal thing. For instance, in **astronomy**, the motion of the **primum mobile** <note>The "first moved" sphere in the old geocentric model of the universe, which was believed to drive the rotation of all other celestial spheres.</note> being equal, measures all times, as does the "mean motion" of the planets measure their own unequal motions. In **arithmetic**, the rule of proportions is the foundation of other rules because it is more "equal" than the rest.

<margin>
The Diapason is the rule in music.
</margin>
In **Music**, the **Diapason** <note>The interval of an octave.</note> is the rule of the **major third** <note>original: "ditoni"</note>...

<summary>Maier argues that alchemical transformation is possible by citing industrial examples like iron turning to copper. He explains that working with pure, homogeneous substances (like gold) is theoretically easier than working with "impure" ones because they follow certain, uniform laws of nature, similar to geometry and music.</summary>

Regarding the other imperfect metals, as with the planets, the operation proceeds with far greater difficulty.

But gold excels the remaining metals in dignity, duration, and in its internal transformation.

Therefore, it can not unfairly be called their **end** <note>Maier uses "end" (Latin: *finis*) in the sense of a "final goal" or the ultimate purpose for which a thing exists, a concept from Aristotelian philosophy.</note>.

*If this is true, then **Chrysopoeia** <note>original: "Chrysopoeia"; the alchemical art of making gold.</note> also appears true from that premise; if it is not true, the art is nonetheless not destroyed.*

For (as you brought up in your next argument) if gold is the end of the other metals, then these other metals seem to be generated by nature so that they may be changed into gold—that is, so they may be led back to their proper end. <margin>Why gold is called the "end" of the remaining metals.</margin>

*The most true proposition of this syllogism is clear in this way:* Man is the end of all bodily creatures because he is more dignified than they are. Because gold also lasts longer and is a sort of incorruptible thing compared to the rest, it appears to be their end for this reason: either because it outlasts their decay—excepting man (who, although he dies, will nonetheless live eternally, and to whom nothing else happens than what happens to gold when it is purged of **foreign elements** <note>original: "heterogeneis"; impurities or substances of a different nature mixed into the metal.</note> by fire)—or because it overcomes other things exposed to fire with an unconquered strength. <margin>When Albert was born.</margin>

He was born in the year of Christ 1193 near Lauingen in Swabia <note>a cultural and linguistic region in southwestern Germany</note>, or as others would have it, in Bavaria, of the noble family of Bollstädt, to most honorable parents. When they had handed him over to the study of letters, he excelled all his fellow students in a short time.

<margin>Albert the Great to be compared with the greatest philosophers.</margin>
Finally, the powers of his genius extended so far that he deserved to be compared with the greatest philosophers, such as *Aristotle* and *Varro* <note>Marcus Terentius Varro was an ancient Roman scholar often called "the most learned of the Romans"</note>.

<margin>What Albert the Great wrote about.</margin>
For he completed the entire Encyclopedia most perfectly, being skilled in both divine and human sciences, which is why he stood out in the admiration of all. He wrote on <term>Dialectics</term> <note>the art of logical argument and investigation</note>, *Mathematics*, *Physics*, *Ethics*, *Metaphysics*, *Medicine*, *Chemistry* <note>here referring to alchemy</note>, *Magic*, and *Theology* (just as all these books are listed by *Trithemius* <note>Johannes Trithemius, a 15th-century Benedictine abbot and famous bibliographer of ecclesiastical writers</note>); and he treated each subject with such diligence and sharpness as if he had touched only these and never any others.

<margin>Albert the Great's commentaries on whom.</margin>
He was the first among Latin writers to write commentaries on the books of *Aristotle*, *Euclid*, *Peter Lombard* <note>author of the *Sentences*, the standard medieval textbook of theology</note>, and those similar to them.

<margin>Albert the Great honored in Paris.</margin>
Wherefore, on account of his supreme learning and the loftiness of his genius, he achieved the most ample honors and a great name in the Academy of *Paris*.

<margin>Albert a professor of physics in Paris.</margin>
Having scrutinized the secrets of nature most clearly, he publicly taught physics in Paris.

<margin>Albert the Great considered a sorcerer by fools.</margin>
At this point, certain eccentric people, either out of envy or ignorance, proclaimed him a sorcerer <note>original: "pro-mago." among these students, *Thomas Aquinas*—who was later accepted as a Saint—stood as his disciple.

<margin>Albert the Great was devoted to Alchemy.</margin>
<margin>The chemical books of Albert the Great.</margin>

Therefore, **ALBERTUS Magnus** put much labor and study into Alchemy, of which *Pantaleon* mentions not even a word, as if recoiling from it; yet this should detract nothing from the truth. He published several books on the subject: one is titled *On Alchemy* <note>original: "de Alchymia"</note>, though it has been expanded and stuffed with many other additions and sophistications by others; another is *On the Concordance of Philosophers* <note>original: "de concordantia philosophorum"</note>, specifically the Chemical ones; and another *On the Composition of the Composite* <note>original: "de compositione compositi"</note>. Besides these and his book *On Minerals* <note>original: "de mineralibus"</note>, there are many others which we do not yet have in published form. How great and perfect a Chemist *Albert* was is sufficiently declared especially by those last three most complete treatises. Even if some of these were ignorantly joined to his collected works by editors, nevertheless, his style alone—aside from the title inscription and the consensus of the Chemists—makes it plain and indubitable that they belong to Albert himself and no other. In the first of those treatises, he himself confesses in this manner:

> *I have traversed,* he says, *many regions and very many provinces, as well as cities and castles, for the sake of the science which is called Alchemy, with the greatest labor; and I have inquired about this art among literate and wise men, so that I might investigate it more fully. Thus says <term>Albert</term>. All these things, spoken according to the mind of the **Chemists**, are suitable to no one else but the craftsman, all other things being equal.*

<margin>Albertus Magnus was a most diligent investigator of metallic nature.</margin>
*<term>Dionysius Zacharius</term> <note>A 16th-century French alchemist known for his autobiographical account of the "Great Work."</note> testifies that <term>Albert</term> was a most diligent investigator of metallic nature above all other **Chemists**; as does the aforementioned <term>Count of Mirandola</term> <note>Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola (1469–1533), who wrote "De Auro" (On Gold) in defense of alchemy.</note> in Book 2, Chapter 7 *On Gold*; who says: "<term>Albert</term>, writing of himself, saw pure gold among river sands, and heard of impure gold arising from mixed stones, like veins," and he adds not long after, that gold born among sands is better, for which fact he brings forward two causes:* 

*One is the greater purity of the sulfur, having been moved among hot and dry sands and being washed more frequently; and also that of the earthy [substance] which is in the <term>quicksilver</term>, which the river both washed and rendered more subtle and pure by the frequent washing of the stream. The other cause he intended to be the closing of the passages, where, shut up in the bottom and the banks, it is rolled into itself and <term>concocted</term> <note>original: "concoquitur." Alchemical "concoction" refers to a process of ripening or maturing through heat, similar to digestion or cooking.</note> into the substance of gold, bringing forth a more noble result,*

...and these things he <note>Referring to Albertus Magnus</note> said while he was mentioning the places in which metals are generated. It appears from many indications that <term>Albert</term> himself visited these places, as he narrates what was found in various metal mines in his own time. Where he discusses the nature of gold, he says a **grain** 

<margin>
Natural gold, that is, a giant grain.
</margin>

was found which exceeded the weight of many pounds; <term>Mirandula</term> <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a famous Italian Renaissance philosopher who also wrote on alchemy.</note> used the term "one hundred marks," which name designates eight ounces, so that those who weighed it found the grain to have been eight hundred ounces. He also recounts that in his time **mountain gold** was found in **Germany**, which, when it was smelted,

<margin>
Mountain gold of Germany.
</margin>

was consumed less than others <note>meaning it was very pure and didn't lose mass to dross during refining</note>, although he reports it was of a cheaper price on account of its novelty. He likewise records that gold was found in the hair of a future human skull and within the teeth. Whether this occurrence was a matter of artifice or a miracle may be doubted; certainly, it was not natural. Although I have often read of the **golden tooth of the Silesian boy** (which was actually fitted by a certain deception) <note>Maier refers to a famous 1593 hoax where a child was claimed to have grown a natural gold tooth; it was eventually found to be a clever gold crown.</note>, of gold generated from a vine and its tendrils like hair, 

<margin>
Gold found in the human head.
</margin>

and of many other such miraculous generations of gold. For gold does not naturally arise from flesh, bones, hair, or wood, but only from its own **proximate matter** in appropriate places. Moreover, the proximate matter is **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> coagulated by its own **sulfur**. If gold were said to be found between the teeth or within the earth alone, it might be excused as a human insertion 

<margin>
Gold is generated only from its own proximate matter.
</margin>

due to the superstition of many. For we find that among the **Romans**, they used to insert a certain type of coin into the mouth of a dying person as a **ferry-fare** <note>original: "naulo"</note> to be paid to **Charon** <note>The mythological ferryman who carried souls across the river Styx.</note> in the underworld. But after this also began to be sought in tombs by the greed of the living, especially soldiers,

<margin>
The Romans used to insert an obol into the mouth of the dying for the ferry-fare.
</margin>

the corpses of the dead were burned on a pyre, which custom endured until the time of Christianity. Why say more? <term>Albert</term> shows himself to be a **Chemist** <note>Maier uses "Chymicus" to mean a practitioner of alchemy.</note> not only in his books (even if he were to deny it), written so learnedly and clearly, that unless 

<margin>
Albert is known as a Chemist not only from his books but from chemical works.
</margin>

they prove him a Chemist, no other man could be judged by his published monuments as to what his doctrine or profession might be. And besides himself, anyone else, and also the effects and works of **Chemistry** most truly performed by him, are celebrated throughout the whole world.

### SYMBOLS

<margin>How Albert the Great, as Bishop, paid off his debts while always devoted to study.</margin>

...they proclaim: For how could the Bishop himself—having already become an old man over 67 years of age, always hiding away in his study among books and letters—show himself to be such a good administrator <note>The Latin *oeconomum* refers here to a household or estate manager.</note> that he freed the Bishopric from its debt? Truly, this is hardly believable; even if annual revenues, moderately spent by him, could have helped a little, yet in those few years in which he presided over the Bishopric, it would have been a meager amount.

<margin>Albert the Great paid off a large debt in a short time.</margin>

For the aforementioned historian says that it was a *large* debt. And it seems even more marvelous that, once the Bishopric was freed from its debts, he abdicated the office and embraced a lowlier condition, namely the teaching and instructing of youth in good literature <note>In the 13th century, "literature" or "letters" referred to the whole of classical and theological learning.</note>.

<margin>Abraham Bucholzer: It is an admirable thing in our times for a Bishopric to be refused by anyone.</margin>

*For we know,* says another chronicler <note>Maier cites Abraham Bucholzer (1529–1584), a German historian and theologian.</note>, *with what labors Bishoprics are acquired; once acquired, it is scarcely ever heard of that they are rejected after they have been marveled at.* Concerning this, several points come to be considered: *First*, that he was made a bishop from being a monk; *second*, how, though occupied with literature, he was able to pay off another's debts; *third*, why he did not rather help his own relatives with his money; *fourth*, why he left such a grand Bishopric; *fifth*, why he chose the office of teaching, which is exceedingly laborious.

<margin>Learning made Albert "the Great," and turned a monk into a bishop.</margin>

*Regarding the first point:* As said before, his diverse and learned teaching in every kind of art, and his published writings, were the chief cause; among physical matters and minerals, however, he dealt both practically and theoretically.

<margin>Alchemy <note>original: *Chemia*</note> presupposes various arts.</margin>

Since this science <note>referring to Alchemy</note> either presupposes all kinds of arts or demands them before anything may be completed with success; hence the <term>Encyclopedia</term> <note>Literally the "circle of learning." Maier argues that alchemy cannot be understood in isolation; it requires a complete mastery of all sciences.</note> was joined with **Alchemy** in *Albert*, as it ought to be. For just as a point without a circular circumference does not make the figure of a circle, so neither can Alchemy be investigated through the reading of its terms without other arts or sciences.

<margin>Albert the Great produced the Phoenix.</margin>

*Regarding the second point:* We state most certainly that *Albert*, having used the furnaces of Alchemy after so many years of investigation and experience, produced from them the **Phoenix** <note>In alchemical symbolism, the "Phoenix" represents the Philosopher's Stone, which is "reborn" through fire and can transmute base metals into gold.</note>, which [wrought] these wonders...

# BOOK VI OF THE GOLDEN TABLE

...might have performed; whether he knew this craft <note>The Latin *artificium* refers to the "Great Work" of alchemy.</note> perfectly before undertaking the Bishopric can be doubted; as for me, I do not think so, but rather that from his youth until that old age he was constant in his investigation, until it seemed good to God to reveal this hidden science to the now-declared Bishop. 
<margin>Albertus Magnus, as an old man and Bishop, rediscovered the art.</margin>
For this reason, he remained in perpetual study, and because he kept his furnaces in a more secret place, he stayed there. It was not necessary for others to know this, whoever they might be. Therefore, it was not the fame, but the **effect** of alchemy that was known by the common people, and this far preceded the fame (which is produced only from books) of what ought to be done. 
<margin>Albertus Magnus’s instruction on observing silence.</margin>
From this, he himself places among the precepts of alchemy to be observed by the initiate: that no one should reveal to others, whoever they may be, that they are practicing chemistry. Otherwise, if those people are nobles, they will ask the working craftsman almost every day: "Master, how are your affairs proceeding?" If they go badly, he will face mockery and laughter; 
<margin>Silence imposed upon all philosophers among all nations.</margin>
if they go well, he will be detained so that he cannot leave. Hence, a perpetual silence under oath was imposed upon the Egyptians, the Pythagoreans, the Brahmins <note>original: *Brachmanis*</note>, the Gymnosophists <term>Gymnosophists: Meaning "naked philosophers," these were ancient Indian ascetics known for their pursuit of wisdom and their influence on Greek philosophy.</term>, and all other investigators and learned masters of hidden doctrine. It did not please him to show himself as knowledgeable in this art in the presence of the Pope or princes, as he was more intent on the instruction and training of others than on his own display. 
<margin>Albertus Magnus was the first to write on the concordance of philosophers.</margin>
For this reason, he was the first of all to write most subtly concerning the *Concordance of Philosophers* <note>original: *concordantia philosophorum*</note>, so that everyone might see in which matters the philosophers agree and in which they do not. This book ought to be considered of great utility among chemists, as it was published not by someone still wandering in the investigation of the art, but by a perfected master. 
<margin>Consideration of concordances in books is highly beneficial.</margin>
Without the collection and consideration of concordances in the writings of all philosophers, no one can achieve the hoped-for end. As to the third point: why did he not help his kinsmen with his money? If it were from the revenues of his domain, he could not; if from alchemy, he both could...

<margin>Albertus Magnus: why do you leave the bishopric?</margin>
And without doubt, he willed it: *Fourthly*, neither old age nor labors were the cause for leaving the Bishopric. For there is no Bishop so old who does not desire to die in his own status rather than in some lower one. Nor are the labors of the Bishops of our lands (who enjoy principal dignity) so great that they cannot be tolerated by anyone, even of a decrepit age. Therefore, it was a contempt for truly worldly pomp in spiritual matters that was in his mind, as he was dedicated to humility before God; thus, he preferred to leave this dignity rather than retain it against the truest conception of his own mind. Nor should anyone think that he did this out of simplicity of mind or hoping for a vacation from cares;
<margin>Albertus Magnus was the most learned in Europe.</margin>
for he himself was the most learned of all in his age, not only of *Germany* (whence *Münster* <note>Sebastian Münster (1488–1552), a famous cartographer and scholar whose *Cosmographia* was the earliest German description of the world.</note> records in his cosmographical writings that *Lauingen* <note>Albert's birthplace in Bavaria.</note> fostered at one and the same time a most learned man—namely, Albertus Magnus—a most beautiful woman, and a most massive horse) but he also stood out in *Europe*, by which reason he knew how to easily preside over a Bishopric. Regarding the fifth point, that he did not desire a vacation from cares, it is evident from this: that he took up a far heavier burden, namely that of teaching, and as the saying goes, *he descended from horses to oxen* <note>A Latin proverb (*ab equis ad boves*) describing someone who leaves a position of honor for one of more grueling, manual labor.</note>. Why this duty seemed more pleasing to him than the Bishopric is perhaps not so clear: *Honors change manners, but rarely for the better, as the proverb goes* <note>Original: *Honores mutant mores, sed rarò in meliores*.</note>. In the case of this Bishop, the opposite occurred. For as a monk and an Academic professor, he did not refuse to be a Bishop when he was elected; yet having been confirmed as such a great man, he submitted his manners and his life to a certain humility, and from Episcopal sublimity, he returned entirely to a lower state.
<margin>Albertus Magnus, leaving the bishopric, underwent greater labors.</margin>
<margin>Why Albert deserves to be called "Great."</margin>
By this name alone—"the Great"—he is most worthy to be called, as some judge. It is the mark of a noble and candid man to clearly teach
<margin>Gratitude and honor are owed to teachers.</margin>
others those things which he himself learned through reading, the use of things <note>Practical experience or experimentation.</note>, and from the instruction of others. Likewise, it is the duty of disciples to offer every readiness of will and benevolence of mind to the one teaching—

...to those seeking <note>Continuing from the previous page's "to exhibit to those seeking..."</note>: For many among the philosophers have left it in writing that an equivalent price of gratitude cannot be offered to teachers and parents. # SYMBOLS

<margin>Albertus Magnus was called a mage by the envious.</margin>
...he recounts the triflers; the malicious, out of envy, called *Albertus Magnus* a "mage" because of his supreme subtlety of mind and his abundance of learning, as if he could not have written such great works of divine and human wisdom by his own strength <note>original: "proprio Marte," literally "by his own Mars," a Roman idiom for one's own efforts or courage</note> unless he had been aided for a long time by the help of the Devil. *Away with you and those blasphemies!* This is the diabolical or slanderous opinion of the common people—or rather, of the "many-headed beast"—by which even the *Savior, both God and man*, was blasphemed for casting out devils by the help of the devil. Every most learned man is forced to undergo the same judgment. O thick-skulled ones, why do you cloak your ignorance with insults against the learned? O heartless breasts, why do you offer infamy to cover your own stupor toward celebrated men? Because you do not grasp a thing, do you think they do not grasp it either—*mice judging elephants, as it were?* But you are deceived, and your madness shall be sent back home to you, along with those unrefined dirges, discarded trifles, and futile scraps.

<margin>One is not immediately a mage who is wiser than the common crowd.</margin>
He is not immediately a mage who is wiser than the common crowd of teachers, but rather he approaches more closely to the *angelic and divine nature* the further he recedes from human dregs and elevates himself. Meanwhile, we do not excuse <term>Necromancers</term> <note>Practitioners of "black magic" or those who supposedly conjure the spirits of the dead</note>, but we detest them in every way as the bondservants of the devil. It is most certain that *Albertus* was by no means such a person. *If as a young man he scrutinized anything in <term>natural magic</term>, it is worthy of the highest praise, not blame; by this I mean knowing the natural virtues implanted in things by God and joining active things with passive ones to produce a natural effect, not opposed to GOD and useful to man.* <note>Maier defines "natural magic" as what we might today call experimental science or physics—using the inherent properties of nature to achieve results.</note> He who counts <term>Chemistry</term> <note>In this context, Maier uses "Chemistry" and "Alchemy" interchangeably to mean the pursuit of the Philosopher's Stone</note> among trifles should prove it first before he asserts it. For this is a "begging of the question," alien to all reason.

<margin>As an old man, Albertus Magnus did not say farewell to Chemistry, but having attained it, he said farewell to his Bishopric.</margin>
As a young man, he investigated <term>Chemical matters</term> through travels, readings, and various experiments; having become an old man, with his judgment confirmed by so many things seen, done, read, and heard, he found the truth. Therefore, he by no means abdicated <term>Chemistry</term>, but having attained it, he abdicated his Bishopric. This alone was...

## THE GERMAN COMPATRIOTS OF ALBERTUS MAGNUS

<margin>How many peoples Germany once encompassed.</margin>
**G**ermany, by its circumference and its communion of language, embraces many peoples—*formerly fifty, now with its borders greatly expanded everywhere*—and without doubt far more: Yet all these are *one Nation, and they enjoy one language (unless distinguished by different dialects), and one supreme Prince (excepting those who, not by compulsion but of their own accord, have subjected themselves to other neighbors or asserted their own liberty).* First...

<margin>Count Bernard, a German.</margin>
BERNARD, COUNT OF TREVISO, is numbered among the *German Nation* rather than any other: For he is not Italian, nor does he write that he is, and he never published anything in Italian, as far as we know. Indeed, his most learned <term>Chemical</term> <note>At this time, "chemical" referred to the art of Alchemy</note> book exists in the German, French, and Latin languages,
<margin>Count Bernard is not Italian.</margin>
(perhaps now even in Italian); however, because he was skilled in all these languages, there is doubt about which one he originally wrote in. We know it was translated from German into Latin by *Michael Toxites* <note>A famous 16th-century editor of alchemical and Paracelsian texts</note>. It is believable that he published his book in both German and French: Moreover, many signs demonstrate that he was a *German*; because he makes separate mention of the Emperor's court, in which he was well known, as if speaking of his own Prince and Lord.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Bernard, Count of Treviso, a famous 15th-century alchemist. The author is refuting common misconceptions about Bernard's origins, specifically arguing against those who confuse him with the Count of Trier or the Count Palatine, while establishing his identity as a German-descended noble from Treviso, Italy, which was then under the Holy Roman Empire.</meta>

### SYMBOLS

<margin>
The territory of Trier was not a county, nor did it obey Bernard.
</margin>
<margin>
Bernard was not the Count Palatine of the Rhine.
</margin>

Rather, he was master of German coinage, and of his own goods and inheritances which were under the Empire. *Others* do not doubt that he was German, but they make him the *Count of Trier* <note>original: "Comitem Treuirenfem." Trier is a city in western Germany. The author argues that because Bernard was called "Trevisanus," people mistakenly linked him to Trier (Treveris) instead of Treviso.</note>, even though the territory and city of Trier is an Electorate and Archbishopric of the same name. Some think he was the *Count Palatine of the Rhine*, an opinion that is entirely erroneous and requires no refutation; for the genealogy and family of those Most Illustrious Princes is well known, and acknowledges no "Bernard" in the age in which he lived. But what sort of man he was, the logic of the name itself shows: for he is most commonly called the Count of Treviso or the Trevisan. **TREVISO**, however, is a town lying near the Gulf of the *Adriatic*, not far from Venice; and it now exists under the power of the Venetians, though in Bernard’s time, 150 years ago, it still obeyed the Empire. 

<margin>
Bernard, Count of Treviso, was under the Empire in his own time.
</margin>

There is no doubt, therefore, that Bernard was a Count in this region, as were his ancestors. He himself admits that he sold a large part of his inheritance, and moreover, while he was at Rhodes, he received another sum of money from a certain man who knew his relatives very well. 

<margin>
The County of Treviso has now ceased to exist.
</margin>

But this county has now ceased to exist along with Bernard's family and Imperial jurisdiction, so much so that not even a memory of it remains. If anyone can more clearly demonstrate that Bernard's county belonged to another nation or country, there is no reason for me to be angry with them. 

<margin>
Count Bernard was not a Frenchman.
</margin>

We presuppose him to be German, since he completely dissociates himself from the French King in his letter to *Thomas of Bologna* <note>Thomas of Bologna was the court physician to King Charles VIII of France and a fellow alchemist.</note>; where he says: *"Your Reverence saw the proof of this saying in the powder formerly sent to the King, whose physician you are."* <note>The "powder" refers to a medicinal or alchemical substance, often associated with the "Philosopher's Stone" or a "Powder of Projection" used to transform metals.</note>

<margin>
The errors and labors of Count Bernard.
</margin>

With how many labors, expenses, experiments, errors, and difficulties this man was led around while he searched for the Art <note>The "Art" refers to Alchemy (the Great Work).</note>, he himself describes quite extensively, and there is no need to introduce them here. 

<margin>
When Count Bernard lived.
</margin>

He lived—as can be gathered from the letter to *Thomas of Bologna*, the physician of *Charles VIII*, King of France—around the year of Christ 1484 (the year in which Charles began to reign, until the year 1508).

1498.) And at this time, Bernard was perhaps over seventy years old. Having attained the Art <note>The "Art" refers to the completion of the Great Work, the creation of the Philosopher's Stone.</note> as an old man, he was solicited by a French physician <note>original: "medico Gallo"</note> and burdened, rather than honored, by the gift of a certain "stone"; nevertheless, he accepted the gift most graciously, as befitted such a great man, as his own words testify in this manner:

<margin>Bernard treats the physician of Bologna politely.</margin>

<margin>Bernard, the Count, a most true expert of Chemistry.</margin>
How much judgment and skill in Chemistry <term>Chemistry: In the 15th and 16th centuries, "Chymia" or Chemistry encompassed both practical laboratory work and the spiritual/philosophical pursuit of alchemy.</term> this good old man possessed—after so many truly Herculean efforts and labors—is demonstrated by this single Letter alone. To all lovers of Chemistry, it is like a torch in the darkness and a statue of Mercury at a crossroads <note>In antiquity, "Herms" or statues of Mercury were used as guideposts; Maier suggests Bernard's writings serve as a guide for lost seekers.</note>. He declares himself to be excellently learned in Aristotelian Philosophy and Galenic Medicine. He discourses most expertly on the generation of metals beneath the earth and their diversity from one another.

<margin>In Chemistry, Bernard joins the Sun (Gold) with Mercury. In a true solution, the solvent and the solute are united without any separation.</margin>
In the works of the art, he affirms that *Mercury is joined to Gold*—namely, the passive to the active—and thus that which dissolves is united with that which is to be dissolved, remaining indivisibly. For he says thus:

> *Indeed, this solution requires the simultaneous permanence of both the solvent and the solute, so that from both—namely, the male and female seed—a new species results. Truly I say to you, that no water by natural reduction dissolves a metallic species, except that which remains with them in matter and form, and which the dissolved metals themselves can recongeal. This does not happen with "strong waters" <term>strong waters: "Aqua fortis" or nitric acid. Bernard argues that acids merely "defile" or destroy the metal's form, whereas a true alchemical solvent unites with it.</term>; rather, it is a corruption of the composite, namely of the body to be dissolved. Nor does a water belong to bodies in solutions if it does not remain with them in congelations. Finally, Mercury is of this kind, and not "strong waters," or what fools think of as a clear and transparent mercurial water.*

<margin>Bernard, profound in chemical matters.</margin>
Indeed, while Bernard appears very clear in these matters, he also remains profoundly deep. His book on *Hermetic Philosophy* is in the hands and admiration of all.

<margin>Bernard’s book should be regarded more for its Theory than its practice.</margin>
And indeed, it is most worthy of being read in this genre, so that the *Theory* of the work might be understood from it rather than the *practice*, even though everyone rushes headlong toward the latter. His *Allegory* <note>original: "Allegoria"; refers to Bernard's famous alchemical parable "The Fountain of the King."</note> explaining the practice is not as easy as it appears at first glance. With the delight of a fable, just as *Orpheus* once drew the oaks and wild beasts, it attracts everyone—the learned and the unlearned alike—but beyond the charms for the ears and the imagination, they rarely bring anything back from it.

<margin>Bernard acquired envy along with old age.</margin>
The reason is that he himself discovered the art when he had become an old man, an age which easily falls prey to envy; he discovered it so that no young man might mock him before reaching his own gray-haired years. *For this reason, names are multiplied,* the old men say in a crowd, *lest venerable old age be pointed out by the fingers of boys.* <note>Maier suggests that Bernard used cryptic terminology ("multiplied names") to hide his secrets from the young and disrespectful, preserving the dignity of his old age.</note>

<margin>The King in the Fountain.</margin>
# **The King**
Indeed, he sits in the *Fountain* washing himself, like a naked *Diana*; both refuse to be seen without their garments. Who is so bold that he would prefer to play the part of *Actaeon* <note>In Greek mythology, Actaeon was a hunter who saw the goddess Diana bathing; she turned him into a stag, and he was torn apart by his own dogs. Maier uses this as a metaphor for the danger of approaching alchemical secrets—the "naked" truth—without proper preparation.</note>, rather than abstaining from things that are not his? He describes the water of the fountain and the fire most excellently.

<margin>Let Vulcan build the fire moderately.</margin>
But care must be taken lest *Vulcan* <note>Vulcan was the Roman god of fire; in alchemy, the name often refers to the heat of the furnace or the "secret fire" used in the chemical process.</note> overheats the summer air, which is already dry and hot by itself. For it would be more prudent to begin the operation when the *South Wind* <note>original: "Noto"</note> is blowing, which glides down from the high mountains; then the heat of that fiery *Deity* would be somewhat diminished, and the *Etesian winds* <note>Cool, seasonal Mediterranean winds that provide a tempering effect.</note> would bring with them a temperate balance of cold and hot, dry and moist.

<margin>When the work is to be begun, and what is required.</margin>
Thus some state the work should be started when the *Sun* enters *Taurus*, and others *Aquarius* (because these two signs are seen at the same declination from the Equator), all of which is said for the purpose of moderating the heat. For if the true matter is held together with its agent, arranged as is fitting, then the *Fire and the Vessel of Hermes* <term>Vessel of Hermes: A specialized glass container (often called the philosopher's egg) used for the Great Work, named after the legendary founder of alchemy, Hermes Trismegistus.</term>—that is, two in one and one in two, fire in fire, vessel in vessel, and each in the other—are sufficient.

<margin>Four types of fires are necessary in Chemistry, and as many vessels.</margin>
Furthermore, according to all who truly philosophize, we require three fires—and if we count correctly, four; and just as many containing vessels. Regarding the fires, the *natural, unnatural, and preternatural* must be properly kindled, so that, of course, this one does not suffocate that one, and that one does not suffocate the other. The *fourth* among all these, like a servant...

...is added, tempered from the *Igneous* and *Aerial Element*: As for the *vessels*, although it is said by many that one is sufficient, it is nevertheless understood that three are contained within that one: for the first is considered opaque, the second less so, and the third even less. # **BASILIUS VALENTINUS**, a Monk of the *Benedictine Order*, a most accomplished German Philosopher, is said to have originated from *Alsace*, and to have lived in the same place—or, as others say, in the capital of *Thuringia*—and to have written his works, which have now finally been made public. He is held to have flourished in the age of our great-grandfathers: for he made no mention in his books of the circumstances of time, place, or persons, from which anything certain regarding his life, actions, and character could be gathered.

<margin>Live hiddenly.</margin>
He preferred to remain obscure to all rather than to become well-known: for that seemed safer to him than *to be pointed out with a finger and have it said, "this is the man"* <note>original: "digito monstrari & dicier, hic est ille"; a quote from the Roman satirist Persius, meaning to be famous or notorious.</note> who, alone among all *Chemists*, devised the little white and red stone <note>The "white and red stones" refer to the two stages of the Philosopher's Stone: the white for transmuting metals into silver, and the red for gold.</note>.

<margin>True masters of Chemistry do not care for popular favor.</margin>
Nor indeed, as was once the case with *Demosthenes* <note>An ancient Greek orator known for his public influence.</note>, is the sweetness of popular favor valued so highly by true masters that they would expose themselves to the common crowd, to be partly admired and partly cursed: for while admiration arises from the novelty of a thing among the well-disposed, so does envy among those of a different mind. But perhaps *Basilius* explained himself sufficiently in his other writings which we have not yet seen, if any such exist.

<margin>Extant writings of Basilius Valentinus.</margin>
However, his *Twelve Keys* are extant, along with the *Theory and Practice* at their beginning; also another *On the Sevenfold Marvelous Birth of the Planets*; a third *On Natural and Supernatural Things*; and a fourth, the *Triumphant Chariot* <note>Referring to the "Triumphant Chariot of Antimony," one of the most famous alchemical texts attributed to Valentinus.</note>...

<margin>The Genealogy of gold and the Tincture.</margin>
it begin its genealogy from an animal or a vegetable? Therefore, the father of gold is the *Tincture*, and the mother is quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuum"; mercury</note>; the grandfather is Mercury, but fixed; the grandmother is likewise mercurial, but volatile. What could be proposed more clearly than this allegory, which is entirely parallel to Basil’s *Twelve Keys*?

<margin>He left 12 Keys to open the Philosophical Fortress.</margin>
...[He] left [the keys] behind, which he set forth for all to see like a most generous *steward* <term>Promus condus</term> <note>original: "Promus condus"; a Roman term for a household manager who both stores and distributes goods, here used to describe Basil Valentine's role in providing the "keys" to knowledge</note>, in order to unlock the innermost approaches of the *Philosophical Fortress*, so that no gate might remain closed. For that FORTRESS is the place where the VIRGIN CHEMISTRY <term>CHEMIA VIRGO</term> <note>Alchemy is personified here as a pure, elusive maiden who guards her secrets from the unworthy</note> resides with all her mysteries and secrets, which have not yet been revealed to the common folk or the unworthy.

<margin>The Gates of the Chemical Fortress, to which the 12 keys belong, and how they are named.</margin>
These gates are each called by their own name: *one* is called MATTER, *the other* FORM. The *third* is TEMPERAMENT <note>original: "complexio"; the balancing of elemental qualities</note> or CONJUNCTION; *another* is COOKING <note>original: "coctio"; the process of ripening or perfecting a substance through heat</note>, *another* VULCAN’S FIRE, *another* RAINING FIRE; there is also one called the HERMETIC VESSEL, and another called the PEACOCK’S TAIL <note>original: "pavonis cauda"; a famous stage in alchemy where the matter in the flask displays many brilliant colors</note>. One is known as SOLUTION, another as CONGEALATION. After these, FIXATION is celebrated, and finally, PROJECTION <note>the final act of casting the completed Philosopher's Stone onto base metals to transform them into gold</note>.

<margin>6 operational and 6 instrumental gates.</margin>
Although all these gates might be called by different names by others, such as *Ripley* <note>George Ripley, a famous 15th-century English alchemist known for his "Twelve Gates"</note>, as if each were a separate operation, they seem superfluous in this regard; for there are at least six that denote an operation, and just as many others that conceal the instruments of the art. Without a doubt, the *Keys of Basil* are meant to be fitted to these gates, which anyone will easily find for themselves. For he who does not know how to join matter to form has not yet begun: Matter is always the passive and manifold one, appearing in a feminine habit; Form is the active and simple one, in a masculine habit.

<margin>How the gates are necessary in order.</margin>
Therefore, join the red servant to his fragrant sister <note>Alchemical allegories for specific substances, often sulfur and mercury</note>, and these two will give birth to the son of the art. Then, there is also a need for cooking, without which nothing ripens. But cooking requires a heat that is hot and dry, which is "roasting" <note>original: "assatio"</note>; or another that is moist and exhaling, which is "boiling" <note>original: "elixatio"</note>. Nor can these things be handled without the aid of a vessel. From there, as the work continues, solution, congealation, and fixation occur—where the "infant" <note>a common term for the emerging Philosopher's Stone</note> is born—and finally its operation or projection.

His *Chemical Monuments* <note>original: "Chymica monumenta"; likely referring to works on alchemy attributed to Alanus</note> are available and widely circulated; he is distinguished as one skilled in the Chemical art. We will not stir up a dispute regarding his homeland; for we group the *Flemings*—as well as neighboring peoples who use the *Teutonic* <note>The Germanic language family</note> tongue as their mother tongue—among the peoples of greater *Germany*. This man is said to have been most versatile in every circle of learning. *Albert Krantz*, the historian of *Saxony*, makes him a contemporary of *John Duns Scotus* <note>A famous medieval philosopher and theologian, c. 1266–1308</note>. Regarding this *Alanus*, who was a man of the most excellent talent, supreme judgment, and erudition most complete in every respect, they recall a certain story: that when Queen *Margaret*, wife of the aforementioned king, once contemplated him sleeping upon a certain chest for a long time (for he was quite deformed of face), she kissed him most sweetly. When all those standing by wondered at this and asked her the reason, that most wise *Lady* answered them thus: that this old man, so deformed in his outward appearance and withered, hid within himself such an excellent and divine soul that nothing in the world is so precious or beautiful that it could be compared to it. Because she herself was unable to grasp or touch the divinity of such a great Spirit, she wished to make use of this opportunity to return, as if in passing, to his outward form to declare her affection toward those things which she so greatly admired in the soul of such an outstanding man.

# THE GOLDEN TABLE. BOOK VI.

<margin>Prophecies attributed to Merlin by monks.</margin>
The prophecies are surreptitious <note>original: "subreptitia"; meaning fraudulent or substituted</note> and were fabricated by certain monks during the time of Henry II to curry favor with the king. They were spread among the common people under the name of Merlin (whom they say was born from an Incubus <note>A male demon believed to have sexual intercourse with sleeping women</note> or Demon before the arrival of the Germanic Saxons in Britain). Albert Krantz <note>A German historian, c. 1448–1517</note> writes that the epitaph of Alanus of the Cistercians survives in these verses:

<margin>The Epitaph of Alanus at the Cistercian monastery.</margin>

> *Here lies ALANUS, whom a brief hour entombed,*
> *Who knew two, who knew seven, and everything knowable.*

<margin>Two and seven, chemical weights.</margin>
<margin>The sayings of Alanus.</margin>
<margin>A double fire for Alanus.</margin>
<margin>Horse dung and its use in Chemistry.</margin>
<margin>The dropsical man is cured without the sun.</margin>
What those monks meant by "two and seven" is not easily apparent. It seems there is some mystery within the words, unless ignorance shaped these songs in such a way that "two and seven" merely denote nine—as if to signify the seven liberal arts <note>Grammar, logic, rhetoric, arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy</note> plus two others. Yet, they should not be accused of such tautology <note>Needless repetition</note>; for generally, at least seven liberal arts are numbered, and no more. Therefore, some secret lies beneath, and it is a Chemical <note>Alchemical</note> one. This is because the philosophers in the *Assembly* <note>original: "in turba"; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note> remember that imbibitions <note>The process of a solid absorbing a liquid</note> must be made according to the proportion of two to seven, or one to three, just as these weights are frequently emphasized by Chemists. Because Alanus knew "two and seven," he stood out as a truly perfect Chemist; likewise, his sayings or his *Book of Chemistry* testify more than enough to this, in which he intermixes Theory with Practice in the philosophical manner. He introduces an Old Man into a Bath to be washed. He establishes a double fire necessary for philosophical work: one hot and dry, the other moist, which is horse dung <note>original: "fimus equinus"; a common source of gentle, steady heat in alchemical laboratories provided by fermenting manure</note>. He prefers this over all other types of fire, and rightly so. For in this dunghill there is more secret and mystery than the common sort of Chemists understand. This is the beginning and cause of putrefaction, without which nothing is changed or born. The "belly of the horse" <note>An alchemical term for the heat of fermentation</note> is the greatest secret. In this, our dropsical man <note>original: "hydropycus"; referring to a substance with an excess of "watery" or "mercurial" humidity that must be dried out</note> hides himself so that he may recover his health and, from all that water, toward the...

<meta>The catchword "folem" (solem) indicates the sentence continues: "toward the sun."</meta>
