...unburden itself of the sun: What the power of the heat of dung can do is apparent in the Egyptian countryside <margin>The power of the heat of dung.</margin> near Cairo, where from most ancient times, many thousands of chicken eggs are hatched all at once into animated, living, and running chicks in certain ovens heated in a long row by burning dung. Almost all philosophers have mentioned this dung with praise; especially **Calid** <note>original: "Calid"; likely Khalid ibn Yazid, a legendary early figure in Arabic alchemy</note> in his *Book of Secrets*; **Morienus**, who chooses sheep’s dung; and **Llull**, who takes equal parts horse dung and quicklime—to pass over the rest. **A whole treatise could deservedly be written on the dignity and utility of philosophical dung**: <margin>*Words to be whispered in the ear of chemists.</margin> Chemists also everywhere have horse dung recommended to them, while according to the mind of **Llull** in his book *On the Fifth Essence*, <margin>Signs of the philosophical dung.</margin> they keep a "philosophical dung-heap" in the corners of their houses, into which they place their well-sealed vessels. They leave them there for forty days, more or less, and thus they make the material ready for undergoing solution <note>The process of dissolving a solid into a liquid state, a key step in the alchemical Great Work</note>. 

But to all these, if they handle philosophical works, I shall say these few words in their ear, or rather their mind: let them see that they choose the best from all dung-heaps, and possess the truly PHILOSOPHICAL one; for unless they do so, they will expect nothing from the dung except the stench. 

But what are the signs of philosophical dung, you ask? That which is sought from animals pastured in the mountains. For since the herbs that grow in the mountains are more vigorous and healthful, so too are the animals that graze upon them. Not without reason did the ancient physicians of Italy banish those suffering from wasting diseases or incurable consumption <note>term: Phthisis; a historical term for pulmonary tuberculosis and other wasting conditions</note> to Mount Tabidum <note>likely referring to the "Milk Mountain" or Mons Lactarius near Naples, famous for its therapeutic air and herbs</note>, so that they might use the milk of animals—especially donkeys and goats—as they were nourished by the most healthful herbs there. Enjoying the dry or rather temperate air, they might lead a longer life. <margin>The use of dungs in medicine.</margin> Thus, there is a peculiar virtue of putrefaction <note>In alchemy, "putrefaction" is the stage of breaking down a substance to its essence through gentle heat</note> in the dung of mountain animals, which perhaps might seem strange to anyone. But those who apply or administer them for medicines experience the diversity of dungs, as in the golden [works] of

<margin>Isaac Hollandus, the father, a chemist.</margin>
**Isaac Hollandus**, *the Father*, was a complete *Chemist*, who instructed his son of the same name in this art. The son testifies that before his father's time, no one had written or published anything regarding the "oil and salt of the philosophers"; however, the father is more easily recognized through the son.

<margin>Isaac Hollandus, the son.</margin>
**Isaac Hollandus** *the Son*, being in no way inferior to his father in the art, wrote various alchemical works in his native Dutch tongue <note>original: "Belgico idiomate"</note>. Two of his books on minerals have been printed and translated into Latin; his work *On Vegetables* is commonly found in German <note>original: "teutonico"</note> manuscript.

<margin>Isaac is recognized as a second Geber at first sight.</margin>
The mineral books of this man are not unlike the books of **Geber** <note>An 8th-century Arabic alchemist whose works emphasize rigorous, repetitive laboratory procedures</note>, filled with various boilings and distillations. For what does he not cook and re-cook, calcine, dissolve, congeal, amalgamate, mix, fix, sublimate, and treat in innumerable other ways? Even an elephant could scarcely endure such labors. Yet, not infrequently, he allows a spark of truth to glimmer among so many clouds of circumlocution, so that the truth is not entirely neglected and the "heads of the hydra" <note>A metaphor for the ever-multiplying errors of false alchemy</note> do not grow too numerous—that is, so that sophisticated falsehood does not prevail.

<margin>Isaac described very many works.</margin>
He treats many operations, one after another, in which he employs a subtle craftsmanship. He does this, of course, to exclude the indiscreet and the ignorant from the art, and to keep those occupied in common alchemical labors until, strengthened by judgment and experience, they understand that these "husks" are not to be mistaken for the "kernel" of Chemistry.

<margin>Everything noble is acquired by labor.</margin>

...recedes, very rarely beyond eight degrees, so in the chemical art, Sol [the Sun] always joins Mercury to itself as a companion; while Luna [the Moon] receives all her splendor and virtue from the Sun.

<margin>The celestial Sun and Moon are compared with terrestrial ones.</margin>

>*The author of the "Sound of the Trumpet"* <note>original: "Author clangoris buccinae," referring to an influential medieval alchemical text</note> *proposes certain beautiful riddles concerning the philosophical Moon in this manner: Ptolemy says in the Almagest* <note>the foundational 2nd-century astronomical work</note> *that the Sun does not heat the earth, nor imprint its virtue upon the earth, except through the mediation of the Moon, which among other stars receives more of the Sun’s light and heat, acting as a medium between the Sun and the Earth. Therefore, as the philosophers say, there are two obstacles to one thing imprinting its virtue upon another: namely, a remote distance and an intervening medium. And so it is between the Sun and the Earth, because the Sun is far distant from the earth, and because the Moon mediates there. Likewise, in our alchemical art, the Sun alone does not complete the tincture* <note>the transformative "spirit" or color sought in the Great Work</note> *except through the mediation of the Moon, because it is remotely distant, having not yet reached that level of subtlety required to tinge, and also because of those same mediums—namely, density and coarseness. Therefore, the Moon is necessarily required there so that she may make the Sun itself subtle, rare, and volatile, and separate its impurity; for she herself stands more in need of his light and nature than the other planets (that is, the metals). Therefore, Hermes and Aristotle say regarding the Planets: the Sun is its father, the Moon is its mother. Thus, the Moon is the mother and the field in which the solar seed must be sown, and so we require nothing else from which our stone and our alchemy might be made, except the Sun and the Moon.*

These things are from the aforementioned author. All the writings of the philosophers tend toward this goal. Among others,

Just as one proceeds with the grafting of trees, so also one proceeds in this art. He says this is the tree that bears the golden apples, guarded in the gardens of the Hesperides <note>In Greek mythology, a garden where golden apples grew, granting immortality</note> by a horrible Dragon (the son of Typhon and Echidna), whose fruit one may enjoy if the dragon is slain. <margin>Two secrets of Greverus not to be revealed.</margin>

Concerning these two secrets, as much as is possible and permitted for us, we will add a few things. The first seems to be a certain *Indian* stone of magnetic virtue <note>original: "magnetinae virtutis"</note> which draws another stone to itself and is called the **Pantaura**; we made mention of this in Book 1 under the Brahman philosophers. This stone, even if not in name, is the same in substance—or certainly in effect—as the **Eagle Stone** <note>original: "Lapis Aquila," also known as Aetites, a hollow stone containing a smaller stone or pebble that rattles inside</note>, which contains another small stone within its belly. It is well known that this stone is sold by many at a low price, but those are not genuine; the true stone is recognized by very few. 

But you might ask, what does a stone have to do with the making of gold? I answer: does not gold arise out of the hardest stones, as is evident in pyrite, <term>Cadmia</term> <note>a term used for various zinc or cobalt ores, or the crusts found in smelting furnaces</note>, garnets, and <term>Lapis Lazuli</term>? What is harder than these individual items? Nevertheless, they are fertile with gold. Thus the true **Pantaura** has within itself the seminal virtue of gold, which is the "father of the work" and the true philosophical sun. If anyone should seek this stone, there is no need to set out for India and search the mountains there, since "the volatiles," as the philosophers say, bring it to us. By "the volatiles," however, they do not mean tiny birds, but rather the largest ones, and perhaps even sail-flying ships. The second secret is the "water of gold," which is expressed in the same aforementioned place. This...

# OF THE GOLDEN TABLE. BOOK VI.

<margin>A secret not to be revealed.</margin>
<margin>Water of gold.</margin>
It is more gold-bearing than the **Hydaspes** <term>Idaspes</term> <note>The Hydaspes or Jhelum river in India/Pakistan, famous in antiquity for its wealth.</note> of India, the **Pactolus** of Asia, the **Tagus** of Spain, or the **Ganges**, the **Arimaspias**, the **Hermus**, the **Po** <term>Padus</term>, and the **Aurigenus**; not indeed in actuality <note>original: "actu"</note>, but in potential <note>original: "potentia"</note>. This is why it is not mixed with gold down to the smallest particles, as other waters are, but only adheres to its surface.

<margin>Where the water of gold is found.</margin>
This "water of gold" <note>original: "aqua auri"</note> is not found in wells or deep places, but in a higher place. On a certain island of the **Fortunate Isles** <note>The Canary Islands</note> called **El Hierro** <term>Ferro</term>, people live even though not a single drop of sweet water can be found throughout the entire land; this occurs in a manner that is almost miraculous.
<margin>Miraculous water on a Fortunate Island.</margin>
For there are many trees there from whose leaves, at a certain time, clear and sweet water drips in abundance, which the inhabitants use. Therefore, just as their water is produced in trees, so is the water of the philosophers produced in the higher parts of the world. He who already knows what and of what kind the parts of the world are—which are higher and which are lower—will easily find the water there. This water, however, does not mix with rainwater, but remains undisturbed in its own substance. For we sometimes see at the confluence of rivers that certain ones preserve their own water for a long distance of their course, so that they can be distinguished from one another by their color. This water, although it is called "of gold," is not however
<margin>Water of gold having the powers of 3 rivers.</margin>
of that color or essence, but it expresses the powers of three rivers: namely, the **Melas** of **Boeotia**, which makes the flocks that drink from it black if they were white (just as the river **Crathis** <term>Cratis</term> does); the **Cephisus**, which turns them from black to white (as do the **Sybaris**); and the **Xanthus** of **Phrygia**, which bestows a red color upon animals. Regarding a certain **Stygian** water <note>The water of the river Styx in the underworld</note>, 
<margin>Water of gold must be kept in a metallic vessel.</margin>
they say it can only be kept in the hoof of a mule, as it penetrates and consumes all other vessels. Likewise, this "water of gold" is kept in no vessel except a metallic one; and the more compact the metal is, the better it is preserved. Let these things we have said concerning the two secrets of **Greverus**—which are neither to be entirely opened nor entirely covered—be sufficient.

# SYMBOLS

<margin>Lambspring.</margin>
**LAMBSPRING**, <note>A famous alchemist, often identified as Nicolas Flamel’s contemporary or a noble German author; his "Book of Lambspring" is a cornerstone of alchemical emblem literature.</note> born of a noble family as he himself asserts, wrote certain verses in the German tongue with great sharpness. In these, as if through emblematic figures, he depicted the whole of the Art, albeit briefly, so that anyone might find with both eyes and mind that which he may delight in. He confesses that he has read and understood Philosophy, and that through the instruction of teachers, he has reached the very foundation of the Work.
<margin>The Emblems of Lambspring.</margin>
In this, he speaks the truth: for he proves what he asserts here in the figures that follow. In these, he says that **two fish** in one sea, a **black beast** in the forest, and a **stag and unicorn** lie hidden in the grove; these must be captured, ensnared, and united. Likewise, he teaches that **two lions** of both sexes, a **wolf and a dog**, and **two birds** are found in the forest; these, though mortal enemies, must be brought back into friendship and bound together by the perpetual bond of concord. His remaining emblems may be seen in their own place. But what is truly understood 
<margin>Two eagles sent from Delphi.</margin>
by these two birds—one of which comes from the East and the other from the West—is evident to anyone. For they are the **two eagles** sent forth by **Jove** from **Delphi** <note>In Greek mythology, Zeus/Jove released two eagles from the opposite ends of the earth; they met at Delphi, marking it as the center of the world or "Omphalos."</note> to fly around the globe in opposite directions. The author of the *Consilium on the Marriage of the Sun and Moon* <note>original: "consilij coniug Solis & Lunæ"</note> brings forward an explanation of this matter 
<margin>Two stones, white and red.</margin>
from the *Epistle of Aristotle* <note>A medieval alchemical text falsely attributed to the philosopher Aristotle.</note> in this manner: *That there are two principal stones of this Art, the white and the red, of a marvelous nature. The white begins to appear at sunset upon the face of the waters, hiding itself until midnight, and afterwards it sinks into the depths. But the red works in the opposite way, for it begins to rise above the waters at sunrise until midday, and afterwards it descends into the depths.*

<margin>Two stones given freely by God.</margin>
**Isaac** <note>Likely Isaac Hollandus, a 15th-century alchemist.</note> and **Arnold** <note>Arnold of Villanova, a famous 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note> testify in various places that God has given two stones—one for the white work, the other for the red—freely; these can be obtained without price in whatever quantity one wishes. **Arnold** adds that no one needs to be asked for them. He, I say, by that miraculous rod of his, shall create and confirm a stable peace between these deadly enemies.

# SYMBOLS

<margin>In Paracelsus, two things are condemned. 1. The change of name.</margin> He possessed much hidden learning beyond others, yet I see him extolled with no praise by many learned men, primarily for two reasons: first, because he cast away his own name (which is *Philippus Bombastus*) <margin>2. Slander directed at other doctors.</margin> and took for himself other pompous and more splendid (but fictional) names. This is indeed an indication of a great spirit, but of little humility. *Secondly*, because by writing in German, thirsting for popular favor, he calls himself a "monarch" <note>Paracelsus famously referred to himself as the "Monarch of Physicians."</note> and judges other doctors—those who do not follow him—to flit about like shadows and to be lighter than seaweed. He tears them apart with long and wordy insults, like an old woman incensed to anger. <margin>3. Some deny Paracelsus the knowledge of Chemistry.</margin> Furthermore, a great part of the more learned, even those who love Chemistry <note>original: "Chemiæ"; here referring to the art of alchemy.</note>, deny him a perfect knowledge of the Hermetic art <note>The "Hermetic art" refers to alchemy, named after the legendary founder Hermes Trismegistus.</note>, the signs of which we shall soon discuss. <margin>4. Others attack his life.</margin> *Fourthly*, these same men take notice of his scurrilous life, stained with many vices, and affirm that it does not befit a true philosopher. We shall discuss these four points individually so that no injury is done to the truth and gratitude for his merits may be ready at hand.

*Regarding the first point:* <margin>Paracelsus the Swiss; the reason for his name.</margin> It is well known that he was born in Switzerland to a noble family, whose father was a *Bombast* and mother was from *Hohenheim*. From this, he seized the opportunity to baptize himself anew as *Paracelsus*, as if this were the equivalent to "Hohenheim." "Hohen" signifies "high" or "lofty," and "heim" signifies "homeland" or "place of dwelling." "Para," however, is a Greek word and denotes nothing of the sort; rather, its use appears in words like *Parasite*, *Paraphrenitis* <note>original: "Paraphenisis"; likely referring to delirium or brain inflammation.</note>, *Parerga* <note>meaning "supplementary works."</note>, *Parable*, and the like, where it always introduces a sense of opposition to another thing—in morals, mind, works, and words. And thus, *Paracelsus* is a composite Greek and Latin word, as if Greece and Latium <note>Latium refers to the Latin-speaking world or Rome.</note> were meeting in Germany.

<margin>To Theophrastus the Aristotelian, honey was carried into his mouth by bees.</margin> He calls himself *Theophrastus* after that ancient Greek disciple of *Aristotle*, for whom (as they also tell of *Plato*) as he lay in his cradle, a swarm...

<meta>The catchword "m" likely begins "mellis" (of honey) or "multitudo" (a multitude/swarm).</meta>

# THE GOLDEN TABLE, BOOK VI

<margin>Aristotle said Theophrastus needed a bridle.</margin> bees dropped honey into his mouth, by which omen it was foretold that he would be most sweet and divine in his eloquence—which indeed came to pass, and thus he earned the name of *Theophrastus* <note>The name Theophrastus literally means "divine speaker" in Greek (from *theos* + *phrazein*). Maier is referring to the ancient Greek philosopher, the successor of Aristotle.</note> among the people, as if he were speaking divine things. He is the noble "Horse" of his teacher *Aristotle*, who said that he [Theophrastus] required a bridle, while others required spurs; he was the one who propagated the Peripatetic <term>Peripatetic: A follower of Aristotle's philosophy, named after the "walkways" (peripatoi) of the Lyceum where they taught.</term> school granted to him by *Aristotle's* will, and who published a highly memorable history of plants and fossils.

<margin>Whether Bombastus was a "divine-speaker" like Theophrastus.</margin> Whether our *Bombastus* <note>Referring to Paracelsus, whose birth name was Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim.</note> shared the same omen, since he desired the same name, is unknown to me. Let us say he is a "divine-speaker," but not in the Latin or Greek language; rather, in his mother and vernacular tongue, the Swiss dialect, which to many does not sound so polished.

<margin>Response in favor of Paracelsus's eloquence.</margin> But I respond on behalf of *Theophrastus* [Paracelsus] that one must look at the subject matter, and not at the language. If the things he treated were divine, it is sufficient, even if he did not bring them forth with divine eloquence.

<margin>Why Paracelsus was called "Aureolus."</margin> He also esteemed himself "Aureolus" <note>original: "Aureolum," meaning "golden" or "little golden one."</note>, perhaps because of his knowledge of the [alchemical] art, or even because of his divine doctrine. For divine and golden things are held in the highest esteem—the former being the greatest of celestial things, the latter the greatest of terrestrial things. Thus he is "gilded," a divine-speaker, and one of those who transcends the common nature or understanding of man. Whence he deservedly took joy in that name. And it was permissible for him to change his name, since it was done without prejudice to anyone else, especially if it was done for his own good or honor. Others may attribute the cause of this act not to arrogance, but to a commendation of the new doctrine which he himself was about to put forward.

<margin>Why Paracelsus wrote in German.</margin> *Regarding the Second point:* He wrote in German because he was German, perhaps for the honor of his own people, and because he begrudged the treasure of his learning to other nations.

<margin>He was not proud, but of a calm spirit.</margin> Whether he was thirsty for popular acclaim, I do not know; certainly he was not proud, appearing more in the garb of a Swiss soldier than of such a great Doctor.

<margin>An explanation of why he insults other physicians and calls himself a Monarch.</margin>
...he walked in a toga. The reason why he slanders and mocks all other physicians is that he could not become a "Monarch" unless the kings (among whom are *Hippocrates* and *Galen*), the princes (among whom is *Avicenna*), and the common people (that is, the practicing physicians) were subjected to him. For a single grove does not nourish two robins <note>The author uses the Latin *erithacos* (robins), referring to an ancient proverb about the bird's fiercely territorial nature; it implies that two great leaders cannot coexist in the same space.</note>, nor does one world support more than one sun. Thus, one earth has but one Monarch. But let us set aside the "Kings of Kings" and those truly called Monarchs, and let us pursue this "literary monarch," which he undoubtedly makes and understands himself to be. Why should this name not suit him, especially in the field of Medicine?

<margin>There can be monarchs within every specific branch of the arts.</margin>
For in as many types of doctrine as there are, and in as many species of manual arts, one may establish just as many Monarchs—one for each specific field—even if, by this reasoning, they were to number over a thousand. But human nature has been so disposed since the Fall of our first parents <note>A reference to the biblical Fall of Adam and Eve, which the author suggests introduced vanity and the desire for power into the human soul.</note> that it gladly seeks to obtain divinity, the highest honors, and great empires above all others.

<margin>Each man is a king to himself.</margin>
Hence *Seneca* <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca, the Roman Stoic philosopher.</note> rightly said: *Every man has the spirit of a king within him, so that he would rather have power over another granted to himself than have power over himself granted to another.* <note>Original Latin: "Regis quisque animum in se habet, ut sibi in alium, quam in se alteri, dari malit imperium."</note> Thus, every man would make himself a monarch if it depended only on his own judgment.

<margin>The cunning of a certain Pope.</margin>
A story is told of the cunning of a certain Pope. When the votes of the electing Cardinals converged upon him, he was told to accept the papal miter and cloak and hand them to whichever man among them was most worthy—one who prevailed in learning, merit, and other gifts—to become Pope. He immediately dressed himself in the Papal attire, affirming that he knew himself (and not the others) best of all. In this way, our *Theophrastus* <note>Paracelsus.</note> called himself a Monarch while he was able and allowed, even though many envied him for such a title and name—and not without cause. For he vehemently attacked *Galen* and his followers in medical doctrine,

<margin>Why he returns insults against the Galenic physicians.</margin>
now calling them "wild asses," or "millstones," <note>original: "onagros, lapides molares"</note> or even more shameful names. But *Theophrastus* could not act otherwise for two reasons: First, because of the envy and slanders which those physicians hurled at him...

<margin>The nature of Paracelsus's accusation.</margin>
Therefore, the rebukes, accusations, and threats of Theophrastus which he directed at other physicians are nothing other than the plowing, turning, ridging, and harrowing of those hard ears and hostile wills into which he desired to scatter his new medicine. If someone wishes to build a marble house in place of a wooden one, does he not first need to destroy the wooden one from its very foundation and then place the marble?

<margin>A double fee for un-teaching.</margin>
*Stratonicus*, a distinguished lyre-player <note>original: *cytharoedus*</note>, demanded a double fee from those students who had already been instructed by others (though incorrectly) in that art: specifically, one fee for "un-teaching" <note>original: *dedocendo*</note> the bad habits they had learned, and another for teaching them better exercises. Thus, Theophrastus seems to have had no less labor in destroying and "un-teaching" unsuitable medical doctrines than in constructing and teaching those that were more appropriate. 

But we shall state no judgment here regarding his medical theories, and we leave them to be freely judged by each individual. However, so that the truth may be revealed, let the judgment of *Bernhard Penotus* <note>Bernard Georges Penot (c. 1519–1617) was an alchemist and physician who, late in life, became a vocal critic of Paracelsus.</note> be heard; a retired old man whose opinion is perhaps not reckless, nor too heated given his great age:

<margin>

Truth is always the same.

Socrates always taught the same things about the same things.
</margin>

Others, if this be so, will condemn his conduct, and they will shove Paracelsus—from the possession of an authority he has held for a long time—like "old men off the bridge" <note>original: *senes de ponte deturbabunt*, a Roman idiom referring to the practice of throwing men over sixty years old off a bridge, perhaps to prevent them from voting or as a ritual; here it means discarding someone as obsolete.</note>. But we believe this deed can be excused, in honor of such a great man, unless it be doubtful or falsely imputed to him. When Hippias, a disciple of Socrates, had heard him for some time and then traveled for several years, he marveled upon his return to find Socrates still lecturing and discussing the same things. The wise old man said to him: "I think and say the same things about the same things." This was as if to suggest there is **one truth** in the things of nature, which does not admit novelty or diversity. 

And that is most true. Therefore, if in the truth of the matter Paracelsus agrees now with one man concerning one subject, and now with another concerning another, and applies it to himself (since truth, like a prize <note>original: *palma*, literally "palm branch," awarded to victors</note>, is placed in the middle; let him who can, seize it), shall he not be judged to have acted correctly? For it is indubitable that God has not given all things to one man, and truth is hidden under dense coverings of opinions and vanities, so that it can scarcely breathe or approach the light. If this is so, then good things must be sought wherever they are to be found, and truth must be investigated in every corner. Not rarely...

-> ## IV. SYMBOLS ## <-

Without any exception, the German is to be excused, who heaps up cups of thirst with those of health; these for the sake of pleasure, and those again for friendship, the others they toast to one another in mutual drunkenness. If only it would stop at the goal of the "friendship-cup" <note>original: "Philothesio", likely referring to a loving-cup or a specific ritual of toasted friendship</note>. Those drinks poured for the health of another have very often undermined the health of their own internal organs. But the prevailing custom of a nation is a tyrant; it cannot be avoided, though it may be blamed.

> "I see the better things and I approve them," says Medea, "but I follow the worse." <note>A famous quote from Ovid's Metamorphoses, expressing the struggle between reason and impulse.</note>

<margin>Each nation has its own vices and virtues.</margin>
Theophrastus <note>Paracelsus’s given name was Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim.</note> therefore, thinking nothing of human or national custom to be foreign to himself <note>A play on the Roman playwright Terence’s famous line: "I am human, and I think nothing human is foreign to me."</note>, accommodated himself to the world. And because he is said to have made little of the ornament and pomp of clothes, he entered taverns and inns with companions of similar habit, indulging his natural disposition, smoothing his brow, and fortifying his belly to satiety with <term>Ceres and Lyaeus</term> <note>Metonyms for bread (Ceres, goddess of grain) and wine (Lyaeus, an epithet for Bacchus, god of wine).</note>.

<margin>Paracelsus, though living more freely, nevertheless cured incurable diseases.</margin>
Even if he employed this way of life, he nevertheless most successfully cured and removed diseases in medicine that were incurable to others—namely, cancer, leprosy, dropsy, paralysis, gout, and other such kinds—using appropriate and most effective medicines, very many of which he left behind in his writings. Yet none of his disciples, as far as we know, has reached this peak of healing.

<margin>None of his followers cured those diseases.</margin>
From this it is to be conjectured that he performed these arduous tasks not without the help of that "great medicine" <note>The Universal Medicine or Philosopher's Stone.</note>; and since it happens that this is very rarely possessed by his followers, the medicinal aid celebrated by them is found to be less effective.

<margin>If Paracelsus's books were purged of slanders, they would not be unworthy of reading.</margin>
His books, if they were purged of all slanders—just as good and fertile fields are cleared of thistles—would without doubt constitute a work not unworthy of reading, in which many things not to be rejected by physicians and surgeons are contained. Lethal enmities ought to become perennial friendships; the former should be cut down, the latter guarded and preserved for the benefit of human life. In ancient times, people shouted insults at one another from wagons, but these have long since perished like a hollow breeze. But those things which are found in vol-

# SYMBOLS

<margin>Different medicines do not create a different medical art.</margin>
...of the art. I greatly value surgeons and physicians, insofar as they proceed without slandering others; but if they are accompanied by slanders and a claim to "Monarchy" <note>original: "Monarchia"; a reference to Paracelsus’s self-styled title as the "Monarch of Physicians," which many traditional doctors found arrogant.</note>, I do not think they should be listened to. For new medicines do not create a new Medicine or art, just as new tools for goldsmiths cannot make their art something other than what it was before. *If he has received certain drugs from others, or discovered them himself, let him gather them into the lap of pharmacy, which is one of many parts of the medical art.* 

<margin>A heavenly way of healing, if such is taught by Paracelsus.</margin>
But if he has most certainly understood some celestial way of curing—derived from the occult properties of things, which we do not doubt depend on the stars and the heavens—and if he has proposed this openly without malice and without suspicion of any evil, we gladly admit and embrace it. 

<margin>Testimony is given to Paracelsus by the unknown German brothers: the Brothers of the R.C., and what they profess.</margin>
However, we notice that testimony is given to this *Paracelsus* beyond all expectation by certain hitherto unknown brothers in Germany. These are the *Brothers of the R.C.* <note>The Rosicrucians (Fratres Roseae Crucis), a mysterious and controversial secret society that appeared in Germany in the early 1600s, claiming to possess secret wisdom and offer free healing to the poor.</note>, who are most skilled in the <term>Chemical</term> <note>original: "Chymica"; in this era, the term encompassed both what we now call chemistry and alchemy.</note> art, and are most well-versed in the entire *Circle of Knowledge* <note>original: "Encyclopaedia"; here meaning a complete mastery of all arts and sciences.</note> and in the true practice (as they tell it) of wonderful things most useful to man. They profess a medicine of occult and astral properties (which we call the "fourth" <note>Maier divided medicine into four categories: legal/traditional, empirical, chemical, and celestial/astral.</note>), and they cure all diseases that are not divinely fated to be fatal for free, removing and driving them away in a very short time using natural yet miraculous and highly proven means. For this reason, we grant him more faith and authority in *Chemical and medicinal* secrets. 

<margin>Colleges in various nations.</margin>
But since we recall that various philosophical colleges and solemn societies were established in ancient times by those knowledgeable in the <term>Chemical</term> art, what wonder is it if something of this sort has occurred in the very populous *German* nation, divided as it is into so many peoples and regions? For like true craftsmen, who [reach their] end from their own invention or the communication of another...

# BOOK VI OF THE GOLDEN TABLE

<margin>Craftsmen are concerned for the propagation of their art.</margin>
Those who have mastered the art <note>The "art" here refers to Alchemy, often called the Royal Art or the Hermetic Art.</note> dedicate and offer a vow of piety to God and a duty of humanity and compassion to their fellow men. Thus, although they maintain silence and reserve the art from the unworthy, they nevertheless look toward the many advantages, good works, and acts of charity that might arise from this art—preserved most secretly through a very long and continuous series of successors. It was therefore reasonable that there were those who directed their thoughts toward the methods and other means necessary for this purpose and put them into effect. For if it is desirable for a human being, in this valley of sorrows, to leave behind children by the guidance of nature—children who will experience the same turns of fortune as their parents, and who are not infrequently destined for wretched ends because of the enormous crimes they commit—why should there not be found at least one among the philosophers of every age, in such great numbers, who would take it upon himself to continue the most secret propagation of the art among his own people for the praise of *God* and the benefit of countless others?

<margin>German Chemical authors and philosophers, unknown and anonymous, hiding under the symbol of the R.C. <note>original: "R. C."; refers to the Rosy Cross or Rosicrucians.</note>, are invited to this symbolic Golden Table. The author struggles with illness (just like the attack of the slandering Pyrgopolynices <note>A "Pyrgopolynices" is a "braggart soldier" character from the plays of Plautus; Maier compares the aggressive nature of his fever to this loud-mouthed literary bully.</note>) every fourth day.</margin>
That this has happened for a long time is now so well known that nothing could be more common. *Lest we, too, remain incredulous for too long after these beginnings*, we have decided to invite, summon, and lead THAT PRAISEWORTHY GERMAN SOCIETY, however many and wherever they may hide among the living, TO THIS OUR TABLE—CALLED THE GOLDEN TABLE ON ACCOUNT OF ITS GILDED GUESTS—*provided they are content with common courses* <note>original: "missibus"; referring to the dishes served at a banquet.</note> (for certainly the cook, while he was entirely occupied in this preparation, was agitated by a quartan enemy <note>A "quartan host" or "quartan enemy" refers to quartan fever, a form of malaria where the fever returns every four days.</note> breathing now cold and now hot, and thus cannot serve you more elegant feasts) *which alone we offer here.*

# COLLEGE OF PHILOSOPHERS
## OF THE GERMANS OF THE R. C.

<margin>
The report of the Brothers of the R. C. passes to foreigners.
</margin>
The so-called **F**AME <note>original: "FAMA"; refers to the *Fama Fraternitatis*, the first Rosicrucian manifesto, which announced the existence of the secret order.</note> of the FRATERNITY, which has for a long time now resounded in the ears and mouths of many here, and having wandered abroad to foreign shores has flown through the widest regions, also reached me while I was then residing in England, keeping a singular watch over chemical matters <note>Maier spent several years in London (c. 1611–1616) at the court of King James I, where he studied alchemy and published several works.</note>. It reached me through certain obscure rumors—unbelievable and far greater than the truth itself—to which I initially gave little credit, depending on the reliability of the person reporting them.

<margin>
Year of Christ 1613. In Barbary <note>Barbary: The coastal regions of North Africa (modern Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya).</note>, a prophetic or certainly magical man performed many wonders.
</margin>
At that same time, certain wonderful innovations were reported from *Barbary*, telling how near *Morocco* and *Fez* a certain prophet from the number of the wise had arisen, named *Mullei Om Hamet Ben Abdela* <note>Ahmad ibn Abi Mahalli (1559–1613), a religious scholar and mahdi-claimant who led a revolt against the Saadi dynasty.</note>. Demonstrating many hidden signs in his person, he attacked and defeated the King of that region, *Mullei Sidan* <note>Zidan al-Nasir, Sultan of Morocco from 1603 to 1627.</note>, who was equipped with a large enough army, even though the prophet was almost unarmed and led only a small band; thus he obtained the seat of the kingdom.

<margin>
The first report was uncertain.
</margin>
When indeed these Brothers were also said by inconsistent rumor to have come from *Barbary* by way of *Spain*, they and that *Barbary* prophet were thought to belong to the same art and institution. But once the book itself concerning their fame and confession <note>original: "fama & confessione"; refers to the two founding Rosicrucian manifestos, the *Fama Fraternitatis* (1614) and the *Confessio Fraternitatis* (1615).</note> had been published and I happened to read through it, I was moved to form a far different judgment concerning them.

<margin>
Frankfurt: Autumn Fair, Year 1616.
</margin>
It is indeed a great matter that is being set in motion by them, and almost unbelievable; if the outcome should manifest it and prove it most true by its actual practice, we shall have enough throughout our lives to wonder at, to praise, and to promote with all our efforts.

<margin>
All the statutes of the Brothers are just and wonderful.
</margin>
*Meanwhile*, since all things correspond to any reasonable person's judgment and to the possibility of the matter, and since nothing is established by them that is contrary to true piety, nature, men of whatever status, or finally to virtue or justice, but instead everything is directed toward the creator’s pra[ise]...

### *The author’s response to the aforementioned doubts.*

<margin>The Confession of the Brothers of the R.C. is refined.</margin>
**A**lthough the *Confession* of the <term>Fraternity</term> <note>The Rosicrucian Order.</note> itself was published in so refined and polished a manner as to dissolve the objections and doubts of all, yet since it is anyone's duty to spring toward the truth and to serve in its camp above all others, I will therefore freely presume and strive to soothe, heal, and remove these "little bites" <note>Maier uses the diminutive "morsiunculas" to characterize the criticisms as minor or stinging nibbles rather than fatal blows.</note> as much as I can. We pass over the incredulous here—whether through ignorance or stubbornness—and therefore we do not dwell on their judgments concerning this whole business.

<margin>Response to 1.</margin>
*To the first doubt*: This does not touch the essence of the matter but is based on accidental details. *Damascus* seems to be the first city at which <term>Brother R.C.</term> <note>Frater Rosae Crucis, the legendary founder.</note> arrived, and there he fell ill and heard various rumors about the Arabian philosophers; and *Damascus* is in Syria, the homeland of Saint Paul. But the other town, where those philosophers were, is not named in the *Fama* <note>The first Rosicrucian manifesto, the *Fama Fraternitatis*.</note>, but is hinted at in the 5th chapter of the *Confession*.
<margin>Damcar in Arabia, a city of wise men.</margin>
There it is said that those who inhabit the city of *Damcar* live by a completely different and diverse government from the rest of the Arabs, because wise men rule it, and they were allowed to establish other laws for them through the king. Therefore, no slander finds a place here.

<margin>Response to 2.</margin>
*To the second*: By *Book M.* I understand the "Book of the World" <note>Liber Mundi</note> or of things existing in the world and their properties, or of <term>Natural Magic</term> <note>The study of hidden natural forces, distinct from "black" or demonic magic.</note>. The Arabs had such a book, which, when it was transcribed, was brought to Germany. Therefore, whether *Paracelsus* <note>The famous Swiss physician and alchemist (1493–1541).</note> read this very book or one similar to it is all the same; nothing—

...it is certain that he was most skilled in this book <note>Probably referring to the "Book M." which Brother R.C. translated</note>. However, because he openly professed this kind of teaching, he was hated by everyone; for this reason, he took no care for himself or for others, but lived in the world with the world, just as it was.

<margin>Response to the 3rd doubt.</margin>
**To the 3rd.** The fact that <term>Brother R.C.</term> <note>Christian Rosenkreuz, the legendary founder of the Rosicrucians.</note> discussed the reformation of the arts with the natural philosophers, physicians, and other learned men of **Spain** was a sign of his great genius, as well as of his laudable purpose. For truth lies hidden in the deep <note>A reference to the philosophical proverb that truth sits at the bottom of a well.</note>, and in the arts, it does not everywhere correspond to standard rules or axioms. If, therefore, such rules or axioms were established that agree with the truth in all things, these should be embraced above all others, and the arts should be regulated according to them. Regarding "new" animals and plants, this should be understood in terms of our own knowledge; they are those whose actions, passions, the use of their parts, and other physical operations and motions do not agree with common, vulgar axioms of physics.

<margin>Response to the 4th doubt.</margin>
**To the 4th.** Those young monks <note>The early companions of Brother R.C. who helped him document his findings.</note> seem at least to have organized into a proper system the secret writings that Brother R.C. had already brought with him from his travels. The volume of those things which a human being could desire contains both celestial and terrestrial goods. Celestial goods are known by the *grace of God*. Terrestrial goods are manifold, among which are health, wealth, wisdom, and the rest. They wrote about each of these individually and revealed how they might be acquired. Since these axioms are true, and truth is eternal and immutable, it is beyond doubt that they remain perennial. **God’s clock** sounds every minute; our own barely sounds the full hours. By this, it is meant that the things God wishes to indicate, which are placed throughout all of nature, differ so greatly from those things which we are able to perceive from nature.

<margin>Response to the 5th doubt.</margin>
**To the 5th.** It does not appear to be stated there that the vocabulary of **Theophrastus** <note>Theophrastus Paracelsus (1493–1541), the famous Swiss alchemist and physician.</note> was in that chest <note>The chest found in the hidden tomb of Christian Rosenkreuz.</note>, but rather that all those brothers also possessed those books along with the vocabulary of Theophrastus; for that is how the words sound, and that is the sense of the passage.

<margin>Response to the 6th doubt.</margin>

<margin>Response 16 to the negative argument.</margin>
# THE RESPONSE OF ALBERTUS MAGNI TO THE 16th
## Negative Argument.

If the proposition is understood to concern the "power of alluring matter"—as if matter always craves a new form and is not satisfied with what it has already acquired—then it is false. This is like what the playwright <term>Plautus</term> <note>Titus Maccius Plautus, a Roman comic playwright. The author uses a bawdy classical joke to illustrate a philosophical point.</note> says of a wanton woman: that she would sooner be content with one eye than with one husband. For there is neither sensation nor appetite in metals—neither that of animals nor of vegetables—but at least a natural movement, which takes its origin from the "light" and the "heavy" <note>This refers to the Aristotelian concept that objects move toward their natural place based on their weight.</note>.

<margin>A memorable question.</margin>
But it is asked: what is the difference between metals existing underground in the <term>mines</term> <note>original: "mineris," referring to the ore veins where metals were believed to "grow."</note> and those transferred above ground for human use, in regards to the "appetite" they have to become a more perfect metal? Is the same force present in both, since those in the mines are said to be "alive" and to grow or be ennobled in their own way, while these...

<header>IV. SYMBOLS</header>

<margin>
Response to the question. The ordinary operations of nature.
</margin>
...[are they] dead outside the mines, and able to grow no further? *I respond:* Nature makes use of different operations, either ordinary or extraordinary. The ordinary ones are those by which imperfect things, solely through the cooking <note>original: "coctione"; a standard alchemical term for the "ripening" of metals through heat, likened to cooking food.</note> of a slow heat, gradually ascend from the lowest to the highest over a very long period of time. In our colder regions, nature is more often hindered in these operations because the metals are dug out of the mines prematurely, and the imperfect grain is separated from the perfect.

<margin>
Extraordinary operations of nature.
</margin>
Extraordinary operations occur when, outside of the mines, lead, copper, or silver—found in rooftops, sands, or rivers—is cooked by the heat of the sun and very often washed by water. These operations tend toward one goal: namely, the stripping away of <term>combustible sulfur</term> <note>original: "sulfuris combustibilis"; in alchemical theory, this was the "impurity" that made metals base and prone to corrosion.</note> and the introduction of the incombustible into the metallic matter of <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argenti vivi"; literally "living silver," the common name for mercury.</note>. From this, it is gradually reduced into silver and gold.

<margin>
The matter of metals, both below and above ground, is purely passive.
</margin>
The potential that exists in these materials is purely passive and in no way active. Therefore, this power depends neither on the stars nor their alignment (except for the heat of the sun), nor on a "seminal" active principle—just as in the seeds of animals and plants, an astral power lies hidden along with the capacity of the matter, which is brought into action by heat if it is joined to its own matter in the proper way in suitable vessels. Truly, this metallic or <term>mercurial matter</term> <note>original: "materia mercurialis"; the "First Matter" of all metals in the Geberian theory of alchemy.</note>, whether existing in mines or in the open air, feels the force of heat for a very long time, which works upon it a small amount of warmth and dryness; from this, a balancing <note>original: "æquatio"; the leveling or balancing of the four elementary qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry).</note> occurs, and the balanced substance is first silver, then gold.

<margin>
The reason why silver and gold can be made from all metals.
</margin>
And this is the reason why silver and gold are generated equally from all metallic materials—such as lead, tin, copper, and iron—and not merely from one specific "seed." This is because, clearly, in all of them resides that mercurial matter from which heat, through a long and continuous operation, can bring forth silver and gold by the balancing of qualities. And this is nature's common process: to generate perfect things from the imperfect. Besides this...

<summary>This page explains that all metals share a common "mercurial" essence and can naturally evolve into gold or silver through the "coction" (cooking) of heat, whether slowly in mines or more rapidly through extraordinary exposure to the sun. The author argues that metals are passive recipients of this transformation, rather than having an internal biological seed.</summary>

<margin>A rare and secret mode of nature's operation.</margin>
There is also another very rare and secret mode of nature, namely, that it generates gold or silver from the matter of <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argenti vivi"; mercury, considered the "mother" of all metals in alchemical theory.</note> when a certain spiritual form, containing in itself either a white or red <term>tincture</term> <note>original: "tincturam"; a potent substance or "medicine" believed to have the power to transform and color base metals into gold (red) or silver (white).</note>, is added to it. This form then coagulates and transforms those two substances into silver and gold. Now it is asked: which path does art <note>original: "ars"; refers to the "Art of Alchemy" or human skill imitating nature.</note> follow? Does it follow those two prior paths <note>referring to the ordinary and extraordinary natural processes described on the previous page.</note>, or this last one? *I respond: not those (unless perhaps one of them in a specific, limited way, without much success), but this last one:* 
<margin>Which operation of nature art follows.</margin>
From this it is clear that what nature achieves in a thousand years or more, art accomplishes in a single hour, once the proper materials and forms are brought together. Therefore, no matter is more eager to receive its form—neither that within the mines, nor this outside of them—but both are purely passive. The difference is this: if metals taken from the mines and treated by fires were placed back into the pits of the earth and left there for a thousand years, they would be consumed by rust or decay <note>original: "situ"; a term for the mold or stagnation that occurs when things are left unmoved.</note> rather than gaining any growth. Conversely, just as they are mixed and impure, if they are taken from the earth without any purification, they could not be brought to gold above ground by the addition of a tincture as effectively as if they had first been purified and cleansed <note>original: "defœcata"; literally "cleansed of dregs," meaning refined to a state of purity.</note>.

<margin>17. A negative argument.</margin>
### 17. The Opponent’s negative argument against Albertus Magnus.

->If one species of metal were changed into another,<-
->the world would not be perfect.<-
->But it is perfect.<-
->Therefore, one species is not changed into another.<-

The <term>minor premise</term> <note>In a logical argument (syllogism), the "minor premise" is the second statement; here, "the world is perfect."</note> is proven thus: because since there are as many species of metals as there are metals themselves, the other species would eventually cease to exist, leaving gold alone surviving.

## Response to the 17th Negative Argument.

<margin>Response to the 17th negative argument.</margin>
**T**hose who argue in this way are far too cautious and provident, fearing "lest the heavens should fall." <note>A classical proverb used to describe those who worry about impossible or highly unlikely catastrophes.</note> It is ridiculous that they fear only gold would remain while all other metals were transmuted.
<margin>Augurello's Hyperbole.</margin>
They seem to have drawn this indeed from the *poet-chemist Augurello* <note>Giovanni Aurelio Augurello (c. 1441–1524), author of the alchemical poem "Chrysopoeia."</note>, who, taking this *hyperbole* <note>An intentional exaggeration used for emphasis.</note> from the reasoning of *Lully* <note>Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1315), a philosopher to whom many alchemical texts were attributed.</note>, asserts that the entire sea, if it were <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury, the liquid metal central to alchemical theory.</note>, could be transmuted into **gold**. Yet no one, for that reason, would dream that the *species of metals would perish, with gold alone surviving*. We have already provided sufficient reason why transmutation is possible: not indeed from some hidden property, but by the nature of the matter itself, which is inherently fit to bring forth a form through nature, or to receive a form brought forth and perfected from elsewhere.

Truly, there is no logical connection in their proposition, because the transmutation of metals into one another takes nothing away from the perfection of the world. For neither the use nor the species of iron or lead will cease to exist in the world, even if this change were a thousand times more frequent than it is. If God gave this capability to metals—that they may be transmuted into one another—then if it were not to happen, the world would not achieve the perfection for which it was destined. *Swallows, spiders, flies, storks, and frogs*, though they are not present with us in winter, nor *silkworms* <note>original: "bombycae".</note> except in their eggs, do not thereby make the world less perfect; for this is the divine order. Nor does it follow that these animals perish entirely from the world just because they are absent or hidden for a time. In the same way, it will not happen that the imperfect metals perish in their own species, even if nature (as well as art) wipes away some small portion of their diseases and dregs, and clothes others in a "purple garment." <note>An alchemical metaphor for the final, perfected state of gold, often associated with the "Red Tincture."</note>
<margin>Gyges with his ring. Justinian.</margin>
If a porter were once made *King of Sicily*, or a cowherd made *Emperor of the East* <note>Likely a reference to Emperor Justin I, who rose from being a peasant swineherd to the imperial throne.</note>, it does not follow that all porters and cowherds will be changed into kings or emperors. The world, therefore, will be

<summary>The author refutes the concern that alchemy will deplete the world of base metals like iron and lead, arguing that transmutation is a natural potential that does not threaten the variety of the physical world. He uses analogies from nature (migrating animals) and history (peasants becoming emperors) to show that individual transformation does not eliminate a class or species.</summary>

<margin>18. Negative argument.</margin>
### 18. *The Opponent's Negative Argument against Albertus Magnus:*

If gold were the ultimate goal of the matter of all other metals, the matter of lead would not exist as "well" under its own form as gold does under its own.

But the matter of lead exists just as "well" under its own form as gold does under its own.

Therefore, gold is not the ultimate goal of other metals, and consequently <term>Chrysopoeia</term> <note>original: "Chrysopopœia"; the alchemical art of making gold.</note> is impossible.

The assumption is proven: because the matter of both lead and gold is tempered in its own way and is suitable for performing its own proper actions. For if lead were not a complete and finished thing, nature would not stop at it—just as nature does not stop at the <term>chyle</term> <note>original: "chylus"; the milky fluid of digested food produced in the stomach during an intermediate stage of digestion.</note> which it has prepared in the stomach, but instead transmits it to the <term>liver</term> <note>original: "epar"; from the Greek word for liver, hepar. In medieval physiology, the liver was believed to turn chyle into blood.</note> so that it may become blood.

---

<margin>Response to the 18th negative argument.</margin>
### *Albertus Magnus's Response to the 18th Negative Argument:*

**IF** by "well-being" <note>original: "BENE ESSE"; a technical term in scholastic philosophy referring to the perfection or optimal state of an object's existence.</note> one understands a certain sense of pleasure, this seems absurd, and is alien to both lead and gold...

<summary>This page presents a logical challenge to alchemy: if lead is a "perfect" and stable metal in its own right, why would nature intend for it to become gold? It uses a physiological analogy (digestion) to argue that nature only pauses at "complete" forms.</summary>
<keywords>Albertus Magnus, teleology, lead vs gold, chyle, digestion analogy, scholastic logic, Chrysopoeia</keywords>

--- Page 334 ---
<meta>This page continues the refutation of the 18th argument, which claimed that lead is just as "perfect" in its own nature as gold is in its own. The author uses chemical and logical counter-arguments to demonstrate that lead is an "imperfect" or "diseased" state of metal compared to the "healthy" and "incorruptible" state of gold.</meta>

<page-num>312</page-num>
<header>SYMBOLS</header>

...foreign. But if indeed it is to remain in a healthy or non-corruptible state, as I believe, then there is no logical connection in the proposition, and the minor premise is not true.

For how could lead be as well-off as gold? Since the former is subject to many mineral "diseases," and is easily converted by fire—as if by a common enemy—into earthy powders, into <term>litharge</term> <note>original: "Lythargyrium"; lead oxide, often a byproduct of smelting, which the author views as a degradation of the metal.</note>, and finally into glassy dross. Gold, however, remains meanwhile free from diseases, pure, constant, and unmoved by fire or other injuries. Not to mention <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>original: "aquis fortibus"; literally "strong waters," refers to nitric acid, which dissolves most metals but leaves gold untouched.</note>, vinegar, and corrosive liquids of that kind, which consume lead just as fires do, but bring no harm to gold. What, then, do you mean by that strange phrase, that "lead is as well-off as gold"? It certainly has its own form, but not the form of gold. We might say of a beggar that he possesses the form of a man just as much as some very wealthy king, but we cannot say of lead that it possesses as perfect a form as gold.

The *Proof of the Assumption* <note>A formal term in a logical debate referring to the evidence for a secondary premise.</note> does not hold—the claim that lead is as well-off as gold because the matter of lead is "tempered" in its own way. It is indeed tempered, but in a temperament and impurity mixed together, which makes it easily corruptible. The matter of gold, however, is most tempered, balanced in its temperament and without any <note>The original Latin "puritate" (purity) is likely a printer's error for "impuritate" (impurity), as the author is arguing gold is perfectly pure.</note> impurity, which is why it is closest to the incorruptible.

If this reasoning sufficed, we would say the same about the beetle and the eagle, the frog and the lion, or even the toad and the man: that the former is as well-off as the latter, because the former's temperament is as balanced as the latter's. But this has nothing to do with the matter at hand. The point brought up regarding <term>chyle</term> <note>The milky fluid of digested food; here used to represent an intermediate stage of development.</note> is a similar comparison, but it does not apply to metals; for metals do not complete their <term>concoctions</term> <note>original: "concoctiones"; the alchemical and physiological process of "ripening" or "digestion" by heat.</note> as quickly as animals do. What if we were to say that the chewing occurring in an animal's mouth corresponds to the <term>coagulation</term> of <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argenti viui"; mercury.</note> into lead; in the stomach, lead into silver; in the liver, silver...

<summary>The author refutes the idea that lead is as perfect as gold, citing gold's resistance to fire and acid as proof of its superior, incorruptible nature. He compares the stages of metal refinement to the stages of animal digestion (chyle, chewing, and organ processing).</summary>

### 16. *The Affirmative Argument for the Truth of Chemistry by* ALBERTUS MAGNUS, *the German:*

**If, in the handling of metals tested by fire, such an accidental occurrence should happen whose cause is hidden and cannot be truly explained by anyone—even the most ingenious—why then should it not be possible, through the proper handling of those same metals in fire from the appropriate material, for a fixed and penetrating <term>tincture</term> <note>original: "tinctura"; a potent alchemical substance, often synonymous with the Philosopher's Stone, capable of "dyeing" or transforming the inner nature of a metal.</note> to be made, the explanation for which can be provided by someone of even moderate talent?**

*Now, the first part is true: that is, when an examination of copper is made by the <term>cupel</term> <note>original: "cupella"; a shallow, porous vessel used in assaying to separate precious metals from base ones. Albertus is pointing out a known chemical paradox of his time.</note>, if all the items placed within are weighed before the operation and then after, they are found to be heavier after the process than before. This is against all reason, since fire always consumes moisture and the substance of sulfur, so the metal body and its contents ought to be rendered lighter.*

*Therefore, by the proper handling of metals in fire from their own material, a fixed and penetrating tincture can be made: because <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argento viuo"; mercury, regarded by alchemists as the "mother" or base of all metals.</note> does not lack fixity, nor flow, nor color. From this, color appears in gold—indeed, fixity and flow and all other things. If these qualities exist somewhere in nature, then why could they not be drawn out by art, or expressed in some other way?*

<meta>catchword: Proposition-</meta>

<summary>Maier uses a biological metaphor to explain why gold does not form naturally in cold climates like Germany and presents Albertus Magnus’s argument that if fire can cause unexplained weight gain in metals, it can surely be used to create the alchemical tincture.</summary>

*The premise of this syllogism <note>A logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two shared premises.</note> is well-connected in its parts; for if that which is less likely to happen should occur, then that which is more likely to happen will also occur. Now, weight is one of the most difficult qualities to acquire through common chemical operations. Indeed, there are those who can impart the color of gold—and even its fixity <note>original: "fixitatem"; the ability of a substance to remain stable in fire without evaporating.</note>—to natural silver, so that it endures the <term>cement</term> <note>original: "cementum"; a dry refining process where metals are layered with powdered reagents and heated.</note> and is not eaten away by <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>original: "aqua forti"; literally "strong water," referring to nitric acid, which dissolves silver but leaves gold intact.</note>, leading it to be thought of as true gold. But because they cannot give it the weight of gold, it is not gold, but merely colored silver: for gold is nearly twice as heavy as silver in the same measure. It is clear, therefore, that if weight can be increased through the operation of fire while the substance remains the same—neither diminished nor increased by adding anything else—so that the matter not only gathers and contracts into itself but also increases in weight; then this requirement is far more wonderful than making something fixed, colored, or fluid:*

<margin>
A very rare and wondrous thing that happens during the test by cupel.
</margin>

For example, I take a <term>cupel</term> <note>original: "cupellam"; a shallow, porous vessel made of bone ash used in assaying to separate precious metals from base metals like lead.</note> weighing 2 ounces, into which I place metallic substances weighing 3 <term>drachms</term> <note>original: "drachma"; a small unit of weight, about 1/8th of an ounce.</note>. I add nothing else, and place them in the fire to stand for two or three hours until the operation is complete. Meanwhile, the fire consumes much of what was contained therein, and smoke visibly evaporates—just as if it had been water or the juice of an herb, half or most of it would have been consumed. Yet, after the operation, I see nothing lost, but rather the weight increased: for I find that if I weigh the whole, it is not 5 drachms as it was before, but 6 drachms. Yet this is not a magical power, but a natural one. What will you say to this—that the fire increased it? It is a most admirable thing that fire, the lightest of all things, could increase weight in such a small space. Whatever the cause may be, it is clear from this that a kind of miracle occurs which is contrary to the discourse of our reason. Let the adversary stand corrected and first find the true causes of this thing (which the most experienced <term>Lazarus Ercker</term> <note>original: "Erkerus"; a famous 16th-century mineralogist and superintendent of mines for the Holy Roman Empire.</note>, the <term>Imperial Assayer</term> <note>original: "Docimastes Cæsareus"; a high-ranking official responsible for testing the purity of ores and coins.</note>, frankly admits he cannot discover).

<summary>The author argues that if fire can "miraculously" increase the weight of metals during cupellation—a phenomenon even the expert Lazarus Ercker could not explain—then the alchemical creation of a gold-making tincture is logically possible. He highlights that weight is the ultimate test of gold, as color and acid-resistance can be faked in silver.</summary>

### But the first can happen.
### Therefore, also the second.

The connection of the parts in this proposition cannot be doubted, even though the progression moves from the vegetable kingdom to the mineral. Whatever serves as the seed in plants, this same thing—be it sulfur or the Tincture <note>The "Tincture" refers to the active alchemical agent or the Philosopher's Stone itself.</note>—is the seed in gold or in the matter from which gold is made. Therefore, nature acts not only when a vegetable—for example, a cabbage <note>original: "brassica"</note>—has reached its proper peak <term>acme</term> <note>The highest point of development or maturity.</note> (that is, when it has produced flowers and the seeds can be ripened while the plant is still green, fixed in the earth, and exposed to the sun's rays), but also when the plant is withered, buried under the earth, or cut off where the sun does not look. Who then would doubt a similar state regarding metallic and mineral things?

For it seems even more contrary to the truth that a growing plant can accomplish this—consisting as it does of organic parts and a vegetable life—than minerals, which neither grow in the proper sense, nor possess life or organic parts. Nevertheless, it happens that seeds are generated and ripened under the earth, and they become far purer and healthier than other seeds born on stalks in the open air; caterpillars <note>original: "erucae"</note> are not harmful to these plants, as those who have experienced it most truly report.

<margin>Slanders regarding the death of Arnold.</margin>
<margin>Because he died well.</margin>
It is an axiom of divine truth: *He who has lived well, cannot die badly.* However, "dying badly" is not understood here as a death far from one's homeland or relatives (otherwise no one would ever dare to travel), but rather a death that occurs without true **FAITH** in Christ and in a horrible manner. It would have been safer, therefore, for those scornful critics <note>original: "nasutulis," literally 'little-nosed ones,' an idiom for those who turn up their noses in judgment.</note> to stay at home, so they might always rejoice in seeing the smoke rising from their ancestral hearths.

<margin>We carry all our things with us; that is, the goods of the soul and body.</margin>

And the way to heaven or the underworld is the same from everywhere; everyone must die by the law of nature. For: *Death makes scepters equal to hoes.* <note>A common medieval trope about the leveling power of death.</note> And: *Pale Death knocks with impartial foot at the huts of the poor and the towers of kings.* <note>A famous quote from the Roman poet Horace (Odes 1.4).</note> If, therefore, we die in our homeland among our own people, it is more welcome; if elsewhere, it is not to be refused. For whenever that supreme *Judge* <note>original: "Arbiter"</note> calls us, we are bound to be ready. Hence, as nothing is more certain than death itself, so nothing is more uncertain than its hour...

at that same hour: and so **Arnold**, having died while traveling, shall suffer no disgrace on that account; for he departed while following his calling, undoubtedly by Divine Will, so that he might not fall into the hands of him who then commanded all Emperors and kings of the Christian name <note>A reference to the Pope, whose temporal and spiritual power was absolute at the time, and with whom Arnold had a famously contentious relationship regarding his "heretical" medical and prophetic writings.</note>, and whose power he could not have escaped unless he had crossed over to the Muslims <note>original: "Mahometanos."</note>. If **Arnold** had lived in a more fortunate time, he would have been a man of even greater virtue and freedom of spirit. How many consciences were stifled in those centuries due to the lack of a freer atmosphere? There, the *God of Silence* <note>Harpocrates, the Egyptian god of silence, often invoked in alchemical and hermetic texts regarding the "Secret of the Art."</note> had to be worshipped just as among the *Egyptians*, unless *Vulcan* <note>The Roman god of fire; here used as a metaphor for the heat of passion or perhaps the fires of the Inquisition ignited by "untamed tongues."</note> should stir up fire from an untamed tongue. Those who thus triumph over **Arnold’s** death—even though it was honorable and Christian—ought to be mindful of that saying of the wise *Solon*: *You know not what the cruel evening may bring: and no one ought to be called blessed before his death and final funeral* <note>original: "Nescis quid ferus vesper vehat: diciq. beatus ante obitum nemo supremaque funera debet." A classical Greek sentiment, famously recorded by Herodotus and Ovid, warning that fate can change until the very last moment of life.</note>. And as the dead say to the living: *What we are, you shall be; we were once what you are.* 

It is also said that **Arnold** had a brother who was not ignorant of the chemical art <term>Chemical art (artis Chymicae): At this time, "chemistry" and "alchemy" were not yet distinct; the term refers to the study of transmuting substances and the preparation of chemical medicines.</term>, namely **Peter of Villanova**. Their homeland was a small village in Provence, not far from **Montpellier** <note>original: "Montepessulano." Montpellier was home to the most prestigious medical school in medieval Europe, where Arnold was a leading figure.</note>, bearing the same name as them, but most famous for the renown of these inhabitants. I shall here include a brief song of praise <note>original: "Encomium."</note> in memory of **Arnold**, who was born there and took his name from that place:

### TO VILLANOVA
### A village of Provence and Arnold’s homeland.

> **O** VILLANOVA, you alone have given a new Honor to the Fatherland,
> From which your name resounds throughout the whole world:
> Although the land is small, and said to be inhabited by few settlers,
> You are greater than all others because of ARNOLD.
> He was a most celebrated Doctor in the Medical art,
> He, through his wise mind, possessed the riches of Chemistry.

He says it is made hot and moist, even though it had first been **sublimated** <note>A process of heating a substance until it becomes vapor and then collecting the solid deposit; in alchemy, this was seen as a purifying death and rebirth.</note> as something hot and dry. But what true philosopher would say that **Mercury**, or any other metal, could be changed in its internal quality of nature by simple water, however hot and boiling it may be? Or that it could acquire its own natural moisture and thus be revived? For whatever nature **Mercury** retained when it was reduced to powder and **mortified** <note>original: "mortificatus"; an alchemical term for "killing" a metal or stripping it of its metallic properties through chemical action.</note> through sublimations, it will preserve that same nature entirely when "revived" by water. I want this to be said out of reverence and honor for the said Arnold; yet I contemplate and defend the truth of nature and experiment. Thus he speaks.*

<margin>Why it is called the Elixir and the stone.</margin>

**The Rose Garden of the Philosophers:** With how much zeal he burned to aid the world of letters with his labors, the matter itself speaks clearly. Just as *Pico della Mirandola* <note>original: "Mirandulanus"; referring to the famous Renaissance philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</note> honorably mentions him in Book 2, Chapter 4, he completed enormous volumes on almost every literary subject. In these, while he treats Nature, he asserts that the true art was not only known to him—by which gold is separated—but also the art by which he believes gold is created. He was perhaps moved by the experience of the thing itself, as one who discovered that it lies hidden within other metals. The same man, in his *Mirror of Nature* <note>original: "Speculo naturali"; a massive medieval encyclopedia by Vincent of Beauvais</note>, Book 6, lists the Chemical authors, and among them *John the Evangelist* <note>It was not uncommon in the Middle Ages to attribute alchemical secrets to Biblical figures; the Book of Revelation was often interpreted as having alchemical symbolism.</note>. He says: *In the first book: In mineral bodies, after the likeness of nature's own operation, the Alchemists have attempted to do in a short time what nature does in a thousand years. Whence they also taught how to make a certain thing which transmutes the bodies upon which it is cast. This is called by them the Elixir, and it is called the Stone, yet not a Stone. A Stone, because it is ground; not a Stone, because it melts and flows in the fire without evaporation, just like gold.* Nor is there any other thing to which that property applies. These words of *Vincent* sufficiently prove that he possessed no common, but a profound knowledge of Chemistry. The fact that he himself affirms he holds the art of separating gold from other metals declares his more abundant experience. And from this it appears that the separation of gold from silver by <term>strong water</term> <note>original: "aquam fortem"; typically nitric acid, used to dissolve silver while leaving gold intact.</note> was in his time still a most secret mystery, and not yet made public as it is now.

<margin>Nicholas Flamel.</margin>
<margin>The writings of Flamel.</margin>
<margin>The hieroglyphic signs of Flamel.</margin>
*Nicholas Flamel*; a Frenchman; just as he possessed the perfection of Chemistry, so he left behind most truthful records of the same. For he published most learned Chemical notes, as well as very rare collections from *Psellus* <note>Michael Psellos, a Byzantine polymath</note> and *Democritus*, in which he made his judgment and experience sufficiently witnessed. Regarding his records, he is said to have founded several Churches and endowed them with annual revenues. His hieroglyphic signs, signifying the mysteries of the art, are still everywhere extant...

...expected, what another might hope for. <margin>3.</margin> 3. That gold is not made by the hands of men, but is born naturally. <margin>4.</margin> 4. That no one has ever been seen or heard of who truly knew or practiced this art of gold-making: Therefore, whatever time, study, labor, and expense is spent on this art, it is all utterly lost. Meanwhile, better opportunities are neglected, one's own resources are consumed, nothing is acquired, and one is reduced to poverty, hiding among the coals—like a soot-stained charcoal burner—and the furnaces.
