All the others are frustrated in it and lose everything they spent on that art. And since that one successful person, for many reasons, does not reveal himself to the public or provide proof of his experience—and since those others, frustrated in their hope and their substance, cannot do so—it therefore seems to everyone most certain that it is performed by no one. But if these individual points are considered by themselves, they are of no value against those devoted to Chemistry: <margin>Refutation of the reasons of the unlearned against Chemists.</margin> For if the art of Chemistry is true, it is worthy of inquiry—not by just anyone, but by him who has already learned the other liberal arts (which serve as handmaidens to Queen Chemistry) and has, as it were, completed their circle. From this, the unlearned and the half-taught are excluded, who value their own doctrine more than what can be brought together by others. Hence, the *Rosarium Philosophorum* <note>A famous 16th-century alchemical treatise, "The Rosary of the Philosophers."</note> says at the beginning: <margin>A chemist who is not a philosopher is a fool.</margin> *Arnold says: "Whoever wishes to reach this science and is not a philosopher is a fool; because this science is only concerned with the secrets of the philosophers." Senior <note>Referring to Senior Zadith (Zadith ben Hamuel), a 10th-century Arabian alchemist.</note> says: "For that art is reserved in the power of God, and is hostile to laypeople." Whence Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the foundational figure of Islamic and European alchemy.</note> says: "Therefore this science does not suit the poor and needy, but rather is hostile to them." In the second book of the Politics, the philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note> says: "It is impossible for an indigent person to philosophize."* <margin>To himself</margin> Therefore, if Chemistry is worthy of inquiry—since it is most true and proven by so many reasons and experiments—minds, as they have various inclinations (some of which give themselves to one art, others to another), find...

This page systematically refutes these claims by distinguishing the character of the practitioner from the validity of the science.</meta>

-># SYMBOLS<-

...are also discovered, which are inclined toward that art more for the sake of knowing the depth of secrets than for the utility hoped for from it. If some look only to utility and the pomp depending on it, they think preposterously and, as they feel, will very rarely obtain their wishes.

<margin>The faults of the person should be blamed on the individual, not the art.</margin>
— Regarding the fact that men who are by nature frivolous, of bad will, of poor intellect, unlearned, and—as they say—"half-lettered Samians" <note>original: "Samij literati." This likely refers to a classical proverb about the people of Samos being pseudo-intellectuals or untrustworthy in their learning.</note> flock to <term>Chemistry</term> <note>At this time, "Chemia" encompassed both spiritual alchemy and practical chemical experiments.</note>, the best of arts, and attempt nothing in it but deceits and frauds according to the nature of their own habits: let this blame remain with the person who brought those qualities with him, not with the art itself. For there are different types of people devoted to this art, and because they are emulators of a single Muse, they should not be confused with the former group.

<margin>On the second point: Why great men rarely reach the truth of Chemistry.</margin>
Regarding the second point—that great and wealthy men accomplish nothing in Chemistry—this is not a universal rule. For not a few of this kind discovered the art in ancient times, as <term>Avicenna</term> <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose works on medicine and alchemy were foundational in Europe.</note> testifies. In our own time, the fact that this happens very rarely is due to many impediments by which they are distracted more than others of moderate condition. Chemistry demands many years of reflection, reading, and continuous operations, so that what the intellect did not first correctly perceive, it may understand through repeated trials, with the hand and the fire showing the way—and this must take place within one and the same man. *Hence, he who works through another's intellect and a hired hand will see works far removed from the truth; and conversely, he who performs servile labor for another, like a slave in the art, will never be admitted to the Queen’s mysteries.* <note>The "Queen" is a traditional personification of Alchemy or the "Philosophical Stone" itself.</note>

<margin>On the third point: Gold is not "born" in the strict sense.</margin>
Thirdly, we confess that gold is not made by human hands, but we also affirm that it is not truly "born" in the usual way. For that which is "born" grows in all dimensions <note>The author distinguishes between biological growth and the chemical "multiplication" or "fixation" of metals.</note>. This is not the case for gold, which is produced in its own unique way from its mother, **quicksilver** <note>original: "argento vivo," literally "living silver" or mercury.</note>, with the **sulfur** "father" approaching—not common burning and combustible sulfur, but a fixed sulfur from the best, incombustible part of the quicksilver. Since this mother is found in common mercury and in all imperfect metals...

<summary>The author argues that alchemical failure is due to the practitioner's poor character or lack of personal labor rather than a flaw in the art itself. He explains that gold is "produced" through a symbolic union of a specialized sulfur (father) and mercury (mother) rather than being "born" like a living organism.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the defense of alchemy (Chemistry) against common objections. Following the discussion on why the wealthy often fail to achieve the Stone, Maier now addresses the "parentage" of gold and the spiritual requirements of the seeker, emphasizing that the art is a gift from God rather than a result of brute force or simple greed.</meta>

-># THE GOLDEN TABLE, BOOK VII<-

<margin>The father of gold is sought by philosophers, the mother being known.</margin>
At the very least, the father must be sought out in his own principles, wherever he may lie hidden. When the true philosophers have found him after long searches and have added him to the mother of metals—that is, to his own wife—will gold not then be produced naturally? Indeed, this entire volume deals with this very subject.

<margin>To the 4th point.</margin>
*Fourthly*, the reason has already been stated previously why true artists do not present themselves to the public to be gazed upon and why they hide their art; whereas those who appear, or desire to appear as such, why they are not true artists but deceivers.

<margin>Those who should be discouraged from Chemistry.</margin>
Persuaded by these petty arguments, common men presume to discourage others from <term>Chemistry</term> <note>In the 17th century, the term "Chemia" encompassed both what we now call chemistry and the spiritual/transmutational practice of alchemy.</note>, not indeed with evil intent, but out of a benevolent affection. And truly, many who attribute more to their own ignorance than to the learning of others, and who cling most stubbornly to even a frivolous and empty purpose, ought to comply with such warnings; not because the art is fictitious or false, but because it remains undiscoverable to them through the reading of authors or the trial of works by fire and hand. *It does not happen to every man to reach Corinth* <note>original: "Non cuiuis homini contingit adire Corinthum." A classical proverb meaning that not everyone has the means or luck to achieve difficult, expensive, or elite goals.</note>, much less to attain the truth of <term>Chemistry</term>.

<margin>The gift of Chemistry is in the hand of God.</margin>
They are most rare to whom this gift is granted by God. It does not lie in human industry, doctrine, or other circumstances alone, but is reserved in the hand of God, who sharpens or dulls the intellect of the seeker, and who gives the "to be able" and the "to will"—all things in all.

<margin>Nothing is extorted from God by force.</margin>
Who then will extort it from Him by threats, boldness, or violence? No giants, even if they declare war on heaven and pile *Pelion upon Ossa* <note>original: "Pelion Ossæ." In Greek mythology, the Giants attempted to storm Olympus by stacking Mount Pelion on top of Mount Ossa.</note>. From Him, nothing is obtained in these matters except through prayer, the zeal of reading and meditation, and practical operation, along with the frequent repetition of the same.

<margin>The nature of Zacharius’s book.</margin>
*Zacharius* <note>Likely Denis Zachaire (1510–1556), a French alchemist who wrote a famous autobiographical account of his many failed attempts before allegedly succeeding.</note> published a most complete book on <term>Chemistry</term> in the French language while still living, after his work was completed not long ago; in this book, he frankly confessed his own fruitless labors, in the manner of Count Bernard <note>Bernard Trevisan, a legendary alchemist who spent decades and fortunes on failed experiments before finding the truth.</note>, so that others, having been made more cautious, might abstain from the said materials and operations. This method of teaching is surely the best in this kind of science, since more is gained by that "negative tradition"—namely, in which things the art is not found—

>*“Lest Zacharius the Parisian be exiled from France at Lausanne, having squandered his goods—”* “Slanderer” and “devil” <note>original: "Calumniator & diabolus." *Jean Fernel of Amiens* <note>Jean Fernel (1497–1558) was a highly influential French physician who introduced the term "physiology."</note> holds the first rank among the physicians of our age, both because of the purity of his doctrine and because of the ornament of his eloquence. By these gifts he obtained the position of primary physician to the King of France. By the King's command, he handed down the entire medical art with a grave style and clear method in two volumes, to which so much authority and faith have been attached that they are esteemed next after the writings of *Hippocrates*, *Galen*, and *Avicenna* in most universal schools. For *Fernel’s* authority is held there as authentic, just like that of *Galen*. Besides these medical writings, he published another treatise *On the Hidden Causes of Things* <note>original: "de abditis rerum causis." For that reason, he sought it in many books and regions, among the learned, with much labor and expense, until finally by the will of **GOD** he recognized it. But just as he acquired glory for himself through his labors, so his glory acquired for him the envy of others. For he did not remain immune from the bites of sycophants or the detractions of slanderers—a man as absolute in virtue as in learning and most worthy of the prize <note>original: "brabeio," a Greek-derived term for the reward given to a victor in a contest.</note> of praise. In other matters, lest I be too *keen-sighted* <note>original: "Lynceus," referring to the mythological Argonaut famous for his piercing vision.</note>, I will at least add some things concerning his last treatise, in which he promises to pass on the hidden causes of things and the *divine element* <note>original: "τὸ θεῖον" (to theion). <margin>
That so great a man as Fernel was not destitute of judgment.

How could he take upon himself so much labor in publishing things he did not understand? It is a work of no common invention or genius, and one that required a circumspect author as well as a circumspect reader. Hence, when a certain person from among those aforementioned critics read it, he wondered what Fernel intended for himself or where he was headed, since he could not see his intention.

### BOOK VII OF THE GOLDEN TABLE ###

<margin>You may drive out nature with a pitchfork, etc.</margin>
...to such an extent that there is no room for slander, except among those whose custom and natural unfairness this is; but let these people delight in their own disposition and practice their dog-like eloquence <note>A common Renaissance insult for critics, comparing their constant barking or snarling to dogs.</note> for as long as they wish. <margin>What of the Divine the Philosopher's Stone truly possesses.</margin>
In itself, because it is the gift of **GOD** alone and proceeds from God to him who is rendered more distinguished by it; and secondly, because it is investigated by a divine intellect alone, not one that is common or foolish:

<margin>The Stone is a gift of God.</margin>
As for diseases, in the curing of them, does it not obtain *something of the Divine*? Let us not fail to add that it presents the image of God and a shadow of the *Divine Trinity* more than any other earthly thing.

<margin>What Hippocrates calls divine.</margin>
Now **Hippocrates** <note>The ancient Greek physician often called the "Father of Medicine."</note> in his books established that the *Divine* in diseases is that which does not seem to happen by a natural and common course—as, for example, the critical days <note>In ancient medicine, "critical days" were specific times during an illness when the body was believed to undergo a "crisis" or turning point toward recovery or death.</note> are the fourth in very acute cases, the 7th, 14th, 22nd, and some intermediate days which are less perfect than those perfect ones:

<margin>Critical days.</margin>

<margin>What "the divine" in diseases commonly signifies.</margin>
But if in some disease something contrary to this happens, it is called *Divine*, because it departs from common nature and proceeds from the governor of nature, **God** Himself. Thus in *Epilepsy*, the suffocation of the womb <note>Historically called *hysteria*, this was a condition thought to be caused by the womb moving or "suffocating" the patient; Maier suggests it involves a supernatural or "divine" element.</note>, and various other diseases, something of the divine seems to be mixed in. <margin>What Fernel calls divine in those books.</margin>
<margin>Fernel's "form" comes from heaven.</margin>
He argues that the form possesses something of the divine and descends from heaven from the stars; nor is there anything born into which a form is not instilled from without. # SYMBOLS #

<margin>*Fernel on disease as form in "On the Hidden Causes of Things."*</margin>
...those called hidden properties; [he says] that in both matter and form, disease can occur. This opinion is unheard of and absurd to physicians: that **disease is a Form**. But I shall presume to interpret Fernel in this matter by this reasoning: that in his entire investigation and division of diseases, he understood the diseases not of men, but of metals. 

<margin>*Fernel understood diseases to be in metals, not men, elsewhere in "On the Hidden Causes of Things."*</margin>
For the so-called imperfect metals suffer a **disease of form and matter** with respect to gold. It is a disease of **Form** because they do not possess the form of gold, which they are destined to receive through "treatment" or projection <note>The alchemical process of "projection" involves casting the Philosopher's Stone upon base metals to "cure" them into gold.</note>. It is a disease of **Matter** because this matter is obstructed by heterogeneous [foreign] substances, acting like superfluous humors <note>In ancient medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids; here, Maier uses the term to describe chemical impurities in metals.</note>, and it perceives an **organic disease** in its path. 

For just as a song expresses its true tone at its conclusion, so Fernel himself—at the end, or rather in the penultimate and final chapters of the second book—manifestly shows that in the preceding parts he spoke and wished to be understood as discussing not man, but primarily metals and the **Philosopher's Stone**, which exists as both the son and the father of metals. 

<margin>*Fernel shows at the end of his book "On the Hidden Causes of Things" what he is actually talking about.*</margin>
If this is true, as it cannot be otherwise, let those unfair censors show what in this treatise does not harmonize with the nature of the reality. 

<margin>*The response of Fernel’s adversaries.*</margin>
But the opponent responds: first, that Fernel used a hundred or more testimonies cited from the writings of physicians, which cannot and should not be understood as referring to anything other than man. Furthermore, if he wrote about the "Stone," a thing which exists neither in nature nor in art, he wrote in vain and without fruit. But if it is granted that this Stone exists, how shall he apply testimonies derived from human medicine to his Stone?

<margin>*Response on behalf of Fernel’s book.*</margin>
I respond: the title of his book fits the writing, and the writing fits the title. For it is *On the Hidden Causes of Things* <note>original: "De abditis rerum causis"</note>, and it was written **hiddenly** [cryptically]. Therefore, he used general testimonies which would correspond to the common nature of medicine and of the substance he undertook to demonstrate, in which no equivocation or falsehood intervenes. In more specific matters, he cited those medical authorities as best he could—not because he was unable to employ other terms, but because he did not wish to, so that there might indeed be an occasion for thinking more deeply about these things. Hence it is that someone writes from the aforementioned [works]:

<margin>*Erastus <note>Thomas Erastus (1524–1583), a Swiss physician and critic of alchemy.</note> in a letter to Crato <note>Johannes Crato von Krafftheim, physician to three Holy Roman Emperors.</note>.*</margin>

*William of Paris* was undoubtedly a Frenchman and a true philosopher. <margin>Christopher of Paris. That God has many means to convert the Turks and resist them.</margin>

Nevertheless, he left behind sufficient witness that he was a philosopher in the chemical book he published, which is obscured everywhere by numbers and "clouds" <note>This refers to the common alchemical practice of using "Decknamen" (cover-names), ciphers, and allegorical imagery to hide secrets from the uninitiated.</note>. For Christopher says that God is able to use far different means, which are at His ready disposal if He so wills, to either convert or repress the Turks, the enemies of His Church, so that He has no need of the [Philosopher's] Stone or its gold-making. Although this may be very true, one ought not to remove or cut off every will to do good based on a noble intention, such as *Lully’s* was. In the giver, that benefit was religious zeal and sincerity in all things; in the receiver—I will not say it was a crime—but it was pretense and treachery <note>Lully famously sought royal patronage to fund Crusades and missionary work, but alchemical legends often claim kings used his gold for war rather than holy purposes.</note>.

*Jean de Meun* <note>original: "Iohannes de Mehu"; a famous French poet and author of the *Roman de la Rose*, to whom several alchemical works were attributed.</note>, who composed the book on the *Lamentations of Nature*, is very often recognized as a true philosopher by other sages, among whom is *Bernard* [of Trevisan]. All these persons, namely four times seven, when reduced to a calculation, are twenty-eight, and all are present here. For they all descend from me, and many others besides these, including their parents. And in these things, the explanation of the riddle appears." <note>This "incestuous" genealogy is a standard alchemical metaphor. It describes how one "root" substance (Mercury/B) is processed and transformed, with the resulting states being viewed as offspring that are recombined with the original material to achieve higher purity.</note>

# IN HONOR OF THE FRENCH.

<margin>Praise of Gaul.</margin>
> *Gaul, rich in resources, I shall show to be foremost in the earth's fertile soil,*
> *In bronze, in men, in fruit, and in honor.*

<margin>The French are of Germanic origin.</margin>
<margin>Worldly wealth is subject to the Tincture.</margin>
**I**t may suffice to have enumerated the chemical artisans <note>Alchemists.</note> of Gaul, both ancient and modern; now, in honor of all the French (most of whom are of Germanic origin, which none but those ignorant of history could deny), we shall add the vastness of that most opulent kingdom, its riches, ecclesiastical revenues, and whatever else pertains to this subject, just as we have borrowed them from French writers. These matters—being worldly riches—are subject to the one Tincture <note>The <term>Tincture</term> is the Philosopher's Stone in its liquid or powder form, capable of "dyeing" or transforming base metals into gold.</note> as their Mistress, and since they are otherwise pleasant and not useless for noble minds to perceive, they will not seem foreign to our purpose.

<margin>How many Archbishoprics and Bishoprics there are in France.</margin>
François de la Noue <note>original: Lanouius; a famous Huguenot commander and writer known for his "Political and Military Discourses."</note> says in his narratives that in *France* there are twelve Archbishoprics, 96 Bishoprics, 600 excellently endowed Abbeys, and 2,000 Priories. He states that all these religious orders possess an annual income of ten times a hundred thousand pounds <note>one million pounds</note>. But others, as mentioned above, claim it is much more—namely 20 million pounds—which seems more likely. For it is established that all the Italian bishoprics, priesthoods, and monasteries combined receive barely as much annual revenue from <term>ecclesiastical benefices</term> <note>property or land held by a member of the clergy that generates income</note> as just a fourth part of the French Church.

<margin>The revenues of France under Charles VI.</margin>
Jean Bodin <note>original: Bodinus; a prominent French jurist and political philosopher.</note> says in his book *On the Republic* that in the year 1444, under *Charles* VI, King of the *Franks*, the entire kingdom paid only thirteen times a hundred thousand pounds <note>1.3 million pounds</note> annually. Under *Charles* IX, in the year of his death (1574), the revenue of the kingdom exceeded fourteen million pounds. Under *Henry* IV, in our modern age, it pays five million gold [crowns] and five hundred thousand crowns <note>5.5 million gold crowns</note>.

<margin>The census of Gaul under Augustus.</margin>
Historical records tell us that *Augustus Caesar*, while he was in *Gaul*, conducted a census of all the provinces of *Gaul*, which then comprised the *Narbonenses*, the *Aquitanians*, the *Celts*, and the *Belgians*. After making an enumeration of the fields, the slaves, and all the collective resources, he imposed an annual tribute upon them amounting to ten million gold pieces <note>original: aureorum</note>.

<margin>The revenues of France under Henry III.</margin>
And Giovanni Botero <note>original: Iohannes Boterus; an Italian thinker and diplomat.</note> writes that *Henry* III also collected ten million crowns from his *France*; although it is certain that this was neither a regular yearly occurrence nor has it been achieved since then, despite it being the most opulent of all kingdoms, both because of the fertility of the region and...

<margin>*The Cabinet of the French King*, a book describing all of France.</margin>
The author of that treatise, which is entitled *The Cabinet of the French King* <note>original: *Conclaue Regis Franciae*; likely a reference to "Le Cabinet du Roy de France," a 1581 work attributed to Nicolas Barnaud</note>, a most exact investigator of French affairs, writes that the Kingdom of **France** has the shape of a **Rhomboid**, and extends from Belgian **Boulogne** <note>original: *Bononia Belgica*; Boulogne-sur-Mer</note> all the way to **Marseille** for two hundred <term>leagues</term> <note>a unit of distance, usually about 3 miles</note>, and just as many from the **Alps of Saint Bernard** to the town of **Saint-Jean-de-Luz**, which is situated at the **Pyrenees** mountains. By this calculation, the kingdom of *France*—or rather the provinces subject to the *Gallican Church*—will have in its total area forty thousand square *leagues*. And each individual *league* contains five thousand <term>acres</term> <note>original: *iugerum*; a Roman unit of area used here as a general term for land</note> of land, which together make two hundred million *acres* of soil.

For a *League* contains 50 measures, which the *French* call *stretches* <note>original: *portees*</note>, each measure being twelve *cords*. A *cord* is twelve *ells* <note>original: *ulnas*</note>. An *ell* is 2 ½ feet. A *foot* is 12 inches. Thus, a *league* will have in its length eighteen thousand feet, and in its square area five thousand acres. An *acre* of cultivated land contains 360 *perches* <note>original: *perticas*; a surveyor's rod or pole</note>. A *perch* is 9 ½ feet. One can measure an *acre* of vineyard and an *acre* of meadow in the same way, but an *acre* of *forest* contains 440 *perches*.

<margin>The three political estates of France.</margin>
The same author describes the three estates of the French Kingdom: the *Church*, the *Nobility*, and the *Common People*. He says the revenue of the political order (that is, of the King and the nobles, who have the common people subject to them) reaches 39 million and five hundred thousand <term>pounds of Tours</term> <note>original: *librarum Turonensium*; the Livre Tournois was the standard currency of France</note>, which exceeds 13 million **crowns**.

<margin>The Kings of France enriched the ecclesiastical order.</margin>

<margin>19. Negative Argument.</margin>
## *19. A negative argument against Chemistry <note>meaning Alchemy</note> set against Arnold of Villanova:*

> If nature cannot make gold from lead, neither will art ever do so.
> But nature is unable to do this.
> Therefore, neither can art. <note>The Latin "necars potest" is a contraction for "nec ars potest," completing the logical syllogism.</note>

### Arnold’s Response to the 19th Negative Argument.

<margin>Response to the 19th Negative Argument.</margin>
**I**t has already been demonstrated before that art is more capable in many things than nature; therefore, this reasoning is not valid: "Whatever nature cannot provide, art cannot provide either, even if it concerns natural things."

Furthermore, the premise <note>original: "assumptio"; refers to the second line of the syllogism ("But nature is unable to do this")</note> must be denied, based on what has already been frequently proven.

## *20. A negative argument against Chemistry <note>original: "Chemiam"; here referring specifically to the alchemical art of transmuting metals</note>.*
<margin>20. A negative argument.</margin>

If the proportion of any mixture, through which its <term>Form</term> <note>in Aristotelian philosophy, the "form" is the essential nature or "soul" of an object that makes it what it is</note> and its perfection exist, is unknown, then the mixing and preparation of that same thing cannot be known.
But the proportion of the elements of silver and gold is unknown.
Therefore, the mixing and preparation of silver and gold also cannot be known.

From these points, they conclude that the art dealing with the preparation of these bodies <note>meaning the metals silver and gold</note> is useless and impossible.

They prove the major premise <note>the first part of the logical argument</note> as follows: The <term>species</term> <note>distinct categories or kinds of being</note> and varieties of things are distinct because the proportions of their elements to one another are diverse and distinct. For a donkey is different from a human in species because it possesses a very different proportion of elements in its composition. This can be inferred in all other varieties of things; therefore, it is also true for minerals.

<term>art</term> <note>original: "ars"; in this context, it refers to human skill, specifically the alchemical "art" that mimics or assists nature</note> never undertakes this; but it receives those things which are already mixed by nature, and into which that required proportion of elements has already been introduced, so that there is no need for some new weighing of the elements to be mixed. For if art sets out to make something, either that very thing has been made elsewhere by nature, or it exists nowhere. If it exists nowhere, then it will not be produced even with the aid of art through human imagination or industry. If it exists elsewhere having been made by nature, it is either perfect or begun: that which is perfect does not need a new making, nor destruction, but perhaps some correction or purification. That which is begun, this is like a <term>seed</term>, <term>embryo</term>, or <term>egg</term> of a thing to be born through nature; if art receives this seed and disposes it in the proper way, then it can produce from it the same thing that nature does of its own accord; but perhaps not as quickly or perfectly as art. The cause is this: because art uses nature’s instruments, such as heat and other aids, and meanwhile adds a significant effort of its own to the natural ones.

->Therefore, the major premise is not true:<- <note>Arnold is rejecting the first part of the opponent's logical argument, which claimed art must know exact elemental proportions to create a mixture.</note>

To the <term>minor premise</term> <note>the second part of the opponent's argument: that the proportion of elements in silver and gold is unknown</note>, I say that the proportion of silver and gold is not unknown to the craftsman in a general sense, but in a specific sense, it is not necessary. That is, while he receives a seed or egg or other natural matter into which he wishes to introduce a form determined by nature, he knows in a general way that in that matter there is a true proportion of those things which he intends to produce. However, in a specific sense—by what weight the vapors or elements are mixed there—this he does not know, nor is it useful for him to
->know.<-

### 21. A Negative Argument against Alchemy.

<margin>Argument 21, negative.</margin>
> **If gold can be made by art from natural principles and materials, then the practitioner who intends this will use either nature’s own process, or one foreign to it.**
> **But he can use neither.**
> **Therefore, gold cannot be made by art from natural principles and materials.**

The *minor premise* <note>the second statement in the logical argument above: "But he can use neither"</note> is proven: because if he used nature's process, he would have to imitate nature in every respect as she works within the earth. This would mean leaving the minerals in the ground and not carrying them out from their "beds" into the light; or, if they were carried out, returning them to the same place and waiting for the vast time required for their perfection. This is impossible and foolish to attempt. If, however, he uses a process specific to <term>art</term> <note>human skill or technology</note> and foreign to nature, then the result will also be different from the natural effect, and thus it will not be true natural gold.

### Response 21. To the negative argument of Arnold.

<margin>Response to the 21st negative argument.</margin>
**I** respond to the minor premise: art does not use the natural process by starting from the very first principles and going to the end; nor does it have any need to do so, since one is permitted to begin where nature left off and thus reach the goal. In nature's case, this goal is gold generated from <term>matter and form</term> <note>Aristotelian concepts where "matter" is the physical substance and "form" is the essential identity or soul of the metal</note>, such that the form is produced from the matter. Therefore, the process is not foreign to nature, since it agrees with nature in the final end, and in both the matter and the form of the compound. Natural principles are also employed, but they are already mixed, since—

The rebuttal argues that alchemy isn't "unnatural" but rather a shortcut that picks up where nature's own work left off.</summary>

### *Reason 19. Affirmative for the truth of Alchemy, by Arnold of Villanova himself.*

<margin>Reason 18, affirmative for Alchemy.</margin> <note>The text labels this Reason 19 in the heading but Reason 18 in the margin, a common numbering discrepancy in early modern printing.</note>
If lead is called **"leprous gold,"** <note>Alchemists often viewed base metals like lead as being "diseased" or "imperfect" versions of gold; "leprous gold" implies it only needs a "cure" to become perfect.</note> and if in Rome there still exists a public epitaph of a collector of gold from lead, and if also, from every piece of lead—before a <term>fire-assay</term> <note>original: docimastica probatio; the technical process of testing the purity of metals using heat</note> is carried out on it—its proportional grain of silver must be extracted, then silver and gold are both naturally born from lead and can be, or are, made from it artificially.
But the first three statements are most true.
Therefore, so is the last.

Three things are connected here with a single intention, and thus form a weaker knot <note>a logical term for a group of linked arguments</note>: Lead is called leprous gold; therefore, if its leprosy is cured, it will be gold. ...and to produce gold, he is able to receive their seeds or the proportioned matter from nature. Therefore, it will not be impossible for him to produce these natural works by ordained means.

*The major premise is true in itself* <note>In a formal logical argument, the "major premise" is the broad general rule. Here, Maier argues that if humans can assist nature in one area, they can do it in another.</note> and is established by countless examples, such as the hatching of eggs into chicks, the production of crops, and the propagation of any trees and vegetables from seeds committed to the earth. Thus in Germany, the raising of <term>Guaiacum</term> <note>original: Guaiaci; a tropical wood from the Americas used in the 16th century as a cure for syphilis. Growing it in cold Germany was a triumph of artificial climate control.</note> shrubs, oranges, and lemons from seeds in summer can be achieved, though the subsequent winter cold destroys them. Likewise, horses and other animals, with human care added, are propagated and raised through their own nature and seeds. Thus mules are generated by the will of man; to say nothing of others.

*To the minor premise:* <note>The "minor premise" is the specific application of the rule—here, that alchemists have access to the "seeds" of metals.</note> there is no doubt that the chemist can receive the seeds of silver and gold, even if he does not take those very principles—that is, the vapors and fumes—from which nature produces the same. For in that regard, he cannot, nor ought he, imitate nature. But what such seeds are is not for this place to determine, as they pertain to another question. We add this: that to produce **sulfur** from the best substance of **quicksilver** <note>original: argenti vivi; literally "living silver," the standard term for mercury.</note>, without the mixture of any external sulfur, is characteristic of the art. Once this is obtained, as if containing the form, it can be mixed with its own metallic **Mercury** whenever desired, and thus gold is generated by a natural mixture.

## SYMBOLS
### VIII.

it remains established: why could gold equal to natural gold not be produced by art?

But the first point is true regarding natural salt dug out of the earth in Poland, and salt made from seawater in Spain and elsewhere by the heat of the sun, or by the heat of fire from natural brine in Halle, Lüneburg, and countless other places in Europe. <note>Halle and Lüneburg were famous German centers for salt production, where salt was extracted from saline springs (brine) rather than mined as rock salt.</note>

->Therefore, the second point is also possible.<-

*To the confirmation of the proposition* it suffices that a natural thing, which elsewhere is born spontaneously, can be made by art. For if this is true, then that universal proposition which denies it will fail. <note>Maier is attacking the common philosophical objection that "Art can only imitate the appearance of nature, not create its essence."</note> The connection of its terms is evident from this: because the process is almost the same in both cases. Among the Poles, salt is dug out in large chunks like rocks; it is somewhat dark and can be purified by art—just as other salts are usually made white by the pouring on of pure water and repeated boiling. So too is sea salt purified by art, which is coagulated from seawater held in a closed trench (so it is not mixed with the waves) by the rays of the sun, provided that heavy rain does not flow in. A coagulation of this kind is made from natural brine under the earth by nature in Poland; in Saxony and other places, it is made from that same natural brine above the earth by art. There are also those who boil down seawater over a fire into salt—specifically in places where the sun's rays are not so strong and there is an abundance of wood. This is to say nothing of salts from willow trees and other vegetables, and even those extracted from the burnt dung of animals by the Chemical art, <note>original: "arte Chymica"; here referring to early laboratory techniques for extracting "fixed salts" from organic matter.</note> some of which are considered medicinal and some not. Nor should this be understood only regarding salt, but regarding many other minerals which are both made by art and generated by nature. If, therefore, one of these is before everyone's eyes—as anyone can see the production of salt—while the other is not, because it wishes and ought to be hidden, why do we not transfer by analogy those things we see in the one to understand the other which lies hidden?

<summary>Maier uses the artificial production of salt in Europe as a logical proof that humans can replicate natural mineral processes. He argues that if we can create pure salt from brine using fire or sun, we should by analogy be able to produce gold through alchemy.</summary>

As once *Truth hung from the neck of the Egyptian Judge* in a little image <note>referring to the "Maat" or Truth pendant worn by ancient Egyptian high priests and judges</note>, so that he might always be reminded of it, so for anyone who would judge sincerely about those things which exist or happen in the world, that same truth ought to hang from the mind, and be so fixed in it that one must not dissent from it for the sake of anyone's favor or hatred. If the adversaries of Chemistry had respected this, they would not have brought forth, for the sake of **St. Thomas**, or out of hatred for Chemistry, those things which are contrary to all truth.

That it is clear from his chemical books that St. Thomas was a chemist.

But to the point: **that St. Thomas was a chemist**, who could prove better than he himself in his own writings, the consistency of public reputation, the consensus of chemical craftsmen, and the assertions of other men of outstanding authority? In addition to these, other circumstances can prove the same thing. Regarding his chemical writings, adversaries immediately cast a doubt, <note>original: "scrupulum inijciunt," literally "to cast a small sharp stone [into the shoe]," meaning to cause hesitation or difficulty.</note> denying that they belong to **St. Thomas**, but are instead surreptitious and falsely attributed to him. Let them go where they wish, then, with their trifling dictates—but not to the chemists, who desire that things denied or affirmed against the Art <note>The "Art" refers to Alchemy or the "Great Work."</note> be demonstrated to them. *If it is permitted to dictate in such a way—that he is a frivolous man, devoted to trifles in his youth; that this man is not a chemist and the books ascribed to him are not his own—what will we not deny or affirm in the arts and sciences without arguments and proofs?* What if I were to say: these new adversaries are not of sound mind when they blabber whatever comes into their mouths; <note>original: "quicquid in buccam venit," a Latin idiom for speaking without thinking.</note> would this proposition not be more probable, with a reason added, than their claim that the chemical books do not belong to **St. Thomas** but were substituted for his?

<margin>
Why the chemical books are said to be substituted for St. Thomas’s by the adversaries.
</margin>
Why substituted? Because they are not gathered into a single body with the other works of **St. Thomas**. But this "little reason" is worth only as much as this: *Virgil did not live in Mantua, but in Rome and Naples; therefore, he was not a Mantuan.* <note>Virgil was born near Mantua, but spent much of his life in Rome and Naples. Maier is pointing out the logical fallacy of judging a person's identity or work solely by where they are currently found.</note> For just as it depended on the will of *Virgil* to leave his native soil and live elsewhere, so it proceeded from the will of **St. Thomas** himself, or from the collector and editor of his works, that the chemical book (whether one or several) was not added or incorporated into his volumes. Who will deny that the chemical books circulated under the name of **St. Thomas** are his own, unless he be one who *seeks a knot in a bulrush* <note>original: "nodum in scirpo quærat," a proverb for looking for a problem where none exists.</note> and *presumes to darken the sun at midday?* <note>To deny the obvious.</note>

<margin>
Why the chemical books of St. Thomas are his and not another's.
</margin>
For unless this were true, doubt would always remain concerning the author of any book—nay, even concerning the father of children. It sometimes happens, indeed, that unlearned deceivers substitute their own offspring <note>Metaphorically, their own poorly written books.</note> for those of the learned, but then the offspring are distinguished from the parents— <note>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page.</note>

<margin>
Other sciences, when compared to Alchemy, are like handmaidens to a mistress.
</margin>
...doubtless to **Thomas Aquinas**, whom he <note>Referring to Albertus Magnus, Thomas’s teacher mentioned on the previous page.</note> found more suitable and skilled for this deepest and most secret discipline than any other, and whom he esteemed for his singular gifts of genius. For it must not be thought that **Thomas** would have adhered to **Albert** as his teacher in other sciences rather than in this most divine of all. For what are the other sciences when compared to this one? Certainly, they are as handmaidens to a Mistress. This science provides the miracles of nature and demonstrates the most certain practice of all contemplative physics through its results. From these facts, it is clear that St. **Thomas** is found to be an Alchemist <note>original: "Chymicum"</note> regardless of how he is considered, though one proof alone would suffice: namely, the evidence of the books on Alchemy published in his name.

<margin>
Testimonies sought from other books of St. Thomas which declare him an Alchemist.
</margin>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;But now we shall proceed to other testimonies of **Thomas** himself, which are found not in Alchemical books, but in his widely accepted works. In his commentary on **Aristotle’s** *Meteorology*, Book 3, toward the end, he says: *The proximate matter of metals is sulfur and quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum," or mercury</note>, as the Alchemists say, such that in the stony places of the earth, sulfur and quicksilver are generated through a mineral virtue; then, from these, diverse metals are generated according to their diverse mixing. Whence even the Alchemists themselves, through the true art of Alchemy—which is nonetheless difficult because of the hidden operations of the celestial virtue called "mineral"—sometimes achieve the true generation of metals, following the aforementioned principles or those derived from them, because these operations, though hidden, can be imitated by us.* These words of St. **Thomas** encompass nature and art together, and show most clearly the manner of operation for both: namely, that metals take their origin from sulfur and quicksilver as if from a father and mother; but sulfur and quicksilver are congealed in the rocky hollows of the earth from various exhaling fumes and hardened into a metallic substance by a mineral virtue.

<margin>
The Alchemists' work is made from sulfur and quicksilver.
</margin>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;From this, the Alchemists, taking nature as their example, produce the same natural result from sulfur and quicksilver, namely gold and silver. For they are not concerned with the other metals, since reason suggests one should focus on the best. There is no need for them to compose quicksilver from fumes, because this is impossible for them from the start, and because quicksilver is produced by nature...

<margin>Common sulfur is useless to Chemists <note>original: "Chymicis"</note>.</margin>
...so great is the quantity of the composite, as much as that of the imperfect metals and quicksilver <note>mercury; original: "hydrargyri"</note>. Common sulfur is a useless defect to them; for this reason, they sought another sulfur through long investigation, great labor, and expense. Once found, from these two—just as fire is struck from steel and flint—they elicited gold. That is, from the proper mixing of these in the fire, they produced gold in a small space of time, scarcely half an hour.

<margin>Gold is made from sulfur and quicksilver in a short space of time in the fire.</margin>
**St. Thomas** admits that this operation is difficult, more by reason of its discovery than its perfection. This is due to the hidden operations of celestial virtue, as he himself asserts; and this is true, for unless this force from heaven were impressed upon the stone, no artisan could ever reach—or would have reached—the end.

<margin>The Triple-Father <note>original: "Tripater"</note> is necessary in the art.</margin>
This is that **Triple-Father**, whom **Lull** <note>referring to Ramon Lull, a famous 13th-century philosopher often associated with alchemical works</note> mentions in the *Theory of the Testament*: namely, the son of the celestial **Sun**, the ingenious **Artisan**, and **Vulcan** <note>the Roman god of fire, representing the heat of the furnace</note>. He is created by the sun, governed by the artisan, and raised by **Vulcan**. This is that "form" without which the same author says any artisan proceeds in the art like a painter who tries to express a person's face to the life, whom he has never seen in person, known in an image, nor heard described by another. Nevertheless, **St. Thomas** says that although these operations of celestial virtue are hidden, they can be imitated by "us." In using the word "us," he does not exclude himself as an artisan; indeed, perhaps he understands himself as unique, speaking of himself in the plural number, as is often done, in place of the singular.

<margin>Products of principles <note>original: "Principiata"</note>, that is, elemented things, and not <unclear>si</unclear> vapors are taken for the art.</margin>
It is certain that the artisan proceeds through "principiata" <note>things already formed from the elements or principles</note> rather than the first principles themselves, since the principles are too remote from the art. He also says that they sometimes perform a true generation of metals—that is, the true artisans, who are very rare; those who are not perfected, however, even if they attempt it, can in no way succeed. Thus, **St. Thomas**, not excluding himself from the art, describes its entire general process most excellently. He does so in such a way that he might not be publicly regarded as an Alchemist (a name held in common with the pseudo-chemists), but at least by true artisans—

<margin>St. Thomas described and treated Chemical <term>Chymica</term> matters prudently.</margin>
...to other artisans, so that he might be recognized as an artisan: this must be attributed to his prudence. For although the art in itself is excellent and a divine gift given to only a very few, yet because so many idle men—squanderers of their fathers' wealth, gluttons, gormandizers, and those overwhelmed by debt—rush and flock to it daily in crowds, as if to *Lucina* <note>the Roman goddess of childbirth, here invoked as a source of relief or the "birth" of wealth</note> bringing help, or to a golden anchor. 

<margin>Why the Chemical Art, though excellent in itself, has a bad reputation.</margin>
These men, according to their own wit, devise something sophisticated <note>meaning adulterated or fake</note>, deceptive, and frivolous; hence our Queen, **Chemistry**, has a bad reputation. Because these pseudo-chemists <note>original: "pseudochymici"</note> claim and appropriate this art as if for themselves alone—though they have not seen even its outward face nor understand the smallest stroke of its letters—the common people judge true Chemists and philosophers under the same name as them. They condemn the true masters for the same fraudulent operations which result in harm to the Commonwealth. From such things, no good man does anything but recoil. 

<margin>Why Chemists do not wish to be recognized as such.</margin>
This is the reason for so many anonymous writings, so many changes of homeland, and so many allegorical treatises—not only regarding their subject matter and contents, but also regarding their purpose—so that no one might be pointed out as an alchemist <note>original: "Alchymista"</note> by the common people. 

<margin>Why the chemical books of St. Thomas were not grouped with his others.</margin>
This is the reason why **St. Thomas** did not group his chemical books—which he treated as if they were illegitimate offspring, though he was their natural father—with his other volumes. It is also why, in his other books, he speaks of Chemistry <note>original: "Chemia"</note> secretly and cautiously, as in the place already mentioned. In those works, he nevertheless brings forth his opinion quite ingeniously—not as a Chemist by profession, but as a physicist who, if necessary, could nonetheless cast his vote <note>original: "calculum ferre," a classical idiom for giving a judgment or vote</note> regarding Chemistry. 

He uses the same approach in another place in his works, namely in the *Summa Theologica* <note>Second part of the second part, question 77, article 2</note>.

<header>BOOK VIII OF THE GOLDEN TABLE.</header>

## BOOK VIII OF THE GOLDEN TABLE.

These very propositions—namely, the <term>major premise</term> <note>the first part of a logical argument</note> of the first <term>syllogism</term> and the <term>minor premise</term> of the second—were a product of his subtle intellect. He does this to prove the point in Question 96, Article 2 of the same book and part: <note>original: "Quod si simpliciter... iis rebus vel effectu uti"</note> *“For if,”* he says, *“natural things are simply applied to produce certain effects for which they are thought to have a natural power, it is not superstitious or unlawful to use those things or that effect.”*

<margin>Natural Magic approved by St. Thomas.</margin>
With these words, he fully approves of **Natural Magic** and declares it to be in no way superstitious or illicit. And in the beginning of the fourth book of the *Meteorologica*: <note>A work on natural phenomena often attributed to or commented upon by Aquinas</note> *“The principal goal of Alchemists is to transmute metals—specifically, the imperfect ones—truly and not sophistically <note>falsely or purely through appearance</note>.”* He likewise says: *“METALS can be transmuted from one into another, since they are natural things and their matter is the same.”* Therefore, no one has doubted that St. Thomas was a **Chemist** <note>here meaning Alchemist</note> and spoke and wrote in favor of **Chemistry** as openly in his alchemical books as he did secretly in his other works, so that it requires no further demonstration. But since there is a controversy among his interpreters, most of whom—being ignorant of Chemistry—assert that he established nothing regarding the truth of Chemistry, we shall bring forward the opinions of these men from Pico della Mirandola and offer them for consideration to any rational person:

<margin>Mirandola reconciles the interpreters of St. Thomas regarding Chemistry.</margin>
Pico della Mirandola <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a famous Renaissance philosopher</note> says in Book 2, Chapter 3 of *On Gold*: *“Saint Thomas, in the second part of the second volume of the Summa Theologica, affirms the truth of Chemistry, which he had not asserted in his second commentary on the theological Sentences. Therefore, he has appeared inconsistent in this matter to many, as will appear more clearly in its proper place when we openly interpret his opinion. As far as the present is concerned, Sylvester <note>Sylvester Mazzolini, a Dominican theologian</note>, a follower of Thomas, is of the same opinion—that gold can be made through art—an opinion which John <note>likely John Capreolus</note> did not maintain.”*

<margin>Sylvester, an interpreter of Thomas, speaks in favor of Chemistry.</margin>
<margin>Cajetan likewise.</margin>
*“But Thomas Cajetan <note>Cardinal Cajetan (1469–1534), a major commentator on Aquinas</note> judges in his Summula that the art itself—provided it is done without fraud—is not to be considered unlawful in itself; nor should the sale of a thing produced through art be counted among sins, if the sale is made for exactly what it truly is. In his commentaries on the Summa Theologica of St. Thomas, he writes that the art is indeed possible, but either it is not human, or it belongs to princes after they have consulted the wise. Regarding the power of the art, nothing...”*

...differs, as he is accustomed to doing acutely in other questions. In this matter, some are amazed that when he confirmed the truth and authority of the Art <note>the "Art" here refers to Alchemy</note> by reason and the authority of St. Thomas, he immediately decreed it possible for man. Thomas's own reasoning proves this very point: if he admits it is possible, why is it not possible for humans? If princes and the wise men they consult can practice it, why should it be considered above the reach of man? As if princes and wise men are not to be counted among men!

<margin>Giovanni Liguri, an interpreter of Thomas, speaks against Chemistry <note>original: "Chemiam", here meaning alchemy</note>.</margin>
The same Pico della Mirandola <note>original: "Mirandulanus", a famous Renaissance philosopher</note>, in his second book, chapter 11, clarifies the opinion of Thomas Aquinas regarding the making of gold, which his interpreters have distorted. He says: *I certainly do not agree with Giovanni Liguri, who excluded the "form of gold" <note>the essential nature or "soul" of gold</note> from the Art for the sake of its nobility, and therefore mocked the art of making gold. For, as we have said, Thomas admits "perfection" as the form—that is, the sensitive soul—of which the Magi <note>practitioners of natural magic and alchemy</note> showed themselves to be the producers of natural things by means of their instruments. Nor am I moved by the fact that the craftsmen do not know how to find those things which properly act and those which properly suffer <note>undergo change</note>. For one need not be ignorant that heat, moisture, and many vapors are the means nature is accustomed to using for the transmutation of metals. Add to this that what Thomas seemed to deny as a young man, he constantly affirmed long afterward—that is, while he was composing the **Summa Theologica**, as if it were the final testament of his opinions. Nor am I moved by the argument used by Sylvester Liguri <note>Sylvester Prierias, a theologian from Liguria</note>, who, along with Petrus Gomas, thought that St. Thomas spoke of "imperfect craftsmen" in his second commentary, but spoke of "perfect ones" in the **Summa**, thus denying the power to the former while granting it to the latter.*

<margin>St. Thomas did not neglect Chemical matters or "great wonders" <note>original: "magnalia"</note>, he who took care of other lesser things.</margin>
For the mention was of the *Art* of making, not of the *craftsmen*. Indeed, since this Art uses the service and instruments of nature, it can be led to perfection by all who are capable of practicing it—whether they be incorporeal spirits or men, whether they are taught naturally or supernaturally. For a variety of ministers does not take away or diminish the Art itself, which relies on the forces of nature; rather, the practitioner sometimes assists that nature and sometimes surpasses it. So much from Pico della Mirandola concerning Thomas. Therefore, St. Thomas is not undeservedly established as the prince of Italian **Chemists**, who with his angelic intellect obstru- <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "obstru-", likely leading to a word meaning "blocked" or "built up"</note>

<header>OF THE GOLDEN TABLE. BOOK 8.</header>

# OF THE GOLDEN TABLE. BOOK 8.

Even though he had penetrated and elucidated the most difficult subjects, he considered his life to be quite bitter unless he also investigated those great wonders of God <note>original: "magnalia Dei"</note> which the whole world gapes at—especially under that teacher <note>Albertus Magnus, who was famously Thomas Aquinas's mentor and a reputed alchemist</note> who was notoriously a **Chemist** <note>here meaning an alchemist</note>. In his aforementioned Alchemical book, two things in particular must be considered: first, what he deduces in the preface by that beautiful example of **Optics**, where solar rays are condensed through concave mirrors to such a degree that they ignite whatever combustible materials they meet. He argues that the celestial virtues descending from the stars—namely from the sun—are communicated to us and are one and the same as the lower elemental virtues.
<margin>*Fire drawn from solar rays is the same as elementary fire.*</margin>
There is no difference between the fire ignited in this way and our common fire. From this, it is clear that the celestial essence can be preserved in these lower elements, just as that **golden Form** <note>the "Form" refers to the essential nature or "soul" of gold that gives it its properties</note> is mixable with all metals, leading the more imperfect among them back into gold.
<margin>*The form of gold descends from the stars.*</margin>
For this Form, as was said a little before, descends from the stars, impressed from heaven into earthly substance. It was brought down to mortals as if by the **stalk of Prometheus** <note>referring to the myth of Prometheus stealing fire from the gods in a hollow fennel stalk</note>, so that they might have a **son of the sun** on earth. When this "son" is well-guided by the genius of the craftsman and properly brought forth by the labor of **Vulcan** <note>the god of fire, representing the alchemist's furnace</note>, he might take the place of his father here; what the father performs in a thousand years, the son himself would perform in a few minutes of a single hour. For just as the rays of the celestial sun are multiplied in the aforementioned mirrors and become, as it were, corporeal and tangible like fire, so when the rays of the **terrestrial sun** <note>the alchemical gold or "Stone"</note> come together and are reflected back into themselves, that which was at first quasi-spiritual and impalpable becomes corporeal and tangible. That which was first produced as a **point** from the sun and heaven has its **circumference** completed and continued by our own fire, or "Vulcan."
<margin>*The center of the Chemical compound is from heaven, the circumference from our fire.*</margin>
There is a *Ray* of celestial light, and there is also a ray on earth, which shines in the darkness like a **carbuncle** <note>a legendary gemstone said to emit its own light</note> gathered into itself. Therefore, our Ray must be taken and its shadow must be destroyed, as **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> advises.
<margin>*The shadow must be removed from the Ray.*</margin>
This cannot happen unless the sun enters **Cancer** <note>the zodiac sign of the summer solstice, when the sun is at its strongest</note>, as it does for those who live in the **Delta**, the island of Egypt, near Syene... <note>Syene, or modern Aswan, was famous in antiquity because the sun stands directly overhead there during the summer solstice.</note>

<margin>The Stone is first an old man, then a youth.</margin>
...[at noon], the sun is vertical and without shadow. Now, **Cancer** is the house of the **Moon**, and the **Moon** is the mistress of the humors <note>The "humors" here refer to the liquid components or "moisture" of the alchemical substance</note>; these humors dominate in our Stone. For this reason, it is white and an "old man" at first; but after these humors have been dried out, it later becomes red and a "bloody youth," as the letter of **Rhazes** <note>original: "Rhasis"; a famous 9th-century Persian physician and alchemist</note> describes it. This **Ray** <note>original: "Radius"</note>, or little fire, dwells in the earth and is not extinguished by water, because it is of celestial virtue. It is nourished by the vilest fuel, just as a fetus in the womb is nourished by the <term>menstruum</term> <note>In alchemy, the "menstruum" refers to a primary solvent or a nourishing fluid that fosters the growth of the Stone</note>. For just as fire, that most precious element, can be fed by any fatty matter—since there are those who use animal dung to foster fires—so the **philosophical fire**, supplied by the Sun to the craftsman, is sustained by a cheaper fodder so that it does not vanish.

<margin>The fire of nature is nourished by vile fodder, by an unnatural fire.</margin>
It exists in a fatty, oily, and incombustible substance which, since it is entirely viscous, does not easily vanish or resolve into the air. This is the **Natural Heat** and the **Radical Moisture** <note>the fundamental life-force and essential fluid believed to exist in all things</note>, joined together in friendship. This is the flame, and that is the oil; this is the horse, and that is the fodder; this is the dog, and that is the hare; this is the active agent, and that is the passive subject, which embraces all things. Secondly, in his *Chemical Book*, **St. Thomas** identifies the matter as a black, "eyed" earth, 

<margin>The Matter of St. Thomas is black earth: or antimony.</margin>
which he calls **Spanish Antimony**. **Democritus**, in the annotations of **Flamel** <note>Nicolas Flamel, the legendary French scrivener and alchemist</note>, calls this same thing **Italian Stibium** <note>original: "Stimmi Italicum"; stibium is another name for antimony</note>, and many others call it by different names. To these may be added the agreement of **Greverus**, **Basil** <note>Basil Valentine</note>, and countless others. There is no doubt that the mind of the philosophers is unanimous and most true in this regard, provided it is correctly understood. What a certain diligent searcher of **Antimony** created from it, he himself left recorded in his little book—namely mercury, lead, copper, iron, tin, "liver" <note>likely "liver of antimony," a sulfurous compound</note>, silver, and gold. Others have made from it the *Regulus of Flowers* <note>crystalline forms of the metal</note>, white, yellow, and red; oil, glass, salt, and innumerable other medicines. 

<margin>What has been made from antimony.</margin>
For this reason, **Basil Valentine** not undeservedly dedicated a *Triumph* to **Antimony** <note>referring to the famous book "The Triumphal Chariot of Antimony"</note>, as if it were the victor and triumpher over diseases; indeed, he called it the **Hercules who slays disease**. From this, many of the more wise have taken their evidence...

# THE GOLDEN TABLE. BOOK VIII. #

They allege <note>original: "pferunt," abbreviation for "proferunt"</note> that there lies in **antimony** more medicinal virtue than in any other **simple** <note>a medicine made from a single constituent, usually a plant or mineral</note>, and therefore also more transforming power, or **tincture**. They have also discovered through experience that a silver spoon dipped into a lye <margin>Volatile gold in antimony.</margin> prepared from it by a simple method becomes gilded, and the same happens with its oil when drawn off through a **retort** <note>a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distillation</note>; however, they note that this gold is **volatile** <note>in alchemy, "volatile" means a substance that easily evaporates or is not yet "fixed" or stable</note>. From this, not a few people conceive great hope. I certainly shall not draw them away from such a good intention; nevertheless, I will not urge them toward that particular goal.

<margin>Various birthplaces of Antimony.</margin>
**Lord Thomas** <note>likely referring to pseudo-Aquinas, to whom many alchemical texts were attributed</note> speaks of **Spanish Antimony**, and **Democritus** speaks of **Italian *Stimmi*** <note>an ancient Greek name for antimony</note>. Others speak of the **Hungarian** variety. **Mattioli** <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, a famous 16th-century botanist and physician</note> reports that there are many mines of the antimony ore in **Siena**; he says the best, however, is found in places near the sea, such as **Messina** and **Sovana**, and near the little town of **Silvena** in the county of **Santa Fiora**. To **Venice** it is brought from **Germany**, appearing as a yellow substance in pots. <margin>Pliny mentions Antimony.</margin> **Pliny**, in Book 33, Chapter 6, also mentions antimony while describing a stone found in silver mines; it is white and shining without being transparent. It is called ***Stimmi*** by some, ***Stibium*** by others, and by some ***Alabastrum*** or ***Larbason***. There are two kinds, male and female, but the female is judged to have the better virtue. It is held in **Schemnitz** in **Hungary**. **Basil of Hungary** <note>referring to the legendary alchemist Basil Valentinus</note> says:
> *Hungary begat me, the sky and stars nourish me, and the earth suckles me, etc.*

<margin>Antimony is found in the gold mines of Hungary.</margin>
There are those who testify that it is found most abundantly there in the gold mines. In **Germany**, the **Torch-bearing Mountain** (the ***Fichtelberg***) and **Altenberg**, and many other mines, produce antimony. But you may ask: which genus among these should be chosen? I answer: the **Philosophical** kind, which is even more effective in its virtues than the others, wherever it may be sought. <margin>Philosophical Antimony suits the art.</margin> The Philosophers do not agree on the "place" of this substance, except to say that it is found everywhere, is of low price, is hidden in the dung-heap, and that ***Adam carried it with him out of Paradise, and the birds brought it to us; it is a stone given for free, to be taken by anyone in whatever amount they please.***

We remember from history that the son of **Margaret**, Queen of the three northern kingdoms <note>original: "Margaritæ"; referring to Margaret I of Denmark (1353–1412), who united Denmark, Norway, and Sweden under the Kalmar Union. And although it represented certain **volatile tinctures** <note>In alchemy, a "tincture" is a substance capable of changing the color or nature of a metal; "volatile" means it evaporates easily and is not yet "fixed" or stable.</note>, as if they were signs of royal offspring, yet in the end it was reduced to ashes and cast aside as useless.

Hence they sit idle at home and care neither for the royal **Treasury** <note>original: "Gazam"; a term for a royal treasure-house or hoard.</note> nor for their own salvation.

<margin>A great part of the work consists in the choice of species.</margin>
**Antimony**, therefore, is not to be rejected by the art, but must be chosen with great care and foresight. For so says **Morienus** <note>Morienus was a legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist said to have taught the Ummayad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> to King **Khalid**: *Similarly, you should know,* he says, *that the greater root of the work lies in the inquiry of species, which are better suited for this mastery.* For every mineral is of many kinds. Thus, <term>St. Thomas</term> <note>original: "D. Thomas"; referring to Thomas Aquinas, though most alchemical works attributed to him are now considered pseudepigraphal (written by others in his name).</note> rightly chose **Spanish** antimony, as it is more excellent than all the others we have listed. However, he did not use it without a singular preparation, since from common things—as **Greverus** <note>Jodocus Greverus, a 16th-century German alchemist known for his "Secretum."</note> says—physical things must be made. <margin>Physical antimony must be used.</margin> For whatever enters the philosophical work must be pure, homogeneous, and purged of all its heterogeneity and superfluous earth into a clear substance suitable for the philosophical work; which, depending on the type of operation, will either fly off entirely <note>referring to sublimation or evaporation</note> or remain entirely at the bottom.

## THE COMPATRIOTS OF ST. THOMAS AQUINAS; ITALIANS.

<margin>Petrus Bonus of Ferrara. Where Bonus lived.</margin>
**PETRUS BONUS OF FERRARA**, a man who corresponds perfectly to his name: for in whatever way he is perceived, whether in character or in teachings, he is *Bonus* <note>The Latin name "Bonus" means "Good."</note>. He lived at Pola in Istria <note>Modern-day Pula, Croatia.</note> more than two hundred years ago. He wrote a chemical treatise, truly called the *New Pearl* <note>original: "Margarita nouella"; refers to his famous work "Pretiosa Margarita Novella," written around 1330.</note>, in which he treats this question so solidly, <margin>The "New Pearl" of Bonus is a most learned treatise.</margin> learnedly, and copiously: whether the art of Chemistry is possible or not. He demonstrates the affirmative through arguments drawn from the nature and properties of the subject, so clear and perspicuous that no one after him has had need to attempt the task. But since abundance indeed clarifies a matter, yet diminishes syllogistic sharpness, others after him—just as new antagonists or wrestlers <note>original: "pancratiastę"; referring to practitioners of pancration, an ancient Greek combat sport.</note> might face new enemies or net-fighters <note>original: "retiarijs"; a type of Roman gladiator who fought with a net and trident.</note>—opposed themselves and defended Chemistry as established and protected with all their strength—

<margin>The "Pearl" is worthy of the honor of a new edition.</margin>
...defended: It would indeed be unworthy to throw so precious a **Pearl** <note>original: "Margaritam"; referring to the "Margarita Pretiosa Novella," a seminal alchemical text written by Petrus Bonus of Ferrara around 1330. The title translates to "The New Precious Pearl."</note> before swine. Only the learned should read and admire it. This is the **Pearl of Cleopatra** left to us from the luxury or voracity of all-devouring time—since one of this kind, namely that of **Petrus Bonus**, a good interpreter of a similar question, has perished—which is more fitting to be adapted to the **Ear of Venus** <note>Likely referring to the *Haliotis* shell or simply an ornament of great beauty, suggesting the work should be displayed with high honor rather than hidden.</note> than to lie hidden in corners, forgotten in dust and smoke. For it is adapted to Venus when it is treated with the highest honor and worn in the sight of all. 

<margin>Bonus has excellently depicted the philosophical sulfur.</margin>
**Petrus Bonus** himself clearly described <term>philosophical sulfur</term> <note>In alchemy, sulfur represents the active, masculine, and "combustible" principle of matter, often associated with the soul or the transformative power of the Stone.</note> among other things, and calls it the "body in union with the spirit and soul." He defines it as sulfur in relation to quicksilver <note>mercury</note>. Although this opinion seems to differ from common views, I believe we should acquiesce to it as most true. On the contrary, so it is in man and animals: the form of man is the rational soul. The form of the philosophical composite is also the soul; but because there is no life in it properly speaking (except by analogy), it should rather be called a **corporeal substance**. 

<margin>The form of the chemical composite is corporeal.</margin>
This is because the body, being more firm and fixed, sustains the volatile parts and embraces them, just as the body embraces the soul. A body does not walk, speak, move itself, or perform other duties without the help of the soul; likewise, the soul does not perform these same things without the body. 

<margin>The soul of bodies, and the body needs the soul's help.</margin>
From the soul comes the beginning and first motion—indeed, everything that is done—but the execution is performed by the body. In the philosophical composite, however, all accidents and properties depend on the corporeal substance, yet not without the assistance of the spirit and soul. 

<margin>In the Stone, body and soul do not exist except by way of likeness.</margin>
If anyone conversely calls the body "matter" and the soul "form," he will not err. However, as **Bernhard** <note>Bernhard Trevisan, a legendary 15th-century alchemist known for his travels and his "Epistle to Thomas of Bologna."</note> warns in his letter to **Thomas of Bologna**, in the **Stone** <note>The Philosopher's Stone.</note> there is neither body, nor soul, nor spirit, except by way of analogy <note>original: "similitudinariè"; meaning these terms are metaphors for physical properties like stability and volatility.</note>.

<margin>The generation of metals.</margin>
...and in other places in the book *On the Generation of Metals*, he says that the vapors of sulfur and quicksilver <note>mercury</note> exhale from the depths of the earth and embrace one another. In their mutual embrace, an unctuous fatness is generated by the action of continuous heat, which is called **Brumaza** <note>A term used in some alchemical texts to describe the "fat of the earth" or the intermediate substance that becomes the Philosopher's Stone.</note>. This is that substance which is not recognized in the mines, though it may be seen, because it exists in a tiny amount. It is the ferment of the whole work, without which no fermentation can occur. 

<margin>What Brumazar is.</margin>
<margin>Brumazar is the ferment of the work.</margin>
Hence the *Clangor Buccinae* <note>original: "The Blare of the Trumpet," a famous alchemical treatise.</note>; likewise the *Rosarius* <note>referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum* or "Rosary of the Philosophers."</note> and **Petrus de Zalento** say: *“The ferment, which is the medium of joining, if it is placed at the beginning or in the middle, the work is completed more quickly and does not require repetition.”* However, they do not say these things as a denial <note>meaning they aren't excluding other necessary steps, just emphasizing the power of the ferment.</note>. 

<margin>What kind of ferment for the work: not common gold.</margin>
The *Clangor* declares what kind of ferment that is: *“Nothing is made from the perfect,”* it says, *“because it is already perfected, just as this matter or craft brings to perfection. We have an example: bread that is fermented and baked is perfect in its state or being and has reached its ultimate end; you cannot ferment it further. So it is with gold: pure gold has been brought through the trial of fire into a firm and fixed body, and for the philosophers, it is impossible to ferment it any further, unless the <term>first matter of metals</term> <note>The "prima materia," the original, undifferentiated substance from which all things are made.</note> is obtained, in which it may be dissolved back into its first matter and into its mixable elements.”* 

Let us therefore take that matter from which gold will be made, and through the craft it is led into the true ferment of the philosophers, and let this be changed with ingenuity into the perfect matter, or into the species of perfect bodies; only then let us begin the operation. 

So much for **Brumazar**. He calls the matter **Blanca** <margin>White Matter [Blanca].</margin> <note>meaning "White," often personified as a woman in alchemical allegory.</note>, because it shows a certain splendor, especially when prepared and mixed with the ferment. Moreover, it is the name of a woman, for **Blanca** sustains the duty of suffering <note>In the sense of "undergoing" or being the passive recipient of an action.</note> and receives into herself the action of the man or agent, which is <term>sulfur</term>. 

<margin>The matter first acts, then suffers.</margin>
For even if the matter first dissolves the sulfur, and in that putrefaction by means of a vaporous fire, it seems to act; nevertheless, that which first draws is soon drawn, and the action itself belongs to the male or the sulfur. This **Blanca**, considered by herself, is of vile origin; for perhaps, before she was raised to any dignity, she was kept for a long time in rooftops, stables, or kitchens, without price or any esteem. 

<margin>Blanca is of vile origin when considered by herself.</margin>
But after she was prepared and clothed in a precious garment, [she] all the dross... <note>original catchword: "squa-"; likely "squamam" or "squallorem," referring to the removal of scales or filth from the raw material.</note>

<summary>This page describes "Brumazar," an oily ferment essential for the alchemical generation of metals, and introduces "Blanca," a personification of the passive matter (mercury) that is transformed by the active sulfur.</summary>
