<meta>This page continues the discussion of alchemical authorities, specifically moving from the work of Petrus de Zalento and the *Rosarius* (Rosary of the Philosophers) to the concept of "philosophical weights" and the poetic works of Giovanni Aurelio Augurello.</meta>

-># SYMBOLS<-

<margin>Once her filth was cast aside, the White Woman appeared beautiful.</margin>
<margin>The weights of the art.</margin>
...she cast off her squalor and filth, and appeared in the likeness of a beautiful woman. If she were to be joined to her husband in marriage, she could deservedly be considered a most beautiful matron, the likes of whom could hardly be found. Here, the author hides the **weights of the art** <note>In alchemy, "weights" often refers not just to physical mass, but to the proportions of elements or the timing of the heat applied.</note> in obscurity, yet hands them down with a certain lucidity. He affirms that the better part of the chemical craft is situated in not revealing these things. "If these things were not hidden," he says, "the science would perhaps perish along with its brothers." And: *The beast with a short tail poorly covers its hindquarters; the fool with a flighty tongue poorly covers his inner thoughts.*

<margin>The weights of the art were hidden by the philosophers.</margin>
> *So says the Rosarius* <note>original: "Rosarius," likely referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous 16th-century alchemical compendium.</note> *citing Rhazes* <note>original: "Rhasi," referring to the Persian physician and alchemist Al-Razi.</note> *who says in his Great Book of Precepts: Whoever is ignorant of the weights should not labor in our books, because the philosophers have set down nothing of their matters, nor hidden anything else, except these weights. He likewise says: Water is the weights of the wise; therefore water and fire are sufficient for you for the whole work. Our water is stronger than fire, because it makes a pure spirit out of the body of gold, which fire cannot do. And fire, in respect to this water, is as water is in respect to common fire. Therefore the philosophers say: Burn our brass with the strongest fire.*

<margin>What the water of the philosophers is called.</margin>
> *And in the same place: The water of the philosophers is called the Vessel of Hermes* <note>The "Vessel of Hermes" often symbolizes the container where the transformation occurs, but here it is identified with the transformative liquid itself.</note> *of which the philosophers have written thus: In our water, all modes are accomplished—namely, sublimation, distillation, solution, calcination, and fixation. In the said water these things are done as if in an artificial vessel, which is the greatest secret.*

The true weight is shown by the figure in that same *Rosarius*, and Petrus de Zalento insinuates the same thing.

### GIOVANNI AURELIO AUGURELLO, of Rimini

<margin>Giovanni Aurelio Augurello, Poet and Chemist.</margin>
As sweet a poet as he was an excellent Chemist, he embraced the art in heroic verse <note>Augurello (c. 1441–1524) was famous for his poem *Chrysopoeia*, which explained alchemy through Latin poetry.</note> with such dexterity of talent that he seems to speak with the mouth of Maro <note>original: "Maro," the family name of the Roman poet Virgil.</note>. He shows the highest skill, both poetic and chemical, in those books, so that it may rightly be doubted whether he was greater in his meter or in his art. Indeed, we believe that he had no equal in either, if we contemplate the arrangement, method, and subject matter of his poetry. Of him, that line of Horace may rightly be said: *Poets wish to both be useful and to delight.*

<meta>This page continues the biography and analysis of Giovanni Aurelio Augurello, an Italian humanist and alchemist famous for his poem *Chrysopoeia* (Gold-making). The previous page concluded by introducing his poetic approach to alchemical secrets.</meta>

# THE GOLDEN TABLE. BOOK VIII. #

<margin>*Where and when he lived.*</margin>
He lived for the most part in *Venice* at that time when *Italy* was being sought in war by *Emperor Maximilian*, the first of that name, around the years 1508 and 1511. For he writes thus at the end:

> *At that time, Augustus, the war held me safe,* <note>original: "Illo Augu: bellum me tempore tutus habebat / Adriacus bacchante sinus per cuncta furore:"</note>
> *While the Adriatic bay was raging with fury through all things:*

<margin>*To whom he dedicated the work.*</margin>
<margin>*Augurello is said to have been gifted an empty purse by the Pope.*</margin>
<margin>*The artist depicted.*</margin>
He inscribed and dedicated his work to the Supreme Pontiff Leo X himself, by whom (if the story is true) he is said to have been presented in return with a most precious purse <note>The Latin "loculo" refers to a small box or purse. According to legend, Pope Leo X gave Augurello an empty purse, saying that a man who could create gold surely did not need any money to put in it.</note>, as if to say he did not lack for money or gold. If this is true, it reveals great flaws even in great men. He introduces *Pietro Lippomano, a Venetian patrician*, as one initiated into his sacred rites by a certain poem, as if he wished to appoint him the heir of the art. In his books, he perfectly depicts the artist—how he ought to conduct himself secretly at home and abroad, lest he become known to the common people as a <term>Chemist</term> <note>original: "Chymico." In the early 16th century, the term "chemist" often carried a social stigma or invited unwanted attention from swindlers.</note>. Because of the multitude of rascals flocking to this most noble art—like crows to a carcass—he is forced to share an ill reputation with them. In handing down the secrets of the art, he is very stingy and guarded, although he does not seem to neglect even the smallest things belonging to the work; and when he has described everything, he playfully eludes the reader in the final four verses in this manner:

<margin>*Augurello closes the book with a joke.*</margin>
> *Now I have played as if awakened from a deep sleep,* <note>original: "Nunc lusi somno velut excitus arcto..." This passage is a sophisticated literary reference to the Gates of Sleep in Virgil's Aeneid.</note>
> *Where the gate is given between the two that guard dreams;*
> *Neither was the horn gate open to us, nor truly the ivory one,*
> *Having been sent out, I sang of dreams in false words.*

<margin>*Augurello sings for himself in the final verses of his book.*</margin>
These words his adversaries interpret as if he were declaring his entire work to be false and a mere joke; but in this they are mistaken. For in this, imitating *Virgil in the 6th book of the Aeneid*, he established a diversion for himself against the malicious and the envious, by which he might escape, if necessary, so that he would not be bound to give an account of the craft to anyone—as if he had described it while playing, not seriously, and with false words, such as dreams. In this he used singular prudence and guarded himself against the traps of the many, who, if they [found] the true art...

<meta>This page continues the defense of Giovanni Aurelio Augurello's "Chrysopoeia," arguing that his poetic allegories contain genuine alchemical truths rather than mere fictions. It then introduces Marcellus Palingenius as another example of a poet-priest who integrated alchemical secrets into his moral philosophy.</meta>

# SYMBOLS #

<margin>Poets describing false and fictional things do not, however, admit to it at the end.</margin>
...if he had professed [falsehoods], they could have been held against him; however, the things he wrote are true, albeit under an allegory. Even if they were not such, but merely fictions like those of other poets, he still would not have added at the end that they were false. For none of the ancient or more recent poets has ever done this—even if they published works that were utterly false and completely removed from all reason—such that they refuted themselves at the conclusion. Instead, they depict everything with the colors of truth, so that no doubt remains about them, as is evident in *Homer's Trojan Expedition*, *Hesiod's Genealogy of the Gods*, *Virgil's Aeneas*, and countless others.

<margin>Marcellus Palingenius, Poet and Priest.</margin>
<margin>Palingenius's moral work.</margin>
MARCELLUS PALINGENIUS <note>Marcellus Palingenius Stellatus (c. 1500–1543) was an Italian poet whose famous work, *Zodiacus Vitae*, combined ancient philosophy, science, and a critique of the Church.</note>, a moral poet and priest, like the previously mentioned *Augurello* the natural philosopher, described human life in easy Heroic verse. In it, he sharply criticized various vices and outrages, sparing no person—neither the *Pope* nor the *Bishops*—but subjected everyone to the most impartial examination of his own judgment. He organized his work into the twelve signs of the heavens and an equal number of books, delivering specific teachings in each of them. After he arrives at the 10th book, or the sign of Capricorn, he describes the *Philosopher's Stone* as a suitable <term>viaticum</term> <note>A "viaticum" traditionally refers to provisions or money set aside for a journey; here, it refers to the Stone as a spiritual and material resource for the wise man.</note> for the learned, with which they may travel through the world, in these verses:

<margin>Palingenius described the Stone as a provision for learned men.</margin>
> *Then men of divine mind, turning over the hidden oracles of the mind with a wavering soul, having at last experienced much over a long time and at no small expense, discovered that art—than which no art is more worthy—of fashioning the Ethereal Stone. This is by no means permitted for the profane to know, and the wicked commoners seek it in vain. He who possesses it is able to live decently wherever he wishes; he fears neither the wrath of fortune nor the arms of thieves. But the Gods deem few worthy of so great a gift.*
> *And a little later: This Arcadian youth, unfaithful and too fleeting, seize him and kill him submerged in the waters of the Styx, etc.*
<note>original: "Tunc mentis diuinæ homines oracula cæca / Voluentes animo ancipiti, vix tempore longo / Experti multa, & non paruis ſumptibus illam / Inuenere artem, qua non ars dignior vlla eſt, / Fingendi Lapidem AEtherium, quem ſcire profanis / Haudquaquam licet, & fruſtra plebs improba quærit: / Quem qui habet, ille poteſt, ubi vult, habitare decenter, / Nec fortunæ iram metuit, nec brachia furum: / Sed paucos tanto dignantur munere Diui: / Et paulò poſt: Arcadium hunc iuuenem, infidum, nimiumque fugacem, / Prendite & immerſum ſtygis occide lymphis, &c." The "Arcadian youth" is an alchemical pseudonym for Mercury (quicksilver), which must be "killed" or fixed to create the Stone.</note>

Ccc 2

From these things it appears that he was not only initiated into <term>Chemistry</term> <note>original: *Chemiæ*; in this period, the term referred to the art of alchemy and the transmutation of metals</note>, but had emerged as a perfect master of it. <margin>Palingenius, a master of Chemistry.</margin> For this reason, he fell into the envy of others—specifically, the ignorance of his fellow brothers—who, since they could not harm him while he was alive, took action against him most cruelly after his death. <margin>Those envious of Palingenius remained hostile even after his death.</margin> For I remember hearing a story of this kind about the death of *Palingenius* from a man worthy of trust; whether it conforms to the truth in all respects or not, cannot be said: *Palingenius* had with him a nephew, still a boy, from either a sister or a brother, <margin>The story of Palingenius's death.</margin> whom he intended—being now about to die—to appoint as the heir of his goods and of the art itself. On account of this, he had made a certain book in unknown letters or figures for the boy's sake, which he handed over to the boy most firmly sealed, along with a paper that contained the complete alphabet in which the book was written; and this was called the "key." <margin>The key to Palingenius's book.</margin> He gave this with a warning and caution: that the boy should never hand over that book and paper into the hands of others, nor open it himself before his twentieth year of age, or even later.

When the boy had promised this to him, the priest met his end <note>original: *diem suum sacerdos obijt*; a Latin idiom for dying</note>. <margin>Palingenius died.</margin> Then his envious enemies and detractors thought they could now seize the opportunity to afflict him with whatever mark of ignominy they could, even after death. Meanwhile, once he was buried, he was proclaimed by these same people to be a mage <note>a practitioner of forbidden magic</note> and unworthy of a place of sacred burial. Having summoned the boy, *Palingenius's* nephew, they questioned him about the life and many other things regarding his uncle, asking whether he had seen various "characters" <note>strange symbols or scripts</note> in his possession. The boy, terrified by this interrogation, made mention of the book left to him. When it was brought forth and opened, they found nothing in it but unknown writing depicted with various characters. Therefore, they persuaded the boy that the book was magical and worthy to be burned along with its author <note>this refers to the historical practice of exhuming and burning the remains of suspected heretics</note>. And so the boy, clearly believing the key depicted on the paper was also magical, threw it into the fire and burned it. A little while later, having examined the book from every side, [they could] read or explain nothing at all...

<margin>Palingenius's corpse was dug up and burned due to envy.</margin>
...they were unable to conclude anything, except that they found a note written in common script in a corner of the book, stating that everything within must be read using an alphabetical key <note>original: *clauem Alphabeti*</note> that had been given separately to the boy. When they demanded this key from the said boy, he replied that he had thrown it into the fire. Thus, the book could not be read by any known skill. Since they could find no use for it, nor understand anything contained within it, they regarded it as a magical work and its author as a sorcerer. They saw to it that Palingenius's corpse was dug up and burned along with the incomprehensible book. Such is the power of envy and slander.

<margin>John of Rupescissa.</margin>
<margin>The childish reasoning of his adversaries.</margin>
<margin>Diligent poverty.</margin>
**JOHN OF RUPESCISSA** <note>A 14th-century Franciscan friar and alchemist, famous for his works on the "quintessence" and his prophetic visions while imprisoned.</note>, a monk of the <term>Minorite order</term> <note>Another name for the Franciscans (Order of Friars Minor).</note>, left behind a chemical book that is held in such high regard that it is accepted and recognized by the learned as legitimate, even though it is filled with many sophisticated trics. He also wrote other treatises, such as one on the <term>fifth essence</term> <note>original: *quinta essentia*; the pure, heavenly substance that alchemists sought to extract from earthly matter to create medicines or the Philosopher's Stone.</note>. In this work, he states that while sitting in chains <note>He was frequently imprisoned by church authorities for his radical views.</note>, he came to know the secrets of nature through divine revelation, constant meditation, and prayer. Because this author is a Minorite, he is judged to be of "minor" value by his adversary through a ridiculous bit of reasoning: "He is from the Minors; therefore, he is an artisan of minor authority." But this does not follow. Not infrequently, the most learned men have been found in this order of mendicants, men who far excelled others. For poverty teaches all the arts, and "the belly is the giver of genius" <note>original: *venter ingenij largitor est*; a quote from the Roman satirist Persius, suggesting that necessity or hunger drives human creativity.</note>.

<margin>Augustine Pantheus.</margin>
<margin>What "Voarchadumia" means.</margin>
<margin>Deceptive and illicit alchemy.</margin>
**AUGUSTINE PANTHEUS**, a Venetian priest, also left a treatise on **Voarchadumia**—that is, true Chemistry—which is most thoroughly prepared with everything necessary and relevant to the art. He changed the name of the art of Chemistry into an unknown Hebrew term <note>The word "Voarchadumia" was a pseudo-Hebrew construction invented by Pantheus.</note> so that he would not seem to have written or dealt with <term>Alchemy</term>, which was forbidden by a certain law among the Venetians. *Voarchadumia*, which signifies "the purification of red gold," <note>original: *auri rubei purificationem*</note> he separates from common alchemy; the latter he calls deceptive and illicit, while the former he calls most true and lawful. A peculiar...

# THE GOLDEN TABLE. BOOK VIII

...in this matter, the author observes a method in the transmission of the art which he describes not allegorically or figuratively <note>original: *tropicè*</note>, but simply, so that it may be understood by all. Nevertheless, he hides the secrets of the art, as is fitting, and takes care that they are not prostituted to the common folk.

<margin>Aloysius Marlianus.</margin>
***Aloysius Marlianus*** illustrated the chemical art under the description of the **Golden Fleece** <note>The *Vellus Aureum*; a common alchemical allegory where Jason's quest represents the search for the Philosopher's Stone</note>. As this allegory is most ancient, having proceeded from Orpheus, so it is so delightful that hardly any other exists that is better suited to this artifice. However, we have already set forth its explanation, consistent with the nature of the matter, in our *Hieroglyphics*, Book 2, and here and there in this present work; therefore, we shall dispense with it on this occasion.

<margin>Janus Lacinius.</margin>
***Janus Lacinius*** brought together the collections of various chemists into a single volume, in which he showed himself to be not ignorant of the art, although it is denied by some that he reached its perfection. However that may be, the author is not to be despised, for he rightfully holds a place among the Italian chemists.

<margin>Johannes Chrysippus Fanianus.</margin>
***Johannes Chrysippus Fanianus*** also published something of a chemical work himself, which should not be rejected but rather credited to his honor.

<margin>Johannes Thebanus.</margin>
***Johannes Thebanus*** transmitted the chemical art in Latin rhythms that are quite sonorous and learned; we place him among the Italians, perhaps not without justification.

***Ludovico Lazzarelli.***
***The Author of the Marriage of the Mass of the Sun and Moon*** <note>original: *massae Solis & Lunae*; referring to the chemical union of gold and silver or sulfur and mercury</note>, ***a true craftsman.***
***The Author of the Lily Plucked from Thorns:*** he published a most complete treatise.
***The Book on the Arts of the Romans.***
***The Author of the Florentine Study.***
***Efferarius the Monk*** also wrote a chemical book, which is found everywhere.
***Clement, on the Secrets of Nature.***

<margin>The revenues of all the Duchies of Italy.</margin>
The **Duchy of Tuscany**, *according to Vigenère* <note>original: "ex Viginario"; referring to Blaise de Vigenère, a French diplomat and alchemist who wrote on history and cryptography</note>, *pays to the Duke of Florence* fifteen hundred thousand; *according to Hieræus* <note>original: "Ex Hieræo"; likely referring to Simon Goulart or a contemporary chronicler of state finances</note>, 1,100,000.
The **Duchy of Milan**, *according to Vigenère*, twelve hundred thousand.
The **Duchy of Mantua and the Marquisate of Montferrat** pay three hundred thousand as *Vigenère* says; but as *Hieræus* says, 849,000.

The **Duchy of Urbino**, *according to Vigenère*, fifty thousand; *Hieræus* adds 10,000.
The **Republic of Lucca**, thirty thousand.
The **Republic of Genoa**, one hundred thousand.
The **Duchy of Ferrara**, 327,000.

<margin>The riches of all Italy.</margin>
Having calculated the accounts according to *Vigenère*, **Italy** would return annually about 9 million in gold; for to the preceding figures he also adds that the **Republic of the Venetians** collects from all the cities subject to its dominion fifteen hundred thousand.

<margin>The annual revenue of the Venetians.</margin>

### *22nd Negative Argument of the Adversary against Chemistry <note>original: "Chemiam"; here meaning Alchemy</note>, against Saint Thomas Aquinas.*

Even if it is conceded that a specific proportion of the elements is not necessary for the art, nevertheless a mixture of two or more is required, without which gold cannot be composed.

But this mixture is just as unknown to the craftsman as the proportion of the elements.

Therefore, gold cannot be produced by art.

# THE GOLDEN TABLE. BOOK VIII.

## Response of Saint Thomas Aquinas to the 22nd Negative Argument.

<margin>Response to the 22nd negative argument.</margin>
**T**hat mixing which occurs in the first natural principles does not necessarily need to be understood by the craftsman <note>original: "artifici"; in this context, the alchemist or practitioner of the Hermetic art</note>, nor can it be known. However, the other kind of mixing, which occurs in substances already mixed by nature, is necessary for the art and is called by the name of weights <note>original: "ponderum"; this refers to the specific proportions or ratios of ingredients required in a chemical recipe</note>. This [the mixing of weights] the craftsman can possess and can investigate either through experience or through reason, since it is perceptible and manageable. But as for whether such a mixture can be obtained or not, do not be anxious, since nothing is being sown or reaped for you here <note>A metaphorical way of saying the opponent has no grounds for their concern or no "skin in the game"</note>.

Therefore, the minor premise <note>In formal logic, the second part of a syllogism; Thomas is dismantling the structure of his opponent's logical proof</note> must be denied as clearly false; for a true craftsman cannot be ignorant of this mixture; and even if he is still ignorant of it, he continues his efforts, so he says, until he finds it.

---

## 23. Negative Argument of the Adversary.

<margin>23rd negative argument.</margin>
Even if the mixture is granted as if it were not necessary, there is still always a need for an efficient heat, which nature uses to produce natural things—namely, natural gold.

However, this heat is unknown to man, both in terms of its quantity and its quality; and even if it were known, it is neither imitable nor measurable.

Therefore, a natural thing, such as gold, cannot be produced by man.

<summary>Saint Thomas Aquinas argues that while the fundamental mixing of elements is a secret of nature, the "weights" or proportions of a substance are discoverable by an alchemist; the adversary counters that man cannot replicate the specific natural heat required to form gold.</summary>

## *Response of Saint Thomas Aquinas to the 23rd Negative Argument.*

<margin>
Response to the 23rd negative argument.
</margin>
**I** respond to the major premise <note>The first part of a logical syllogism. Aquinas is breaking down his opponent's formal argument piece by piece.</note>, that if a natural work is to be drawn out from the first natural principles, then the same degree and kind of heat must be used as nature uses; in that case, the major premise is true. But if art does not use those same principles, nor in the same manner, then the major premise is false. We have often demonstrated that this latter method is characteristic of art, while the former belongs to nature.

To the minor premise <note>The second part of a logical argument that applies a general rule to a specific case.</note> I say: the heat of nature is not unknown to man, whether we consider its quantity or its quality, but it is not meant to be imitated exactly. For since nature has at least one regular path which she follows to bring metals to perfection—namely, a uniform and equal cooking <note>original: "coctionem"; in alchemy, this refers to the slow "ripening" of metals within the earth through heat</note> caused by subterranean heat circulating around the minerals—she required two kinds of heat to introduce that third internal heat into the mercury (which is the "fire of nature"), or to gradually produce the form and tincture of gold in imperfect substances. 

The first is, as has been said, the subterranean heat, which nourishes the minerals from the outside, just as elementary fire cooks our food. The second kind of heat is enclosed within the minerals themselves and mixed like a vapor with the matter to be cooked, which is quicksilver <term>quicksilver: also known as mercury (argentum vivum), considered by alchemists to be the "womb" or primary matter of all metals</term>. This second heat is that burning and combustible sulfur <term>sulfur: in alchemical theory, sulfur represents the active, masculine principle that acts upon the passive mercury to determine which metal is formed</term>. 

Depending on the greater or lesser quantity of this sulfur, or its differing quality, it distinguishes the quicksilver of the "imperfect" metals, so that one becomes iron, another copper, a third tin, and a fourth lead—to say nothing here of the others, which are like semi-metals. This sulfur acts upon its own quicksilver, into which it has been mixed, with a continuous action, being moved and stirred up by the surrounding subterranean heat; and in this way it produces a third heat, which is the metallic embryo <note>original: "Embryo metallicus"; the nascent state of a metal before it is fully "born" or perfected</note>, equa- <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "æqua-", likely continuing "æquabilis" (uniform/even) on the following page.</note>

<summary>In this passage, the author (writing as Thomas Aquinas) argues that while nature and art use heat differently, the alchemist can still achieve natural results. He explains the alchemical theory that metals are formed in the earth through a "cooking" process involving subterranean heat, sulfur, and quicksilver.</summary>

### 24. Negative Argument of the Adversary against Alchemy.

If this science were true, it would more likely have been discovered by kings and princes—who keep a great number of scholars and laborers in this art in their service—than by anyone else.
But it is established that it was discovered by none of them.
Therefore, it was not discovered by anyone else either; and consequently, it is a non-entity and false.

### Response of Saint Thomas to the 24th Argument.

<margin>Response to the 24th negative argument.</margin>

**I**t is believable that if something were to be discovered or perfected by labor, cost, and expense alone, it could more easily be discovered and perfected by a king, prince, or any wealthy man—since they can provide all the necessary things pertaining to the discovery or perfection of that matter—rather than by a private citizen or someone of modest means. However, there are many reasons why such men very rarely attain this art, although some have indeed possessed it; thus, the **minor premise** <note>The second part of the opponent's logical argument, which asserted that no prince has ever found the secret.</note> of the **syllogism** <term>Syllogism: A formal logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two given or assumed propositions.</term> is false. For so great is the...

...of individuals <note>The text continues from the previous page's discussion on the scarcity of masters even among the wealthy.</note>, such that out of ten thousand, scarcely one acquires the **true matter** and the genuine way of handling it, and brings it to a successful conclusion. Whether that one person would then enter the service of another <note>i.e., a King or Prince</note> is scarcely consistent with the truth. It is necessary, moreover, that one and the same person has performed many experiments, and not merely that many individuals have performed a few each, if anyone is to pass judgment on each and all of these matters. But the principal cause of this attainment is **God Himself**, who illuminates the human mind for whom and when He wills, and not for another. Hence, not every man—even the most learned and experienced in the common practice of distillation—necessarily acquires the truth of this science, since it is a **gift of the Most High**, who gives to whom He wills and withdraws it from whom He pleases. We know, however, that many of the most ancient kings of the *Egyptians* possessed and practiced this art, as they were enumerated previously in Book I.

### *22. Affirmative Reason.*

<margin>
Affirmative
Reason 22
for Alchemy.
</margin>
If it is possible to **coagulate** <term>Coagulate: In alchemy, this refers to the process of turning a liquid or volatile substance, like mercury, into a solid or "fixed" state.</term> common **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"; literally "living silver," the standard term for mercury.</note> by a slight artifice—namely, by the smoke of sulfur from lead as if in a moment—which smoke is nonetheless foreign to the quicksilver, it will not be inconsistent to draw out from quicksilver, through a greater artifice, a smoky, fixed, hot and dry, dyed, and penetrating substance. This substance may alter and coagulate this and all other metallic quicksilver according to its powers, and thus convert the same into gold.

But the first is true by daily experience.
Therefore, the second is also possible.

*This reasoning is not frivolous, but being partly deduced from the nature of the thing, it reveals not a few secrets of nature. For the same proportion exists in both cases: if the smoke of raw lead accomplishes so much <note>referring to the previous page's argument that lead vapors can solidify mercury</note>, what if this smoke were not leaden, but golden? Not raw, but "cooked" <term>Cooked: In alchemy, 'coction' refers to the process of maturing or purifying a substance through heat, mimicking nature's own processes underground.</term>? Not white, but red? Not volatile, but fixed? Not sulfurous, but mercurial? Would it not then alter the **mercury** <note>original: "argentum vivum," literally "living silver"</note> according to these differences? If so, it will therefore become gold, which consists of all these properties. If not, then whatever is lacking must be investigated and added until the intended result is achieved. There are those who say that with mercury thus coagulated, a transmutation of mercury into lead could occur, increasing successively to infinity, although this would be done at a loss. But let him who wishes experiment with this; I scarcely agree with them. It is enough to have demonstrated the possibility of the matter through a certain "idea" <note>an archetypal or theoretical model</note>, which, although it is not the same as the thing it expresses, nevertheless leads the intellect from the senses toward contemplation.*

### *23. Affirmative Reason for Alchemy.*

<margin>Affirmative Reason 23 for Alchemy.</margin>
If the color of gold—which is truly red in its depth—can be extracted by the skill of certain "waters" <note>likely referring to acids or solvents like *aqua regia*</note> so that the white substance of the mercury is left behind, then once that red color is obtained, whole and not corrupted by corrosives, a **projection** <term>Projection: The final stage of the alchemical process where the "Philosopher's Stone" is cast upon a base metal to transform it into gold.</term> can be made upon mercury, and gold can be composed from both.

But the first can be done,
Therefore, the second too.

*The connection of this proposition is evident from the fact that in those composite things which are of a composite color, such as red, yellow, blue, green, and so on...*

—[red], those colors can be separated, not entirely as accidents without a subject <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, an "accident" is a property like color that cannot exist without a physical "subject" or object. ## But the first is true. Therefore, the second follows as well.

And consequently, since this must be demonstrated by the senses, they should wait and suspend their judgment until it is proven to them by their own senses; or, they should place their trust in others who have drawn from the experiences of the senses, which is essentially the same thing.

Avicenna <note>Avicenna (c. 980–1037) was a Persian polymath whose works on medicine and philosophy were foundational in Europe; here his "De Anima" is cited.</note> calls this argument the *reasoning of vision* in his *Book on the Soul*, discourse 1, chapter 2, which we mentioned above in Book 5. Lull <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315) was a Majorcan philosopher and mystic. Many alchemical works were attributed to him in the centuries following his death.</note> recognized such great efficacy in this argument that he did not wish to assert the truth of the art through words or reasoning alone, but simply said: "That which is seen by ocular experience requires no further proof." Hence I also (Thomas Aquinas) <note>This refers to "Pseudo-Thomas Aquinas," an anonymous author whose alchemical writings were falsely attributed to the famous Saint and theologian.</note> said to my brother Reginald: *Do not concern yourself with the words of modern and ancient philosophers who disagree about this science, since <term>Alchemy</term> <note>The medieval and early modern precursor to chemistry, focused on the transmutation of matter.</note> has established its seat in the capacity of the intellect and in experimental demonstration.* 

Truly, among those who deny this art, some would claim that even if they saw truthful experiments, they were performed either by magical power or by deceit. But if they are allowed to trifle in this way, why should not everything known through the senses be called into doubt, so that nothing certain about reality could be affirmed or denied? Regarding these people, Mirandola <note>Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola (1469–1533), a scholar who wrote extensively on both the validity of alchemy and the dangers of witchcraft.</note> says in Book 3, Chapter 3: *For what is there,* he says, *that cannot be turned into doubt if the power and cunning of a demon are brought into the conversation? If someone who is not unskilled in the <term>Chemical</term> <note>In the 17th century, "chemical" and "alchemical" were often used interchangeably to describe the study of substances.</note> faculty, and not ignorant of the higher sciences, does not silence such detractors, then even the birth of their own mother—from whom they themselves were born—might be placed in ambiguity.* For a wicked demon could have taken the form, not of Amphitryon <note>In Greek myth, Zeus disguised himself as the general Amphitryon to seduce Amphitryon’s wife, Alcmene.</note>, but of a husband or anyone else, and embraced the mother while she believed she was working with her husband to produce children. The stories are well known concerning the conception and embrace of Alexander the Macedonian and King Seleucus, and much later, Merlin. Furthermore, the wickedness and deception of succubus and incubus demons <note>Incubi and succubi were male and female demons believed in folklore to have sexual encounters with sleeping humans.</note> in these matters have been recorded in many ways by our theologians, both ancient and modern. Shall even health derived from the medical art suffer such slander, since [a demon] might be able to involve itself...

# SYMBOLS

<meta>catchword: tempus</meta>

<margin>The first blackness is known to few.</margin>

...[blackness] <note>The text here completes the word "nigredine" from the previous page.</note> known to few, desiring to gather the kind spirit, winning the battle of fire (and not being overcome by it). Although we have many times felt it with our bodily senses and seen it with our own eyes, we still did not possess the knowledge of its extraction through any science or art. Feeling ourselves still supported by a certain lack of refinement <note>original: "rusticitate"; implying a lack of technical or spiritual sophistication.</note>, we were in no way able to fully comprehend it until another spirit of prophecy, breathing from the **Father of Lights** <note>A biblical title for God, from James 1:17, often used by alchemists to emphasize that true knowledge is a gift from the Creator.</note>, descended. He never abandons his own, nor fails those who ask of him. In the heights of our vigilance, he shed such clarity into the eyes of our mind that he deigned to reveal that spirit within and without—once the outward form was removed—by his insatiable goodness, restoring us.

<margin>How the blackness is made.</margin>

He demonstrated that, to fulfill this, we should prepare the body for one **natural and secret decoction** <term>decoction: the process of heating a substance in a liquid to extract its essence; here, it refers to the prolonged heating of the alchemical "matter."</term>. In this process, the "net-bearer of nature" <note>original: "retiarius naturae". A 'retiarius' was a Roman gladiator who fought with a net and trident; here it is used metaphorically for a force that captures or binds the spirit of nature.</note>, acting entirely in a reverse order with a piercing lance, is immediately and visibly dissolved into pure blackness. We have expressly handed down the method for this in the present volume through excerpts, as we have received from the custom of the ancients, although we have been forced to conceal the locations where we placed them. We reveal these sacred things only to those who honor God's secrets by keeping them properly.

<margin>It belongs to God alone to reveal secrets.</margin>

For it belongs to God alone to reveal them; man strives to steal from the Divine Majesty when he makes such things—which belong to God alone—public through human speech or a series of letters. For this reason, you cannot perform that operation unless you have first been spiritually approved by the merits of the Divine. And shortly after: "Because this secret is to be revealed by no mortal, except that it be inspired by the nourishing Spirit who breathes where He wills."

The same author [Llull] in the same book, chapter 63, testifies that he was **"mortally wounded"** by an ignorance of the **circles** <note>original: "circulorum". This refers to the process of 'circulatio', a continuous distillation where vapors rise, condense, and fall back into the vessel, mimicking the cycles of nature.</note>. He specifically names **Arnald** <note>Arnald of Villanova.</note> as the one who taught him, in these words: "From which the philosophers elegantly said that the **Great Work** is nothing but **solution and congealing** <note>original: "solutio & congelatio". The two fundamental processes of alchemy: dissolving the solid and solidifying the liquid.</note>. 

<margin>Llull was mortally wounded while he was ignorant of the weights.</margin>

But these things are done through the **way of the circles**, in ignorance of which many great men of letters were deceived in their mastery. They believed with notable confidence that they understood the form of these sayings and the method of circulating through their own knowledge. Among these, we do not intend to hide that we were one 'mortally wounded,' when by the mere presumption and rashness of knowledge we believed we firmly understood the nature of the 'Other,' yet we had not understood it in any way until..."

<summary>Ramon Llull describes the "nigredo" stage of alchemy as a divine revelation rather than a purely intellectual achievement, admitting that he was once "mortally wounded" by his ignorance of the "way of circles" (distillation cycles) until instructed by Arnald of Villanova.</summary>

<margin>Llull confesses that he learned the secret of the art from Arnald.</margin>
The time came in which the spirit was breathed into us—not directly, but through the mediation of **Master Arnald of Villanova** <note>A famous 13th-century physician and alchemist to whom many influential texts were attributed.</note>, who by his immense generosity refreshed and inspired us. Indeed, in many ways and by many methods, we moved through the circulations of the wheels, taking up again the **vegetative exemplar** <term>vegetative exemplar: in Llull’s alchemy, this refers to the "life-force" or organic principle within minerals that allows them to "grow" into gold.</term>, the mineral work of which was never fully revealed until it recently sprouted under its own governors. By these, true nature is constrained under the preservation and successive strengthening of its virtues within the **magistery** <term>magistery: the mastery of the alchemical process, or the "Great Work" itself.</term>. Regarding this, I do not dare to speak to you with my own tongue for now, bound as I am by chains, though I used to speak favorably at this stage; for although I have received the license to reveal it, I am restricted by the usual gift: namely, an **alienated tongue** <note>original: "alienata lingua"; this suggests Llull is writing in a coded or symbolic language rather than his natural style.</note>. Llull also mentions his partnership in his *Latest Testament* in this manner:

<margin>p. 133.</margin>
<margin>Llull was in the company of three others in Milan for 3 years.</margin>
> Just as he says, we saw through the work of a certain companion, whom we found while traveling through the world, who made known many beautiful and wonderful things; but later he was hindered in his art, since we knew more through **sensory perception** <note>original: "sensualitatem"; referring here to practical, hands-on experience rather than theoretical study.</note> than he understood through art or intellect. Therefore, after him, we provided instruction in many other matters with a kind of influence and great virtues, until we were associated from above in refining the **virtuous stone** <note>original: "lapide virtuoso"; the Philosopher's Stone.</note>. We were together for three years in great legal standing; thus in **Milan** the whole year was spent in perfecting it. In the year 1330 the work was completed. Wherefore, those three later departed, but the art and the vessels remained with the fourth, who stays in his kingdom, regenerating as before. And if God has given this to you in any way, hold it secretly, so that the world knows nothing. Thus he writes there.

<margin>In what year Llull completed the venerable work.</margin>
Where it should be noted that he expresses the year of the completed work as 1330 here, but above in the *Book of Mercuries*, he records the same as the year 1333. However, in the *Book of Mercuries* there is an error, because in the year 1332 the author himself was not in **Milan**, but in **London** in England, as we shall say later. Concerning the perfection of the work, Llull himself relates in his *Last Experiment* near the end, the reason why the companions departed from one another; where he says:

<margin>What Llull and his companions did when the work was completed.</margin>

<margin>Arguments of those who deny that Llull supplied any gold to the King of England.</margin>
Those who deny this—namely, that <term>Llull</term><note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315), a Majorcan philosopher and mystic to whom many later alchemical works were attributed.</note> supplied any gold to the King of <term>England</term><note>The legend claims Llull transmuted base metals into gold for Edward III on the condition it be used for a crusade.</note> for the purpose of waging war against the Turks—first doubt which **Edward** he lived under, whether the Second, Third, or Fourth. Second, if it is understood to be the Third, they argue that he imposed an annual tax on wool (which was then being exported from England to <term>Brabant</term><note>A region in the low countries, modern-day Belgium and the Netherlands.</note>) which amounted to three hundred thousand pounds **Sterling** every year, and therefore the King was wealthy enough on his own. Indeed, that annual sum amounts to about 6,000 pounds of gold. However, one must respond to these <margin>Response to the objections.</margin> objections. Regarding the first: let those who are ignorant of this search the Chronicles, and they shall find that in the year 1332—the year in which Llull shows in many places in his books that he lived in England—**Edward III** was reigning there, still a young man. Regarding the second: it is <margin>Edward III reigned from the year 1327 to 1377, for 50 years.</margin> true that Edward collected so much money from taxes that he had a thousand pounds available to spend every single day; but even this was not sufficient for waging war against a most powerful kingdom. If, therefore, Llull doubled that sum, he could have provided it with six pounds of <term>tincture</term><note>original: "tincturae." In alchemy, the "tincture" is the Philosopher's Stone in liquid or powder form, capable of "dyeing" or transforming base metals into gold.</note>. Truly, Edward III did not take up that war by himself and for his subjects alone, but because he held the favor of almost all the princes of **Germany**, the whole Empire, and **Belgium**, he made use of their help. Therefore, he had need of a vast sum of money, which perhaps he did not receive from wool alone. Others insist that this is not found recorded in the Chronicles, nor...

-> ### SYMBOLS <-

<margin>The truth is suppressed.</margin>
...that any writer makes mention of "Lullian gold," <note>original: "Lulliani auri"</note> nor of the war to be moved into Barbary, <note>Barbary refers to the North African coast, then under Muslim rule. The legend claims Llull intended the gold for a crusade there.</note> nor of the captivity of Llull. I answer: I admit this is because the truth in these matters is either suppressed by choice or ignored. For it is believable that these things were handled so secretly between the King and Llull that a third party intervening would hardly have known. And even if someone did know, who would have dared to publish or write about it?

<margin>Pretense is not free from deceit.</margin>
Since this simulation and dissimulation <note>The author suggests the King practiced "simulation" (pretending to be what he wasn't) and "dissimulation" (hiding what he was actually doing).</note> does not seem to be free of deceit or broken faith—even if toward a private man—it was nonetheless toward one to whom the King was bound by oath for other purposes than what he later perpetrated. The one [Llull] gave for the defense of Christian blood; the other [the King] used it for the shedding of Christian—and indeed innocent—blood.

<margin>Two people doing the same thing is often not the same.</margin>

<margin>The glory of the martyrs</margin>

<margin>A death worthy of a Christian.</margin>
We have reviewed above the case of Democritus <note>The Greek "laughing philosopher," often cited in alchemical texts.</note>, who, being weary of this life due to his great age, took away his own breath of life through starvation and hastened his death. Surely that is neither worthy of praise nor becoming of a Christian. But this—that Llull, already worn out by age, went to the enemies of the Christian faith and preached Christ to them, even though he saw immediate death before his eyes—this ought to be considered most worthy of praise and not unbecoming of a Christian man.

<margin>Why Llull preached Christ to the Moors.</margin>
The cause which incited Llull to this undertaking is, without doubt, this: that he was led by repentance for the "French slaughter" <note>A reference to the legend that Llull produced gold for the King of England for a crusade, but the King instead used the funds to wage war against the French.</note> committed by the King of England, for which Llull had, as it were, provided the occasion; when he saw that not by arms...

<margin>Llull’s Chemical books.</margin>
Llull’s Chemical books <note>The term "Chymici" here refers to Alchemy, which in the 13th and 14th centuries was considered a branch of natural philosophy.</note> were written for the understanding of anyone rational and skilled in the arts, but they are certainly a specific specimen of his own Lullian Art. <note>The "Lullian Art" (Ars Lulliana) was a complex system of logic and combinatorics using rotating diagrams to combine concepts, intended to prove the truths of Christianity.</note> For if the entire art, as it is simple in itself, ought to have been proposed in plain words, Llull instead composed individual volumes for individual words. However, through that elegant speech, he ensures that all those who follow him are frustrated in their ultimate goal; they find nothing in their hands, even if they have much in their minds. <margin>Llull is very long-winded in his Chemical writings.</margin>

<margin>A method of writing secretly through perforated membranes.</margin>
>*There is a certain method of writing secretly and signaling to another by mixing words of no value with a word that signifies something, so that a continuous series of things and words is observed; if someone reads it as it is written, they interpret it unknowingly, because it holds nothing contrary to reason; but if someone else looks through it using excerpts, they understand by omitting those things which do not pertain to the matter.* <note>This describes a "null cipher" or a "Grille cipher," where a hidden message is embedded within a seemingly normal letter.</note>

<margin>
Excerpts from the Codicillus: The 4 Principles
</margin>
We will briefly collect these points and present them to the reader’s mind—namely, those from the *Codicillus* <note>The "Codicillus" is one of the most famous alchemical texts attributed to Ramon Llull, likely written by a follower in the 14th century.</note>, in which, in Chapter 5, he establishes four practical principles: two natural and the remaining two contrary to nature. The natural ones, he says, are **Sulfur** and **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum," also known as mercury.</note>, and from these two, a "metallic love" is born, through which the generation of the desired object <note>The Philosopher's Stone.</note> occurs, when their own specific individuals are joined together in a natural covenant. In Chapter 6, he proposes four principal 
<margin>
The 4 Colors.
</margin>
colors, which are **blackness**, **whiteness**, **yellowing**, and **redness** <note>These represent the stages of the alchemical "Great Work": nigredo, albedo, citrinitas, and rubedo.</note>. In Chapter 7, he declares four 
<margin>
The 4 Fires.
</margin>
fires: the **Natural**, the **Unnatural**, the **Against Nature**, and also the 
<margin>
The 3 Mediums.
</margin>
**Artificial**. He says there are natural, unnatural, and "against nature" mediums. The entire art is encompassed within these stated fires and mediums. For the **natural fire** denotes the "form," the **unnatural** denotes the "matter," and the fire **against nature** denotes the fire in the vessel; all of these must necessarily concur. 
<margin>
What is understood by the 4 fires of Llull.
</margin>
For how could the form act without matter, or the matter be informed without a form? How could these two be brought into action without an efficient cause, or a "cause without which not" <note>original: "causa sine qua non," a necessary condition.</note>? Nothing here is superfluous, nor is anything lacking. An example of this is found in human generation, in which the seed of the male and female concur—the former having the formal power within itself, the latter being the material; these will achieve nothing unless a third element is added, acting as a mover and impeller toward the action: namely, the tempered and moist heat of the womb. Therefore, it is necessary for these three to concur in every natural action. Regarding the four colors that appear, 
<margin>
The 4 colors are like statues of Mercury on the roads.
</margin>
there is no ambiguity; they show the way to perfection, just like **statues of Mercury** <note>original: "Mercuriales statuae." In antiquity, stone pillars topped with the head of Hermes (Mercury) served as road markers and signposts. Here, Maier uses them as a metaphor for the visual changes that guide the alchemist.</note>. For everything that is altered internally shows its visible character externally, or makes it perceptible to another 
<margin>
Color is the subject of the eyes or vision.
</margin>
sense. Concerning colors, the eyes judge them as they show through the transparent vessel. Other senses cannot judge their own objects in this operation, and therefore they are omitted. In Chapter 9, he says: "Because of this, two things are found to be more purified than others, namely **gold** and **silver**, 
<margin>
Without gold and silver, the art cannot be completed.
</margin>
without which this art cannot be integrated, since in them resides the purest substance of sulfur, perfectly purified by the ingenuity of nature; the art is weaker than nature for such purification and is not able to match it, though it labors much in the task." In the art, therefore, it is said: *Its Father is the Sun* <note>original: "Pater eius Sol," a famous quote from the Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus, identifying gold (the Sun) as the source of the Work.</note>.

<margin>The first act precedes the second.</margin>
For a "second act" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "first act" is the potential or the readiness of a thing, while the "second act" is the actual performance or the completed state.</note> to be achieved, it is necessary that a "first act" or "proximate potential" comes before it. We see this in the workshop of **blood-making** <note>original: *sanguificationis*</note>—the liver—where even before the **chyle** <note>The milky fluid of digested food.</note> reaches it, it has already received the first rudiments of blood within the **mesenteric veins**. In the same way, for the "Form" or the **Sulfur** <note>In alchemy, Sulfur represents the active, masculine, and "combustible" principle of a substance.</note> to be created through the "cooking" of the Art, it must first have received some natural potential and aptitude from Nature, just as is seen in the seeds of plants and animals, in eggs, in the branches or shoots of trees to be grafted onto another trunk, and indeed in almost all of Nature.

<margin>Care lies in the selection of seeds in which Nature delights.</margin>
All the care and labor, therefore, consists of selecting and drawing out from the whole universe and from the depths of the earth that in which Nature delights for the production of the perfect kinds of metals.

<margin>The seeds of Clover are near the roots.</margin>
They say that the herb called **Clover** <note>original: *Trifolium*</note> keeps its seeds near its root in the earth; this was so fashioned and ordered by a provident Nature so that if it is mown down by harvesters before the seeds are shed—as often happens—it has the means from which to sprout again.

<margin>The seeds of metals are in the depths.</margin>
In this very way, metals have their seeds near their roots, which must be sought there—that is, in the deep bosom of the earth, where fumes and vapors are contained, which are perpetually stirred up by subterranean heat.

<margin>On the mixing of sulfur and silver.</margin>
<margin>The destruction of quicksilver is its generation.</margin>
<margin>Bodies must be reduced to prime matter.</margin>
> Concerning the mixing of **Sulfur** and **Quicksilver** <note>original: *argenti vivi*, or Mercury.</note> in the following sections, he speaks thus in the same Chapter: *Let the power of the transforming Quicksilver take over the roles of the transformed Sulfur, so that before its own transformation, it is mixed at the smallest level into its own Sulfur—non-burning, white or red—and that Quicksilver will then possess its own proper material.* And in Chapter 33: *Because the sulfurous elements, when mixed with the watery parts of the Quicksilver at the smallest level, are now converted, they are changed equally and "corrupted" into one another. Such a **corruption** of our Quicksilver is its solemn **generation**, which cannot be achieved except after **putrefaction** <note>The stage of alchemical "death" or "blackening" (*nigredo*) where the substance breaks down to be reborn.</note>, which is the mother of all things.* And shortly after: *Let all craftsmen of this Art know, therefore, that perfect species cannot be transformed, nor can the craftsman perform a transformation, unless he first knows how to reduce the bodies into their **Prime Matter** <note>original: *primam materiam*; the formless, original substance from which all things are created.</note>. If the craftsman knows how to convert such things, then he will easily know how to transform their individuals by the help—*

<margin>Just judgment; a just and an unjust judge in the same nation.</margin>
...with his new wife, he was forced to kneel and was thus beheaded. <note>Maier is likely referring to a famous legal anecdote where a superior judge forced a corrupt official to marry the woman he had wronged—making her his legal heir—before executing him for his crimes.</note> This example of "high law" is consistent with justice; and just as the conduct of the previous *Spanish* man (namely the lower-ranking Captain) is judged detestable, inhuman, cruel, and unjust, so the conduct of this governor of the same nation, but of a nobler spirit and nature, is considered laudable and most worthy of the highest praise for equity.

<margin>Public trust must not be violated.</margin>
<margin>Greed and cruelty destroy.</margin>
<margin>An Italian proverb.</margin>
<margin>The prudent and the simple.</margin>
<margin>The leopard lures wild beasts to itself by its sweet scent.</margin>
<margin>Spain was once very rich in gold and silver mines.</margin>
Nor indeed is this told to insult the *Spaniards*—from which we think one should entirely abstain—but rather to their praise. For that *Milanese* governor received more honor from this judgment than the other who was beheaded felt of shame. What was done in *America* <note>Referring back to the execution of the Inca ruler mentioned on the previous page.</note> is to be ascribed to a greedy and inhuman military commander, who, if that matter had been reported to the King as it truly happened, would undoubtedly have found little favor with him. Indeed, those very deeds and that greed destroyed more in the initial building of the church there than the sword ever built up. 

There is an Italian proverb: *Beautiful words and bad deeds deceive both the wise and the fools.* <note>original: "Belle parolle è cattiui fatti Ingannanno è saui e matti"</note> Under the direction of *Christ*, we ought to be as prudent as serpents, but also as simple as doves—not wild like bears and leopards. Among these, the leopard attracts small beasts to itself by the sweetness of the scent it spreads from its skin, and then seizes and consumes them as prey. In the same way, tyrants invite people to themselves with flattering words when they are actually thinking of slaughtering them. In the leopard, the scent does not match its predatory nature; here, the words do not match the deeds.

The gardens of the *Hesperides* are also imagined to have been toward the West and the shores of *Spain*. These gardens possessed trees bearing golden apples, which were guarded by an ever-watchful Dragon.

<margin>The Phoenicians taught the Spaniards the use of gold.</margin>
The *Phoenicians* were the first to teach the *Spaniards* to recognize gold and to search for mineral veins. For as *Juan Luis Vives* <note>A prominent Spanish humanist and scholar (1493–1540).</note> notes in his commentary on *Augustine’s City of God*, the most ancient *Spaniards* were a very simple people. They lived at home in peace, quiet and without war, and they ignored that "shining earth." Even if some had seen it, they did not understand its use.

<margin>The Phoenicians gathered gold from Spain.</margin>
But the *Phoenicians*, arriving there every year with ships, collected whatever gold they could gather from the mountainous regions and from the rivers, taking it with the permission of the local inhabitants and carrying it back home.

<margin>Many Phoenicians migrated to Spain.</margin>
As a result, other *Phoenicians* were stirred up and moved to *Spain* with their entire families. They began to seek out minerals by digging mines, and as one group followed another, they settled there in great numbers and joined themselves to the *Spaniards* through marriage.

<margin>Phoenician vices were passed to the Spaniards.</margin>
From this contact, the vices of the *Phoenicians*—such as greed, luxury, gluttony, lust, and other such things—were eventually passed on to the *Spaniards* through trade. These vices then grew over time to such an extent that they seem to have reached their peak long ago. This is what *Vives* himself, a *Spaniard*, left in his writings. It is likely that the same thing happened to the *Americans* <note>Meaning the indigenous peoples of the Americas.</note> upon the arrival of the *Spaniards*.

<margin>The simple Americans were taught by the Spaniards.</margin>
For those people were at first simple and content with what they had, but now they have undoubtedly adopted the customs of those they called *Viracochas* <note>original: "Viricochias"; a Quechua term used by the Incas for the Spanish, originally the name of their creator deity.</note>. In a certain part of that Western...

<margin>The words of a barbarian man, not lacking in wisdom.</margin>
> *Your Lord, by whom you say you were sent, must be very wealthy, since he says he possesses so many knives, so many bells, and so many other things. We have no need—nor are we so insane—to go to you through so many perils of life to collect gold there. For what is gold to me, when I have enough here to live on? Certainly, you must be very foolish to seek through such long journeys that which you do not need, and with such great labors, under which you very often succumb. I think you are miserable and ignorant of what it means to live quietly, since you waste yourselves with cares you could be without, and torment yourselves with a desire that can never be satisfied.*

<margin>

With these words, this barbarian declared himself content with the gifts of nature—and meager ones at that—and to despise great weights of gold, no less than that famous **Crates of Thebes** <note>A Cynic philosopher (c. 365–285 BCE) who famously gave away his fortune to live a life of poverty in Athens.</note>, who threw a significant weight of gold and silver into the sea so that he might better practice philosophy; or **Democritus** <note>The "laughing philosopher" (c. 460–370 BCE), known for his atomic theory and for valuing intellectual pursuit over material wealth.</note>, who left his fields and allowed them to become public pastures. Likewise, **Lysander**, King of the Spartans, refused the costly garments sent to his daughters by **Dionysius**; and the Romans **Marcus Curius** and **Fabricius** <note>Both were Roman generals and consuls (3rd century BCE) celebrated as models of ancient Roman frugality and incorruptibility for refusing bribes and living simply.</note>, both of whom rejected the gold offered by the **Samnites** <note>An ancient Italic people who fought several wars against the Roman Republic.</note>. Whether he spoke falsely, let others judge. If we were only to look after the belly, he would have spoken truly. But since each man must maintain his honor, educate and provide dowries for his children, and necessarily possess clothing and buildings, our reasoning is far different from theirs, who live in the manner of wild beasts in caves or huts constructed of mud and tree branches.

<margin>Spain had the first gold mines in Europe. Britain long ago had tin mines. Germany gave a great abundance of silver. The Pyrenees of Spain are metal-bearing. The Alps toward Germany have metallic mines.</margin>
*Spain* indeed had the first mines of gold, silver, and other metals; *Britain* also, now *England*, in *Cornwall*, had very rich tin mines in the time of the historian *Dionysius of Halicarnassus* and *Diodorus Siculus* (who lived 60 years before the birth of *Christ*), which have remained so to this day. Then *Germany*, which for a hundred years from now has supplied all of *Europe* with an incredible abundance of silver from various places, such as the *Joachim Valley* <note>Jáchymov in the modern Czech Republic; the silver "Joachimsthaler" minted here is the origin of the word "dollar."</note>, *Mount St. Ann*, *St. Mary*, *Schneeberg*, *Freiberg*, and countless others; meanwhile, I shall say nothing of *Slavonia*, *Hungary*, *Transylvania*, *Sweden*, and other kingdoms. It is clear from experience that the *Pyrenees* mountains of *Spain* were metal-bearing, as were the *Alps* toward *Germany*, at *Sterzing* and elsewhere, the *Sudetes* around *Bohemia*, the *Harz mountains* <note>original: "montes Hercinios"</note> near *Zellerfeld*, *Wildemann*, *Mount St. Andrew*, and elsewhere; and the *Apennines* in *Italy*.

->*Now we shall add the revenues of Spain:*<-

<margin>The revenues of Spain.</margin>
*Spain*, as *Vigenère* <note>Blaise de Vigenère (1523–1596), a French diplomat and scholar famous for his work on cryptography and alchemy.</note> reports, pays only two million in gold annually to its King; besides the huge sum of gold brought to him from *India* and *America*.

<margin>Revenues of the 9 kingdoms of Spain.</margin>
*Abraham Ortelius* <note>A famous Flemish cartographer and geographer (1527–1598) who created the first modern atlas.</note> writes that five million ducats are collected from the nine kingdoms of *Spain*.

<margin>How many Archbishoprics and Bishoprics Spain has, and what their revenues are.</margin>
*Spain* has *8 Archbishoprics* and *48 Bishoprics*, whose annual revenues amount to one hundred and forty thousand ducats; these make approximately four hundred and twenty-seven thousand *French livres*. A meager sum (says *Boissard* <note>Jean-Jacques Boissard (1528–1602), a French antiquarian and poet.</note>) if compared with *French* revenues.

<margin>Belgian revenues.</margin>
The *Netherlands* <note>original: "Belgicum." In the 16th century, this term referred to the "Low Countries" generally.</note>, according to *Vigenère*, pays sixteen hundred thousand crowns. *Bodin* <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French jurist and political philosopher.</note> reports that in the time of *Charles V*, the *Belgians* paid only thirteen hundred thousand livres.

### *The Response of Raymond Lull to the Adversary’s Negative Argument.*

<margin>
Response to the 26th negative argument.

**I** respond to the proposition: if it had been useful for all to know it without distinction, then the authors would have handed it down, just as they did with other doctrines. But since it was not useful, they did not dare. If you ask why it was not useful, you seem to understand nothing—neither the vices of the world nor the customs of men—or certainly, you are entirely ignorant of the primary cause of this thing. Many others have produced more than ten reasons from the books of the philosophers, by which it is proven that it is not useful for this knowledge to be handed down like other arts, so that those reading their *a, b, c* <note>Equivalent to "learning the basics" or "the alphabet."</note> might immediately understand; anyone can investigate and consider these reasons. Very many have wished to expose the matter in plain words, but they were divinely prohibited, as they themselves testify. <margin>Many nations obscured their dogmas.</margin> Likewise, it is well known that many nations obscured almost all their dogmas with allegories, tropes <note>In rhetoric, a "trope" is a figurative use of a word or expression.</note>, and figures, no matter what they were. Such were the Egyptians, Phoenicians, and Syrians, who did this lest the treasure of a precious thing be seen without a chest, or a naked body without clothing. Are not the sacred scriptures themselves mere oracles and figurative in most places? The reason is this: if wheat were without chaff, and the kernel without its hard shell, it would be prey for the swiftest little birds.

*To the minor premise I say:* That the writings of the <term>Alchemists</term> <note>original: "Chymicorum" — refers here to the authors of alchemical texts.</note> are both false and true in different respects. They are false if they are understood literally; they are true if understood according to the suitability of the subject matter and the consensus of the authors. For they did not dare to hand down the truth for the reasons stated before: because the literal word would have brought more harm than benefit to men, if it had been naked and true; now, since it is clothed...

## Affirmative Reasons for the Truth of Chemistry <note>original: "Chemiæ" — in this context, the term refers to the art of alchemy.</note> by Ramon Llull.

### 25. *Affirmative reason for Chemistry by Ramon Llull.*

<margin>
Reason 25.
Affirmative
for Alchemy.
</margin>
If this report, which has been spread from the most ancient ages until now concerning **gold-making** <term>aurificio|the alchemical art of transmuting base metals into gold</term>, were about an imaginary or fictitious thing that existed nowhere, then so many highly respected men would not have produced testimonies, agreeing across all ages and nations in their published books.

But no one can deny that these testimonies exist in such great number, with such great authority and consensus (as is evident from this volume and elsewhere), unless they are someone who has read or seen nothing at all.

Therefore, this report is not based on nothing, but on a real and possible art.

<meta>This page continues the logical defense of alchemy begun on page 442. The author uses a syllogism (a formal logical argument) to prove that the "report" or reputation of alchemy is based on truth. This page explains the "Major premise" (that long-standing traditions usually have a basis in reality) and the "Minor premise" (that alchemy has such a tradition), then moves into a new argument by Ramon Llull based on legal testimony.</meta>

The **major premise** is clear: For things which can be proven true by the experience of some would collapse of themselves if they were not eventually stabilized by experiments. This is the kind of truth that is grasped not only by the **faith of the mind**, but also by the **work of the hand**. What the ancients and moderns have handed down concerning the *Phoenix* <note>In alchemy, the Phoenix is a common symbol for the Philosopher's Stone, representing the process of chemical death and rebirth through heat.</note> is well known from what was said above. If a true thing had not been hidden under this purely fictitious and fabulous bird, it would not have been so consistently handed down by the ancient *Egyptian* writers as to reach the age of *Pliny*, *Tacitus*, and our own time. Where *Pliny* <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), a Roman naturalist whose "Natural History" was a primary source for medieval and Renaissance science.</note> writes that this bird was once brought alive to Rome, he is mistaken, as he is in many other matters he knew only by hearsay. 

Therefore, this report is not spread without cause, especially by those writing on the **philosophical art** <term>arte philosophica|a common synonym for alchemy</term>. These writers, being grave and serious men, were not led by an empty desire for glory, but moved by the benefit of posterity. They left behind, as if they were public monuments, works on the most hidden secrets of nature and art. To these secrets, access is open only to the **initiated**—that is, to those who have been most proven by virtue, learning, labor, expense, and a long passage of time.

*The minor premise is most true*, and it requires no proof other than the reading and comparison of authors, whose names and great works are for the most part collected and preserved here.

### 26. *Ramon Llull’s Affirmative Reason for the Truth of Chemistry.*

If, by the production of two or three witnesses of proven faith, it is permitted by every law to judge the life, reputation, and wealth of any man; and if a testator, when composing <note>original: "condente"</note> a testament of his last will in the presence of several witnesses, must have that will held as legitimate and indubitable, why then should we not <note>The text continues on the next page, likely concluding that the testimony of many alchemical "witnesses" should also be judged as legal truth.</note>

<margin>The difference between those treating Chemistry.</margin>
The **proposition** of this argument, and its connection, is most firm: For if in divine and human matters one must acquiesce to the testimony of even a single writer, why not in **Chemical** sayings? How great the credibility of public Notaries is among the *Germans* and *Italians* is well enough established: for if neither the words nor the writings of some proven man were to be trusted, human affairs would always slip into uncertainty, nor could any certainty be produced by anyone that could not be contradicted. What now should be said of the writers of **Chemistry**? Are they alone without any credibility? We know a distinction must be made among those who treat of **Chemical** matters: Some are most frivolous men; who, as they are unlearned, treat these things without judgment until they utterly despair of reaching the goal of perfection. Hence, to seek a remedy for their own poverty, they turn themselves to sophistical and deceptive practices. And of these—like drones <note>original: "fucorum." In natural history of the time, drones were seen as parasitic bees that ate the honey produced by others; here, it refers to "charlatans" who live off the gullibility of others.</note>—the number is greater than that of the learned and upright men. Small books can be published by both types, just as both types are encountered in the world. But both types of books easily testify to the character of their authors, and express their doctrine and their experience in **Chemical** matters. 
<margin>Let the reader judge cautiously concerning the books of the Chemists.</margin>
Concerning these, it is necessary that the reader judge cautiously and attentively whether they possess enough truth that they should be read and imitated in actual work.

### 27. The affirmative argument of Raymond Lully himself, which he proposes in the book *On the Fifth Essence*, in the third distinction, in the final part concerning questions:

->The First Question.<-

<margin>Lully’s 27th affirmative argument from the book *On the Fifth Essence* <note>The "De Quinta Essentia" is a seminal alchemical text attributed to Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315), a Majorcan philosopher. Modern scholars usually attribute these chemical works to a "Pseudo-Lully" from the 14th century.</note></margin>

*Whether Alchemy is a real entity, or if it is a fiction?*

*I respond: the goal of Alchemy is to make gold, to make silver, to vegetate <note>To "vegetate" in an alchemical sense means to cause a substance to grow or come alive, as if it were a plant rather than a dead mineral.</note>, or to transmute. It is demonstrated according to its condition—namely, that Alchemy is a real entity and not a fiction—because its existence is composed of gold, silver, and a vegetable <term>menstruo|menstruum: A technical term for a solvent, believed to be the "blood" or "life-force" that dissolves and prepares substances for transformation.</term> menstruum. This is indeed compelled by the definition of a "principle":*

*Since, just as fire is the principle of heating, so gold is the principle in the logic of gold-making, and silver of silver-making, and the vegetative power is the principle of vegetating.*

*Therefore, since the goal is to make gold, it is necessary for gold, silver, and vegetative elements to be present in Alchemy. And this is that which is the "substantive" <note>The underlying material or essence</note> in Alchemy, in which the vegetative elements are planted.*

*And if Alchemy were to make gold and transmute, and yet gold, silver, and vegetative elements were not within it, the definition of a principle would be false. This is because no principle would exist before the result in any order of priority, and all things would have a single property; thus, one thing would be many in number, which is impossible.*

*And if gold, silver, and the vegetable substance are present in Alchemy, and yet it does not make gold or silver, and does not transmute the primary <term>quidditatem|quiddity: the "whatness" or essential nature of a thing.</term> essence through the primary location: then the science would be false. This would be because gold, silver, and the vegetative elements would be actually present in something where it would not be proper for them to make gold or silver or to transmute—which is against the course of nature. For it would follow that there could be some place in nature where principles could naturally be so empty in nature <note>original: "in natura vacua." This refers to the philosophical "horror vacui," or the idea that nature cannot allow a vacuum or a purposeless existence.</note> that nature could not endure it; because it would be against its own...*
