<margin>It is difficult to balance the primary and secondary qualities of the elements.</margin>
<margin>In gold, the measure is found in the balancing, not within the tincture.</margin>
<margin>In gold, there can be no inequality of qualities.</margin>
<margin>The balancing of qualities is the key to the veil of truth.</margin>
Therefore, it is necessary that all qualities of the elements, both secondary and primary, be balanced, which is the real labor of this work <note>original: "hic labor est," a famous phrase from Virgil’s Aeneid regarding the difficulty of returning from the underworld.</note>. For if one part, or a sixteenth degree of fiery quality or heat, is taken, and just as much of the remaining primary qualities, there would be twenty-two degrees of heat, twenty-two of cold, twenty-eight of moisture, and twenty-four of dryness. But this balancing is presupposed to occur in the gold itself, rather than in the Tincture <note>The "Tincture" or "Elixir" is the potent substance alchemists sought to create for transmuting base metals into gold.</note>. For if it were in the Tincture, when mixed with moist and cold mercury in a great or thousand-fold quantity, a supreme imbalance would occur in the gold, from which its destruction in fire and other elements would be caused. For if there were such an unequal battle and internal discord of qualities in gold, nothing else would follow but the death of the weaker part. 

Indeed, Bacon gives warnings in those *Letters* to those to whom he writes, that they should direct all sayings and writings toward the possibility of nature, covering the truth under a cloak, so that those who hear may think they grasp something, when they are found to have nothing in their hands. <margin>What the animal called Sloth does.</margin> <margin>The unworthy are those unwilling to labor for the knowledge of the art.</margin> For very many are unworthy, who wish neither to work nor to meditate on matters because of their laziness and the stupidity of their character. These people, he says, are very much like the animal called the *Sloth* <note>original: "Pigritia." Maier is using the sloth as a moral allegory for those who want the rewards of alchemy without the effort.</note>, which, though it suffers the greatest hunger under a tree whose fruit could satisfy it, nevertheless remains lying there and does not try to climb, even though it is endowed with claws suitable for climbing, lest it be forced to descend again with labor. For it would be unworthy to provide such people with food already chewed in their mouths, for whom it is a sin to touch coals, or for whom keeping watch through the nights in the service of Vulcan <note>The Roman god of fire; here meaning the demanding work of tending the alchemical furnace.</note> seems an intolerable servitude. When I speak the truth, says Bacon, think it a lie; when a lie, the truth. This is the reasoning behind the method and inscription of Geber and Avicenna: it is therefore necessary to extract the lies from them...

<margin>Truth lies in the depth of natural writings; falsehood on the surface.</margin>
...boldness to collect and elicit deep truth from there, while neglecting the truth in what is manifest: These words of Bacon agree with the confession of Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–c. 815), the legendary father of Islamic and European alchemy.</note>, who affirms that where he spoke plainly, he said nothing, but where he spoke in allegory, he hid the truth. Similarly, Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose works on medicine and alchemy were foundational in the Middle Ages.</note> declares that he will tell a *Great Lie* <note>original: "Mendacium magnum"</note> when he intends to bring forth some truth. These are paradoxes and are foreign to the treatment of Peripatetic <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, which generally favored literal and logical categorization.</note> philosophy, but, if <margin>The Key of Chemistry, which.</margin> we consider it well, it is the *Key of Chemistry*, without which no one can penetrate the hidden and obscured mind of the *chemical practitioners*. For the *alchemists* write either <margin>Falsehood is found in figures and tropes understood literally.</margin> simple truth or falsehood. Not the former; therefore, the latter. But they present falsehood in the manifest sense—through figures, tropes, allegories, and metaphors—while the truth remains hidden. It is therefore necessary to struggle through those things, as if through hard shells, toward the truth, like a kernel.

<margin>*Art does not transcend nature*</margin> *[Art] completes its own stage, which it can naturally perfect, and it cannot go beyond that unless it is impeded by a contrary force; although art certainly does not transcend nature by creating a new nature through simple labor.* <margin>*Art begins where nature ends.*</margin> *And therefore it is said that art imitates nature, not that it builds a new one, but that it refines the power of that nature. *In the morning when I rise and see my urine is white, I judge that I have slept too little; then I lay myself down to sleep again, and after taking sleep, the urine <term>turns yellow</term> <note>original: "citrinatur"; the "citrine" or yellow color was a vital sign of "digestion" or maturation in both medieval medicine and alchemy.</note>. Thus, follow nature through art: likewise boil, digest, and ripen substantially, since nature already actually contains within itself the natural fire by which it is ripened. Other things do not have this, and therefore they cannot give it. <margin>
The better ought to perfect the worse.
</margin>
But a kind of fire is covered and hidden, acting in it more by art than by nature: And therefore it is not impossible that art, with nature as the intermediary, might digest and perfect this further, since it naturally intends to be perfected, but cannot do so on its own unless it is moved by art and operation. But these labors, I believe, do not reach the stubborn man <note>original: "homini durae cervicis," literally "man of a stiff neck," a biblical idiom for those who are obstinate or unreceptive.</note>: And therefore true gold is not produced unless it is so digested and cooked <note>In alchemy, "digestion" and "decoction" refer to the application of steady heat over a long period to mature a substance.</note> that the better might improve the worse: Because the intention of all philosophers is to perfect the worse with the better: which fools understand in reverse, because they strive to perfect the better with the worse, and they seek something in a substance that was never in it—namely, gold and silver in combustible things, etc.

<margin>
Whether sulfur can be obtained from sick bodies.
</margin>
And in the tenth chapter: It may not without reason be asked whether this white and red sulfur, used for tingeing <note>To "tinge" or "color" in alchemy means to fundamentally transform the internal nature of a metal, as if by a concentrated dye or medicine.</note> Mercury, can be drawn out of other "sick bodies"? <note>Alchemists referred to base metals like lead, iron, or tin as "sick" or "infirm" because they lacked the "health," purity, and stability of gold and silver.</note> I say it cannot, because it was said before that no other thing of greater balance <note>original: "temperantia," referring to the internal equilibrium of the four elements.</note> is found than in these two bodies [gold and silver], in which the tingeing rays reside; since it was said before that "sick" bodies contain within themselves a foul and combustible sulfur, and not an essential <note>original: "virtualis," meaning possessing "virtue" or inherent power.</note> nature, as in these [gold and silver], etc.

<margin>
Sick bodies contain foul and combustible sulfur.
</margin>
Since all art is of no value unless nature is had beforehand, which it follows: You could nonetheless purge metals with lesser minerals; though once they are purged, they still do not have the nature of gold and silver in them, because the golden digestion and cooking was not in them as it was in the others, nor was the sulfur so mature: And therefore these immature things must be helped with mature things, so that they may be matured:

<margin>
Mature things ought to help immature ones.
</margin>
Therefore they do not tinge, but are tinged, because the tincture <term>tincture</term> <note>The "tincture" is the potent alchemical substance (often identified with the Philosopher's Stone) capable of transforming base metals into gold or silver.</note> of gold and silver has a nature proportional with them—that is, with the immature or imperfect ones—because they drew their origin from Mercury:

<margin>
Sick bodies do not tinge, but are tinged.
</margin>
From these things it is clearly manifest that the lesser minerals cannot tinge, because imperfect metallic bodies, which do not agree with gold and silver on the part of mature Mercury, cannot tinge nor infuse the nature of gold or silver: And therefore one must not tinge except with those things in which the power of tingeing exists: Tinge therefore with gold and sil... <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "gento," completing the word "argento" (silver) on the following page.</note>

<margin>Ripley's books: which ones:</margin>
...partly in English, partly in Latin, namely: the *Treatise of the Twelve Gates*, the *Chemical Marrow*, *On Mercury and the Philosopher’s Stone*, and *The Song*. If there are other manuscripts of his, they have not become known to us. *The Song* is in the Latin language, while the rest are written in the vernacular <note>Ripley wrote largely in Middle English, which was unusual for the time but helped spread his fame in England.</note> and in verse.

<margin>Ripley handed down the art completely in the Twelve Gates.</margin>
He seems to describe everything necessary for the art accurately and diligently in those twelve gates, the keys of each of which we have handed down above.

<margin>Ripley's gates are locked.</margin>
To be sure, he himself has shown the gates; let him enter who can. But what if they are made of iron and secured with a bolt? Truly, entry is granted to no one unless he is among the household <note>An "initiate" or someone deeply familiar with the secret language of alchemy.</note>.

<margin>Ripley gives warnings for acquiring the keys to the gates.</margin>
Yet he does not leave the seeker entirely stranded at that point, but gives many warnings everywhere regarding the acquisition of the keys. Therefore, in the beginning, he says: "I will certainly teach you so that you understand that <term>the Mercuries are three</term> <note>These are not literal quicksilver, but three distinct stages or forms of the alchemical substance.</note>, which are the **KEYS** of the science; these Raymond Lull <note>A 13th-century polymath and mystic to whom many alchemical works were later attributed.</note> calls his 'menstruums' <note>Solvents used to dissolve the material of the Stone.</note>, without which nothing is done correctly."

<margin>Three Mercuries are the keys of the art.</margin>
But two of these are superficial; the third is essential, of the sun and the moon, etc. We naturally calcine <note>To reduce a substance to powder through heat.</note> perfect bodies with the first mercury; but no unclean body enters, except for one, which is commonly called by the philosophers the <term>Green Lion</term> <note>Usually refers to vitriol or an acidic solvent capable of dissolving gold, often associated with the raw, "unripe" state of the matter.</note>.

<margin>The first Mercury is the Green Lion, the medium for joining the Sun and Moon.</margin>
This is the medium for joining the tinctures between the sun and the moon with perfection, just as Geber himself testifies.

<margin>The second is the Lunar Mercury.</margin>
With the second, which is a vegetable moisture <note>Likely referring to a life-giving or "growing" spirit within the matter.</note> that brings back to life what was previously dead, both the material and formal principles must be dissolved; otherwise, they would be of little importance.

<margin>The third Mercury is sulfurous and solar.</margin>
With the third, which is a most permanent moisture—incombustible and oily in its nature—the <term>Tree of Hermes</term> <note>A metaphor for the alchemical process or the growing Philosopher's Stone.</note> is burned into ashes. This is our most certain natural fire, our mercury sulfur, our clean tincture, our soul, our stone raised with the wind and generated in the earth <note>This is a direct reference to the "Emerald Tablet," a foundational alchemical text.</note>.

<margin>The stone raised with the wind.</margin>
Store these things in your mind: I dare to tell you that this stone is the potential vapor of a metal. You must be cautious in how you acquire this, for this menstruum is truly invisible, although with the second water...

<margin>As the Basilisk is from the egg, so is the tincture.</margin>
The **Basilisk** <note>A legendary serpent-king said to be hatched from a cock’s egg and capable of killing with a glance; here, it symbolizes the potent, finished Alchemical Tincture.</note> is truly this: for as the *Basilisk* is said to come forth alive from an egg, which then infects and kills living things by poisonous rays emitted from its eyes, so the tincture is produced from the philosophical egg. By the lightest touch, this tincture coagulates metals that have some Mercury within them, renders them "stupid" <note>original: "stupida"; in alchemy, this refers to a metal losing its metallic "life" or reactivity during a transformation.</note>, and strips them of their sulfur. <margin>Why the Tincture is called a Dragon.</margin> At other times it is called a *Dragon* for the same reason, or because when the celestial Sun and Moon <note>Gold and Silver.</note> are joined, it is necessary for it to happen in the head or tail of the dragon <note>An astronomical reference to the lunar nodes where eclipses occur; in alchemy, this signifies a perfect union or "eclipse" of properties.</note>; in this, the conjunction and unification of the Sun and Moon is achieved, with an Eclipse occurring.

<margin>How the spirit is fixed.</margin>
Gate 1. *Every spirit, he says, is fixed with the ashes of its own kind; if you observe this well, you will gather fruit:* <margin>Birds are enticed by their like.</margin> *For just as birds gather with those similar to themselves and are captured by the same decoys, so it happens in this philosophy: for Nature acts by the similarity of things according to genus and species.* <margin>Nature does not compose a Centaur.</margin> *Nature never procreates a hippocentaur* <note>A mythical creature, half-man and half-horse; used here to argue that alchemy must follow natural laws and not mix unrelated "species" of matter.</note>, *yet the imagination of the craftsman not infrequently composes very diverse things and hopes for a union from them, which will never follow before the final fire. For this reason, he adds later:* <margin>Heterogeneous things and those diverse from metals are not to be taken for the art.</margin> *If you therefore strive to fashion the Sun and Moon by the philosophical art, you should take for that purpose neither eggs nor blood, but the Sun and Moon, which—having been naturally and prudently calcined* <note>Burned to a fine powder (calx) through chemical heating.</note>, *and not by hand—bring forth a new generation, increasing their own kind and all natural things.*

<margin>Sister and brother, patient and agent, Mercury and sulfur.</margin>
*In Gate 2: There is nothing here except a sister and a brother, which is to say, if you interpret it: the agent and the patient, Sulfur and Mercury, which are of the same essence as our purpose. Between these two, in their contrary qualities, a most admirable medium is generated, which is our Mercury and an oily solvent* <note>original: "menstruum unctuosum"; a powerful chemical liquid used to dissolve solids.</note>, *our secret sulfur, working invisibly, burning bodies more violently than fire until they are dissolved into mineral water, which we call "night," on account of its darkness, and "the North."* <margin>What the North is.</margin> *And soon: Observe how ice is resolved into water, and rightly so: for it was water before. In the same way, our earth is again turned into water...*

<margin>Examples worthy of note concerning two men who were selling the bear's skin before it was caught. <note>An idiom similar to "counting one's chickens before they hatch."</note></margin>
Then, in the second chapter, he presents examples of two men who were fantastically triumphing over the Art before they had even found it. These are not unpleasant to read, and we shall bring them forward as a caution to others, lest they trust too quickly in their own imaginations and the reading of one book or another: *In Normandy,* he says, *there lived very recently a certain monk who deceived very many people of every status. After he had preconceived in his imagination that he knew this Art perfectly, he was filled with such joy that he almost began to go mad; concerning his absurd joy (though it did not last long), I shall relate this moral fable as an example:*

*This monk had wandered through France as an apostate <note>A monk who has abandoned his religious order or vows without permission.</note>, indulging his own desires. Afterward, he came into this kingdom [England], wishing to persuade everyone that he fully understood the foundation of all alchemy, which he had found in a certain book of recipes. Therefore, he fully set his mind to leaving behind certain magnificent deeds and noble acts, so that his honor, name, and praise might remain forever. And from this point, he often speculated on how he would spend such great wealth, or in what things he would invest it—wealth which he expected to have soon. He thought to himself: "Behold, I know this thing; where shall I find certain men who will be faithful to me?* <margin>The dreams of a waking monk.</margin> *Who might assist me with counsel to fulfill my will? Then, on the Salisbury Plain <note>An expansive plateau in southern England, famous for being the site of Stonehenge.</note>, I would most magnificently construct fifteen abbeys in a very short space of time, so that each would be one mile distant from the others."*

*For this reason, approaching me, he said that he had been assured of my loyalty by others, and therefore he would tell me the conception of his mind. He asked that I assist him with counsel. I promised by the image of Saint James that I would not reveal his name. Nevertheless, I am permitted to write without fault concerning his so empty a desire. When he had revealed his knowledge to me, he added that nothing was lacking to him except the opportunity and the means of working for the King's benefit, so that he might obtain license from him and the whole state to purchase fields and lands for the said abbeys; for he himself would settle all the expenses. # ON OTHER ARTISANS GATHERED TOGETHER IN LONDON at one time for the space of ten days; from the same Author, chapter 5.

<margin>Three true masters of Chemistry gathered at one time in London.</margin>
**A**t that time, he says (*while a certain Brice held the coinage in his power* <note>original: "Briseo." Likely referring to Sir Hugh Brice, who was the Governor of the King’s Mint at the Tower of London and later Lord Mayor in the late 15th century</note>), a marvelous thing happened concerning this science. Namely, that three masters of this art lay in one bed not far from the lead-covered hall (that is, **Leadenhall** <note>A famous historic market and landmark in the City of London, known then for its lead-tiled roof</note>), who possessed the white and red **Elixir** <note>The "white elixir" was believed to transmute base metals into silver; the "red elixir" into gold</note>. It is a wonder that three of such a kind rested in one bed, and that for the space of ten days; since among hundreds of thousands of men, scarcely one is found.

<margin>The artisan from Lorraine.</margin>
One was a native of the Duchy of Lorraine; the second was born near the middle of England; the third was born under a Cross at the boundary of three counties, being younger in age than the others. It was predicted of this youngest man by the learned—after his birth chart had been cast—that he ought to adorn the whole land of England. One could travel through the entire world and scarcely find so many and such great masters in this art meeting together. Two of them are about to depart; this one, younger in age, will remain and will confer much benefit upon this region, unless the sins of princes hinder those good things which he himself was once destined to provide.

<margin>A certain artisan prophesied in London.</margin>
The eldest of the masters predicted in a certain song that the youth would suffer much injury from friends. And he told of many other things which have happened since that time, and some which are yet to come. Among these, he said one shall be most true: that after great troubles, there shall be great joy in every **tetrarchy** <note>original: "tetrarchia." Referring here to the four-fold division or regions of the kingdom</note> of this realm.

<margin>When the cross is honored, the art will be shared with the king.</margin>
The younger in age asked when this would happen. Then the elder replied: when men see the most holy **Cross** honored night and day in the region of God and light. This could happen soon; but if it is deferred, it will not be convenient. This will be proven true by experience itself: here the science shall be communicated to the king, and many graces shall come to him,

Above all human things I love knowledge; and the <term>red medicine</term> <note>Another name for the completed Philosopher's Stone, emphasizing its power to heal the body and extend life</note>, the best preservative of my life: The red stone, I say, seems more precious to me than the gold of the whole world": To these things he responded, that I was too young in age, handsome in body, and prone to excess; scarcely 28 years of age, such as the philosophers do not have as peers.*

## left as a token of gratitude,

It is said that among peoples no law was observed more solemnly
Than that which was kept for sacred guests.
This law, once the salt was tasted, remained renewed,
And the joining of right hands held firm a mutual faith.

hospitable.

guests.

Both the horrible *Scythians* and the pitiless hearts of the *Thracians*
Bear names worthy of their own ferocity.
**ENGLAND**, for your merits, a greater gratitude remains for you,
To whose pleasing fields every stranger comes.
Because you have sheltered me safely in your hospitality for so many years,
There is cause for me to celebrate your praises.
Indeed, you are a beautiful Nymph, and no other more beautiful

But while good form blesses many goddesses, one gift

The Judge of the earth did not grant all gifts to one alone;
Your fortune is joyful in many ways:
Rejoice in your rich soil; *India* sends gifts to you by ships,

But if you say that this happened before **Maximilian** was made **Emperor**: I respond, this could happen, because as a youth of 18 years he wished to undergo his first <term>apprenticeship in warfare</term> <note>original: "tyrocinium militiæ"; this refers to Maximilian I serving as a volunteer under King Henry VIII of England at the Battle of the Spurs in 1513, though Maier disputes the implications of this service.</note> under the **English** king against the **French**, but this has nothing to do with the **Emperor** or the **Empire**. 

<margin>A greater slander against the **Emperor** cannot be written: yet it is read daily.</margin>

Why then do those forgers write that the **Emperor** did this? Similarly, a trifling monk-writer, called **William of Newburgh**, is found in **England**, who, in order to excuse the deeds of that **Richard** <note>King Richard I, "the Lionheart."</note> in the Holy Land, invents marvelous fables, which even a blind man could feel out on a wall. 

<margin>5th Slander.</margin>

Then, when this King himself was hiding in **Vienna** in another habit <note>Disguised as a humble traveler or kitchen-boy.</note> and, being recognized, was captured by the Duke of **Austria**, his enemy, and handed over to the **Emperor**, this gossip-mongering writer inveighs wonderfully against the greed of the **Caesar** <note>The Emperor Henry VI, who held Richard for ransom.</note>; but he was a monk educated in a monastery, who knew nothing except what he had heard most falsely reported by his own people. 

<margin>Marvelous fables about the green children and others.</margin>

He tells the same marvelous fables of **green children** <note>The "Green Children of Woolpit," a legendary 12th-century account of two children with green skin who appeared in Suffolk.</note> coming out of the earth, of two dogs from a stone quarry, and a toad with a golden chain coming out of the same place; he is more worthy of being numbered among storytellers than historians. 

<margin>6th Slander.</margin>

There is still living the historian **Camden**, a most learned and otherwise circumspect man, who wove together the history of **England** in an excellent style and with great dexterity of judgment. He, based on the false reports of others, writes in that place where he deals with the **Counts** <note>In an English context, these are "Earls."</note> of **England**, that the **Counts** and **Barons** in **England** are not such as they are in **France** and **Germany**, but are **peers** <note>original: "pares"; Maier is critiquing Camden's "Britannia" regarding the status of the Peerage.</note>. 

<margin>Ignorantia excusat, si non sit calumniosa.</margin> <note>Ignorance excuses, if it is not slanderous.</note>

These words were brought forth from the ignorance of such a great man rather than from malice. For they are openly false: An **English Count** or **Baron** has at least some fields and a title, and nothing besides...

<margin>How an Earl of **England** and a Count of **Germany** differ:</margin>
A **German** Count is equal to a King in jurisdiction, authority, and dignity: for he possesses a most extensive region, in which there are cities and very many villages, as well as nobles, citizens, and peasants. He commands these as a king; he has his own chancellor, marshal, secretary, treasurer, and all the officers just as a king does. He holds the jurisdiction of life and death over all his subjects, and furthermore, other <term>Regalia</term> <note>Royal rights or privileges belonging to a sovereign, such as minting coins or collecting certain taxes.</note> which are by far the most extensive. 
<margin>A **German** Count is equal to a King in all things, except for the size of his territory.</margin>
Indeed, he is so similar to a king that nothing could be more like one. The appeal of judgments from nobles and cities reaches him. Under our counts, in a slightly lower order, are the **Barons**, who hold the same status but in a smaller form. Then there are those called **Nobles**, who have the same but in an even smaller manner.
<margin>**German** Barons.</margin>
Next are the **Feudal** tenants in the cities, who hold the same, yet in a far lesser way.
<margin>**German** Nobles.</margin>
After them are the **merchant citizens and craftsmen**. 
<margin>Feudal tenants.</margin>
Then there are the **free peasants**, who, living in the **Marshes** <note>Likely referring to the wealthy independent farming communities in the marshlands of Northern Germany, such as Dithmarschen.</note>, are very wealthy and sometimes possess as much land as one of the Magnates of **England**, but they lack the title. If they had it (as it could easily be given to them by the **Emperor**), they would be **Barons in title only**, without subjects or their own jurisdiction. 
<margin>Citizens.</margin>
Finally, there are the **hired peasants**, who are entirely the servants of the nobles and cultivate the fields, which they nevertheless possess by hereditary right. 
<margin>Free peasants.</margin>
From among these, which is an **English** baron more like? Certainly those who have lands without jurisdiction.
<margin>Barons in title only.</margin>
Many **Feudal** tenants have jurisdiction and the right of life and death over their subjects. This is much more the case for the **Nobles**, who are truly noble by all lineage and affinity, and not solely by their clothing. 
<margin>No one will deny these things are true: hence the **English** inquire about the surnames of the princes and counts of **Germany**.</margin>
In **England** (if it is permitted to speak the truth) there is no **Count**, **Baron**, or <term>Knecht</term> <note>original: "Knecht"; here used to mean a servant or lower-ranking attendant, though etymologically related to the English word "Knight."</note> or servant who is not connected by lineage and affinity to craftsmen and men of the lowest order. Our nobles are such by eight great-grandparents <note>Referencing the strict German "proof of ancestry" (*Ahnenprobe*) required to maintain noble status.</note>. And here, riches do not make one noble, but rather military or literary virtue. Therefore, **Camden** <note>William Camden (1551–1623), an influential English historian and author of *Britannia*.</note> is mistaken in these matters—not, I believe, because he tries to take away deserved honors from others, but because he [writes] from a lack...

...unless, through a <note>The text likely refers back to a traveler or critic.</note> lack of travel, he should not know otherwise. **In England, the sons of an Earl** are distinguished by degrees: the eldest obtains the father's title and most of the goods; the second is of a lower order; the third is lower still; the fourth is merely a <term>gentleman</term> <note>original: "gentelmānus"; meaning a man of good family but without a specific title of nobility</note>, that is, someone having some income or born of a good lineage; and the fifth will perhaps be a craftsman, a mechanic, or a merchant.

<margin>*The sons of Great Lords in England are unequal.*</margin>

<margin>*In Germany, there is greater equality among heirs.*</margin>
**In Germany, if there is a Count who has five sons, the first succeeds in the county; the other four are equally Counts, just as he is.** For they hold the same title, even if they do not hold the jurisdiction; and this is done so that if the first dies without male heirs, the second may succeed, and so on for the rest. Therefore, that title looks toward the inheritance and not always to the immediate jurisdiction. However, these four remaining sons are called to various high offices: one might be a great commander of the military; another becomes a <term>canon</term> <note>A member of the clergy serving a cathedral or collegiate church.</note> or a <term>provost</term> in those great metropolitan churches; a third might perhaps be a bishop. And the same is to be judged for the others; thus, all remain in dignity and wealth.

<margin>*Great Lords in Germany are promoted in many ways.*</margin>
What has been said here regarding Counts must also be understood for those of higher rank, such as the Princes—specifically the <term>Palatine Counts</term>, <term>Margraves</term>, and <term>Landgraves</term> <note>These are specific German titles: Pfalzgrafen (associated with the palace/court), Markgrafen (lords of border territories), and Landgrafen (lords of a significant province).</note> of Germany—as well as for **Barons** and **nobles**.

<margin>*The number of German Princes is great.*</margin>
Indeed, the Princes in Germany who hold some jurisdiction are more than 50; there are nearly 120 Counts; twice as many Barons; and the nobles who hold jurisdiction and use the German language are over 20,000. Perhaps <term>Camden</term> <note>Referring to William Camden (1551–1623), a famous English antiquarian and historian whose works often compared English and continental customs.</note> saw some Count or Baron traveling without a large retinue, which is why his judgment was false. But he should have used discretion, noting that those traveling do not always enjoy a large retinue, or rather that the Germans look toward providing an equal inheritance for their sons rather than displaying external pomp.

<margin>*In Germany, annual revenues are not all spent on the belly and pomp, but a large part of them is reserved for the children.*</margin>
I know a place or region in Germany where the nobles (not to speak of Barons or Counts) would wish to consume their annual revenues entirely (as is done in England), and leave only the principal patrimony to the eldest—

Therefore, there is no real patron of *England*, and the feast of *George* is merely worldly pomp.

<margin>13. The English pronunciation is most faulty, though they are unaware of it.</margin>
Those who speak ill of others should also look to their own letters and pronunciation, in which they are so faulty that if they speak in Latin, they are scarcely understood by other nations around them. For example, when they wish to say *propino tibi* <note>original: "propino tibi"; "I drink to your health"</note>, they say *propino teibei*. Indeed, there is no vowel or consonant that is not corrupted and distorted; where other people pronounce a **u**, they say **oo**; where others say **i**, they say **ee**. Where others say *charitas* <note>Charity</note>, they say *Tiaritas* as a three-syllable word; where others say *Abimelech*, <margin>The English can neither write nor pronounce many words, e.g., Chamech. They say Tiamectz.</margin> they say *Abimelecz*, and so on with other words. 

In this distortion of letters, there are many thousands of words that, when pronounced by other nations, the English cannot even write down in a way that allows them to pronounce them the same way later. They pronounce the word *Church* <note>Maier uses the English word here to illustrate the phonetic gap between English and Continental European ears.</note> as *Tziurtz*, a single syllable, yet they are unable to write our pronunciation of *Church*. And so it goes with other things. I recount these matters because the English consider anyone who does not pronounce words as they do to be "barbarians," believing themselves to be in possession of the true pronunciation of the Latin language—in which they are quite mistaken. <margin>English who have left their country learn a different pronunciation.</margin> **However, those who have once left their fatherland for France or Germany** soon correct their Latin pronunciation.

Let these remarks suffice as a brief defense against those English detractors. I do not wish, however, to include the Great Men or the nobles in this critique, for they are far wiser in these matters; rather, I speak of the dregs of the common people, who, out of a lazy ignorance, behave injuriously toward other nations.

# THE GOLDEN TABLE. BOOK X.

...it is possible in all things to follow the footsteps of nature, since Art chooses a shorter, middle path, borrowed from those same principles of nature, toward the same goal. From this, it follows that it does not need as much time as nature will require, but a far shorter time. Nature’s time is very lengthy, and its method of cooking <note>original: "coctio"; a term for the application of heat to mature a substance</note> is uniform, and its fire most gentle. Art, on the contrary, is brief, and the cooking must be moderated by the skill of the artist, just as the fire must be increased or decreased. Furthermore, Art mixes two or more things together with the hands of the artist, which nature produced in different places and would never have joined into one, since nature lacks the power of locomotion, separation, and judgment. All these things belong to the artist, who brings together certain things from different mines into one, mixes like things, separates unlike things, and judges the fires, vessels, colors, time, maturity, and all other circumstances until he arrives at the desired goal. Hence it is that nature does not produce perfect tinctures <note>The "tincture" is the refined alchemical agent used for transmutation</note> in the abstract, but only in the concrete; just as it does not produce the purest spirit of wine <note>original: "spiritum vini"; distilled alcohol or ethanol</note> in the abstract, but in the concrete, in wine, from which it is separated by art.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;To the minor premise <note>Maier is responding to the second part of a logical syllogism</note> I say that the artist does not need 100 years for the perfection of the art, much less a thousand, since a few days, which do not even <term>complete</term> <note>original: "conficiant"; to finish or fulfill a span of time</note> a whole year, can be sufficient for him, once the art is perfectly known and discovered. However, for the discovery itself, unless one receives it from another, many years are required, and for many, even an entire life was not sufficient for its perfection. <term>Ulysses</term> <note>Odysseus, the hero of Greek myth known for his ten-year journey</note> spent 10 years traveling through various seas to return home from <term>Troy</term>, which he could have reached within 20 days if it had been pleasing enough [to the gods]. Likewise, some have sailed around the entire world in a few years, which one hundred years ago, before <term>Magellan</term> <note>Ferdinand Magellan, the explorer who organized the first circumnavigation of the Earth</note>, no man could have traversed in his whole life. The reason is that it is easier to follow a path once found than to find one that has not been discovered. Thus in the art, [he] is a Ulysses...

### 29. A Negative Argument Against Chemistry.

<margin>Negative Argument 29.</margin>If metals are composed of vapors <note>original: "fumi"; literally "smokes" or "fumes." In alchemical theory, these are the exhalations within the earth that condense into minerals.</note>, as if from their constituent principles, and those vapors require a tempered cooking <note>original: "decoctio"; the process of maturing a substance through steady heat.</note>—since they are most subtle—lest they flee from the fire under a stronger heat, and so that they may be thickened within themselves and reach a state of uniformity; then Art, which intends to compose those metals (especially the perfect ones), requires a tempered cooking that extends over several hundred years.

But the first premise is true.
Therefore, so is the second.
And consequently, since the artist cannot endure in his work for such a long time—or, if he increases the fire, he deprives those vapors of their moisture or puts them to flight—it follows that the efforts of his art are inconsistent and in vain <note>original: "frustraneus"; fruitless or failing to produce the desired result.</note>.

*The antecedent <note>The "antecedent" refers to the first part of the logical proposition being argued by the critic.</note> is proved:* For if, by your artifice, you wish to shorten nature’s time of cooking in mineral and metallic bodies, it will be necessary to do this through an excess of heat; this heat will not balance the substance, but rather [the] moisture... <note>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page.</note>

## Response to the 29th Negative Argument:

<margin>Response to the 29th Negative Argument</margin>
The difference between Nature—which draws metals out from their own principles—and Art—which takes them where they were left imperfect and perfects them through a Medicine <note>In alchemy, the "Medicine" refers to the Philosopher's Stone or Elixir, which "cures" base metals of their imperfections.</note> originating from quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"; literally "living silver," the common name for mercury.</note>—has been sufficiently and abundantly demonstrated above. Art, therefore, does not take the raw principles, but rather compounds already formed from those principles; from these, it composes the matter and form of gold, and thereafter gold itself. We grant, then, that Nature employs a long digestion to coagulate and balance those vapors; but Nature also possesses another path which she uses to generate perfect metals, a path that is swifter than the first. Art directs its operations according to this swifter path and reaches the intended goal far more quickly than Nature does.

Therefore, the major premise [of the critic's argument] does not hold together in its parts, nor does the minor premise introduce any truth. Consequently, the conclusion of the resulting syllogism <note>A form of logical argument consisting of a major premise, a minor premise, and a conclusion.</note> is not true; for Art differs from Nature in many respects, yet these differences cannot alter the final goal or the effect produced. In Nature’s case, the time required is longer; the vapors must be coagulated and balanced by themselves without any external aid, and the method of digestion is simple. In the case of Art, the time is shorter, and the vapors—partly coagulated and partly purified—are balanced by mutual assistance, because the fixed substance provides stability <note>original: "fixitatem"; the quality of being resistant to fire and not evaporating.</note> to the volatile, and the volatile substance provides mobility to the fixed: and thus the method of operation is different.

## 30. The Adversary's negative argument against Bacon and Alchemy.

<margin>30th negative argument.</margin>
If the **Chymical** art were true, then the practitioner would have to possess within himself the power of all the stars—through which an "infusion" is made into things being born—in order for a perfect metal to be produced.

But this last point is absurd and improper. Therefore, the first point is also false, and the art is not true.

*The major premise <note>The first part of a logical argument (syllogism) that states a general rule.</note> is proven* because "being" and perfection are granted by the stars, as they are the primary finishers and movers of the nature of generation and corruption <note>The traditional Aristotelian framework for the birth and decay of all physical things.</note> regarding the existence and non-existence of species. This, moreover, happens suddenly and in an instant, when one or more stars reach a determined position in the firmament <note>The sphere of the fixed stars; the heavens.</note> through their movements, from which the "being" of perfection is granted; because every single thing acquires its existence in a moment from a specific arrangement of the stars. And there is not just one arrangement, but rather many that differ from one another, just as their effects are diverse. We are unable to fully note the diversity and distinction of these arrangements from one another, since they are unknown and infinite to us. How, then, can you make up for the defect in your work that arises from your ignorance of the diverse positions of the stars in their motion?

### Response to the 30th Negative Argument.

<margin>Response to the 30th negative argument.</margin>
**I** respond that it is not necessary for us to know this celestial arrangement, because there is no species among things that can be generated or corrupted that does not [emerge] from indi- <note>The text cuts off here mid-word, likely "individualibus" (individuals).</note>

...generation and corruption of any of its individuals occurs every day; by which, certainly, the position of the stars is every day perfecting and corrupting any species of individuals. Therefore, it is not necessary to wait for a specific position of the stars.

Therefore, there is no logical connection in the opponent’s proposition. Nor is it necessary in other practical arts to consider the position of the stars: because the stars operate in too general a manner upon the things subject to this art <note>The mineral kingdom</note>, which possess neither a vegetative nor a sensitive soul <note>In the Aristotelian tradition, plants had a "vegetative" soul for growth, and animals had a "sensitive" soul for movement and feeling. Minerals were considered "inanimate" and thus less dependent on the specific celestial "infusions" required for life.</note>. In other matters, the stars undoubtedly instill a soul by their influences into the female or into matter disposed toward a specific plant or animal. There are those who deny that these souls are made from mere elements, and this is consistent with reason.

Those who make Salt from natural brine <note>muria naturali</note> work every day and night throughout the whole year; meanwhile, the natural work—namely, salt—is produced without a determined position or influence of the stars. Those who wish to propagate plants and animals cannot accomplish this every single day, even with suitable materials or seeds kept in their vessels, but must look to the "appetite of nature"—that is, to the cycles of the Sun and Moon, and to the readiness of individual animals. Thus in **Chymistry**, the change of one metal into another can occur any day, once the <term>Tincture</term> <note>A potent substance or "philosopher's stone" capable of transforming base metals into gold or silver.</note> is obtained: the **Tincture** can also be prepared from its materials at any time.

### 29. The Affirmative Argument of Roger Bacon the Englishman in Favor of Chemistry.

<margin>Affirmative Argument 29 for Chemistry.</margin>
If those who deny the truth of Chemistry <note>In the early 17th century, "Chemia" referred to the art of alchemy as well as what we now call chemistry.</note> against so many who affirm it are not all-knowing, but are ignorant in many arts and sciences—even those which the common people know—it follows that Chemistry can be true, even while they are ignorant, unaware, and see nothing in it.

->But the first [premise] is true.<-
->Therefore, also the second.<-

To confirm this proposition, it must be considered that he who denies any thing or proposition ought to have clearly perceived all those things which could affirm it. This is evident by a common example: if someone is sent into a stable to see if a horse is there, upon returning he can negatively and truly answer that there is not; for if it had been there, he would have seen it. But if he is asked whether some mouse is there, even if he responds negatively that there is none, it could nevertheless be hiding, unseen by him. In this way, all those who argue against Chemistry—claiming it does not exist—pretend themselves to be altogether like <term>Lynceus</term> <note>original: "Lynceos." In Greek mythology, Lynceus was an Argonaut renowned for his superhuman sight, capable of seeing through stone, trees, and even into the earth.</note>, as if they themselves could see and penetrate all the recesses and caves where such a small

...mouse: But we do not believe them, even if they deny the presence of such a hidden mouse (which one of us has seen); even if such deniers were a thousand in number and only one affirmed it. Or surely, they should prove themselves to be so **Lyncean** <note>original: "Lynceos"; referring to Lynceus of Greek mythology, who was said to have sight so keen he could see through stone and into the earth.</note> that they have perceived all the smallest and hidden things as clearly as the large and obvious ones. Therefore, let those learned men—**Erasmus, Scaliger, Lipsius, Erastus, Guibert,** and others like them—be silent or rather hang up their censorial rods <note>A metaphor for putting aside their harsh judgment.</note>. Let them not hear from the Chemists, "**shoemaker, stay at your last**," <note>original: "ne sutor ultra crepidam"; a famous Latin proverb used to tell someone to stop offering opinions on things they know nothing about.</note> and realize that they are to be laughed at even by children when, through their own [supposed] perspicacity, they think that because they themselves do not understand something, no one else has understood it, does understand it, or will ever understand it.

<margin>The adversaries of Chemistry among the learned.</margin>
<margin>Hippias wished to be held as all-knowing but was ignorant of many things.</margin>

To present the **minor premise** [of the argument], it must be considered that even that **Hippias**—the Socratic disciple who wished to be considered all-knowing because he boasted that he had made with his own hand everything he wore on his body: his rags, clothes, shoes, rings, and the rest—was not truly all-knowing. Instead, he was ignorant of infinite things, many of which are now known to us, including the art of **gold-making** itself. The same must be said of other most learned men of our age: let them first learn the arts known by that Hippias, and then those not known, and prove themselves to be all-knowing so that we might truly believe them. Otherwise, we shall say that they are rather ignorant for denying the **Mastery** <term>Magisterium: The completion of the Philosopher's Stone or the "Great Work" of alchemy.</term>, which has been asserted by so many wise men, simply because they do not understand how it is or is not possible. Hence, by the philosophers **Geber, Avicenna, Bonus** and others, these very men are likened to children who, having been shut in a certain house from the beginning of their birth, do not think the width of the world extends beyond the house in which they are enclosed, or beyond what they can see with their eyes. And while these "eyebrow-raisers" <note>original: "superciliolati"; referring to their haughty or skeptical expressions.</note> and those "wise only as far as their cloak" <note>A common idiom for someone who looks like a philosopher but lacks true wisdom.</note> boast, they are held as fools by the Philosophers themselves; for **Avicenna** affirms: "**No wise man has ever denied the Mastery.**" Indeed, if one were to put them under oath...

<margin>Those denying the Mastery are like certain children.</margin>
<margin>He is not wise who denies the Mastery.</margin>

...if I were to ask whether the aforementioned horse <note>The author is using a hypothetical scenario where a person denies something exists simply because it is hidden from their view.</note> were there or not, they might deny it under oath. But if they were to deny it under oath, I would say that those men were unreliable and perjured for claiming a mouse was there. We must speak of the truth of **Chemistry** in the same way: if it were something that ought to be publicly known through reasoning and experiments, then they would see it; but since that is not the case, and they do not see it, if they therefore deny it and wish to persuade others by an oath that it does not exist, they will not succeed. Rather, they will prove themselves to be false and perjured instead of proving **Chemistry** to be entirely deceptive. <margin>Plautus.</margin> *As the comic poet says,* <note>original: "Vbi oculato testi... plus fidei adhibendum est, quam decem auritis"; a quote from the Roman playwright Plautus.</note> *more faith should be placed in one eyewitness than in ten who have only heard of a thing. For those who have seen can bear witness to the matter as it stands; those who have not seen cannot do the same. This is because a thing can exist even if many do not see it, but it cannot be absent if even one person sees it.*

### 30. An Affirmative Argument for Chemistry.

<margin>Affirmative Argument 30.</margin>
If the chemical art were not true, but merely a fiction, it would not possess certain precepts consistent with reason and conforming to the very nature of metals; nor would **vegetable or growing gold** <note>original: "aurum vegetabile"; Alchemists used the term "vegetable" to describe the way the Philosophers' Stone was thought to "grow" or multiply gold, much like a seed produces a plant.</note> be found in its color, **fixity**, and **ingress**.

But this latter point is beyond doubt: that it possesses precepts consistent with reason and nature themselves, as well as a matter that can be increased in color, **fixity**, and **ingress**. <term>Fixity: The quality of a substance (like gold) that allows it to remain stable and non-volatile even under the most intense heat.</term> <term>Ingress: The ability of the alchemical medicine to penetrate into the "pores" of a base metal to transform it.</term>

**Therefore, the first point is also true.**

**T**he connection of this proposition is clear; because that which is not a true art does not agree with itself in its means, nor its principles, nor its end, nor does it possess...

<summary>Maier uses a quote from Plautus to argue that the testimony of one successful alchemist outweighs the skepticism of many who have never seen the Work. He then begins a formal logical proof arguing that the consistency of alchemical theory with the nature of metals proves its validity.</summary>

...precepts consistent with these things: The art of the Augurs <note>The practice of "augury" involved interpreting the will of the gods from the flight of birds; the author considers it a false science because it lacks a basis in nature.</note> is not a true art, as is proven by the fact that it possesses rules that conform neither to nature nor to reason. # THE STONE, LIKE AN INFANT, MUST BE NOURISHED

**M**elchior of Sibiu <note>original: "Melchior Cibinensis"; a 16th-century Hungarian priest and alchemist famous for writing a "Mass of the Alchemists."</note>, a Hungarian—or, if we consider the specific branch of his people, he is otherwise held to be a Transylvanian—was a religious man initiated into the priestly order. ...color <note>The text begins mid-word, likely completing a word like "color" or "labor" from the previous page.</note>. For nothing among earthly things is more similar to that great heavenly work—if it is somehow permissible to compare these lowest things with the highest, and fleeting things with the eternal—than the preparation of the <term>Tincture</term> <note>The "Tincture" or "Medicine" is another name for the Philosopher's Stone, emphasizing its power to "tint" or permeate and transform base metals into gold.</note>, which is regarded as the greatest and most precious of human achievements, just as Salvation is in the divine realm. 

But since we know there have been those who abused this comparison (which is otherwise lawful) and, by a truly diabolical instinct, applied all the axioms of the Christian Faith to the earthly or gold-making Stone—about which they had not the slightest knowledge—and thereby shrouded the mystery of our Salvation in darkness; therefore, setting aside the "Form of the Mass" or its allegory as applied to the Stone, we shall instead—and not without reason—compare the production of the Tincture to human birth, activity, life, death, and resurrection, making no mention of Christ in this matter. This can and may be done without causing any scandal. 

The **Stone**, therefore, like a human being, is conceived from the mixture of two seeds, masculine and feminine; through impregnation, it is turned into an embryo; it is born into the light; it is nourished by milk; it grows; it reaches its peak; it is joined in marriage (though in a different sense); it generates from its spouse; it is afflicted by the cross or the heat of tribulation <note>In alchemy, "tribulation" often refers to the intense heat of the furnace required to purify the matter.</note>; it dies; it is buried; it remains in the tomb for some time; from there it rises and enjoys a new, incorruptible life, and can die no more. 

We will demonstrate all these things in their proper order, and then we will proceed to explain the advantages and disadvantages of this nation <note>The "nation" refers here to the community of alchemists or "Philosophers."</note>, as far as the purpose of our study is concerned. We will, however, provide only a few testimonies from the philosophers on this subject, because the individual points are self-evident and well-known: *The Rosary* <note>original: "Rosarius"; likely referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum* (The Rosary of the Philosophers), one of the most famous alchemical texts that uses the metaphor of human generation and resurrection.</note>

<margin>When the pregnancy of the Stone occurs.</margin>
When the water arrives—that is, the **arsenic** <note>In alchemy, "arsenic" usually refers to a philosophical spirit or a specific stage of volatile matter, rather than the common poison</note>—it grows and increases greatly in the earth. This happens when the earth has been whitened <note>A reference to the *albedo* or whitening stage of the alchemical process</note>; it is then called **pregnancy**, because it is now pregnant.

<margin>When the nourishment of the Stone occurs.</margin>
And **nourishment** follows, so that he may increase more, for the more he is nourished by his own milk and seed, the more abundantly they are produced. He is soaked with arsenic <note>The philosophical "water" or spirit</note> again and again, until he drinks two parts, and let this be sufficient.

<margin>Morienus's comparison of the Stone with human birth.</margin>
**Morienus** <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist</note>, from whom the things said so far have been translated, puts it this way: "*The first of these (the arrangement of parts) is intercourse; the second is conception; the third is pregnancy; the fourth is birth; the fifth is nourishment.*" Therefore, if there is no intercourse, there will be no conception; and if there is no conception, there will be no pregnancy; and if there is no pregnancy, birth will by no means follow. For this is the direction of this arrangement, which is truly likened to the creation of a human being.

<margin>The Sun and Moon unite.</margin>
Thus he spoke. But it may be asked, if there is intercourse, between whom does it occur? The answer is: between the **Sun** and the **Moon**. For in this marriage, these spouses are considered to be the Suns <note>meaning the "shining ones" or the perfect principles</note> who are coupled in the bed or bridal chamber. From their joined seeds is born he who is sought by thousands upon thousands, yet is most rarely found. The reason is that people are ignorant of his parents and do not know the way to join them in their lawful marriage bed.

<margin>Where the Sun and Moon are joined.</margin>
But from where can they be obtained? One of them comes from the East and the other from the West into a single land, adorned and conspicuous with various flowers, which is not unlike the **Elysian Fields** <note>In Greek mythology, a paradise for the blessed; here it describes the idealized environment of the alchemical vessel</note>. For whatever the human appetite might desire, it is not lacking here. If anyone by chance or fortune should come into this land, he will see these two walking here like a bridegroom and a bride. <margin>The union of the Sun and Moon occurs in a temperate place.</margin>
<margin>The son of the Philosophers is born.</margin>
The Kings, now united, lie together in a place where the Etesian winds <note>Strong, cool Mediterranean winds that blow in the summer</note>, the West Winds, or southern breezes might be felt in the heat, so that some cooling might reach them. For unless the place of their union were temperate, the seeds would either be dried out by excessive heat or hindered by cold. Therefore, their bed is a grassy turf under the open sky, which contributes much to the pleasure of the new spouses. Hence, when the time of her gestation is complete, the joy and longing of the philosophers is born: a legitimate son, full of vitality and most beautiful, to whom we shall rightly join this Birthday Poem <note>original: "Genethliacum"</note> here.

# A BIRTHDAY POEM FOR THE BIRTH
## sung for the little Philosophical son.

<margin>Congratulation on the birth of the philosophers' son.</margin>
*Little lad, leave your mother’s womb happily,*
*and may you deign to bless us with your birth.*
*Be born, and once brought forth, quickly catch the heavenly breezes,*
*so that you may be both the care and the hope for the company of Philosophers.*
*They adopt you as their little son (as is the custom),*
*for they hold the rights over you in the place of a father.*
*For the Sun is your natural parent, but without*
*the guidance of the Artificer <note>The alchemist himself, who directs the natural process</note>, you would scarcely have been well born.*
*He established the regimen for your mother and father,*
*which was suitable for you, the offspring to be born.*
*And Mulciber <note>A name for Vulcan, the god of fire, representing the heat of the furnace</note> was present then with a gentle fire,*
*whose care it was to warm your mother's lap.*
*From this, you are ours because of such merits toward you, even before*
*you were able to enjoy the gift of life and the light.*
*As you grow in age, produce fertile, golden offspring,*
*and may the wishes of Midas be granted to you.*
<margin>The wishes of Midas are appropriate for the tincture.</margin>
*So that, Golden One, whatever you deign to touch with your hand...*

# WEDDING SONG
## Dedicated in honor of the marriage of Mother Beia and her son Gabricus, to be joined in union under good omens.

*While the mother herself is joined to her son in a marital bond,*
    *let the work not be seen as an incestuous deed.*
*For thus Nature commands, thus the nourishing*
    *Law of Fate requires, nor is this matter displeasing to God:*
*For if only one seed remained in the whole world,*
    *it would be lawful for it to be committed to its own soil.*
*Likewise, if there were no man but one son,*
    *and only one mother, it is better that these enjoy love;*
*Than that the world should afterwards be without human offspring,*
    *or one who might rule the empty earth with reason.*
*Let that bond be believed happy for the spouses, so that from it*
    *a progeny increased with good fruit may go forth:*
*He shall be the one born from you who soon, by his merits*
    *and gifts, shall draw the love of all.*
*He, crowned with the red diadem of a King,*
    *shall walk forth providing various riches.*
*O happy mother, who rejoices in such a great pledge,*
    *O happy spouse, with a spouse so like yourself.*
*And you, husband, scatter the nuts <note>A Roman wedding tradition where the groom threw walnuts to children, symbolizing the end of childhood and the assumption of adult responsibilities</note>; now a wife is bound to you*
    *by the chains of Venus <note>original: "Cypriae" — the Cyprian goddess, Aphrodite/Venus</note>, equal to you in character.*
*This bride, through kindred desire, shall bear from her womb*
    *an offspring just such as you are yourself.*

<margin>Mother, sister, and wife of her own son.</margin>
We have demonstrated above that this mother, Beia, is also the sister of Gabricus; although this may seem contrary to nature, it is nonetheless true in the hidden philosophy <term>philosophia occulta; the secret tradition of alchemy</term>. Hence the philosophers so often advise that our "red servant" <term>seruum rubeum; a term for the masculine principle or sulfur in the work</term> is the spouse to be joined—

<margin>The red servant is to be joined with his sister.</margin>
He must be joined with his fragrant sister, and these two joined together will beget a son far more powerful than his parents. Thus the *Rosary* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum*, or "Rosary of the Philosophers," a seminal 16th-century alchemical text</note> says from the vision of Arisleus <note>A legendary alchemist often cited in the *Turba Philosophorum*</note>: *Therefore join your son Gabricus <note>Representing the "Sulfur" or the masculine, active principle</note>, who is dearer to you than all your other sons, with his sister Beia <note>Representing "Mercury" or the feminine, receptive principle</note>, who is a shining, sweet, and tender girl. Gabricus is the male and Beia the female, who gives to him everything that is of herself.* And presently: *Join therefore our servant to his fragrant sister, and between them they shall beget a son who will not resemble the parents; and although Gabricus is more precious than Beia, nevertheless there can be no generation without Gabricus. For the intercourse of Gabricus with Beia resulted in immediate death: For Beia climbed on top of Gabricus and enclosed him in her womb, so that nothing at all of him could be seen; and she embraced Gabricus with such great love that she conceived him entirely into her own nature and divided him into indivisible parts.*

<margin>The son will be more noble than his parents.</margin>
<margin>Beia encloses Gabricus in her womb.</margin>
And a little later, Senior <note>Zadith ben Hamuel, an 11th-century Arabic alchemist known to the Latin world as "Senior"</note> says: *The red servant took a white wife, and in the joining of these two, the wife remaining pregnant, she gave birth to a son who preserved his parents in all things, and is more splendid and radiant.* Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical father of Hermeticism and alchemy</note> also mentions this marriage when he says in the second treatise: *Know this, my son, that unless one knows how to lead, to make pregnant, and to generate species, nothing happens, nor is anything accomplished. <margin>The marriage of the mother and son ends in the death of the son.</margin>

*...then it is dead, but the body is alive by reason of heat and dryness. For everything having heat has life: And because of this, alchemical lime <term>calx</term> <note>The powdery residue left after a substance has been roasted or "calcined"</note> is said to have life: because the philosophers strived to kill their imperfect life and restore it to eternal life. From the same Rising Dawn <note>original: "Aurora consurgens," a famous 15th-century alchemical manuscript</note>, in the final chapter; Of the Lesser Heat: "It behooves us," it says, "to kill him wisely, that is, to burn him; because death* <margin>To burn is to kill.</margin> *will reveal it." Let us do this many times, until it dies and is softened."*

Now, what kind of mortification <note>In alchemy, "mortification" refers to the breakdown or "killing" of the raw material to prepare it for transformation</note> this is and how it occurs, the *Rosary* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum*</note> explains when it says: <margin>How mortification occurs.</margin> *"Quicksilver <term>Argentum vivum</term> [mercury] by itself is worth nothing; but when it is mortified with its hidden body, then it is worth much and lives an incorruptible life. And this body is of the nature of the sun; therefore it is necessary that it converts the whole quicksilver into the nature of the sun, just as leaven converts the whole dough into the nature of leaven, and not the reverse, because the mastery is always transferred to the dominant principles."*

It is mortified, moreover, when it is given a black robe by Saturn <note>In alchemy, Saturn represents the metal lead and the "nigredo" or blackening stage, which signifies death and decay</note>, which, as a dark color, is seen to be appropriate for those who are dying. But it must be considered that the mother, namely Isis, was not the primary cause of Osiris's death, but Typhon, who, like a furious whirlwind, kills him and divides him into various parts. <margin>Isis was not the cause of Osiris's death, but Typhon.</margin> The *Egyptians* pursued his death with weeping and wailing, just as the *Syrians* did for *Adonis*, as we have related in the appropriate places above; For *Osiris* and *Adonis* are one and the same—namely the Sun—not the celestial sun, as the ignorant among the pagans <note>original: "Ethicis," literally "ethnics," used here to mean non-Christian or pre-Christian writers</note> have thought, but the philosophical Sun. <margin>Osiris and Adonis are the philosophical Sun.</margin> Upon the death of the one, we celebrate with joy instead of tears, and with gestures of gladness instead of wailing, not doubting that he will be restored to life. Therefore, we shall set up a funeral song <term>Epicedion</term> for him as a monument, not of grief, but of the hope already conceived for his future life.

...by night. The philosophers transmit what revivification truly is:
The same **Rosary** <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum* (The Rosary of the Philosophers) is a famous 16th-century alchemical treatise that uses metaphors of marriage, death, and rebirth to describe chemical processes.</note> says: *Revivification is the restoration of the perfect humor <note>In alchemy, "humor" refers to the vital moisture or fluid within a substance</note> and rectifying humidity by means of nourishment—that is, by the expulsion of the imperfect humor itself.* And **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the founder of alchemy.</note> says: *He wishes the dead to be made alive and the sick to be cured.* So the *Aurora* <note>Referring to the *Aurora Consurgens* (The Rising Dawn), a medieval alchemical manuscript known for its rich allegorical and biblical imagery.</note> states in its last chapter. It is also called "revivification" by reason of nourishment, or by reason of the **metallic humor**. For everything that is nourished is nourished by reason of a deficiency: And that which is made alive is made alive for two reasons. Moreover, the philosophers wish to nourish their grain with a humor natural to it, until it grows and brings forth such fruit as it possesses within itself; and they wish to revive that which is "dead" from its metallic form <note>Alchemy often describes raw or "crude" metals as being in a state of death; the process of "revivification" brings them to the "living" state of gold or the Philosopher's Stone.</note>, until it provides a perfect metallic fusion; and such revivification or nourishment is called **ingress** <note>original: "ingressum"; in alchemy, "ingress" refers to the ability of the Stone or tincture to penetrate and transform base metals</note> by some philosophers.

From this it is established that the **Little King** <note>original: "Regillus"; a diminutive of Rex, referring to the nascent gold or the Stone</note>, having been endowed by **Venus**, appears revived, which signifies the red ornament:

For Vulcan, as it is transmitted among the **Egyptians**, was the master of **Mercury** and, along with him, the author of laws; so he exists as the educator and guardian of this Royal son, who is nourished by fire. # SYMBOLS

<margin>When Sulfur begins to act, life is resumed.</margin>
[The text] says that the **Medicine** <note>In alchemy, the "Medicine" refers to the Philosopher’s Stone in its curative or transformative state.</note> is to be roasted longer over the fire and nourished, *like a child at the breasts*: **Death** indeed flees together with the shadows—that is, the **blackness** <note>original: "nigredo"; the first stage of the alchemical Great Work, representing decay and the stripping away of old forms.</note> which appears in the dissolution of the body, vanishes as other more joyful colors, namely **whiteness** <note>original: "albedo"</note> and **redness** <note>original: "rubedo"</note>, succeed it; and the **sulfur** <note>The active, masculine, or combustible principle in alchemy.</note>, which was first drawn and suffered from the **quicksilver** <note>original: "argento vivo"; mercury, the passive or feminine principle.</note>, begins to react and demonstrate its prevailing powers. <margin>What the Sea is.</margin> The **Sea** also flees—that is, the superfluous humidity, which is dried up, whereas before, like a sea, it abounded in the compound. <margin>What the Dragon is.</margin> To these things the **dragon** flees, who is the horrible **Typhon** <note>In Egyptian mythology (via Greek interpretation), Typhon/Set is the chaos-monster who murdered and dismembered Osiris. In alchemy, this represents the forceful breaking down of matter.</note>, and who divided the limbs of **Osiris** into the smallest parts; hence he is said to watch the openings, as if hiding in the shadows. He cannot endure the solar rays—that is, the burning fire of the sun existing in **Leo** <note>The astrological sign of Leo is the "domicile" of the Sun, representing its maximum heat and power; here it symbolizes the intensity of the alchemical furnace.</note>—since he is cold by nature. He becomes a **warrior** by fire; for just as a soldier casts down and plunders the enemy, so he destroys imperfect metals and strips them of their corruptible sulfur. <margin>Fire is the sword for our warrior.</margin> Fire, however, is his sword: for without fire he performs nothing, just as a warrior cannot without weapons. He stands above all **tinctures** <note>A "tincture" is a substance capable of infusing its color and quality into another body; here, it refers to the Stone itself.</note>—that is, above all others sought from wherever, which are not true, or if true, are not universal.

# CONGRATULATORY POEM TO THE PHILOSOPHICAL HERO
## Who, after black death, was gifted with a purple life; dedicated for the sake of joy.

<margin>
A congratulation
made to one
restored to life.
</margin>

*Behold the welcome changes! He who lay conquered by death,*
*Now by the right of return* <note>original: "postliminio"; a legal term referring to the restoration of rights to a person returning from captivity. Here, it signifies the substance returning from the "death" of the black stage.</note> *has escaped into the upper air,*
*And the great-souled Hero has again sought his friendly garments of life;*
*He who is wondrous in his first birth and marriage,*
*Being both father and son to himself.*
*He is the victor over death, which was at first victorious,*
*From which he brought forth a noble Trophy from the purple War* <note>original: "purpureo Marte"; Mars represents iron and the color red. This refers to the "Red Work" or Rubedo, the final stage of alchemy.</note>;
*Now let us celebrate these good joys with a secure mind,*
*And let us strike our hands in resounding applause toward the heavens.*
*For the Phoenix of the Arabs has now returned, sent from its shores,*
*And the cold Salamander* <note>In alchemical lore, the salamander was a lizard-like creature that lived in fire and could extinguish it with its coldness. It represents the "fixed" substance that cannot be destroyed by heat.</note> *leaps from the heart of the furnaces—*
*She who is called "Incombustible" by the Art, nor can she be tamed*
*By any power of the flames (which master all other things).*
*Behold, he shines from afar in a golden cloak, and appearing*
*Resplendent with gold, he is held to be the terrestrial Sun.*
*You come as the long-desired one, most beautiful and great hope*
*Of the wise, for whom the entire world burns with longing.*
*We shall scatter flowers stained with the blood of Venus* <note>A reference to the red color of the Stone; mythologically, the white rose was turned red by the blood of Venus.</note>,
*And we shall offer baskets full of the sprigs of amaranth,*
*Lest honor be lacking to you, or glory to your deeds.*
*We shall heap more songs upon our songs,*
*And we shall sing your praises in a perpetual hymn.*

And thus we shall appear to have satisfied the intention of the man from Sibiu <note>original: "Cibinensis"; referring to Melchior Cibinensis, an alchemist active in the early 16th century who famously composed a "Mass" where alchemical transformation was compared to the Eucharist.</note>, while we [examine] each of those things he mentions in his *Mass* in formal terms...

...lest they perhaps involve themselves in the movements of wars: But now we shall add several things regarding the <margin>Advantages and disadvantages of Hungary.</margin> advantages and disadvantages of this nation: That **Hungary** was, and in part still is, abundant in gold, and that it had fertile veins or mines, the name itself, **Hungarian** gold, easily demonstrates. For this is held as the gold <margin>Hungary was fertile in gold mines.</margin> of Hungarian ducats, in terms of its value and degree of estimation. It is most certain that such natural gold is sometimes found there, just as *Rhenish* gold is found near the *Rhine*, though of far less value. For before the use and invention of nitric acid <note>original: "aquarum fortium"; literally "strong waters," the alchemical term for nitric acid used to separate gold from silver.</note> or antimony <note>Antimony was used in a smelting process to purify gold by removing silver and other base metals.</note>, all gold, as it was found, had to remain mixed with silver, because there was nothing by which one could be separated from the other. Fire or <margin>Different kinds of gold, because it could not formerly be separated from silver.</margin> cupellation <note>original: "cineritium"; the process of refining ores in a cupel, a porous vessel that absorbs base metals when heated.</note> produced no separation of them. Hence we see in a certain city of *Saxony* a golden tablet made of natural **Hungarian** gold, from which, one part having been removed, other gold was substituted which is pale in color, like *Rhenish* gold. But if they had then possessed the art of separating silver from gold, the whole table would be <margin>Lüneburg <note>The marginal note "Luneb." refers to the city of Lüneburg in Lower Saxony, famous for its treasures.</note></margin> or could be made of pure gold <term>obrizum <note>Refers to "aurum obrizum," gold that has been refined and tested to the highest possible purity.</note></term>, the best, finest, of the highest value, and there would have been no need to patch it together from parts of different colors. However, so that this may be better understood and the nature of gold more perfectly perceived, besides the <margin>The external accidental qualities of purification surveyed.</margin> treatise which we published on its internal essence—that is, on the *squared physical circle* <note>Michael Maier's own work, *De Circulo Physico Quadrato* (1616), which compares the properties of gold to the human heart.</note>—we shall here survey, as if in passing, certain external accidental qualities of gold by which it is purified and brought to the highest and equal grade, if ever it is brought forth raw from the mines; lest we seem to have invited the **Hungarians** to this golden table in vain, who were formerly and are still celebrated for their gold mines; which we, in order to see them firsthand in *Transylvania*, undertook a journey as far as **Hungary**, but on account of the war which was then flourishing...
