...flourished, it was not possible to pass through the mountain regions between the late **Emperor Rudolf of divine memory and the Turks**, as bandits raged against everyone they met. <margin>Schemnitz in Hungary has gold-bearing mines.</margin> In the region of *Zepus* <note>Spiš, a historical region in present-day Slovakia</note> is the most famous **Schemnitz**, renowned because its mines are gold-bearing and yield copper, antimony, and vitriol, as well as other metals and minerals. <margin>At Schemnitz, iron is changed into copper.</margin> Here, iron is truly transmuted into copper by means of natural vitriolic waters collected in the mountain cavities. Within a few days—perhaps three, as at *Goslar* in *Saxony*—these waters convert iron plow-handles or rods of considerable thickness into a reddish mud. When this mud is melted by intense fires, it reveals the finest copper, and this in a fixed proportion relative to the amount of iron put into it. <note>This "transmutation" was actually a chemical displacement reaction where copper in the solution precipitated onto the iron, which dissolved—a famous marvel to early modern scientists.</note> <margin>In how many ways gold grows.</margin> Gold is also dug out here and purified through various labors. Now, gold grows in various ways with respect to its matrix <note>The surrounding rock or material in which a mineral is embedded.</note>:

<margin>1.</margin> First, as pure, or nearly pure, from very hard stone, pyrites <note>iron sulfide, often called 'fool's gold'</note>, garnets, **Lapis Lazuli**, and others of that kind.

<margin>2.</margin> Second, it is found as pure grains in certain streams flowing with great force from the gold-bearing mountains.

<margin>3.</margin> Third, it is found invisibly in the mud and the water itself of the streams, and is captured by its "mother," the common **Quicksilver** <note>mercury</note>; however, these two methods hardly relate to the actual generation of gold, since it is washed down to those places from elsewhere rather than being generated there.

<margin>4.</margin> Fourth, gold is found produced in muddy earth, not as hard as stones, but easily crumbled by the hands.

<margin>5.</margin> Fifth, it is found mixed with the poisonous fumes of <term>Cadmia</term> <note>a term used for various zinc or cobalt-bearing ores</note>, arsenic, and others, which—unless handled with skill—carry the gold away with them into smoke and make it volatile <note>meaning the gold would evaporate or be lost as vapor during smelting</note>.

<margin>6.</margin> Sixth, it is sometimes seen mixed with imperfect metals, especially copper.

<margin>7.</margin> Seventh, with silver, which is its own proper mother and more frequently adheres to it.

<margin>Method of separating gold from hard stones.</margin> If it is born with the first type—namely, hard stone—it is separated from there through various labors, such as by fire and iron. Fire is applied to the sides of the mountain using flammable wood, by which the invulnerable stone is made more manageable. Then, with iron—

...with a sharp tool, by which it is cut out; afterward, fire is applied as often as necessary to heat the pieces so they can be crushed. From here, they are ground in mills designed for this purpose. The dust or sludge is washed so that the mere earth flows away and the metallic part settles. For this, they use linens of thick thread, in which there is an unevenness between the weft and the warp—they call these "figured" <note>likely referring to a specific weave or texture used to trap heavy particles</note>. They spread these over a floor made of inclined boards; then, water is poured onto the sludge placed there, which washes and rinses away—or carries off with it—the lighter parts of the earth, while the metallic parts stick to the linens in the pores or the rough threads. From here, the linens are cleaned of the adhering metallic substance in waters where the metallic sludge remains; once collected in this way by boys and girls of eight or nine years old, or older, it is reserved for smelting. 

This is the method they use in **Germany** to extract **silver** mixed with stones and earth, which is considered the same for **gold** in this regard. **Lapis Lazuli** <note>a deep-blue metamorphic rock used as a semi-precious stone and pigment</note> endures heating, yet it is finally overcome by fire.

<margin>Gold hidden in garnets is scarcely separable.</margin>
In those **garnet** gems found in **Germany** not far from **Marienberg** <note>a mining town in Saxony</note>, they report that gold lies hidden imperceptibly, but because of their hardness, it cannot be drawn out from there. Furthermore, the gold is so meager and the price of the garnets so high that it is not worth the effort to destroy those little stones for that purpose.

<margin>Fine gold found in this way melts by itself and becomes pure.</margin>
**Fine gold**, which is found in pieces or grains, is recognized on its own and easily becomes workable and malleable through smelting, once certain foreign parts—vapors and other substances that were still imperceptibly clinging to it—have been separated.

<margin>Natural gold that has not felt the fire gives much great hope for gold-making.</margin>
Many hold high hopes for this gold which has never felt the fire, as if it still contains within itself a **gold-making and vegetative spirit** <note>original: *spiritum aurificum & vegetabilem*; a reference to the alchemical belief that metals "grow" in the earth like plants</note>, which is separated from common gold by the heat of fire and smelting; they believe this spirit ought to perform much—indeed, everything—in the [alchemical] work <term>aurificium</term> <note>the art of making gold</note>. In all things there is an innate spirit by which they are quickened and grow; whether this is so in gold, let the seekers of nature inquire...

Indeed, I have known the opposite experience in these matters: 

<margin>The gathering of gold dispersed through water.</margin>
Thirdly, when particles of gold are dispersed through the water or the silt of rivers, they are collected here or there in a large vat, and whatever gold is contained therein is drawn out using quicksilver <term>mercury</term>. A weight of several pounds of mercury is cast into this silt which has settled; then, like a magnet pulling iron, the mercury attracts the gold particles into its bosom. From this, the gold remains in a piece of soft leather <note>original: *aluta*; a supple leather or chamois used as a filter to squeeze out liquid mercury, leaving the solid gold amalgam behind</note> once the quicksilver is squeezed out, to be melted down by the proper application of fire. In this manner, in **Hungary**, **Slavonia**, and other places in **Germany** and **Bohemia**, certain men possessing knowledge of these things secretly station themselves at gold-bearing streams—or by paying a price to the owner of the land—and they gain or "hunt" enough gold in a day to allow them to live well. In **Slavonia**, says **Mathesius** <note>Johannes Mathesius (1504–1565), a German minister and author of *Sarepta*, a famous collection of sermons that used mining metaphors to explain theology</note>, even a peasant could earn one or more ducats <note>a high-purity gold coin used throughout Europe</note> daily by this route. The same occurred in the **Bohemian** mountains toward **Silesia**, and in **Bohemia** not far from the small town of **Eule** <note>original: *Eila*; Jílové u Prahy, a major historical gold-mining center near Prague</note>, where some years ago many emerged wealthy from this washing process.

<margin>Rodlevvius, a wealthy miner in Bohemia.</margin>
Here, **Rodlevvius** (also known as the "Red Lion" <note>Johannes Rotlöw, a prominent 14th-century citizen of Prague</note>), a man of the mining trade, acquired such great riches during the time of **Charles IV** <note>Holy Roman Emperor and King of Bohemia, r. 1346–1378</note> that he lent several hundred thousand ducats to the aforementioned King of Bohemia and later gave them as a gift. Having risen from a poor commoner to the wealthiest of men along with his wife, he reached such a point of madness that they are said to have blurted out that it was impossible for God to make them poor again. Truly, it happened otherwise.

<margin>Made most poor from being most wealthy.</margin>
For he himself is reported to have been shut in a prison and nearly died of hunger, and to have passed away most miserably in the deepest poverty, after all their goods had been confiscated.

<margin>Another story about a very wealthy peasant made very poor.</margin>
Something similar to this happened in **Prussia** <note>original: *Borussia*</note>, where a peasant living on the island of **Neringa** <note>The Curonian Spit, a long sand-dune spit in the Baltic Sea</note> collected so much money from the pasturing of livestock that he had eleven and a half tubs full (of the kind used in **Germany** for preserving butter or herring). Concerning this matter, when the **Master of the Order** <note>The Grand Master of the Teutonic Knights, who ruled Prussia at the time</note> spoke to foreign princes after a meal had concluded...

->...for the sake of amusement, they set out to visit this peasant.<- He appeared poor in his dress and diet (for he would not spend even a half-penny <note>original: *obolum*; a small coin of very little value</note> in the taverns, but always satisfied everyone with small cheeses). They demanded that he prepare a meal for them while they returned from the hunt. The peasant, sensing a trap <note>original: *insidias*; literally "ambush" or "snares"</note> was being set for his money, brought out all his barrels full of money into a spacious room and arranged them in order. Above them, he placed a long board to serve as a table and prepared a meal—sumptuous, as was his custom.

Then the **Master of the Order** <note>The Grand Master of the Teutonic Knights, a powerful crusading military order that ruled large territories in Prussia and the Baltics</note> returned with the foreign princes, reclined at the table, and satisfied himself with the prepared food. When the dinner was finished, he said to the peasant, "Hey you, I have been told that you are so rich that you have eleven barrels full of money, and even more?" 

The peasant replied cautiously, "**Lord**, I know that goods which are denied pass to the superior Lord <note>A reference to feudal law where hidden or unclaimed wealth could be legally seized by a sovereign; the peasant admits his wealth to avoid immediate confiscation</note>; hence I freely confess that I have that much money." 

"Where are they?" asked the **Teutonic Master**. 

"They are here before you," the peasant replied. When the table was removed, all the barrels were discovered and opened, and as much money as had been reported was found. 

Then the **Master, seeing** that a twelfth vessel was only half-filled, immediately sent for enough copper <note>original: *ære*; can refer to bronze, copper, or small change</note> to fill it, so that he might be able to say he had a peasant so wealthy that he possessed twelve full barrels of money. 

In truth, however, the money brought there had the nature of <term>tame pigeons</term> <note>original: *columbarum cicurum*; decoy birds used by hunters to lure wild flocks into a net</note>, which by their tameness circumvent and entice other pigeons, leading them back home with them where they are often captured and killed. 

For so it happened to this peasant; for that prince, who was called the **Teutonic Master**, first borrowed one or two barrels from the peasant, then more, until he had transferred all twelve of those barrels to himself. Nor could this be denied him without the risk of the peasant losing his head. Hence, this rich peasant was rendered so poor that he is said to have died of hunger in the dung—

...declared: These are divine judgments, which we observe are exercised at times either because of ingratitude or on account of other vices, most worthy of anyone's notice. **Fourth**, when gold is found generated in crumbly earth, at least washing is needed and a reduction into metallic mud, once the filth has been separated.

<margin>How gold is separated from poisonous fumes, which carry it away with them into the air.</margin>
**Fifth**, if it is mixed with poisonous substances, then by the ingenuity of the craftsmen, pieces of iron are thrown to that gold-devouring dragon; once the iron is devoured, the dragon releases the gold and allows it to be incorporated and reduced into a solid substance. This is indeed very similar to the labor of *Jason*, *Cadmus*, and *Hercules*; when the dragons were lulled to sleep, the first gained his wish for the ever-watchful golden fleece, the second for the fountain of Boeotia, and the third in the gardens of the Hesperides for the golden apples they were guarding. This poisonous Cadmia <note>original: *Cadmia*; a historical term for various metallic ores or furnace crusts, often containing zinc or arsenic</note> or arsenical fume can be likened to the dragon's poison; for it kills just as that does:

<margin>Arsenic is the dragon, and its smoke is the poison.</margin>
and therefore, like a dragon, it must be guarded against and removed from the midst by a suitable remedy. That this remedy is iron is known from actual use: for just as the sharp iron directed by the hands of the said heroes killed the dragon, so here the matter is accomplished with iron:

<margin>Why iron consumes metallic poison.</margin>
For iron has within itself a burning and very hot sulfur; when this is set on fire, that dragon is ensnared and killed. While those two are held by mutual connections, the gold is saved by flight or liquefaction, so that it is not forced, as before, to fly away together with the winged dragon <note>This refers to "volatilization," where the gold is lost as vapor along with the arsenic unless a "fixing" agent like iron is used</note>. There are also other means by which this offspring, or rather embryo, is preserved from miscarriage, lest it perish and return to nothing, just as various craftsmen have found various ways and devices:

<margin>More gold and silver is reserved in a very small test than in a large cupellation.</margin>
Where it should be noted, that more gold or silver is usually left behind from this kind from a very small test or cupel <note><term>cupella</term>: a small, porous bowl made of bone ash used by assayers to separate precious metals from impurities</note>, than in a large ash-furnace <note>original: *cineritio magno*; a large-scale version of the cupellation process</note>, namely because of the difference of the fires and the addition of (as they call them) metallic fluxes. For the fire in a small cupel is not so strong, therefore it does not despoil as much, and the flux is more precious and useful; therefore more will be preserved here than there. <margin>Method of preserving silver from volatility in Saxony.</margin>
To prevent this, in *Goslar, Saxony* and elsewhere, they work by means of **the raw layer** <note>original: *the rohe schicht*; a German metallurgical term for a specific smelting charge or process stage</note>; that is, during the smelting of metals filled with these poisonous spirits (such as copper, lead, and silver), a hole is made in the bottom of the furnace. From this, the molten material may be immediately saved and flow out to cool itself, so that nothing of the silver is lost, which is what usually happens otherwise.

<margin>Method of separating gold from imperfect metals, namely copper.</margin>
Sixth, gold mixed with imperfect metals is reduced in the same way as first mentioned—from earth and other foreign substances—namely through fire, grinding, washing, and similar operations, into a metallic mud <term>metallic mud: a concentrated sludge of ore particles ready for smelting</term> which is suitable for melting. In this context, copper is primarily understood, for iron, tin, and lead hardly ever hide any perceptible amount of gold. They say that *Mansfeld* copper often contained gold; this copper is extracted from fissile stone <note>original: *lapis scissilis*; likely copper-bearing shale or slate</note>, from which tables are made and the roofs of houses are covered.

<margin>Gold is regularly contained within silver.</margin>
In other cases, gold regularly remains within silver, as if in a mother's womb. Because of this, since that silver still has its mother with it and has not yet been emancipated from her, it is extracted in the same way as from imperfect metals, or treated until it becomes mud. For this silver may contain much copper or lead, or both together, yet it does not take its name from them—it is not called lead or copper ore—but rather silver ore. Even if those other metals far outweigh the silver in weight, since the silver excels them in value, the name is taken from the more precious part.

<margin>When lead ore may be called silver ore.</margin>
For example: a hundredweight <note>original: *centenarius*; a traditional unit of weight</note> of lead ore containing one or two ounces of silver is named for the prevailing lead; but if it contains 12, 16, or more ounces of silver, it is named for the silver. Thus, these seven types of gold ores having been reduced to a meltable mud that can be turned into metal, we shall add the method of melting, separating, and testing it:

...mixed with foreign matter. We shall therefore make a three-fold distinction of these mixtures: the first contains mostly gold and very little of another metal or substance; the second contains more additives; and the third contains even more. We say, then, that the first can return to pure gold by the melting of fire alone; the second not by fire alone, but by adding a metallic flux; and the third, by the addition of lead to that flux.

<margin>
Metallic flux: why it excels the metal and how it is made.
</margin>
For flux aids the melting process and makes it easy. Such a flux is made from equal parts saltpeter <note>original: *sal petræ*</note> and glass <note>original: *vitrido*</note>, burned with charcoal in a large vessel and afterward saved for use. One should take half a portion of this flux for every full portion of the metallic mud <term>metallic mud: the concentrated ore or 'slime' resulting from washing</term> that is to be melted. Then, in a fierce fire, lead performs the same role as mercury <note>original: *argenti vivi*</note> does outside the fire (which collects gold); it gathers all the metallic parts of the mud into itself.

<margin>
Saturn the father gathers all metals into himself.
</margin>
In this, lead acts as Saturn <note>In alchemy, Saturn is the symbolic name for lead</note>, the father of all metals. Thus, as the fire <note>original: *Vulcano*, referring to Vulcan, the god of fire</note> presses upon it, all the metallic material is forced out along with the lead into a button <term>button: a 'regulus', or the solid mass of metal found at the bottom of a crucible after smelting</term> at the bottom of the vessel, either by itself or with the flux alone. This button is still impure, for it has other metals mixed with the gold which must be separated.

<margin>
Separation is perfected in the final stage through cupellation.
</margin>
This separation must be carried out by cupellation <note>original: *cineritium*</note> in a large-scale operation, or by a cupel <note>original: *cupellam*</note> in a small-scale work. These differ from one another only in the "more and less"—that is, in the quantity of the material, not the quality of the method.

<margin>
Cupellation and the cupel differ according to greater and lesser scale.
</margin>
Geber <note>A famous 8th-century alchemist, often cited as an authority on metallurgy</note> treated cupellation at length, which anyone may see for themselves in his *Book of Examinations*, chapters 22 and 33. But we shall briefly explain what we ourselves have seen and done many times, as it is currently in use, along with the reasons for the said examination or separation by cupellation.

Ash is a porous body.

There are therefore pores in the ash which are filled with the water. The same must be said of bones burned into a friable powder. With these...

<margin>
From what and how the ash-bed is made.
</margin>
Having considered these things, the **Assayers** <term>Assayers: specialists who test the purity of metals</term> take wood ash and, after the salt has been separated from it through washing, they take the finest and most distinct portion. They mix this with a half-part of burnt bones that have been ground into an extremely fine powder, and then they dry it. To this dried mixture, they sprinkle drops of rich beer <note>original: *cerevisiae pinguis*; likely a thick, unrefined ale used as a sticky binding agent</note> until it is just damp enough that, when squeezed in the hand, it holds its shape. Then they press this into large or small earthenware vessels, which are unglazed and capable of enduring the fire. Taking a polished marble sphere, they roll it around the top to create a moderate cavity. However, they first sprinkle the surface with the finest powders of burnt calf-skulls or various fish bones, which have been ground for a long time on a stone (just like a painter's pigments). Finally, these ash-beds <note>original: *cineritia*; the porous floor or lining of the furnace</note> or vessels are dried.

<margin>
The ash-bed in the hearth or furnace.
</margin>
When a large ash-bed is prepared in a hearth or furnace, they do not prepare everything with as much labor as they do for the vessels and cupels. For the smaller the work, the greater the diligence required; thus, this small-scale method is more certain for conducting an assay <note>original: *probatione*; a test to determine the metal content</note>, whichever you prefer. Once the ash-beds are dried, they are put to use.

<margin>
How and from what cupels are made.
</margin>
The material for cupels <term>cupels: small, porous bowls used in assaying to absorb base metals</term> is the same, but the purification is different. These are shaped using a pestle and what they call a "monk" <note>original: *monacha*; a technical term for the tool used to stamp the hollow into the cupel</note>, made of polished brass <note>original: *latone*</note>.

<margin>
The assay-hundredweight is equal to one dram in common weight.
</margin>
In these properly prepared and dried vessels, the assay-hundredweight <term>assay-hundredweight: a miniature scale weight where a tiny amount represents a full hundred-pound load for testing purposes</term> is placed, part by part. The assay is conducted in a separation furnace with the fire lit from above, and the cupel covered by a curved, perforated tile. This continues until the "fixed grain"—the steady bead of gold and silver—flashes <note>original: *fulguret*; this refers to the 'blick,' the sudden brightening seen when the last of the lead oxide film disappears</note> and rests upon the surface of the cupel. While still glowing, it is removed along with the cupel and sprinkled with drops of water to extinguish it.

<margin>
Where the ash-bed of the vessels is made.
</margin>
The ash-bed in vessels is made in a different furnace, specifically a larger one. The hearth process occurs in one even larger still. For in the hearth, several hundredweights are processed at one time, whereas in the ash-bed, several pounds are used.

<margin>
What kind of fire is used for separating metal via the ash-bed.
</margin>
It is necessary that the fire be a flaming one, which is reflected <note>original: *reverberetur*; the heat is "reverberated" or bounced off the furnace roof</note> onto the molten metal so that it can be swirled and moved about. <margin>Quartation, or separation by strong water, is established to distinguish gold from silver.</margin> Let these things suffice concerning separation by the <term>ash-bed</term> <note>original: *cineritium*; the process of cupellation where base metals are oxidized and absorbed into a porous bed of ash, leaving only precious metals behind</note>. In the mass thus left on the surface, two perfect metals <note>gold and silver</note> remain mixed in greater or lesser proportions, which the color of the mass indicates. From here, one must proceed to perform <term>quartation</term>; which is the separation of silver from gold through the corrosion of <term>strong water</term> <note>original: *aqua fortis*; the historical name for nitric acid</note>. For silver, being a less compact and more porous body, is penetrated by that water and dissolved into a liquid consistency, while the gold remains at the bottom as a powder.

<margin>Why it is called Quartation.</margin> It is called *Quartation* because there must be at least three parts of silver to one part of gold if the acid is to work. If there is more gold and less silver, then it is necessary to add more fine silver until the silver exceeds the gold contained in the mass by that three-to-one proportion or greater. 

<margin>How quartation is performed.</margin> This operation is performed in a glass vessel placed in warm sand for a few hours. Once the solution is made, the blue-colored silver <note>silver nitrate solution appears blue-green when copper impurities are present or due to the concentration</note> is poured with the liquid into a thick stone vessel. At the bottom of this vessel, a copper plate is placed, and a little spring water is added; then the silver seeks the bottom and gathers on that plate, becoming a solid body once again. From here, it is washed several times and melted, and it is held to be fine silver. 

<margin>What fine silver is.</margin> Likewise, the yellow substance of gold which remained in the glass is washed and melted, and it is recognized as fine gold. 

<margin>What fine gold is.</margin> Truly, since some silver always remains with the gold—as if with its mother, from whom it cannot be sufficiently separated by the acid—there exists a bond of nature by which the more perfect metal is indivisibly bound with the less perfect. This is also the "door" through which one nature passes into another. Because of this, craftsmen have found two further ways to purify gold more thoroughly. They also use these methods if a small quantity of gold is to be separated from silver without a preceding quartation, such as a single ducat...

<margin>
What cementation is, why and how it is done.

...or several [methods], for gilding or the creation of gold leaf; and these are **Cementation** and **fusion by antimony**. 

**Cementation** is performed in various ways, but the most common is with powdered tiles <note>crushed bricks or ceramics</note> moistened with human urine. The gold is beaten into thin sheets and placed in an earthen vessel, with those powders layered above and below it. It is then heated in a fire for several hours. By this process, the silver is separated from the gold and "hides" itself within the brick powders, from which it can be recovered by another skillful method. If one cementation is not sufficient, a second or third is performed. Others add salts, iron dross <note>slag or waste from iron smelting</note>, and many similar things to the brick powders, but for a different purpose.

<margin>
What fusion through antimony is and how it is done.
</margin>
Fusion through antimony, like cementation, is a specific test for gold. Other tests include: not being dissolved by **strong water** <note>original: *aqua forti*; nitric acid</note>, not being changed or consumed by burning sulfur, and not being discolored by the breath or warm vapor of vinegar. However, the strongest and most exquisite of all tests is said to be that which is performed through antimony, in this manner:

<margin>
Many tests of gold.
</margin>
About six parts of <term>antimony</term> <note>specifically stibnite, the sulfide mineral of antimony used to scavenge impurities from gold</note> are placed in a crucible—a strong, unglazed vessel that can endure the fire, narrow at the base and wider at the top. These are melted, and then one part of gold is cast into the liquid. Once melted, the vessel is removed from the fire and tapped firmly on the surface where it stands, so that the heavy gold may seek the bottom. 

<margin>
How fusion through antimony is done.
</margin>
When the vessel has cooled, it is broken open. At the bottom (or the "apex") of the antimony, a **golden regulus** <note>original: *regulus aureus*; a "regulus" is the metallic button or lump found at the bottom of a crucible after smelting</note> is found. It will be white in color. This is then placed in an open vessel and subjected to the fire or the flame of bellows to be purged of the antimony. The result is the purest, reddest gold, perfect in all its measures.

<margin>
Common works of purging gold are worth the Chemist's knowing.
</margin>
Truly, the types of separation, examination, and purification of gold mentioned so far are also known to common metalworkers, smelters, and goldsmiths. They comprise a great part of their labor. Nevertheless, it does not seem foreign to the purpose of philosophers and seekers of <term>Chemistry</term> <note>original: *Chemiæ*; here referring to the high art of alchemy</note>—indeed, it is most necessary—that these things be understood by them, if not through manual practice, then certainly through intellectual consideration. For this reason, we have inserted these matters here as if in passing, so that through these...

...looking toward the greater works of authors of this kind—namely **Ercker**, **Fachs**, <note>Lazarus Ercker and Modestin Fachs were renowned 16th-century experts on mining and assaying.</note> and others—readers should be encouraged to study them, and if possible, to drink in the experience itself through sight and manual practice. However, lest we linger on these common practices without meditating on their causes, we, as philosophers, shall weigh and examine these principles. Of these, the common class of craftsmen understands little or nothing, since they perform their tasks merely according to use and custom, as they have learned from others.

<margin>What the causes are for the separation of metals from one another through incineration.</margin>

Thus, the separation through <term>cupellation</term> <note>original: *cineritium* or *cupella*; a refining process where ores are heated in a shallow porous cup to separate noble metals from base metals</note> occurs for five reasons: 

<margin>Separation through cupellation occurs for five reasons.</margin>

First, because **heat is a gatherer of like things and a scatterer of unlike things.** <note>A classic Aristotelian principle often cited in alchemy: *calor est congregator homogeneorum et dissipator heterogeneorum*.</note> Hence, heat gathers the pure substance of <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: *argenti vivi*; mercury, viewed here as the "spirit" or "seed" of the metal</note> which is found in gold and silver, but separates the impure and heterogeneous substance found in other metals by reason of their great abundance of combustible and earthy sulfur. 

<margin>1. Heat gathers like things.</margin>

This heat operates in the same way within the bowels of the earth in imperfect minerals: namely, by ripening the immature over a long period, coagulating the liquid quicksilver, and segregating from it the combustible and burning sulfur. From this sulfur, a certain "sulfurous idea" <note>In this context, an "idea" is a formal property or essential character imprinted on the material.</note>—that is, a hot and dry quality—is imprinted upon the quicksilver. 

<margin>A sulfurous idea is imprinted on the quicksilver by combustible sulfur.</margin>

When this happens, some small particle of the quicksilver expires, abandoning its habitation where it was merely a guest and not the master. 

Second, this same heat coming from above—since it is far greater than at the bottom, where the fire cannot reach—repels and beats back from itself that which it has separated as "unlike" from the "like." 

<margin>2. Heat repels the unlike from itself.</margin>

Thus, a double cause of ordered heat concurring in this way renders the separation of one from the other easier—separating the imperfect from the perfect. 

Now, the reason why the imperfect flees and the perfect remains is twofold: One is the **combustible and heterogeneous sulfur**, as mentioned. The other is because the imperfect is **immature** and less accustomed to the heat of the fire. 

<margin>3. 4.</margin>

Hence, it flees the fire as its opposite by a natural instinct, just as we see all watery and moist and cold things do...

...and cold, such as the <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: *argentum vivum*; in alchemy, this refers to the "mercury" or "spirit" within a metal rather than just the liquid element.</note> of imperfect things: Let there be, for example, two perfect metals, gold and silver, and just as many imperfect ones, copper and lead, in the <term>cupel</term> <note>original: *cineritio*; a porous vessel made of bone ash used in the process of cupellation to separate precious metals from base metals.</note>;

<margin>The quantity of lead in the assay.</margin>
it is therefore necessary that the quantity of lead be three times greater than all the others; namely, if there is one part of gold, one of silver, and one of copper, then nine ounces of lead, or a little more, must be added. Otherwise, the copper will not be entirely separated from the perfect metals. In this proportion, the melting of all these becomes easy. From these, the first which attempts to depart into the bottom of the cupel due to the intensity of the fire is the lead, being watery and very quick to melt;

<margin>Lead as the charioteer of copper in the assay.</margin>
This lead carries away with it something of its own relative—by reason of the earthy and foul sulfur and the mercury not yet mature in the copper—and like a *charioteer*, leads it down to the bottom of the cupel, and continues to do so until it has carried it all away; but it leaves behind the silver and gold, with which it has nothing in common:

<margin>5.</margin>
Fifth, the cupel, formed in that manner described above, is suited to receive the imperfect metals when they are afflicted and tortured by the fire, lest these be burned into ashes, on account of its porosity; yet this porosity is not so great that, by reason of weight (which is greater in gold than the others), the perfect metals would descend or be absorbed:

<margin>Perfect metals do not feel the force of fire.</margin>
For these do not feel the violence of the fire; therefore, they do not seek to flee, but because they were born and balanced in heat, they rejoice in it. Furthermore, their viscosity is so great that they are not easily separated from one another into parts that would descend:

<margin>The cupel is a hospital for sick metals. The cupel is the Field of Mars for the perfect metals.</margin>
The cupel is therefore a *sanctuary* or a *hospital* for sick metals, not healthy ones, if we consider its inner base and capacity; but if we consider its upper surface, it is like a *Field of Mars* <note>original: *campus Martius*; a reference to the Roman training grounds, suggesting a place of trial and athletic contest.</note> or a *gymnasium* in which the perfect athletes are tested, and the imperfect ones are distinguished from them and driven away.

<margin>Silver is more porous than gold.</margin>
...for the reason that <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>literally "strong water," now known as nitric acid</note> made from salts, such as <term>saltpeter</term> <note>potassium nitrate</note> and <term>vitriol</term> <note>sulfate minerals used to create acids</note>, or others, is of a most penetrating power, so that it seeps into the innermost pores of any metal. Furthermore, it possesses a corroding and fiery sharpness. For this reason, when external heat is applied, it acts upon silver, which is of a more porous body than gold, and it corrodes it and transforms it into a meltable liquid so that it appears like water. There is in vitriol not only an opening force, but also an astringent one: by which it is held back from sinking into the water by its own weight, and thus remains with the gold.

<margin>Why gold is not dissolved by aqua fortis.</margin>
This [gold], being the heaviest, very compact, and solid without pores, does not admit this astringent water into itself on account of the vitriol or alum, but excludes it entirely; wherefore it remains whole, as it is separated from the silver, namely in very thin particles.

<margin>What aqua regia is, how it is made, and why it dissolves gold.</margin>
But if you indeed make the so-called <term>Aqua Regia</term> <note>literally "Royal Water," a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids capable of dissolving gold</note> from aqua fortis by adding one ounce of <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>ammonium chloride</note> to a pound of it, then there is a greater penetration from this salt, and the astringent force of the vitriol is blunted; thus gold is similarly corroded and reduced into water. The recovery of the silver occurs when common water is poured in, because the strength and power of the strong liquid is weakened, and hence it releases the silver; just as through re-distillation, once the common water is separated, the aqua fortis becomes effective again as before.

<margin>Why copper makes silver descend.</margin>
The recovery by copper occurs because of an affinity of natures: for on account of the sulfur existing in the copper, the already weakened water descends to it; and on account of the <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: *argentum vivum*; referring to the alchemical "mercury" or spirit of the metal</note> of the copper, the silver [descends]. For it is clear from sight and experience that there are many dregs of aqua fortis in the silver, which must be separated through melting.

<margin>What is the cause of cementation.</margin>
The cause of <term>cementation</term> <note>a dry refining process where gold is heated with salts to remove silver impurities</note> is almost the same, but in this process, corrosion does not occur. However, the compaction of the gold and its greater habituation to heat cause the gold to remain; and the rarity of the substance and the lesser maturity of the silver cause it to depart. *Geber* <note>an influential 8th/9th-century alchemist</note> in his *Book of Investigations*, chapter 34, gives this reason where he says: *We have said, however, that some bodies [are affected] more, but others truly less, by*

## The Adversary, now prepared for battle, has brought forward this Argument.

### *31. The Adversary’s negative argument against Chemistry and Melchior of Sibiu, the Hungarian.*

<margin>Negative Argument 31.</margin>
If every perfection, and the introduction of a "form" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "form" is the essential nature that makes a thing what it is (e.g., the "form" of gold makes it gold).</note>, occurs in an instant, then the operation and preparation of Chemistry <note>original: "Chemiæ." In this period, the term refers to the art of alchemy.</note>, which does not occur in an instant, is useless, and the art itself is vain.

->But the first premise is true,<-
->Therefore, so is the second.<-

*The proposition is evident: Because it is the form that gives being to a thing. Moreover, the essence of a thing does not accept "more" or "less" <note>original: "magis nec minus." This is a standard Scholastic principle: you cannot be "more" or "less" of a specific species. A thing either possesses the essence of gold or it does not.</note>, but in a moment it becomes that which it was not before, as is clear in the study of physics. Otherwise, either two forms would exist at the same time and all at once in a single piece of matter, or forms would undergo expansion and contraction, which is not permitted. For an infant of one hour is no less a human being than a man of fifty years, as far as the "form" of a human is concerned. In this same way, the Chemist <note>The Alchemist.</note> does not introduce a form to metals, but merely prepares them over a long period of time.*

### *The Response of Melchior of Sibiu to the 31st negative Argument.*

<margin>Response to the 31st negative Argument.</margin>
**I**t is true that the introduction of a form occurs in a moment, and also that the operation and preparation of Chemistry does not occur in an instan— <note>The text cuts off here due to the page break; the catchword "instan-" indicates the sentence continues on the next page with "instanti," meaning "instantaneously."</note>

<summary>This page presents a philosophical challenge to alchemy, arguing that because nature creates the "essence" of a thing instantly, the long, labored processes of alchemists cannot be responsible for creating true gold.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the rebuttal to the 31st argument posed by the "Adversary" on the previous page. instant; and therefore it does not follow that the art is vain: For the introduction of a form and the preparation for it differ, both according to nature and according to art. For example, a cabinet-maker <term>Scriniarius: a joiner or furniture maker</term> who makes a table: while he polishes the planks, he has not yet imposed the form of the table; when he joins the planks with glue, not yet; nor even when he has added the legs; but then, the perfect form is imposed. The same must be said of a house: while the foundations are being laid, while the walls are being raised, it does not yet have the form of a house; when the roof is being made, the form is not yet present; but when it is finished, it is a perfect house. 

Thus, according to nature, a human being does not yet exist while the seeds <note>original: "femina," likely a typesetting error for "semina" (seeds/semen)</note> of the male and female are held separately, nor even when they are joined. And so the embryo <term>embryo</term> grows in the womb by a vegetative soul <term>anima vegetatiua: the basic life force shared with plants</term> and a sensitive soul <term>anima sensitiua: the soul shared with animals, involving perception</term>, until it pleases the Creator to instill the rational soul <term>anima rationale: the uniquely human soul</term> into it in a single moment; in that moment, it becomes a human being. 

Let these things be transferred to the work which is both natural and artificial at once, namely the Chemical art <term>Chymicum: Alchemy</term>. In this, the preparation takes place until the perfect form of gold <term>forma auri</term> is ready to be sent into its matter. When, however, it is now introduced through projection <note>The final stage of the alchemical Great Work where the "Philosopher's Stone" is cast onto base metal to transform it</note>, in that moment the generation of gold occurs through the stripping away of combustible sulfur <term>sulfuris combustibilis: in alchemical theory, the impurity that causes metals to be "base" or "imperfect"</term> from the matter of quicksilver <term>argenti viui: mercury</term> within the imperfect metals. Therefore, that argument concludes nothing against Chemistry, but rather is on its side.

<margin>Geber's sharp response to the 31st negative argument.</margin>

> *Geber <note>An influential 8th-century Arabic alchemist (Jabir ibn Hayyan), whose Latinized writings were foundational to European alchemy</note> responds quite sharply to those reasoning in this way: "Even if they say that perfection is given in an instant, and our preparation does not happen in an instant, and they conclude from this: 'It will not be perfected by art; therefore, the art is nothing'—we say their heads are foolish and empty of human reason, and they are more like beasts than men. For they conclude from premises that have no relation to the conclusion drawn. This argument holds as much weight as: 'The donkey runs, therefore you are a goat.' This is because even if the preparation does not happen in an instant, it does not prevent the form or perfection from being given to the prepared material in an instant. For the preparation is not the perfection, but the making-ready to receive the form."*

## 32. A Negative Argument against Alchemy.

<margin>Negative Argument 32.</margin>

> **If the alchemical art cannot destroy gold, it will be much less able to construct it.**
> **But it cannot do the first <note>meaning: it cannot destroy gold</note>.**
> **Therefore, it cannot do the second <note>meaning: it cannot create gold</note>.**

*The reason for this proposition is clear:* For everything is more easily destroyed than it is constructed, as is evident in houses, which we can destroy in a single day and yet scarcely build in a hundred. Thus, all things which nature has made, nature itself again corrupts and destroys—except for gold, which is brought by nature to such a great firmness and connection of all **four elements** <term>the four elements: earth, air, fire, and water, which the ancients believed composed all matter</term> that it remains as it is without any breaking down of those elements.

---

### Response to the 32nd Negative Argument.

<margin>Response to the 32nd Negative Argument.</margin>

## 33. A Negative Argument of the Adversary against Alchemy.

## Response to the 33rd Negative Argument.

<margin>Response to the 33rd Negative Argument</margin>
All philosophers affirm that **T**inctures <term>tinctures: in alchemy, these are powerful elixirs or substances capable of "staining" or transforming base metals into gold</term> exist in nature and are made by nature: *Raymond <note>Raymond Lully (c. 1232–1315), a major figure in medieval logic and alchemy</note>, as cited in the Rosary <note>referring to the "Rosarium Philosophorum," a famous 16th-century alchemical compendium</note>, says: "Although this stone contains the Tincture naturally; for it was created perfectly in the body of magnesia <term>magnesia: here referring to a primary mineral substance or "the mother" of the stone, not the modern chemical element</term>, yet it does not possess movement by itself unless it is perfected by art and operation."* The philosophers say that the potential for the tincture, or sulfur, exists in nature, but it is spoken of to no one except those to whom it is revealed by God: *Thus Alphidius <note>an Arabic alchemist often cited in medieval Latin texts</note>, as witnessed by the Rosary, says: "Know that God did not set a great price for the purchase of this stone, which is the subject of this secret; for it is found cast out in the way, so that it may be held by the poor as well as the rich, in order that everyone might easily reach it through reason and knowledge."* Furthermore, there are many things which nature began but did not lead to the end, as is clear in those who naturally lack certain limbs because of a defect of heat or matter; even if these are not among the ordinary works of nature, they are nonetheless her works just as much as the others, which she would have produced as finished things had she not been hindered. In the same way, that matter which is so hidden by the philosophers has the potential to become a tincture and is called the gold of the philosophers, but it suffers from a lack of heat and mixing with its own kind: It was enough, therefore, that nature introduced the first virtue and power into it, even if she did not perfect it.

### 33. An Affirmative Argument for the Truth of Chemistry.
<note>In this context, "Chemistry" refers to the art of alchemy.</note>

<margin>Argument 33: Affirmative for Chemistry</margin>
->By the same means that gold can be destroyed,<-
->it is presumed it can also be constructed.<-
->But gold is destroyed by Chemists alone.<-
->Therefore, it is constructed by the same.<-

**T**he major premise of this syllogism is the common opinion of the philosophers, and the opinion of the common people agrees with it. Thus the *Rosary* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous 16th-century alchemical florilegium or collection of authorities</note>, citing other authors such as Johannes de Aquino <note>A 14th-century alchemist, not to be confused with the theologian Thomas Aquinas, though works were often falsely attributed to the latter</note>, states: *He who is ignorant of the destruction of gold, must necessarily be ignorant of its construction according to the course of nature. Thus, it is easier to construct gold than to destroy it.* And a little later: *The Philosopher says: He who knows how to destroy gold so that it is gold no longer, has arrived at the greatest secret.* Another philosopher says: *It is difficult for gold to be destroyed, and most difficult for it to be constructed; it is easier to destroy what is accidental than what is essential.* For everyone believes that whoever is able to "open" <note>In alchemy, "opening" a metal means breaking it down into its primary matter or "mercury"</note> that most tight and solid compound of nature—gold—is likewise able to join its parts together. Although philosophers say that nothing is composed simply from its own destruction, there are otherwise two species of method: one is called **Analytical**, and the other **Synthetic**. The **Analytical** begins from what is later in nature and proceeds toward what is prior in nature; the **Synthetic** does the opposite. In this way, the road from Rome to Naples is the same as the road from Naples to Rome. Whence many think that from the resolution <note>The process of breaking a substance down into its component parts</note> of gold...

<summary>Maier argues that because alchemists (chemists) are the only ones capable of "opening" or dissolving gold into its primary components, they are logically the only ones capable of creating it. He uses the philosophical methods of Analysis and Synthesis to explain that the path to creating gold is simply the reverse of the path used to decompose it.</summary>

<margin>Democritus and Heracletus indulged in different emotions. <note>In the Renaissance, these two Greek philosophers were often paired: Democritus laughed at the absurdity of human life, while Heracletus wept for its misery.</note></margin>
When I had already spent the better part of my life in the study of the humanities <term>literarum humaniorum</term> <note>The study of classical languages, literature, and rhetoric.</note> and the liberal arts, and in conversations with all manner of learned men who seemed to possess some wisdom beyond the common crowd, so that I seemed to myself to have acquired a firmer judgment—partly through constant reading and partly through the actual experience of things—I began to consider more acutely the various actions of men. I saw that these actions were for the most part directed toward the pomp and lust for dominating others and being preferred in honors, or toward the promotion of gluttony and bodily luxury, or other such enormous vices. I saw that most men were preoccupied with accumulating riches alone, by hook or by crook <note>original: "per fas & nefas," meaning through divine or human law, or regardless of right and wrong.</note>, setting aside all respect for conscience and zeal for piety or virtue. # SYMBOLS

<margin>All is vanity of vanities.</margin>
...to that same cause I should subscribe, or whether I should instead pronounce with the Preacher, *All is vanity of vanities.* <note>original: "Omnia vanitates vanitatum," a reference to Ecclesiastes 1:2.</note> But after weighing each thing, I finally returned to myself. <margin>Nothing is better than the investigation of hidden things.</margin>
This investigation may be undertaken in whatever way: whether at home through books left by others, with meditation leading the way and manual experience following as a servant, or abroad by leafing through that *great book of the World.* <note>The "Book of Nature" or "Book of the World" was a common Renaissance metaphor suggesting that God's wisdom could be read in the physical creation just as in the Bible.</note> I abstained from none of these ways of seeking knowledge; but by indulging now in one, now in another, the more I drank, the more—*like Tantalus*—I thirsted. <note>In Greek mythology, Tantalus was punished with eternal hunger and thirst, with water and fruit always receding just as he tried to reach them.</note>
<margin>The Phoenix bird has always been most celebrated in the writings of the wise.</margin>

<margin>A remedy for Anger and Grief.</margin>

Therefore, to track down this bird, wherever it might lie hidden, I was seized by a certain impulse of my nature and mind, and as if willing, I was compelled. It was not because I hoped to gain possession of this bird whole (for I foresaw that would be impossible for me), but at least that I might obtain even a small feather of it, through whatever labor, expense, and travel.

<margin>Diodorus Siculus makes mention of this medicine.</margin>
...although I had perceived mention of it being made by several most trustworthy men, I nevertheless thought it—with a certain perverse obstinacy of mind—to be either counterfeit or entirely legendary, just as such things brought forth by the ancients or from distant lands, which lie outside the common order of nature or custom, are often seen to be. For who, I said, ever professed a <term>cure for anger</term> <note>original: "medela irae." Maier is debating if a physical alchemical substance can treat an emotional or "spiritual" state like rage.</note> except in words alone, and not by natural remedies? Who does not know how to remove pain with soothing <term>Narcotics</term>, <term>Opiates</term>, and <term>Laudana</term> <note>Laudanum was a tincture of opium, famously promoted by Paracelsus as a "pain-killer."</note>, unless they are poorly experienced in medicine? To these points, we read in the commentaries of the ancients 
<margin>Moral aid against anger.</margin>
how a certain philosopher <note>This refers to Athenodorus Cananites, who advised the Emperor Augustus to recite the alphabet before acting on anger.</note> attempted to correct the headlong anger of **Augustus Caesar**, namely, that he should do nothing while hindered by anger until he had silently run through the twenty-four elements of the letters <note>The 24 letters of the Latin alphabet.</note> within himself. <margin>Francis Petrarch, *On Remedies for Both Good and Bad Fortune*.</margin>
promising remedies for both grief of the soul and for anger. <margin>That remedies for anger are useful.</margin>
even the Theologian prescribes precepts for moderating anger if the temperament of the body rebels—being, for instance, hot and dry, and boiling with <term>bilious</term> and parched humors. ## SYMBOLS

<margin>Anger arises from an abundant hot humor.</margin>
Therefore, in such cases, let the physician temper or purge the immoderate humors, and the madness of anger will cease, no differently than how all combustion ceases when fire is extinguished by water. Whence that leader of physicians, *Galen*, left it attested—not inelegantly—in a particular book: *That the characters of the soul follow the temperament of the body.* <note>original: "Quod mores animi sequantur temperamentum corporis." <margin>The mind suffers from the body.</margin>

<margin>Things that produce a good intellect.</margin>
*Therefore, the things that produce a good intellect are those that produce good digestion and strengthen the brain and the principal members, purging superfluities, preventing vapors from ascending, clarifying the blood, and those things which regard the head and brain and have a property [conducive] to the goodness of the intellect: Furthermore, once the things said above are understood, you will find all these things, from which you may make for yourself a table for every operation, if you wish: And according to this, you will find many authors saying of their recipes that they produce a good intellect, because they broadly prevent superfluities from multiplying, or they repress vapors, or they strengthen the brain generally; rectifying...*

# SYMBOLS

<margin>The doctor made a spendthrift out of a miser</margin>
*One is gladdened and made good by another, but by yet another, one was corrupted. Thus, the doctor makes a spendthrift out of a miser, a lecher out of a chaste man, a bold man out of a fearful one; and generally, just as he changes the <term>complexion</term> <note>original: "complexionem"; in medieval medicine, this refers to the specific balance of the four bodily fluids (humors) that determines a person's temperament.</note> of the blood, it is necessary to change the resulting inclinations and dispositions of that person.*

<margin>What the ultimate secrets of medicine are.</margin>
*And these are the ultimate secrets of the art of medicine itself. Sometimes, however, medicine only achieves these things as a major consequence. When the foolish read in the books of the wise and elder physicians—who knew these were already the secrets of medicine—and see them creating good intellect, or making a person faithful and fortunate, they mock them loudly. Having mocked, they are distanced far from the secrets of medicine; they do not wish to hear, nor do they believe, that such things belong to medicine. They believe medicine is only for curing a headache, an <term>abscess</term>, <note>original: "apostema"; a swelling or internal collection of pus.</note> or a fever. They themselves ought to cure their own dullness of intellect until they can understand these things. Because of such people who disparage the discoverers of secrets, you have heard what Hippocrates commanded the physicians he taught:*

<margin>Those who mock the secrets are distanced from them.</margin>
<margin>Secrets must not be revealed.</margin>

<margin>A remedy for anger not sought out seems useless</margin>
If anyone expects such a **Remedy**, it seems entirely useless and superfluous: To this it can be responded; it is sufficient that the medicine exists in nature to temper personal <term>passions</term> <note>original: "affectus"; in this context, it refers to powerful emotions or states of mind that influence behavior.</note>, even if it is not recognized or valued by others: For this detracts nothing from its utility or necessity: For even if it is not held in high regard at this time, nevertheless in some other place, just as it was once before, it can afterwards be held in greater esteem.

<margin>The vicissitude of all things.</margin>
In the same way, in his own time, the aforementioned *Galen* <note>Claudius Galenus (c. 129–216 AD), the influential Roman physician. Maier is pointing out how historical reputations change over time.</note> declared the *Germans* to be alienated from all medicine; as they were a fiercer people, he was not going to publish the precepts of Medicine for them. Now, however, those same people both embrace and cultivate medicine, while the Greeks, on the contrary, have been reduced again to a kind of barbarism and are greatly removed from almost all literature of <term>humanity</term> <note>original: "humanitatis literatura"; refers to the liberal arts and classical learning.</note> under the *Turkish yoke* <note>A reference to the Ottoman Empire's control over Greece during Maier's life in the early 17th century.</note>. <margin>Innumerable evils from anger.</margin>
Hence, the Medicine which takes away or averts that anger is of immense utility.

<margin>Pain is the sharpest of symptoms.</margin>
What has been said concerning anger ought also to be understood concerning pain: For just as anger seems to be the most evident and immense of the passions of the soul, so pain is the most sensible and significant of the symptoms of the body—so much so that a Physician must not infrequently, by some inevitable necessity, turn his care toward it even before the disease has been conquered or the cause expelled.

# SYMBOLS

...and may cast out anger from the soul. This, I say, is the **Medicine**, which far surpasses gold, provided only that the **Phoenix** <note>In alchemy, the Phoenix is a common symbol for the Philosopher's Stone or the Universal Medicine, representing rebirth and perfection through fire.</note>, from which it is sought, can be found. Where shall I seek it? Where shall I investigate? Whom shall I ask? He who knows will scarcely reveal it; he who knows not will be unable to tell of it. Meanwhile, the die must be cast and the way attempted; for those who sit idle at home learn almost nothing of secrets, while fortune favors the bold.

<margin>Medicine must be tracked down through travel.</margin>
Hence, I have resolved with the most certain determination of mind to leave my homeland, which is dear to me, and set out for foreign lands, so that I might either consume my life in travel or finally bring home with me that longed-for medicine with joy.

<margin>Objection against traveling.</margin>
It is difficult, I confess, to change soil and sky; to migrate from the known to the unknown, from neighbors to barbarians, from kinsmen to the **Antipodes** <note>original: "Antipodas"; literally those on the opposite side of the earth, used here to mean the most distant and alien peoples.</note>, for the sake of a doubtful hope for a pre-conceived medicine. Many will say that whether such a thing even exists in the nature of things is a matter still before the judge <note>original: "sub iudice lis est"; a legal metaphor meaning the case is undecided or still under debate.</note>. But I have nothing to respond to these people, except what **Tullius** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman orator.</note> once said to his friend **Trebatius** <note>Gaius Trebatius Testa, a Roman jurist and friend of Cicero.</note> while he was living outside Rome: *Many have managed their own affairs and those of the state well while far from their fatherland.* Every beginning is difficult; and he who has never been saddened will not rejoice, and he who has never wandered will not be led back to the true path.

<margin>*The Rose Garden of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Rosar. phil."; refers to the *Rosarium philosophorum*, one of the most famous illustrated alchemical treatises, first printed in 1550.</note></margin>
For as the **Chemists** <note>original: "Chymici"; refers to the alchemists.</note> say, there is in **Chemistry** <note>original: "Chemia"; here used interchangeably with Alchemy.</note> a certain noble body which is moved from master to master, in the beginning of which is misery with **vinegar** <note>In alchemical processing, "vinegar" often refers to a caustic acid used for dissolution or a state of initial suffering and purification.</note>, but in the end joy with gladness. I have likewise presupposed that this would happen to me: that I would first taste, endure, and experience many harsh, bitter, sad, and tedious things, but would eventually see everything become more joyful and easy.

<margin>There is no doubt that the Phoenix exists.</margin>
Regarding that **Medicine**, or the **Phoenix**, I have not doubted whether it exists; for if I had doubted, how would I have sought it? If I had not sought it, how could I have had hope of finding it? Let it suffice for me to have seen the shadow of the sun or its rays, even if I have not touched the sun itself with my fingers. Perhaps it would be useless for us, hedged about by this earthly dross, to be joined and immediately...

<margin>*Majestic.*</margin>

Let me look at the heaven itself, and its great traveler, the **Sun**, how he rejoices in continuous motion <margin>*The Sun, the great traveler of heaven, rejoices in motion.*</margin> and illustrates, illuminates, warms, and governs all creatures of the sun and the pole. Indeed, I shall direct my mind to the very center of my chest, to the **heart** itself: <margin>*The human heart continues life by motion.*</margin> how it is driven by this perpetual motion as long as life remains. For just as motion measures life while it is unharmed, so life ends when motion is taken away, damaged, or hindered. It is therefore natural <margin>*It is natural for man to travel.*</margin> for man to move from place to place, from region to region, while he looks within himself, above himself, and around himself. But since every movement is made toward a goal—especially that of sensible and rational beings, directed by appetite or will from the imagination or intellect toward a certain end—hence, for the sake of his profit, through sea and through lands, the merchant runs to the Indies, fleeing poverty; and others...

<margin>One must travel for the rewards of the mind.</margin>

<margin>The delight of travel.</margin>
For he who has grown old at his own home will also bury his wisdom at home, and will recognize nothing of those things which are in the world, nor will he be recognized by others—unless he becomes a child twice over <note>original: "bis puer"; an allusion to the proverb that "old men are twice children," suggesting that those who never leave home remain intellectually immature or become senile without experience.</note>. <margin>The honor of travel.</margin>
*What is more honorable* than to have outrun the celestial Sun in its daily course—that is, by surveying the whole globe from the east to the west and then returning to one's homeland once the circle is completed—to have anticipated its usual journey or shown oneself as its companion?

<margin>A day is missing or abounds for those circumnavigating the globe.</margin>
For a day is missing for all who circumnavigate the earthly globe from east to west, while from west to east, a day is superfluous <note>Maier is describing the phenomenon of the International Date Line; when sailing around the world, one "gains" or "loses" a day relative to those who stayed behind.</note>; the cause of which was obscure at first, but is now sufficiently known. Indeed, the closer something approaches a spiritual essence, being purged and purified <note>original: "defœcatum"; literally "strained of dregs," a term from alchemy and chemistry meaning to be refined or cleared of impurities.</note> from earthly weight, the faster and more capable it becomes in its movement.

<margin>The more spiritual, the more mobile.</margin>
The idle Earth rests, and rightly so, because it is the immovable center of the world. But the water moves, and the whole Ocean flows and ebbs, and that four times in the space of twenty-four hours; thus the springs and rivers, like the parents of that great offspring, move in a fixed order, and by running they bring their "sweet delights," as it were, to the Ocean to temper the salt sea <note>original: "salum"; the open sea.</note>.

<margin>The three elements are in motion. 117.</margin>

Our Fire passes away in continuous motion, so that it cannot be retained unless it is always generated anew from flammable materials. <margin>The rush of the heavens is incomprehensible to the imagination.</margin>
An iron ball fired from a cannon by the force of gunpowder <note>original: "pulueris Pyrij"; literally "pyric powder," an early term for gunpowder</note>, if it were to circle the entire earth while maintaining that same constant speed, would perhaps require eight full days before it completed its 5,400 German miles <note>The "German mile" was much longer than the English mile, approximately 7.5 kilometers. Indeed, it perhaps does so in a quarter of an hour—a speed which no man can measure in his thought, not to mention the higher heaven of Saturn or the *Primum Mobile* <term>Primum Mobile (the "First Moved"): In the old geocentric model of the universe, this was the outermost sphere that moved all the inner heavens.</term>, which are placed far higher than the sun.

<margin>Human thoughts are the swiftest.</margin>
What is swifter than human thoughts? Nothing in human affairs. Yet it is said that intellectual substances <note>Referring to angels or pure spirits.</note> are equal to these thoughts in speed, and move in the "Now" itself, or in an instant.

<margin>Angels are said to move in the "Now."</margin>
Inasmuch as they are indivisible, they move in an indivisible point, not in time <note>In scholastic philosophy, spiritual beings like angels were thought to move instantaneously from one place to another because they were not bound by physical mass.</note>.

<margin>God does not move, because He is everywhere.</margin>
*God* truly, who is free of all motion, is everywhere; nor does He need to move to where He already is. Therefore, since it is impossible for a man to be in many places at the same time and at once (which is the property of God alone), it is closest to divinity to be present in those various places at different times, as far as it is permitted. Therefore, let it not be tedious to me, but rather most pleasant; not dishonorable, but in many ways most honorable; not useless, but joined with the highest utility, to have traveled through many regions of this world—

<margin>Why one must travel.</margin>
not so that I may see rocks and forests among foreigners, but so that I may search for the *Phoenician Medicine* <term>Phoenician Medicine: A pun on the "Medicine of the Phoenix," a common alchemical metaphor for the Philosopher's Stone, which was said to grant rebirth and health.</term> in the world by consulting the wisest men and conferring with them about things which the ignorant common people do not so much admire as they despise.

<margin>What the intention and order of the journey should be.</margin>
And so I prepared myself for a long journey, having prepared all things which seem necessary, which need not be listed here. First, I decided to travel through the kingdoms and borders of *Europe*, then if there be need, to cross into *America*, then into *Asia*, and finally into *Africa*; for I deliberated within myself that I might find that medicinal bird in some part of these vast regions of the earth's globe...

<margin>*Why Europe is called a virgin.*</margin>

This is that land which I venerate; this is that mother who is always recognized as a virgin. She is the most ingenious nurse of peoples, who has supplied many gifts discovered by her own most subtle craftsmanship.

<margin>*Germany, the fat belly of Europe.*</margin>

In *Europe* there are various miraculous talents, which this is not the place to recount, except insofar as they agree with the element of Earth which we are discussing.

<margin>*The wonders of Europe.*</margin>
In certain places in *Pannonia* <note>A Roman province covering parts of modern-day Hungary, Austria, and the Balkans.</note>, they write that men live under the water, because tufa stones <note>Porous rock formed by the precipitation of water.</note> have hardened and grown together from the water. In the *Carolingian* mountains <note>likely referring to Karlovy Vary (Carlsbad), famous for its hot springs and mineral deposits.</note>, boiling waters similarly turn to stone. 

<margin>*The walls of Madrutius.*</margin>
Elsewhere, they assert that living mortals dwell within fire, if indeed flints contain actual fire within them, as in *Castile* <note>A region in Spain. Maier is likely making a metaphor about the "fire" (sparks) trapped within flint stones used for building or tools.</note>.

Who would not marvel at amber <note>original: "succinum"</note>, a transparent and fragrant stone produced from subterranean juices and driven to the shores by the waves of the sea, as in *Sudavia* <note>The text reads "Sudania," likely a variant or error for Sudavia/Sudovia, a region in Prussia famous for amber.</note>, the maritime coast of *Prussia*?

<margin>Leonine Earth indicated.</margin>
And to have hinted to the wise, who grasp our words with the mind and not just the ears: Moreover, just as Earth endures in fire and is not resolved into air even if the flame be very strong, but like precious **Gold** resists any injuries, so also our *Europe*, made equal and fortified by its own powers, like the most ancient *Boundary of the Gods* <note>original: "Terminus Deorum." Terminus was the Roman god of boundary markers who famously refused to yield his place even to Jupiter.</note>, yields to none.

<margin>Why Europe is like Gold.</margin>
If we have not spoken of her praise in a manner equal to her dignity, we have nevertheless illustrated her according to the truth of our purpose as best we could. Having traveled through many famous places, I could find no one who could inform me more certainly about the *Phoenix* and its Medicine; instead, I encountered many who mocked me as if I were wasting my effort and my oil <note>A Latin idiom, "oleam et operam perdere," referring to wasting both the oil in a student's lamp and the labor of study.</note>, rather than helping me with words, much less with deeds.

<margin>The words and reasons of those who wished to deter the seeker of the medicine.</margin>
> "What you seek," they said, "you will find nowhere, and what you find is not what you seek. You have been deceived by others who urged you to hunt for what does not exist. Spare your labor, expense, and the investigation of a vocal booming that has no weight—a sound which, like *Echo*, follows you, the *Narcissus* of your own genius, and responds to every call in a way that seems fitting, but is most unfit for the actual thing you seek."

<margin>Chemical sayings apply themselves to all concepts of the mind.</margin>
Some of them said, "This matter is more hidden and intricate than is suitable for you and your studies. For let us grant that such a Medicine is to be sought from the *Phoenix*, yet human life, being quite short in itself, perishes before it can be tracked down. Meanwhile, many other profitable vocations...

# SYMBOLS

<margin>Things to be neglected while this Medicine is sought.</margin>
...and professions are neglected, expenses are worn away, time passes, and finally nothing is found in the hands. To spend certain money and the precious time of life on uncertain things is the mark of an uncertain and vain man. Another suggested: "I would wish to bestow nothing upon this medicine, unless by seeking it in passing <note>original: "obiter," meaning incidentally or as a side-project</note>, while I dealt with other most truthful works from which profit might come to me; for if you do the same, you will always remain without loss."

<margin>Response to objections.</margin>
With my ears closed to the harsher warnings of the first group, I replied to the others thus: To search for this Medicine is the task of a man who is exceptionally industrious and hardworking, and who is strong in intellect and the knowledge of things. 

<margin>Chemistry requires the whole man.</margin>
If he applies himself to this only in passing, it is the same as if he does nothing: for he will never even reach the first outer bark <note>The "cortex" or bark refers to the most superficial, literal layer of alchemical secrets.</note>. The reason is clear: because the matter is most hidden; it is finally noticed only through profound speculation and the use of many things not dissimilar to it, after various previous errors concerning the same subject. Nor is it ever found by a chance accident by unlearned **Empirics** <term>empirics: "Emphyricis," refers to practitioners who rely on trial-and-error experience rather than a systematic, theoretical understanding of nature.</term>. Whence it is necessary that one gives himself entirely to this, or abstains from it entirely. 

And although I do not recognize such and so great gifts in myself, nevertheless I know not by what guidance or nod (I believe it is surely divine) I am swept into these difficulties, whether willing or unwilling, with an indubitable hope already conceived that I shall at last, by the grace of God, find the sought-after **Medicament**. 

<margin>Chemical Medicine is to be preferred above other goods.</margin>
Just as his own Queen seems beautiful to any King, or a bride to a groom, so this Medicine smiles upon me above all the goods of the world; and by a certain magnetic virtue, it fascinates and binds my mind to itself, so that I would be willing to go without life, friends, and kin, if I must lack her. 

What **Hippocrates** elsewhere pronounced concerning Medicine—that *Art is long, life is short, judgment difficult, and experiment fallacious* <note>The famous aphorism: "Ars longa, vita brevis, iudicium difficile, experimentum periculosum."</note>—this can be most truly understood regarding this [Alchemical] Medicine. To the former [general medicine], very many arrive; yet to this, very few. The reason is that beautiful things are difficult, and sweat is placed before virtue and glory.

Who Hercules is.

The marriage celebrated under what conditions. The **Diamond** and **Ruby** are given as pledges and dowries by the spouses to each other.

Agreement was reached by the virgin’s side, and the nuptials were soon celebrated under these conditions, confirmed by both: first, that she would bring with her as a dowry an **Adamant** <note>original: "Adamantem"; in alchemical allegory, the "Adamant" or Diamond represents the fixed, indestructible nature of the perfected matter.</note> of immense price and size, and he in turn would give as a gift for this a **Ruby**, called a carbuncle from its radiating splendor <note>original: "Rubinum, carbunculum"; the Ruby or Red Carbuncle represents the "Red Stage" (Rubedo) or the final perfection of the Philosopher's Stone.</note>, of far greater value and esteem; which mutual gifts were worth one million and more; that is, ten hundred thousand gold ducats.
