## AMERICA, WATER.

<margin>
*America, water.*
</margin>
To hasten by ship to America—called the New World, or the West Indies already well-known—does not seem a matter of great difficulty, since constant habit and use have found, as it were, a Royal Road through the Ocean by the indication of the magnet <note>original: "magnetis indicio"; a reference to the mariner's compass, which revolutionized navigation.</note>. Truly, however, to have first tracked it out and brought it to the knowledge of others, "this was the work, this was the labor" <note>original: "hoc opus hic labor fuit"; a famous quote from Virgil’s Aeneid regarding the difficulty of a task.</note>.

<margin>
*A black eagle on the stern of the ship by which America was sought.*
</margin>
Having left the Fortunate Isles <note>original: "Insulis Fortunatis"; the Canary Islands, traditionally the jumping-off point for Atlantic crossings.</note> to approach it, I boarded a ship, on whose stern was a **Black Eagle** <note>original: "Aquila nigra"; in alchemy, the "Eagle" often represents sublimation or the volatile spirit, and the "Black Eagle" specifically relates to the stage of putrefaction or the extraction of the "mercury of the philosophers."</note>. Having traversed the waves of the Ocean, which grew horribly black by night, and having endured many dangers inflicted by sea monsters, contrary whirlwinds, and storms;

<margin>
*What Brazil is.*
</margin>
at last we joyfully put in at the shores of **Brazil**, which is a great province of America filled with continuous forests. The huts of the settlers are few, the towns very rare, and the men are most estranged from the teachings of the liberal arts. Shall I consult these people here, I say, concerning the most hidden secrets of nature?

<margin>
*The Americans were ignorant of letters or writing.*
</margin>
Where the inhabitants, not so long ago, held the reading of a letter written and sent to one another by the Spaniards as a miracle, and thought the paper was "talkative" and a betrayer of deeds? Whom shall I ask about the **Phoenix**, the rarest of all birds? This is indeed beyond doubt: that birds of various kinds and colors are found there, such as are not seen in these places or parts of the earth; but since the **Phoenix** is of a far different nature and property, there is no reason for us to seek it among common birds.

*Allegory.*
</margin>
The forests here are crowded with fragrant and variously colored trees, into which I sometimes walked while occupied with meditations; partly so that I might refresh my eyes with the more joyful sight of the trees and flowers, and partly that I might relax <note>original: "relaxarem"; the text breaks here at the catchword "rela-".</note> my mind from cares with the natural music of the chirping birds...

# SYMBOLS OF THE GOLDEN TABLE. BOOK 12.

<page-num>581</page-num>

<margin>Discovery of the apple.</margin>
...while I was relaxing, I happened by chance upon an apple of unusual and wonderful elegance. While I was contemplating it from every side, I found an inscription of this sort:

<margin>Riddle inscribed on the apple.</margin>
> *Within is the grandmother, whom you should hand over; rising from there,*
> *The son can enter his mother’s embrace.*
> *Shortly thereafter, a noble tree will be reborn,*
> *Which will give gold-haired fruit to the farmer.*
<note>original: "Intus adest auia... Agricola fætus quæ dabit auricomos." This riddle uses familial terms to describe alchemical stages: the "grandmother" is the Earth (the base element), the "mother" is the tree (the matrix or metallic body), and the "son" is the seed or the transformative spirit. The "gold-haired fruit" represents the final successful transformation into alchemical gold.</note>

<margin>Explanation of the apple's riddle.</margin>
After considering these things for a long time, I finally understood that the seed lurking within must be entrusted to the grandmother—that is, the earth—since the tree appeared to be the mother of that apple, and the earth the mother of the tree. Therefore, I took this up as a gift offered by divine power until I had the opportunity to put it to the test and prove it, just as the inscription teaches. I believe the method of proceeding is as follows: I ought to take the seeds of this apple (which were perhaps brought there from the Garden of the Hesperides <note>In Greek mythology, the Hesperides tended a garden with a tree that grew golden apples; alchemists often used this as a metaphor for the pursuit of the Golden Fleece or the Stone.</note>) and place them into the earth.

<margin>The process of grafting trees.</margin>
Then, in a short time, shoots will grow from that same tree to which the apple belongs. Afterward, another tree of the same kind must be sought, or one that is very similar to the first; it must be "decapitated" or cut down to the trunk, and the aforementioned shoot, cut off, must be inserted into the trunk as a <term>scion</term> <note>A "scion" (surculus) is a young shoot or twig of a plant, especially one cut for grafting or rooting.</note>.

<margin>Another allegory. The process of breeding from different species of animals.</margin>
When these two have grown together into one tree, that trunk will turn out far more noble than it was before because of the grafting of the scion. This is because it will be entirely converted to the nature of the grafted scion; and the fruit that arises from it will reflect the nature of the scion or the apple found previously. No one can deny that this is a natural artifice, which is perfected by the benefit of both nature and art. It is well known that in that same region, before the arrival of the Spaniards, there were no horses, and a rider was first seen by those people as a some kind of miraculous animal. But later, when these were brought along with donkeys, and the wealthier people used the labor of these beasts of burden, they heard that there was also a third animal produced from both, but...

->...different, called a mule: Therefore, they applied all their strength to produce this.<-

There was especially a certain man born of noble rank who took charge of this matter and had already procured for himself the most noble horses; he also raised many donkeys devoted to the labor of the mills. The method of breeding horses from mares was well known, as was that of donkeys from their own kind; but it was not so for mules. For this reason, the matter had to be 
<margin>Experience is dangerous.</margin>
put to the test. However, all experience is dangerous or full of errors when it is done without a prior example of the known thing, or without a most true investigation conducted through reason. Fodder was provided to the horse with great care and in abundance, but from his mounting of the female donkey, nothing was produced—without doubt, because there was no proper proportion between the seeds of both. And when this had been tried often in vain, all hope of breeding a mule failed. At last, when one of those who examine the nature of things and 
<margin>The philosopher examines the natures of things more sharply than the common people.</margin>
animals more sharply than those common people had arrived at that place, and had noticed the repeated complaints of the said lord regarding that matter, he said: "Although I am not a doctor or veterinarian for mules, but a philosopher, nevertheless I think I know the cause of the frustrated conception of the mule." And when he was begged by the lord to declare it, he said, "I will speak as I have learned and am able," and thus he began:

<margin>A riddle concerning the conception of the mule.</margin>
> *To produce a mule, let him be made like his father, the little donkey,*
> *With his ears and slow steps; do it in this way:*
> *Let his own food be given to each according to the weight of their nature,*
> *Which, if by chance you wish to ask, how great will it be?*
> *Add half of that of the active agent, and double that of the other,*
> *Then the mare will produce a mule from the donkey.*
<note>This riddle describes the "proportions" of materials needed for a successful chemical reaction. The "agent" and the "patient" (the two substances being combined) must be balanced according to a specific numerical ratio (1/2 of one to 2 of the other) to produce the "mule"—the desired alchemical result.</note>

Believing in these words, which held little obscurity, and after multiple experiments were performed, he finally produced a mule—an animal more like its father than its mother—from both...

<margin>The mule is different from its father and mother.</margin>
...yet he obtained something different: who does not see that these are privileges of nature—that from two things a third is generated, which does not agree in species with either, but has a form distinct from them? In these matters, if anyone were to imitate nature, he would without doubt produce many other types of animals, vegetables, and metals; it is affirmed as certain that many of the sharpest searchers of nature have long since proven this by experience itself. For there are those who say that from a *Panther* <note>original: Pardo</note> and a *Lioness* <note>original: Leæna</note> the *Leopard* is thus generated; from a wolf and a female dog, a *hound-wolf* <note>original: lycisca</note>; from a horse and a female donkey, a *hinny* <note>original: hinnus</note> or a mule different from a [standard] mule. From a shoot or branch of one tree and the trunk of another, a tree is produced similar to the former, but not the latter; from flowers of certain mixed colors, other colored flowers; from a Tincture or very red metallic powder mixed in fire with quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, gold is produced, which is not similar to this or that in all respects; and so it must be judged concerning other things.

<margin>Leopard, hound-wolf, hinny: mixed species.</margin>
<margin>The craft of the Americans concerning the softening of gold.</margin>
In metallic matters also, especially regarding gold, they say these *American* peoples <note>referring to indigenous South Americans, particularly the Incas</note> are skilled in a singular craft above others—namely, how gold can be so softened by a certain water that it can be handled like wax with the fingers, and indentations can be pressed into it, and gemstones inserted, with the edges and rims being firmed up on all sides. This craft, which is certainly more common in *Peru*, is a secret of nature and art not to be despised. Indeed, that water does not seem to be made of corrosives; otherwise it could not be handled with the fingers, or if it were, the gold would have to be shaped with some glass stylus.

<margin>American chemical water for softening gold.</margin>
However it happens, no one will doubt that it is an invention of Chemistry <note>original: Chemiae</note>, since such waters proceed hardly from nature, but from the art of distillation. Having looked into all these things, since no hope remained here for the medicine sought <note>the Philosopher's Stone or universal cure</note>, I thought to leave these parts as soon as possible and cross over into *Asia* when the opportunity was given. The most precious thing I saw here in *Brazil* was a wood as black as *Ebony* <note>original: Hebeni</note> (to pass over that red wood called *Brazilwood* <note>original: Brafiliarum; a wood used for red dye</note>), of great weight and value,

Concerning this, the most learned physician *Monardes* <note>Nicolás Monardes (c. 1493–1588) was a Spanish physician and botanist famous for his study of medicinal plants from the New World.</note> writes similarly in his book on medicines brought from the West Indies:

<margin>The various and wonderful colors of the American earth.</margin>
> *The variety of colors of the Peruvian earth is wonderful and worthy of consideration. For if anyone observes it from a distance, he will see many parts of the soil tinted with different colors, so that they appear like cloths of various colors exposed to the sun to be dried; for one part of the earth is green, another blue, another of another color, such as yellow, white, black, and red or even others, all of which are different minerals of the earth. Concerning the black earth, a portion of which they sent to me, I can affirm that I made from it the best ink—if it were mixed with water or wine—very suitable for writing; it has, however, a little blue in it, which makes it appear better. He says the red earth is a mineral of quicksilver <note>original: "argenti vini" — likely a scribal error for "argenti vivi," a common term for mercury</note>, with which those Indians painted themselves.*

Once a ship was available, the ensign of which was a white unicorn, I left *America* and hastened toward *Asia*, looking out at the Cape of Good Hope on my left side; from there I arrived at the Persian Gulf.

## ASIA, AIR.

<margin>Asia, Air.</margin>
<margin>From where the four parts of the earth are named.</margin>

# THE GOLDEN TABLE, BOOK XII

<page-num>585</page-num>

<margin>Asia, the aerial land.</margin>
Asia is the third continent of the world, or the aerial land, being of a more temperate nature than the remaining parts. For just as *Europe* is troubled by cold on certain coasts, and *Africa* by heat, *Asia* participates in neither the most intense cold nor the most intense heat.
<margin>Why Asia represents the element of air.</margin>
Hence it represents the element of air to us most excellently, because air is hot and moist—with its heat tempering the cold and its moisture tempering the dryness.

<margin>Why islands are less hot and cold.</margin>
For regions situated in the sea, even if they are quite hot, have their heat mitigated by the moisture of the waters; if they are cold, the cold is likewise softened by the same moisture.

<margin>The genealogy of hot and moist air.</margin>
For if we carefully consider the nature of hot and moist air and examine its genealogy from its causes, we find that fiery heat is its father, while watery moisture is its mother.
<margin>Air, the son of whom.</margin>
From these parents, *Air*, like a son, retains the more active qualities—namely, heat and moisture together.

<margin>Air, the mediator between opposites.</margin>
Hence it is the mediator between the contrary elements already mentioned, and, being joined to both by kinship, it makes them friendly and unites them in every mixture <term>mixture</term> <note>original: "mistione" — in alchemy and natural philosophy, this refers to the blending of elements into a unified substance.</note> of bodies.

<margin>Asia joins Africa with Europe.</margin>
In such a way, *Asia*, the most powerful part of the earthly world, binds *Africa* and *Europe* together with a kind of intermediate bond, much like connecting fire and earth—the thinnest and the thickest elements. For otherwise there would be no coherence between the two, nor could one provide its natural virtues in a mixture without the other. Fire indeed clings willingly to earth as its fuel and hearth, but take away the air for it to breathe, and it will soon vanish.

<margin>The prerogatives of Asia.</margin>
Therefore, it is considered the prerogative of *Asia* to be in the center of the earthly world, to experience the temperament of the air, and to provide us with "aerial fruits"—such as dates, balsam, all kinds of spices, and even gold itself. In *Asia*, just as the first *Monarchies* began here and there under *Nimrod* <note>A biblical figure described in Genesis as a "mighty hunter before the Lord," traditionally credited with founding the first empires.</note>, the "hunter before the Lord," so too was the first man created. And, what is the most excellent of all things, our *Savior*, as a man, drew his first breath of light there, lived his human life, and underwent death...

### FIERY AFRICA.

<margin>Africa always brings something new.</margin>
**WHEN** I had landed in *Africa*, and one full year and more had passed, the *Solstice* had already entered *Leo* <note>The "Solstice" here refers to the height of summer; the Sun enters the zodiac sign of Leo in late July.</note>, while the *Moon* held *Cancer, the height of its own house* <note>In traditional astrology, Cancer is the "domicile" or home of the Moon. This positioning was considered a powerful and lucky omen.</note>. This gave me great hope of a most favorable sign. Now, *Africa* stretches toward the midday sun [the South] relative to *Asia* itself; for this reason, the seasons of the year are far hotter there than elsewhere, especially the summer, which is felt to be most burning. And this is the chief cause why the greatest part of it is uncultivated, parched, thirsty, barren, and empty. In this land, as rivers are rarer, so wild beasts are more frequent; they gather together at the fresh waters, wherever they may be, and there they even mate with one another across different species. From this, new offspring and animals with strange faces are born, and it is not without reason that it is said: *Africa always brings something new.*

<margin>Africa abounds in mountains and minerals.</margin>
In this place, *Panes* <note>Nature spirits resembling the god Pan.</note>, *Satyrs*, *Cynocephali* <note>original: *Cynocephali*, legendary creatures with the heads of dogs and bodies of men.</note>, and half-humans are said to dwell, besides innumerable species of beasts. There, the *Oryx* is said to loathe the heat of the sun in the greatest scorched season with a flood of tears and repeated groans. There are the *Mountains of the Moon* and *Atlas*, who supports the heavens on his shoulders; they abound in minerals as well as serpents. In that same place, "dragon's blood" is collected, which the dragon sucked from the Elephant; when the Elephant falls dead, the dragon is crushed and forced to give back the blood it drank <note>In ancient and medieval natural history, "Dragon's Blood" (a red resin) was believed to be the literal mixture of blood from a dragon and an elephant who died in a mutual struggle.</note>.

<margin>The *Ortus*, an animal whose head is red, eyes black, and feet white.</margin>
In that same region, near the *Erythraean Sea* <note>The Red Sea.</note>, a certain wild beast was seen, named the **ORTUS**. Its head was red with golden lines reaching all the way to the neck; its eyes were black and its feet—especially the front ones—were white, while the hind ones were darker; its mouth was white all the way to the cheeks. While I was held fixed in contemplation of this creature's outward form, there occurred to me the words of the philosopher *Avicenna*

*Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior, Cross* <note>original: *Iefous Christos Theou vios soter stauros*. <margin>The Sibyl's poems were not fabricated by Christians.</margin>

...who reigned for 56 years <note>referring to Augustus Caesar</note>, and that Tiberius succeeded him, in whose time the light of Christ’s coming shone forth, and a new succession of people was established. And again in another place in his *Bucolics* <note>The *Eclogues*, specifically the famous Fourth Eclogue often read by Christians as a prophecy of Christ</note>, where he adds:

<margin>Where Cicero mentions the Sibyl prophesying about Christ.</margin>
These are the words of Eusebius. The passage from Cicero, which Eusebius cites, is found in Book 2 of *On Divination*: *“We observe the verses of the Sibyl, which she is said to have poured out in a frenzy. Their interpreter <note>the official guardian of the Sibylline Books in Rome</note> was recently thought, by a false rumor, to be about to state in the Senate that if we wished to be safe, we must call the one whom we already truly had as King, a 'King' by title as well.”*

<margin>Cicero interprets the Sibyl’s words spoken about Christ—that through him we shall be saved—as referring to an earthly king.</margin>
*“If this prophecy is in those books, to what man or what time does it refer? For whoever composed them did so craftily, so that whatever happened might seem predicted, since specific definitions of people and times were removed. He also employed the concealment of obscurity, so that the same verses could seem to be adapted to one thing at one time and another thing at another. Furthermore, the poem itself declares it is not the work of one in a frenzy; for it shows more of art and diligence than of divine inspiration and agitation, since there is that which is called an **acrostic** <term>acrostic</term> <note>original: ἀκροστιχὶς; a poetic form where the first letters of each line form a name or message</note>, where a sequence is connected from the first letters of the verses; as in certain works of Ennius. That is certainly the sign of an attentive mind rather than a frenzied one. And in the Sibylline books, the entire poem is woven together from the first letters of the start of each sentence. This belongs to a writer who is diligent, not one who is raving or insane.”*

<margin>Cicero wrongly tries to refute the Sibyl’s verses because the initial letters signify something, as they say she was in a frenzy; but we say they are not from a frenzy, but rather are true in the Sibyl.</margin>
These are Cicero's words. However, the axiom that Cicero uses—namely, that this poem is not the Sibyl's because it is not the product of a frenzy, and that the Sibyl must have spoken her poems while in a frenzy—is false and unworthy of his reputation. We grant that the Sibyl was not seized by a frenzy when she produced that poem, but how does this detract from the truth of the matter? For we say she was moved by the breath of the Holy Spirit, not by the "enthusiasm" or madness of the devil. After I approached her, [I found her] sitting...

<margin>Conversation with the Erythraean Sibyl</margin>
...in a cave, surrounded by branches of trees and green turf, I greeted her most dutifully. Although she was a little terrified at first sight and stepped back further inside; nevertheless, giving way to my prayers, she said, "Whom do you seek here, stranger? It is not permitted for a man to approach a virgin." 

"Driven by no headlong rashness," I replied, "but having taken certain aim with mature deliberation, I have hurried to you, so that you might dissolve certain doubts clinging to my mind, and instruct me with the most gracious lessons of your guidance; for which, if I find you not opposed to my wishes, I promise and bind myself in turn to all the duties of kindness and service owed to you." 

At these words, appearing more merciful with a milder expression, she said, "What is it that you ask of me? I can deny nothing to you and those like you, who are so eager for learning." 

<margin>The question of whether the Phoenix exists in the world and if Medicine should be sought from it.</margin>
"There are two things," I replied, "divine virgin, which I hope you would deign to teach me candidly, without any evasion or circumlocution: namely, whether here in the borders of *Egypt or Arabia* that bird, unique in all the world, called the *Phoenix*, was once and still is to be found (as rumor spreads); and whether a certain Medicine for *Anger and Grief* <note>original: "Iræ & doloris." In alchemical literature, "anger" and "grief" often symbolize the volatile or corrosive states of matter that must be "healed" or stabilized into the Philosophical Stone.</note> was ever or is to be sought from it. And if so, where are both the bird and the medicine to be investigated?" 

<margin>Doubt is the first step of knowledge</margin>
"You do well," she said, "to doubt not of trifles or worthless things, but of things of great price; for doubt is the first step of knowledge; with which I promise to bless you as far as I am able. 

<margin>What is the homeland of the Phoenix?</margin>
Many have sought these same things through means that have nothing to do with the matter; but you have strayed neither in place nor person. For the region in which you now stay is *Arabia Felix* <note>meaning "Fertile" or "Happy" Arabia, the classical name for the southern Arabian Peninsula</note>, bordering Egypt, which is considered the unique homeland of the *Phoenix*. 

Know also that the person whom you question <note>the Sibyl herself</note> is not ignorant of this matter; since you have entrusted your fortune to both the place and the person, neither will deny you the truth of the thing you seek. I shall make you blessed with teaching, while this region—or Egypt—shall make you so by visual demonstration. Therefore, apply your ears to my warnings and your mind to these matters: Which—

I first betook myself to the *Canopic* mouth, on which road I proceeded past a hill notable for the burials of *Christians* who were once slain there by barbarians. I cannot pass over the annual miracles of this place, which are most worthy of being related:

<margin>A miracle occurring annually not far from Memphis in Egypt involving the rising and sinking of bodies from the earth.</margin>
For on a certain day in the month of *May*, the corpses or bones of those buried, from sunrise until midday, are gradually raised by themselves to the surface of the tomb, until they come into the sight of the people gathering there—some more, others less—then from midday toward the setting of the sun, they are lowered in the same way until all have returned to their original state. If anyone should assert that these things happen not by divine power, but entirely by diabolical means, let him take care lest, by departing too far from superstition, he incline toward unbelief or impiety, and deny or subtract these or similar miraculous deeds from the omnipotence and most free will of God.

<margin>A model for the Resurrection of bodies.</margin>
If these things are true, as many who have seen them testify in their published writings, they exhibit a most evident example of the *Resurrection* of human bodies, just as does the revival of the new *Phoenix* from its dead ashes.

<margin>Egypt is the image of heaven, according to Hermes.</margin>
Coming to the island of *Canopus*, and the *mouth of the Nile* opposite it, I inquired about *Mercury* <note>The Roman name for the Greek Hermes, here referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage and father of alchemy.</note>, whether he might have a seat there. Truly, the people of that little region could scarcely find anything to answer. The more learned among them said, "*Egypt* is the image of heaven..."

# THE GOLDEN TABLE. BOOK 12.

<margin>Saturn is the grandfather of Mercury.</margin>
With Hermes as witness, the sky reflects back to us, and the seven mouths of the Nile represent the same number of planets, of which the Canopic is the highest, and is subject to the younger son of the sky <note>original: "coelique filio iuniori," referring to Saturn, who was the son of Caelus (Sky/Uranus).</note>. As Canobus, the pilot of Menelaus’ ship, was buried here and gave his name to the island and the port, so the highest of the planets <note>Saturn, often associated with the highest sphere in ancient astronomy.</note> is like a favorable old inspector. Since he is the grandfather of the Mercury you seek, it is no wonder if Mercury sometimes passes to his grandfather’s house. But he reported that Mercury was not to be found here now, but resided perpetually at another mouth of that same Nile. Astonished by this response, after much time and error committed, I realized that I had to approach another place, one more familiar to Mercury.

<margin>2. The Bolbitic mouth of the Nile.</margin>
Therefore, I did not hesitate to proceed straight to the second, called the *Bolbitic*. But when I had questioned some people I met there whether they had seen *Mercury*, the son of the Nile, and whether I should meet him, and they replied that they knew nothing of the *Mercury* of that place, I did not wish to proceed further, lest I waste both time and expense in vain.

<margin>3. The Sebennytic mouth of the Nile.</margin>
Having thus been informed about two mouths of the Nile, I ran with a hurried pace to the third. Near this is the city of *Sebennytos*, from which it is called the *Sebennytic* mouth; it is inhabited by residents who are not very numerous, whose customs I found to be so barbaric and rigid that I judged them far removed from all refined humanity. I did not wish to linger there any longer, nor inquire further about the seat of *Mercury*. For how, I asked, could *Mercury*, the author of all more refined literature and learning <note>Mercury/Hermes was the traditional patron of language, writing, and the "liberal arts."</note>, stay among such wild people? For either these people would make him fierce and barbaric like themselves, or he would make them mild and human through a long stay and proximity. Therefore, after I had departed and left the town, I asked a certain farmer of that place: "Does *Mercury* not have a court here?" He replied: "He certainly has a very well-fortified court here, but he never lives in it."

## SYMBOLS

<margin>4. The Pelusiac mouth of the Nile.</margin>
And so I traveled to the fourth *mouth*, called the *Pelusiac*, the most famous of all because of the city of the same name lying next to it. Its founder, as rumor has it, was Peleus, the father of Achilles. This mouth divides Asia and Arabia from *Egypt*, and was once most abundant in riches. After I had heard about it and understood its virtues and conditions, I did not doubt that I would find the seat of Mercury there. For as it is said, just as *Troy* could not be besieged without the *son of Peleus* <note>original: "Pelide," a patronymic for Achilles, the son of Peleus.</note> or *Achilles*, so *Mercury* cannot be obtained without *Pelusium*. This is the most noble emporium of *Egypt*, which especially abounds in Arabian gold. When I arrived there, I asked where *Mercury* might reside. But one of the inhabitants replied that *Mercury* is not always present in this place, although he is a most welcome guest when he is here. Taking it poorly that so many journeys had been undertaken here in vain, I did not wish to settle my feet until I had visited the remaining mouths, not despairing that I would finally meet the longed-for *Mercury* face-to-face in those that followed.

<margin>5. The Tanitic mouth of the Nile.</margin>
The fifth in order was the *Tanitic* mouth. Although its name was more obscure, I still wanted to go there so that I would not seem to have provided any excuse for avoiding it. But I brought back just as much from there as from the previous ones—namely, nothing at all—except for the fact that I learned that the *Mercury* I was seeking lived there not at all. "O unhappy me," I said, "must I follow him so far, one who either is nowhere or flees from me as I pursue him, just as the beautiful *Alexis* fled from *Corydon*?" <note>A reference to Virgil’s *Eclogues* (Eclogue 2), where the shepherd Corydon fruitlessly pursues the youth Alexis. It underscores the narrator's growing frustration.</note> Would it not have been better to progress from the last to the first by imitating a crab <note>Moving backward.</note>? Does that fleeting and *hat-wearing* <term>petasatus: wearing a petasos, the winged traveler's hat characteristic of Mercury</term> youth, foreseeing my arrival, feel such disdain that he takes flight before I even approach? But he shall not escape in the end, nor can he be hidden for long, wherever he may be. Two mouths remain for me out of all those of the *Nile*, which, God willing, I shall also survey, and then I shall bid farewell to all of *Egypt*.

# THE GOLDEN TABLE. BOOK XII.

<margin>6. The Phatnitic mouth of the Nile.</margin>
Therefore, I set out for the *Phatnitic* <note>The text spells this "Phanniticum" or "Phäniticum," referring to the sixth of the traditional seven outlets of the Nile Delta.</note> mouth, the sixth of the *Nile*, which I believed was owed to *Mercury* by the reasoning of the heavens <note>A reference to the astrological or "celestial" correspondence between physical locations and planetary influences.</note>. I was led by a firm hope in my soul that now, at last, there would be an end to my many labors. But that confidence also failed me, as it had so often before. For I received an answer from the inhabitants of that place that *Mercury* had indeed lived here, but had long ago changed his residence and migrated elsewhere. They said many people had frequently searched for him there, but he was never found at home.

<margin>7. The Mendesian mouth of the Nile.</margin>
After this, I undertook the final journey as far as the *Mendesian* mouth. When I arrived there, I asked about *Mercury*, but he was not found here either. Indeed, many replied that they did not even know a *Mercury*.

And so, having surveyed the seven mouths of the *Nile* in order, and since I did not find the one I sought, I thought I had been deceived by the *Sibyl* <note>A Sibyl was a prophetess in ancient Greece and Rome; here she represents a guide who provides cryptic or difficult instructions.</note>. I suspected she had thrown me into these labyrinths just to lead my spirit around, delighting it with false hope—perhaps out of envy or a preconceived hatred toward strangers. However, when I reconsidered every single thing that had happened on the journey, I conjectured that I might have been surrounded by deceptive answers by the inhabitants of every location. I realized that, due to a certain innate ferocity, they all loathed and hated foreigners. Therefore, I carefully reconsidered what they had answered regarding the first, second, third, and other mouths. Many things occurred to me that increased my previous doubts rather than removing them. Consequently, retracing my steps from the last mouth back toward the first, I finally found *Mercury* before I had even returned to the first, in one of those very mouths where the inhabitants had previously seemed to deny his presence.

<margin>Where Mercury was found.</margin>
<margin>Many things learned from Mercury.</margin>
<margin>Where the Phoenix lies hidden.</margin>
<margin>The Phoenix was not found at home.</margin>
Approaching him, and after many conversations held between us, those things which I had been ignorant of were told by him. First, he showed me the *Phoenix* and where it ought to be met. He told me most openly where it lay hidden—a place I had not even thought of before. But when I arrived there, by my misfortune, the bird had gone out (perhaps having been appointed as an Arbiter between... <note>original: "Arbiter conſitutus inter," suggesting the Phoenix was acting as a judge or mediator in some dispute.</note>)

# EPIGRAM DEDICATED TO PHILOSOPHICAL
## Mercury.

<margin>Philosophical Mercury <note>In alchemy, "Philosophical Mercury" is not common quicksilver, but the vital, transformative spirit or "living silver" believed to be the soul of all metals.</note> praised in verse.</margin>
**T** *he Latins call you Mercury with a fitting name,*
*Because you yourself run as a mediator between the Gods.*
*Among the Greeks, you are held as the interpreter and the Greatest Hermes <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary "Thrice-Great" founder of the hermetic and alchemical traditions.</note>,*
*And you are said to be of the land of Thoth <note>original: "Teuthius." Thoth is the Egyptian god of wisdom and writing, often identified with Hermes.</note> in the soil of Egypt.*

*Bringing joy to the lands, he who left great wealth to you.*
*You duly brought laws to the peoples of Egypt,*
*Which Vulcan <note>The god of fire and craftsmanship; in alchemy, he represents the controlled heat of the furnace.</note>, your confidant, gave to you through his art.*
*To all nations in the whole world you appear*
*Pleasing, yet you desire to be known only by a few.*
*O, how many secret gifts of nature were entrusted*
*To you, and are revealed by your treasures!*
*A red face is your own, and a yellow neck,*
*But your breast shines with a powerful white color.*
*Black winged sandals <note>original: "talaria"</note> are fitted to your feet,*
*And the staff with the twin snakes <note>The Caduceus, Mercury's staff, which symbolizes the reconciliation of opposing forces (like sulfur and mercury).</note> does not weigh down your hand.*
*This is your appearance, by which you are known to all as Hermes;*
*That fourfold color <note>The four colors mentioned—black (feet), white (breast), yellow (neck), and red (face)—correspond to the four traditional stages of the alchemical Great Work: Nigredo, Albedo, Citrinitas, and Rubedo.</note> is fitting for you.*
*You showed me the Phoenix <note>The Phoenix represents the completion of the work: the Red Stone capable of rejuvenation and transmutation.</note> with your interpreter’s voice;*
*As your debtor, I return the grateful thanks I am able.*
*Meanwhile, receive these small gifts written on talkative paper;*
*If you grant something greater, you yourself shall receive the reward.*

# PRAISE TO THE PHOENIX
### Expressed in an epigram.

> *O Miracle of the World, Wonder <note>original: "Monstrum"; here used in the classical sense of a divine omen or supernatural marvel rather than a "monster" in the modern sense.</note> without flaw, unique Phoenix,*
> *Who are suited only to the great sages:*
> *Clad in purple feathers and a golden neck,*
> *You excel among all birds and all treasures:*
> *For your nest is built of cassia and Sabaean incense <note>Incense from the land of Sheba, famous in antiquity for its high-quality resins.</note>,*
> *And thus you are richer than any other bird.*
> *You appear, conscious of your fate after several centuries,*
> *Which nature granted, that you might be renewed.*
> *Then, willingly, you present yourself at the altar in Thebes <note>The Egyptian city of Heliopolis/Thebes was traditionally the site where the Phoenix was said to undergo its fiery rebirth.</note>,*
> *So that Vulcan <note>The god of fire; in alchemy, this refers to the transformative heat of the furnace.</note> may grant you a new form through his art.*
> *The golden beauty of your feathers is called the Medicine of health,*
> *And is said to bring relief to human ills.*
> *The only hope for incurable disease resides in you,*
> *And you make the old walk in the manner of youths.*
> *Lest I recount your other most divine gifts,*
> *Even the Persian Treasury <note>original: "Gaza"; a term for the royal treasury of the Persian kings, used here to represent immense wealth.</note> is scarcely equal to your riches.*
> *I prefer you, blessed bird, above all riches,*
> *Because you provide the medicine of powerful aid.*
> *I have desired these delights for many years,*
> *Without you, I have no care for any worldly thing.*
> *Hidden in secret places, you are concealed in retreats*
> *Lest you become prey; and you are accustomed to go out without a witness.*
> *Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman naturalist who recorded the Phoenix appearing in Rome during the reign of Claudius, though he expressed some skepticism.</note> writes that you were seen in Rome in ancient times,*
> *But (alas) he is deceived in marvelous ways.*
> *Who would be so bold as to drag you from your nests, or who*
> *Would uncover you, unless he were a boy of foolish mind?*
> *You shall be safe hereafter, as you have been safe until now;*
> *May he be wise, I pray, to whom you shall give your feathers.*

...owls <note>original: "noctuas"; a reference to the practice of using a tethered owl as a decoy to attract and trap other birds.</note> for catching the gold of others—namely, of richer men—and they themselves are like bird-catchers, whose pipe sings sweetly so that they may deceive the bird:

From this I construct the following Argument:
If Alchemists use their furnaces as decoys, with which they might catch the gold of other wealthier men, the art itself is deceptive and to be condemned.
But the first premise is true.
Therefore, the second is also true.

*The minor premise is proved by the already mentioned authority of Scaliger and by experience itself*, nor does it need a long demonstration: For we see how those who properly claim for themselves the title and name of <term>Alchemists</term> <note>Here used by the critic to mean fraudulent "gold-makers."</note> decorate their so-called laboratories, and how they place furnaces of various shapes, instruments, glassware, and other things there for all to see. They do this for no other reason than to entice the ignorant, who are caught by these external displays, thinking that something great and true lies hidden beneath this decoration: But they do not know that these are merely nets, decoys, and captured little birds attracting others of their kind to themselves.

<margin>Response to the 34th Negative Argument.</margin>

**I**F we must argue by the authority of others, a single Scaliger counts for nothing against two true philosophers attesting to the truth of <term>Chemistry</term> <note>original: "Chemiæ"; at this time, chemistry and alchemy were often considered the same discipline of matter-transformation.</note>, much less against a hundred or more whom we have cited and produced up to this point: Therefore, the authority of one falls against so many who contradict him: Truly, so that [we may regard] Scaliger...

...nonetheless, we salute this man <note>referring to Julius Caesar Scaliger, a famous 16th-century scholar and critic of alchemy</note> who is outstanding in singular erudition regarding his intentions. We say that he speaks of a certain "carbon-waster" <note>original: "carboniperda"; a derogatory term for a fraudulent or incompetent alchemist who "wastes coal" without producing results</note>, a deceptive Alchemist, of whose ilk there are countless numbers in almost all places, and therefore Scaliger spoke most truly: For this race of men composes all their words and deeds for the purpose of deceiving others; and since this is their very nature, it can never be absent from them.

<margin>The nature of deceptive Alchemists.</margin>
These men truly have furnaces as decoys <note>original: "pro noctuis"; literally "for owls," referring to the practice of using a tethered owl as a decoy to lure birds into a trap</note> and tongues for bird-calls, their trifling works—distilled, if it please the gods, from gold or other secrets—as little birds, and laboratories splendidly adorned as nets. Scaliger did not say as much about them as ought to be said. We have depicted these men in their true colors, as best we could, in a special treatise titled *The Examination of Drones or False-Chemists* <note>original: "Examen fucorum seu Pseudochymicorū"; "fucorum" refers to drones—lazy bees—symbolizing frauds</note>, which you may read.

<margin>False-chemists fly to bright things like flies.</margin>
But these same <term>False-chemists</term> <note>original: "Pseudochymici"</note> are as far removed from the truth of Chemistry as the earth is from the heaven—except that they fly to it like flies to defile it with their own filth. For who can resist such a tiny animal—a fly, I say—or prevent it from sitting upon vessels that are bright and polished, made of tin or <term>latten</term> <note>original: "latone"; a brass-like alloy used for household vessels</note>, or even of silver and gold, and contaminating them with its squalor? Much less can anyone resist these men, who are fugitives from their own duties or trades, to keep them from flying toward <term>Chemistry</term>—which promises to its inventors riches, wealth, honors, and health as the most precious and splendid of all things—and from defiling it, infecting it, and forcing it to have an ill reputation. These men claim the name for themselves, though they possess not the least bit of the reality. This may be forgiven in them; but it is not to be forgiven in those who confuse names and things, mistaking true artists for false ones, and deceptive Alchemistry for true <term>Chemistry</term> <note>The author distinguishes between "Alchymia" (the fraudulent practice of gold-making) and "Chemia" (the legitimate philosophical and medicinal art)</note>, which brings harm or loss to no one, except that it must be sought over a long time with great labor and expense, and is scarcely obtained by one in a thousand; which occurs because of its excellence.

## 35. The Adversary's negative argument against Chemistry.

<margin>Argument 35. Negative.</margin> The authority of <term>Canon Law</term> <note>the body of laws and regulations made by ecclesiastical authority for the government of the Christian organization and its members</note> is so great that, deservedly, what it condemns ought to be condemned, and what it belittles ought to be belittled.
However, it judges Alchemists as counterfeiters and liars; for in the chapter *Spondent* <note>original: "C. spondent"; referring to the decree "Spondent pariter" issued by Pope John XXII in 1317</note>, found in the *Extravagantes* <note>original: "Extrauagante"; a collection of papal decrees that were "wandering" outside the primary official codifications</note>, it set down these words: "Poor Alchemists promise riches which they do not provide."
Therefore, Alchemists are to be condemned and regarded as liars.

### Response to the 35th negative Argument.

<margin>Response to the 35th negative argument.</margin> **W**e do not infringe upon the authority of Canon Law as long as it contains itself within its own boundaries. But if it wishes to interpose its authority regarding temporal matters, the secrets of nature, and other things of this kind, though we may admit its authority is doubtful, we are not bound to believe it. For this reason, we bind ourselves to its authority in ecclesiastical matters at least, but not in others.
Regarding the <term>Minor premise</term> <note>the second part of the adversary's logical syllogism</note>, I say that those chapters in the *Extravagantes* are outside of the body of Canon Law, added by a certain interpreter as an appendix; therefore, they may either be accepted or not. Furthermore, the text speaks of false Alchemists, deceivers, and liars, who, while receiving money from others, promise them mountains of gold—not even the smallest bit of which they can provide—while they themselves in the meantime are poor, vagabonds, and destitute of all things. Concerning these...

<summary>The author addresses a legal objection against alchemy based on a 14th-century papal decree (Spondent pariter) that categorized alchemists as frauds. He argues that Canon Law’s authority is limited to spiritual matters and that the decree specifically targets fraudulent "get-rich-quick" pretenders rather than true natural philosophers.</summary>

The **major premise** <note>original: "MAior"; in a syllogism, the major premise is the broad general rule</note> is true in itself; if it were not, no truth would be evident from experience.
The **minor premise** <note>original: "Minor"; the specific case being applied to the rule</note> is proven by a thousand experiments of <term>projection</term> <note>The act of casting the "philosopher's stone" or a "tincture" onto molten base metal to effect transmutation</note> published in various places, which may be sought partly from the things mentioned scattered above, and partly from the books of others published on this matter—such as the letter of *Theobald of Hohenland to his brother* and others. Moreover, that this gold, thus made by the projection of a true and legitimate <term>tincture</term> <note>The alchemical medicine or substance used to "dye" or transform metals</note>, is true and similar to natural gold in all respects, is demonstrated as follows: *It is the opinion of Aristotle in the 4th book of his Meteorology:* <note>original: "lib. 4. meteor"; Aristotle's Meteorologica, which was a standard text for discussing the composition of minerals</note> *That everything which produces the same operation as some composite thing is identical to it and similar in all respects, just as everything that has the operation of an eye is an eye.*
*In no different a way, says Zacharius,* <note>likely referring to Dionysius Zachaire, a 16th-century French alchemist</note> *since our gold composed by our art is similar in all respects to the mineral gold (in which lies the whole controversy of the dispute, whether the gold composed by us is true gold), we seem to have sufficiently shown* from the philosopher’s opinion that our art is true and most certain; they will sufficiently admit it has been proven to them, those who have seen the experience of it, but to others, truly not.

### 35. *Affirmative reason for Chemistry and its truth.*

<margin>Reason 35. affirmative for Chem.</margin>
**J**ohannes Andreas <note>A celebrated 14th-century Italian canonist, known as "the fountain and trumpet of the law."</note>, an interpreter of Canon Law who is beyond all exception, powerful in authority and faith, is called the most excellent of all men by Ludovicus Romanus. Likewise, Thomas Aquinas, the most perfect philosopher and theologian, felt in favor of Chemistry and pronounced his affirmative judgment of its truth, as we demonstrated above under Arnold <note>Arnold of Villanova</note> in the seventh book and Thomas in the eighth book. Besides these, there are countless other illustrious men, most highly skilled in other sciences—philosophers, physicians, theologians, and legal experts—who have approved the same by their testimonies and reasons. The number of legal experts favoring the art is greater than can be produced here as a list of their opinions; we shall at least make mention of one: Oldradus <note>Oldradus da Ponte (d. 1335), a famous jurist whose "Consilia" often addressed the legality of alchemy.</note>, the legal expert, in his book of counsels, the seventy-fourth question, where he speaks in affirmation of Chemistry. "For we see," he says, "that sometimes the living is produced from the dead matter, as we see from worms, from which silk is produced, and many other things; and glass is produced from grass <note>original: "ex herba producitur vitrum"; referring to the use of plant ash (potash) in glassmaking.</note>. Much more so from metals, in which there is a greater correspondence and similarity. For (as they themselves hand down, and as is held in the book *On the Properties of Things* <note>A famous medieval encyclopedia by Bartholomeus Anglicus.</note> in the chapter on Alchemy) all metals proceed from the same principle, namely from <term>sulfur</term> and <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argento viuo"; the "mercury" of the philosophers, considered the two parent components of all metals.</note>. Since, therefore, art imitates nature (as per the Digest <note>original: "ff. de adopt. l. si adoptio"; a reference to Roman Civil Law regarding adoption, used here as a legal maxim that "art imitates nature."</note>), these alchemists do not seem to sin. For since they are as if from the same principle into similar things, in those things having a shared <term>symbol</term> <note>original: "symbolum"; here meaning a shared quality or common element between substances.</note> the transition is easier." For there are, as Augustine says in the book *On the City of God*, in things...

### 36. Affirmative reason for Chemistry and its practitioners.

<margin>Reason 33. affirmative <note>While the previous page listed Reason 35, the original text here labels this as Reason 33, likely a printer's error in the original manuscript.</note></margin> Against all the authorities who oppose Chemistry, we rightly oppose them with the authority of one man who is most outstanding in his lineage, learning, sharpness of judgment, and experience: Giovanni Francesco Pico della Mirandola, the Count <note>Giovanni Francesco Pico della Mirandola (1469–1533), nephew of the more famous Giovanni Pico, was a philosopher who wrote "De auri confectione" (On the Making of Gold) to defend the art from a Christian and empirical perspective.</note>, whose words are as follows:

<margin>The authority of Francesco Pico della Mirandola in favor of Chemistry.</margin> **B**OOK 3, chapter 2, concerning the makers of gold who have held the chemical art in high esteem: "They knew," he says, "that God and nature have made nothing in vain. They held it as a proven fact that man was established as the prince of lower nature; through his ingenuity, things could be achieved through nature that would never occur by nature’s own accord if nature were left without man’s intellect. This is clearly seen in the grafting of trees, in painting, in medicine, and in almost every duty of life. Why then should it be considered obscure in the case of metals, which are bound together by such a great fellowship <note>original: "societate"; referring to the shared properties or "affinities" between different metals.</note> that one frequently lies hidden within another? They knew that the clever nature of human intellects ought to look toward this goal: not to be content merely with a general and common knowledge of natural things, but to aspire by its own impulse toward a knowledge that is introduced through individual parts and submitted to the evidence of the senses." <margin>That logical disputes for and against are vain.</margin> "Circular disputes wander in uncertainty, and those who surrender themselves to them more than is proper are accustomed to worshiping their own imaginations as truth. But it is plain to the senses and confirmed by the common consent of men that from the art of Chemistry a great and excellent benefit can arise for human society, by which the various needs of mortals may be relieved, when—"

Therefore, he can easily help mortals in many ways, both in the goods of the body and in external goods. Will not he who possesses these things surpass talkative debaters as much as a body surpasses the shadow of a body? As much as truth surpasses changing and fickle operations? For if deeds excel words, if it is better to do great things than to speak of them, the name of philosopher more truly and excellently belongs to such a man. Or would a fair judge of things prefer him who demonstrates a thing and places it before one's eyes over him who—relying only on his own imaginations, whether through common topics of the faculty of* <term>Dialectic</term> <note>The art of logical argument and investigation of truth through discussion.</note> *or through metaphysical conceptions—seems to himself to know something, yet is never certain, always doubtful, and always occupied with metaphorical arguments?*

<margin>The Chemist is a wise man, the talkative debater is a "philosopher."</margin>
*To this latter man [the debater], antiquity would certainly have given the name of sophist; to the former [the chemist], the name of Wise Man. This would be without objection from the* <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle, known for walking (peripatētikos) while teaching.</note>*, whose doctrines fall back upon the senses, from which they strive to bring forth their proofs. By these same senses, those skilled in the Chemical art—though scorning the mere debater—bring forth evidence against a resisting adversary and prepare a victory for themselves from it.*

<margin>Riches from Chemistry, which are otherwise acquired with great labor.</margin>

No one ought to regret this great delay by which we have been detained, since it is better to manfully attack and conquer the enemy <note>In alchemical literature, the "enemy" often refers to the impurities of metals or the intellectual errors that prevent successful transmutation.</note> once and for all, rather than to merely irritate him with countless incursions without ever overcoming him. Therefore, it shall be according to your own discretion and will to return to your respective homes and homelands as soon as the prayers have been recited by me. The royal maiden Chemistry <note>Maier personifies Alchemy (Chemia) as a noble virgin or goddess who oversees the work.</note> promises that she will be favorable and merciful to each and every one of you, and compliant with your vows in the future just as she has been until now; she wished for me to offer, in her name, the greatest thanks that can ever be given.

### Hermes’ Hymn of Regeneration from the Pimander, Chapter 13.

<margin>Hermes’ hymn of regeneration <note>The *Pimander* (or *Poimandres*) is a foundational text of the *Corpus Hermeticum*, a body of Egyptian-Greek wisdom traditionally attributed to Hermes Trismegistus.</note>.</margin>

> *Let the whole nature of the world hear this hymn.*
> *Hear, O earth; hear, O whirlwinds of rain; be silent, O forests; I am about to sing of the Creator of all, the whole and the one.*
> *Hear, O heavens; rest, O winds; let the immortal circle of God hear this prayer.*
> *I sing now of the Creator of all, the distributor of lands, the one who balances the heavens, who commands sweet water to flow from the Ocean everywhere for the nourishment of men, and who commands fire to shine from above for the actions of men and gods alike.*

<sig>Iiii 2</sig>

<summary>Hermes Trismegistus concludes the assembly of the Golden Table by praising the personified "Lady Chemistry" and beginning a solemn Hymn of Regeneration sourced from the Hermetic Pimander.</summary>

<header>SYMBOLS</header>

<meta>catchword: And-</meta>

*Let us all with one voice give thanks to Him, who passes through the heavens and creates nature.*
*Here is the eye of the mind; here He will willingly receive the blessing of the powers.*
*O my powers, praise Him who is the One and the All.*
*Sound together with my joy, all you powers of the soul.*
*Holy Knowledge <note>original: "Cognitio sancta"; in Hermetic thought, Gnosis (knowledge) is a divine gift that allows the soul to see the light of God.</note>, which shines by your light, singing through itself the intelligible light, I exult in the joy of the mind.*
*All powers, sing together with me.*
*Constancy, sing with me.*
*Let my Justice sing of the Just through me.*
*Let my Fellowship praise the whole; let Truth sing of Truth through me.*
*Finally, let our Goodness sing of the Good.*
*O Life, O Light, from you the blessing flows into us.*
*I give thanks to you, Father, the activity <note>Latin "actus," referring to the divine energy or "energeia" that puts all things into motion.</note> of all powers.*
*I give thanks to you, God, the power of all activities.*
*Your Word <note>original: "Verbum"; Maier is translating the Greek "Logos," the divine reason or speech that structures the universe.</note> praises you through me; through me the rational world receives this sacrifice of words <note>The "sacrifice of words" (logikos thysia) is a central Hermetic concept where the seeker offers hymns and prayers instead of the blood of animals.</note>; my powers cry out, they sing of the whole, they fulfill your will.*
*Your will is from you; receive from all this entire sacrifice of words.*
*O Life, save all that is in me.*
*O Light, illuminate the whole, O Spirit God.*
*Your Word rules me, O Spirit-bearing Craftsman <term>Spiritifer Opifex</term> <note>A title for the Creator who "brings the spirit." Maier uses "Opifex" to translate the Greek "Demiurge" (the divine craftsman).</note>.*
*You alone are God.*
*Your Man <note>In the Poimandres, "Man" (Anthropos) refers to the divine, pre-cosmic human being who fell into nature and must now be redeemed.</note> cries these things through fire, and through air, through water, and through earth, through spirit, and through all created things.*
*I have found a blessing from eternity, by which I shall find rest through my desire in your will.*

<summary>This page concludes the Hermetic Hymn of Regeneration, a mystical prayer of thanksgiving where the speaker's internal powers (Justice, Truth, Knowledge) harmonize to praise the Creator. It emphasizes the "sacrifice of words" as the highest form of worship in the alchemical and Hermetic tradition.</summary>

<header>THE GOLDEN TABLE. BOOK XII.</header>

->*And near the end of the Asclepius:*<-

It is similar to sacrilege when you ask God to burn incense and other such things; for nothing is lacking to Him, who is Himself all things, or in whom all things exist. Instead, let us adore Him by giving thanks.

For these are the highest "burnings" <note>original: "incensiones"; Maier is contrasting the physical smoke of incense with the spiritual "burning" of a thankful heart</note> of God: when thanks are offered by mortals.

*We give thanks to you, O Most High and Most Exalted.*

*For by your grace alone have we attained the Light of your kinship <note>original: "cognationis tuae"; this refers to the Hermetic belief that the human mind shares a direct family-like essence with the Divine Mind</note>, that holy and honorable name by which God alone is to be blessed according to the religion of our fathers. Since you deign to provide to all people fatherly piety, religion, and love, and whatever efficacy is sweeter, you gift us with sense, reason, and intelligence: Sense, so that we may know you; reason, so that we may track you through our inklings <note>original: "suspicionibus"; in this philosophical context, it refers to using mental clues or intuitions to seek the divine</note>; and intelligence, so that knowing you through cognition, we may rejoice.* 

*And let us rejoice, having been saved by your Divine Power <term>Numen (the manifest will or presence of a deity)</term>, through which you have shown yourself entirely to us; let us rejoice that you have deigned to consecrate us to eternity while we are still situated in these bodies.*

*For this is the only human thanksgiving: the knowledge of your Majesty.*

*We have known you, and we understand you, the greatest Light, perceptible only by the intellect.*

*O life, the true way: O fertile pregnancy of all natures, we have known you; by the conception of your whole nature most fully, we have known you, the eternal perseverance.*

*For in all this prayer, adoring the good of your goodness, we pray only for this: that you wish to keep us persevering in the love of your kinship, and never to separate us from this kind of life:*

<sig>Iiii 3</sig>
